case_summary.text: INCOME TAX: Where assessee, diamond trader, imported diamonds and purchases were executed through banking channels and in compliance with statutory provisions, furthermore sine purchases were accepted as genuine with proper supporting documents, expenditure on such purchases could not be treated as unexplained merely because sales were made in cash or buyers could not be fully identified, and thus, disallowance under section 69C was unjustified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of gold and diamond jewellery deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs during demonetization period in his bank accounts and claimed that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales,

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made an addition in hands of assessee on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three concerns were bogus purchases, since assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers etc., such purchases could not be treated as bogus

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in sarafi business, purchased diamonds from a company and sold them to other entities, since assessee had received payments from separate entities for diamonds sold, which suggested that purchases were genuine, transaction could not be treated as bogus

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made an addition in hands of assessee on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three concerns were bogus purchases, since assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers, such purchases could not be treated as bogus

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected,

IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

INCOME TAX: Where AO made addition for unexplained cash purchases in diamond trading business solely based on third-party software recovered from search on another entity without providing corroborative material or opportunity for cross-examination to assessee who maintained proper books and banking records, such addition under section 69C could not be sustained.

INCOME TAX: Where assessee engaged in diamond trading was alleged to have made bogus purchases from two entities based on third party investigation, but furnished all purchase and sales records, payment proofs and export documents correlating purchases with export sales and sales were not doubted, entire purchases could not be disallowed and only profit element relating to disputed purchases could be added to income.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization period and claimed that same arose out of cash sales of jewellery, since other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT and books of account of assessee were accepted by AO, said deposits could not be said to be unexplained cash deposit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

INCOME TAX : Where assessee received loan from various creditors who had sold their old jewellery to jewellers and gave loan to assessee out of said sale consideration, and assessee had disclosed name of jewellers to whom jewellery was sold and also established mode of payment through banking channel and further no inquiry was made from jeweller to whom jewellery was sold by creditors,

INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed that purchase of jewellery during year was made by her relative using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his savings, since onus to prove genuineness of transaction lay with assessee which had not been discharged, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69

IT: Where assessee proved genuineness of share transactions by contract notes for sale and purchase, bank statement of broker, demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, as also abstract of transactions furnished by stock exchange, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit
Additions u/s 69C deleted as genuine diamond purchases can't be disallowed merely due to cash sales: HC

INCOME TAX: Where assessee’s long-term capital gains from sale of diamonds were supported by declaration under IDS, 2016 and valid holding period, additions under sections 68 and 69C treating sale proceeds and alleged commission as unexplained were unsustainable and liable to be deleted.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of trading in bullion and jewellery, deposited cash in its bank accounts during demonetisation period, since assessee had successfully explained source of such cash deposits as sales/advances duly recorded in its books of account and comparative sales data dispelled allegation of abnormal cash sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating same as unexplained cash credits under section 68

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery, claimed that cash deposited in bank account during demonetization period pertained to sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers, since assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences, impugned addition made under section 69A, read with section 115BBE treating cash sales as bogus was to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee-jeweller deposited huge amount of cash in bank accounts during demonetization period and had presented evidence of available stock and depletion of said stock on account of sales and Assessing Officer had not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of receipts on account of sale of that stock were unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 was made out

INCOME TAX : Where shares were purchased by assessee on floor of stock exchange and not from broker, payment was made through banking channel, deliveries were taken in DEMAT account where shares remained for more than one year, contract notes were issued and shares were also sold on stock exchange, there was no reason to add capital gains as unexplained cash credit under section 68

IT: Where assessee duly proved genuineness of share transactions by bringing on record contract notes for sale and purchase, bank statement of broker and demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, Assessing Officer was not justified in bringing to tax capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee sold jewellery inherited from her father and substantiated transaction through banking channels, a government-approved valuation report, matching sale bills and a notarised affidavit, since sale transaction was duly explained, absence of purchase bills or a will could not justify addition of sale proceeds as unexplained cash credit under section 68

INCOME TAX: Where assessees claimed exemption under section 10(38) on LTCG from sale of shares alleged to be penny stock scrips, but transactions were through stock exchange, supported by Demat records and banking channels, and revenue failed to establish any direct evidence of assessees' conscious involvement or nexus with brokers, entry providers or share-rigging activities, additions made as unexplained money were unsustainable and liable to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited huge cash during demonetization period in his bank accounts contending that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales
Sale of shares couldn't be treated as unexplained when AO failed to prove that share transaction was bogus
Receipt of share application money couldn’t be held unexplained if it was routed through banking channel: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where cash deposited in bank by assessee during demonetization period was out of cash sales and realization from trade debtors which was duly shown in books of account and Assessing Officer did not point out any specific defect in books of account maintained by assessee and no inflated purchases or suppressed sales were found, such cash deposit could not be treated as unexplained money of assessee was to be deleted

IT: Where neither huge cash in hand over Rs. 20 lakhs was substantiated by wealth-tax return of other documentary proof nor photocopies of shares purchased or share numbers were furnished, impugned transaction could not be held to be genuine and explained
High value shown in stock statement sent to banks couldn't be held as unexplained investment
Disallowance on alleged bogus diamond purchases restricted to profit element as sales and documentation undisputed:ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee duly proved genuineness of sale transaction by bringing on record contract notes of sale and purchase, bank statement of broker and demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, Assessing Officer was not justified in bringing to tax capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit

IT : Value of diamond jewellery received by assessee from family members and partners only for exhibition and covered under VDIS could not be added to assessee's income as unexplained investment in jewellery

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was trading in diamonds and Assessing Officer made disallowance at rate of 100 per cent of purchases made by assessee on account of unexplained purchases being accommodation entries, in view of judicial precedent on identical issue disallowance at rate of 6 per cent of disputed purchases would be sufficient to meet possibility of revenue leakage
Share application money can’t be deemed as unexplained if identity and creditworthiness of applicants are proved
IT : Where transaction of sale of shares at stock exchange through demat account could not be proved to be bogus, capital gain arising therefrom could not be added as unexplained income

INCOME TAX : Where assessee sold shares through stock exchange, paid STT, disclosed transaction in return, held shares in demat account and routed payments through banks, addition of sale proceeds as unexplained cash credit based solely on generalized penny-stock investigation findings without direct nexus to assessee's involvement was arbitrary and liable to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee duly proved genuineness of sale transaction by bringing on record contract notes of sale and purchase, bank statement of broker and demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, Assessing Officer was not justified in bringing to tax capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit.
Receipt of share application money via banking channel couldn't be held as unexplained

INCOME TAX : Where two entities from whom assessee made purchases were found to be bogus but assessee had shown from its audited books of account, stock statement as well as material receipt register that it could not have sold equivalent quantum of diamond jewellery without these two purchases, addition on account of bogus purchases was to be restricted to 3 per cent of total purchases

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had furnished various details including bank payment details for purchase of shares, subsequent consolidation statement and also contract notes for sale of shares through stock exchange and proved genuineness of transactions of purchase and sale of shares of company SCL as an ordinary investor, addition made by Assessing Officer treating sale consideration received for sale of shares as unexplained money was to be deleted

INCOME TAX :Where assessee had sold goods and deposited cash in bank during demonetization period and part of said cash was deposited in SBN and remaining part of cash was directly deposited into bank account by seller, though SBN, since same had not been received by assessee directly and same was received by bank which was permitted till 31st December to be received by bank, said amount could not be considered as unexplained money in hands of assessee

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer made an addition in respect of sale proceeds of shares as unexplained cash credit under section 68, since shares were purchased by assessee on floor of stock exchange and not from broker, payment was made through banking channel, deliverables were taken in DEMAT account where shares remained for more than one year, contract notes were issued and shares were also sold on stock exchange, Tribunal had rightly deleted impugned addition

INCOME TAX : Where during search conducted at premises of one S, gold jewellery which was to be received by assessee as consignee was seized, since payment for purchasing said gold was made through banking channels and purchases were duly accounted for in books of account of assessee, no additions could be made for unaccounted investment with respect to said gold jewellery and same was to be released in favour of assessee

IT : Where assessee failed to prove that cash deposits in his bank was out of sale proceeds of alleged gold gifted to him by his parents, such deposits were rightly treated as unexplained cash credits

INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified
Addition for unexplained cash payment on jewellery purchase unsustainable as no incriminating evidence found in search: ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where, assessee-medical practitioner, deposited cash in bank out of her professional income which was already reflecting in return and same was supported by entries passed in books and by patient register containing all required details, merely because assessee had deposited said sourced income in form of SBNs during demonetization, same couldnot be considered as unexplained in hands of assessee

Where assessee proved sale transaction of shares by filing mass documentary evidence and payment of sale price was made through bank channel, sale transaction could not be disbelieved only because assessee could not give identity of purchasers

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had paid commission to four entities on export of diamond and had furnished all relevant details in respect of said commission alongwith details of service tax collected thereon, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure as non-genuine and bogus

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer received information from investigation wing that assessee had debited expenses in form of commission from four different parties - Enquiries were conducted and found that all 4 companies had same address and they were not available on addresses mentioned in income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises - Based on said information, Assessing Officer disallowed commission expenses claimed by assessee - It was noted that all four entities were assessed by same Assessing Officer and commission income shown by them was accepted - It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes FACT: The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

The assessee–individual filed the return for assessment year 2020-21 declaring total income of about Rs. 87.3 crores, including long-term capital gains of about Rs. 76.19 crores on sale of diamonds. On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

On second appeal :

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

FACT: The assessees were dealers in diamonds. Each of the assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997. The said declarations were accepted by the Department and a certificate was issued to the respective assessees under the VDIS, 1997. The assessees claimed to have sold the jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 in the year relevant to the assessment year 1998-99 and offered to tax the capital gains arising from the respective sales. On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

In aforesaid circumstances, it was to be held that the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessees' claim. [Para 7]

On revenue's appeal:

HELD: Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 69A, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained Moneys (Demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery - During demonetization period, assessee deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers in its bank account - Assessing Officer observed that cash sales were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by assessee company merely to build an explanation for cash deposits in to bank account and made an addition of total cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE - Assessee furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for relevant period and cash sales made by assessee had been credited in books of account and, thus, assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences - Further, no defect had been pointed out in books of account of assessee - When sale had been offered to tax, adding same again would amount to double taxation - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving source of cash deposited in bank, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of retail sales of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited certain amount in specified bank notes to the bank account. The case was selected for scrutiny to verify the source for cash deposited and certain details were called for.

■

The assessee submitted that it had deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers and had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period and demonstrated that the cash deposited in bank was out of sales proceeds of stock on hand.

■

The Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee and observed that cash sales entered in the cash book and sales register were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by the assessee company merely to build an explanation for the cash deposits in to the bank accounts and made addition of total of cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the assessee had explained the sources of cash deposits as cash sales received on 08-11-2016 against the sales and the assessee also produced the sale bills and books of accounts and that when there was sufficient stock to effect the sales and no defect had been found in the stock as well as the sales and purchases and since, the assessee has already admitted the sales as revenue receipt, there was no case for considering cash deposit as not explained and adding the same and deleted the addition.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The fact with regard to the impugned dispute are that the assessee has deposited a sum in specified bank notes during demonetization period to the bank account. In response to notice under section 142(1), the assessee had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period. The stock moved out of the books on account of sales made by the assessee has been established from stock registers. The VAT returns and annual audit report under TNVAT Act for the relevant period reflected such sales which have been accepted by the VAT authorities. The assessee has maintained proper books of account which are subjected to tax audit under section 44AB. The assessee also maintained quantitative details of the stock of Gems, Gold and Diamond separately and furnished before the lower authorities, which have not been rejected. The books of account of the assessee have been accepted by the lower authorities while framing the assessment and not rejected by pointing out any defects. [Para 8]

HEADNOTE: Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32] As regards the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998, the assessee had stated in response to a question that he was at Surat on most of the dates and not necessarily on all the dates. In view of the fact that preceding the date of 15-3-1998, there was sales of diamonds on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 24-1-1998 of other family members of the assessee, sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998 was to be accepted as genuine. [Para 33]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 25-3-1998 after perusal of statement and rejoinder of the assessee, it was found that Rs. 5,00,000 was not drawn on 25-3-1998 but was credited to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and it was a transfer entry on 25-3-1998 from the bank account of ‘H’ in State Bank of India to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and, therefore, the contention of the revenue that the assessee was at Hyderabad on 25-3-1998 was not correct. [Para 34]

As regards letters filed by the departmental representative, it was to be held that these were internal correspondence between the Income-tax Department at Surat and at Hyderabad which were never put to the assessee. None of these letters, which were in the form of general statements, pertained to ‘S’ with whom the assessee had transactions. A specific reference to letter dated 5-3-2001 showed that the Dy. Commissioner, Surat, clearly mentioned that the jurisdiction qua ‘S’ lay with Mumbai office and not Surat and, therefore, nothing turned on this correspondence. As for the postal remark that the letter addressed to ‘S’ at Surat was returned, it was to be held that the correct address of ‘S’ at the time was at Mumbai and not at Surat and the letter was, therefore, returned ‘unserved’. Nothing turned on this issue as far as the genuineness of the transaction was concerned. [Para 35]

The contention of the departmental representative that the books of account, computer floppies and other evidences relating to purchase of diamonds by ‘S’ could not be verified on the pretext that these were washed away in floods in the heart of Surat and that the purchaser could not retrieve the same, was contrary to the facts and evidence on record. ‘S’ co-operated in all enquiries of the Department. The transaction was confirmed by ‘S’ in response to summons under section 131. The purchase of diamonds was reflected in the stock register maintained by ‘S’. The payments were made by DDs from Mumbai. The facts that the assessee himself removed the diamonds at his own risk and that the payments were received a month after handing over of the diamonds which was again a risk taken by the assessee, could not be a ground to hold that the transactions of sale of diamonds were not genuine. The initials placed on the business purchase invoices of ‘N’ Textiles, in which the assessee was a partner, were the dates meant for payment and the endorsements were made earlier. This had been demonstrated by the assessee with documentary evidence. In respect of huge deposits of amounts in the bank account of ‘S’, the assessee could not be called upon to comment on the same as the department ought to have examined ‘S’ as summons under section 131 was issued. The proceedings thereafter had not been placed before the Tribunal by the revenue. [Para 37]

Thus, the identity of ‘S’ Jeweller, genuineness of the transaction and creditworthiness of ‘S’ Jeweller had been amply established by the assessee. [Paras 37 & 38]

As stated in earlier para, some diamond studded jewellery have been purchased during this year. The difference in weight can be reconciled only after the diamonds are valued by an approved diamond valuer."

The specific items which the assessee had clearly identified as purchased by her are as under : After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order, as under :

issuing cheques to various parties including the assessee. [Para 13]

T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14] In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

Assuming the revenue was right in its contention that the sale did not involve actual delivery of diamond jewellery, then unless it was established that the assessee had passed on his undisclosed income to T, it could not be said that the amount received by the assessee from T represented the undisclosed income of the assessee. Neither T in his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 had stated that the assessee had given the cash amount to T nor in the reassessment proceedings the Assessing Officer had gathered any evidence to that effect. Perusal of the reassessment order showed that the Assessing Officer had not made any efforts to link that the cash received and deposited by T in his bank account was, in fact, paid by the assessee. In those circumstances, in the absence of any cogent evidence brought on record, the decision of the Tribunal in holding that the Assessing Officer had failed to establish the nexus between the cash amount deposited in the bank account of T was attributable to the cheque issued by T in favour of the assessee could not be faulted. [Para 18]

In the instant case, cash credits were not introduced in the accounts of the assessee. From the fact that the cash credits were introduced in the accounts of T, it could not be inferred that the said cash belonged to the assessee. The assessee was not under any obligation to prove the cash credits in the accounts of 'T'. The assessee had proved that he was in possession of the diamond jewellery which was duly declared and certified under the VDIS, 1997. He had proved the identity of the person to whom the said diamond jewellery was sold, his creditworthiness and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from the sale of the diamond jewellery. [Para 19]

The sale transaction of diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 between the assessee and T had been accepted by the Sales Tax Authorities and the assessments made them had attained finality. In any event, in the facts of the instant case, the view taken by the Tribunal that the retracted statement of T was corroborated by the pay-in-slips/cash deposits in the bank account of T and the non-availability of the jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee to T was a reasonable and possible view. [Para 20]

Therefore, the appeal filed by the revenue was without any merit and was liable to be dismissed. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading in bullion and jewellery. During demonetization, the assessee had deposited a significant amount of cash in its bank accounts. The assessee explained that the cash deposits were out of cash advances received from customers against cash sales of jewellery/bullion.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and treated the amount of cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68, read with section 115BBE, and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The entire case of the revenue is built upon the basis of suspicion regarding the sales booked by the assessee prior to the start of demonetization period. The Assessing Officer has rejected the books of account merely because there was a spike in cash advances on three dates. However, the comparative data furnished by the assessee clearly dispels this suspicion. A perusal of the chart reveals that the cash sales in the year under consideration were in fact significantly lower than the preceding year. When the assessee has demonstrated that in the previous year, during the corresponding period, the cash sales were much higher, the allegation of ‘abnormal’ sales during the demonetization period falls flat. The data furnished by the assessee shows that the assessee’s total sales as well as cash sales during the year under consideration including the relevant demonetization period were comparatively very less than the preceding financial year. This data shows that the assessee’s cash sales were not abnormal during the relevant period and Assessing Officer’s suspicion of cash sales is not based on any reliable material. [Para 11]

■

Further, the Assessing Officer has not pointed out any discrepancy in the stock register, and the assessee was evidently possessed of the requisite stock to effect the impugned sales. It is a matter of record that the purchases have been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income. The notices issued under section 133(6) were largely complied with, and the mere fact that one party went into bankruptcy does not make the entire purchases bogus. Though the Assessing Officer has doubted the purchases, it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had not debited the amount of purchases from its books or that the assessee had made purchases out of its unexplained income. Once the purchases are accepted and the stock is not disputed, the sales flowing out of such stock cannot be treated as non-genuine. The sales have been recorded in the books of account and the profit arising therefrom has been offered to tax. Therefore, the entire receipts from the corresponding sales cannot be treated as unaccounted income of the assessee; only the profit element embedded in such sales can be taxed, which the assessee has duly offered for taxation. Taxing the gross receipts again under section 68 would amount to double taxation of the same amount. [Para 12]

■

Even, at the most, it can be alleged, though not proved, by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had made certain sales and accepted SBN/demonetized currency during the relevant period. Even assuming so, the assessee may have breached or violated the relevant circular/notification of the RBI/Demonetization Scheme, however, even then it cannot be held a case of income from unexplained sources. [Para 14]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-HUF filed its return of income for assessment year 1998-99 and declared long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds - Assessee submitted that said diamonds had been declared under voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced VDIS certificate issued by Commissioner - Assessee further submitted that sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts and was deposited in savings bank account of assessee and he also placed before Assessing Officer confirmation letters from buyers of diamonds; sale invoices; copy of extract of bank account and valuation report of diamonds - Assessing Officer, however, found that (i) main activity of purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries; (ii) demand drafts were purchased by depositing equivalent amounts of cash in bank account; (iii) assessee travelled to Surat alone in unreserved compartment carrying diamonds and stayed in dharamshala under a fictitious name; (iv) 'G' who was connected with purchasing parties in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between - In view of said details Assessing Officer concluded that assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold diamonds to Surat based parties and he, accordingly, rejected claim of capital gains of assessee and made addition under section 68 - Whether since diamonds were declared in VDIS which was supported through certificate issued by Commissioner and further, buyers had confirmed to have purchased diamonds and sale invoices; copy of bank account giving full description and details had been placed on record, which were not controverted by Assessing Officer, it could be said that there was a strong presumption in favour of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes

assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor. Thus, these so-called proceeds of cash sales deposited in bank accounts of the assessee are cash credits appearing in the books of account of the assessee sources of which are not satisfactorily explained by the assessee keeping in view detailed factual matrix of the case and onus cast under section 68 on the assessee is not fulfilled. The genuineness of these cash receipts could not be satisfactorily proved by the assessee as there is no third party evidences to substantiate the authenticity of these cash deposits as no details of the said persons to whom cash sales were allegedly made by the assessee was revealed by the assessee. It is incomprehensible and unacceptable that the assessee having issued cash sales invoices of average value of around Rs.3 crores per single invoice in majority of case and at the same time the assessee is claiming that the name of the said alleged buyers of gold bars is not known to the assessee rather it is the assessee who is actively concealing the identity of these so-called buyers of gold bars. It is incomprehensible keeping in view factual matrix of the case that the assessee have extended credit of Rs. 27.55 crores to its so-called buyers of gold bars out of sale of gold bars of Rs. 48.99 crores concluded in April 2005 as the said amount of Rs. 27.55 crores was realized in the months of May, June, July and August 2005 which does not inspire confidence. The genuineness of the business of gold bars carried on by the assessee of such huge magnitude keeping in view background of the assessee based on material on record and infrastructure facilities maintained by the assessee as well no experience in this field itself cast serious shadow of doubt on the genuineness of said business carried on by the assessee. The onus was on the assessee to prove genuineness of the business of gold bars conducted by the assessee. Provisions of section 68 is a special provisions and is a deeming provision which cast obligation on the assessee to satisfactorily explain the cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee by revealing identity, creditworthiness of the creditor and genuineness of the transaction which has not been fulfilled by the assessee and burden cast on the assessee is not fulfilled by the assessee in the instant case as detailed above.

The assessee failed to satisfactorily explain the sources of these cash deposits in bank accounts of the assessee which are in the nature of cash credits in the books of account /bank accounts of the assessee, which is stated to be from cash sales of gold bar wherein identity of the buyers is not revealed by the assessee and is a devise used to convert undisclosed income/money into gold bars without disclosure of the identity of depositor of cash in bank accounts, and thus burden cast on the assessee under section 68 did not stood discharged and the said cash credit will be deemed to be income of the assessee from the undisclosed income chargeable to tax within deeming fiction of section 68, which in the instant case it is held this issue against the assessee and in favour of revenue based on factual matrix of the case detailed above.

The whole controversy can also be seen from the another angle, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases to the tune of Rs. 48.78 crores during the subject assessment year as the payments for these purchases were stated to be made out of cash deposited in bank accounts out of so-called cash sales of gold made by the assessee of which identity of the buyers was not revealed by the assessee.

Further, payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel - He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances - Whether in light of factual context and balance of probabilities, issue would be adjudicated in favour of assessee, and disallowances made on this count were to be cancelled - FACT: The assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery. Pursuant to a search conducted at the premises of the assessee the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N'.

The assessee contended that the allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer had ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties were placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. Further, the payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances.

The Assessing Officer was however, dissatisfied with the documentary evidences filed to support the purchases made from these two parties, and treated same as bogus and made addition.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition on account of bogus purchases.

On second appeal:

HELD: As noted above, the assessee contends that the allegation towards bogus purchases is wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contends that the Assessing Officer has ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties are placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. The payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. It is also the contention of the assessee that both the parties from whom the assessee has made purchases are existing parties and such parties have independently filed their confirmation with regard to the supplies made by such parties to the assessee and mere non-attendance per se after a lapse of time could not be viewed adversely.[Para 9.1]

Having regard to the nature of business, i.e. trade in bullion, where stocks are identifiable and the price is also governed by market forces with little scope for manipulations; the purchases duly accounted for; the transaction of only 2 parties doubted despite extensive enquiry on 122 parties etc. there was potency in the plea of bonafides. There can be variety of reasons for non-attendence by unrelated third parties and it is not always within the domain of assessee to enforce attendance of third parties. Nothing adverse need to be imputed in such circumstances, more so, where the payments have been made through banking channel. [Para 9.1.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 69, read with sections 40A(3) and 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee a trader in diamonds and VCD rights, declared that during previous year it had earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on purchases and sales of diamonds - Assessing Officer noted that profit earned by assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher as in assessee’s line of business normally profit was 6 per cent; that all parties from whom assessee made purchases, on examination, had confirmed transactions but none of them could reply satisfactorily about amount of credit given; that though all suppliers to assessee’s sellers were based at Surat, none of those parties were traceable and that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to assessee - Accordingly, Assessing Officer concluded that assessee made purchases of diamonds from open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC - Assessing Officer further held that assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and, accordingly, worked out peak credit; HEADNOTE: II. Section 69A,  read with section 158BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Block period 1-4-1995 to 13-9-2001 - Diamond was found in business premises of assessee - Only after several months, assessee explained that diamond stock was received on approval basis from an entity - Proprietor of said entity stated that said transactions were only by way of accommodation for which he received commission equivalent to tax paid by him - No receipt or encashment slip was made available by assessee - Whether assessee failed to discharge burden cast upon him to explain diamonds in his possession - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition made on account of unexplained diamonds was sustainable - Held, yes [Para 14][In favour of revenue]

FACT: In course of search and seizure, the department found 338 carats of diamonds from the business premises of the assessee. He explained several months after the search action was conducted that diamond stock was received on approval basis from an entity.

Statement was made by the proprietor of the entity to the effect that said transactions were only by way of accommodation entries for which he received commission equivalent to tax paid by him. Statement made was shown to the assessee who chose not to cross-examine the proprietor. The assessee rather modified his earlier statement made to the effect of availability of quantity of diamonds. The revenue sought copy of the entrustment slip for the alleged receipt of diamonds but same was said to be unavailable with the assessee.

The Assessing Officer held that neither the transaction nor the explanation tendered was bona fide. Accordingly, a sum of Rs. 67.75 lakhs was added as an undisclosed income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, the Tribunal reversed the order of the Assessing Officer on the ground that addition was made solely on the basis of statements made by the proprietor of the entity and since the statement was not shown to the assessee and an opportunity of cross-examination was not afforded, the addition was liable to be deleted.

On appeal before the High Court by the revenue.

HELD: The sequence of facts as narrated would make it clear that the explanations tendered by the assessee have been made several months after the time of search. This, coupled with the fact that primary documents such as the entrustment slips have not been produced, lead to a belief that the explanation tendered is a mere after thought. The statement of the proprietor of BE who confirms that the transaction was not bona fide, but an accommodation for commission. No opportunity has been sought to cross examine the proprietor and in any event, this aspect of the matter is merely incidental and in addition to the overwhelming evidence already available to disprove the version of events adduced by the assessee. The totality of circumstances support the conclusion that the assessee has failed to discharge the burden cast upon him to explain the diamonds in his possession. [Para 14]

The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted the aforesaid sequence as elaborated, in confirming the addition. The assessee appears to have, retracted the sworn statements. The retraction has not been accepted on the ground that it is made after inordinate delay and is not supported by any material contrary to the facts set out in the sworn statements. That view is endorsed. [Para 15]

In any event, the statements of 'M' and 'H', proprietor of BM are, but one spoke in the entire wheel and the totality of the events that transpired have to be taken into consideration. Viewed in this light, the conclusion of the Tribunal on this account is unsustainable. [Para 18]
