■

On appeal, the CIT(A) accepted the assessee's cash-flow statement and records, noted that the audited books, purchases, sales and VAT returns had not been rejected or found non-genuine, held that the deposits stood explained as arising from recorded sales and that taxing them again would result in double taxation, and accordingly deleted the addition of Rs. 2.64 crores.

■

On revenue’s appeal to the Tribunal

HELD: ■ The Tribunal duly considered the facts and circumstances of the case. The Tribunal noticed from the assessment order that the AO has proceeded to hold the sales of the assessee to be bogus, primarily on account of the fact that the figures of purchases and sales in the period immediately prior to demonetization were at wide variance with the figures of purchases and sales in the corresponding period of the previous year and also at variance with the figures of the previous months in the present financial year. The AO also noted that the purchases on the basis of which the sales were made were effected from certain sister concerns and that too, only upto the period of demonetization. He could not find any nexus between the purchase and the payment made to the persons from whom the purchase had been made and from the same he came to the conclusion that a channel of purchase and sale was created just to give colour to unexplained cash deposit under the garb of sale and for this the VAT return had been utilized as a tool. In consideration of these findings, the Tribunal observes that a departure in trading patterns cannot in itself be a ground to make an addition by holding such departure to be bogus. It can at best be a ground for further investigation to determine the reason for such departure and if the assessee is unable to prove that the enhanced figures were genuine, then only could the credits purported to be made on account of such sales be brought to tax under the provisions of section 68. However, before section 68 could be invoked, the AO was obliged to demonstrate with evidence as to why the explanation furnished by the assessee for cash sales in that particular period were not acceptable. Such evidence could be the fact that the assessee did not have the inventory to make the sale that it claimed, or that the assessee had not made corresponding purchases which stood subsequently effected by way of sales. Unless the AO could find sufficient material to disturb the trading results declared by the assessee in the audited accounts, he would not be at liberty to regard the explanation offered by the assessee for the said cash deposits as unexplained. The Tribunal noticed that in the instant case, the AO had voiced suspicion that the purchases had been shown to have been made from sisterconcerns only so as to create a channel of purchase and sales to explain the deposit of money. He comes to this conclusion on account of the fact that he was unable to relate payment for such purchases to the actual purchases made. The Tribunal again notes that the suspicion could only be a starting point for further investigation and the purchase of goods on credit cannot in itself be a ground to reject the genuineness of the purchase. The Tribunal further notes from the assessee's submission that the AO had issued notices under section 133(6), but could not find anything adverse in this regard. On the contrary, the Tribunal notes from the paper book filed by the assessee that the assessee had inventories amounting to Rs. 4.61 crores as on the first day of the accounting year and that the assessee is able to explain an opening stock of worth Rs.4.41 crores as on 1-10-2016 as per the perpetual inventory method, prepared on the basis of its VAT returns filed upto September, 2016, which the Tribunal notes had been filed on 20-10-2016 i.e. before the date of demonetization. In the circumstances, there do not appear to be any reasons to question the sales made by the assessee in the month of October, 2016 were not due till later, out of those stocks or even in November, 2016 out of the residual stocks that remained on 31-10-2016 and purchases made during the period. The AO has pointed out that there was possibility for manipulation in sales on account of the fact that the VAT returns for the month of October, 2016 but the Tribunal notes that even if that were so, it would not change the nature of the receipt from being realization of sales of stocks that was available unless it could be demonstrated that such sales were not made or that the stock to make such sales was not available. No credence can be given to the AO's views that such sales were shown only with a view to deposit cash during demonetization and the stocks were later on actually sold outside the books of accounts as no such evidence has been brought on record by the AO to back up this suspicion. The Tribunal is therefore in agreement with the decision of the ITAT Chennai Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. Viswa and Devji Diamonds (P.) Ltd. [2025] 171 taxmann.com 474 (Chennai - Trib.) wherein the ITAT Chennai Bench has held that if no defect could be pointed out in the books of accounts and the cash deposited had been stated to be made out of sales, since the assessee had discharged the burden of proving the source of cash deposited in the bank, the impugned addition was fit to be deleted

HEADNOTE: Section  69C,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing, buying and selling of jewellery - During relevant assessment year, assessee had entered into transactions with five parties - Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in books of assessee - Assessing Officer further presumed that assessee had earned additional gross profit by procuring diamonds from grey market and accordingly made addition being 8 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases -  Commissioner  (Appeals) restricted profit estimation to 3 per cent - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating detailed evidences filed by assessee including quantitative details, purchase and sales registers, bank statements, confirmations, sales-tax registration, and income-tax returns of supplier parties, came to conclusion that sales and closing stock figures were duly accepted by Assessing Officer - Commissioner (Appeals) further observed that without corresponding purchases, assessee could not have affected sales - Thus, only profit element embedded in such alleged purchases could be brought to tax, not entire purchase value - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly restricted addition to 3 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases was fair, reasonable and in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing, buying, and selling jewellery. During relevant assessment year, the assessee had entered into transactions with five parties.

■

The Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated the entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in the books of the assessee

■

The Assessing Officer further presumed that the assessee had earned additional gross profit at the rate of 8 per cent by procuring diamonds from the grey market, and accordingly made an addition of certain amount being 8 per cent of the alleged non-genuine purchases.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restricted the profit estimation from 8 per cent to 3 per cent, thereby partly allowing the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Investigation Wing that diamonds shown by the assessee as purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14 were bogus. Accordingly, he made an addition in the hands of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ A perusal of the record would suggest that the assessee is engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. It has been maintaining its proper books of account. The accounts were duly audited. The assessee has filed its return of income on the strength of those accounts. When the Assessing Officer has confronted the assessee for explaining its position with regard to certain purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14. The assessee has submitted copy of the audited balance-sheet, Profit & Loss account along with auditor’s report, the complete stock tally of the ornaments. It has also filed copy of the stock register exhibiting opening stock, purchase, sales and closing stock. The assessee thereafter filed purchase bills issued by Daksh Diamonds, Jewel Diamonds and Nazar Impex in the respective years. The assessee has made the payments to its suppliers through banking channel. The seller of the diamonds was having PAN, VAT, TIN and CST no. Those details were submitted by the assessee to the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings. The assessee had made request that the person, who has disclosed from its back that he was engaged in providing bogus entries, then, such a person be subject to cross examination. The Assessing Officer had issued summons under section 131 to Bhanwar Lal Jain for appearance, he never appeared. The assessee thereafter brought it to the notice of the Assessing Officer that a perusal of the statement given by Bhanwar Lal Jain would suggest that he has not specifically taken the name of assessee disclosing therein that the assessee has availed accommodation entries. The information disclosed by him is a general nature whereby he disclosed that he controls 68 firms mentioned therein and such firms were engaged in providing accommodation entry. It is not specific whether such firm has specifically provided accommodation entry to the assessee or not. The assessee further produced details of the sales made by it. [Para 19]

■

It is also pertinent to note that in assessment year 2013-14, the assessee has requested that Sanjay Chaudhary managing the affairs of Nazar Impex be produced for cross examination. The Assessing Officer has issued the summons for the appearance of Sanjay Chaudhary before the Assessing Officer. However, he has expressed his inability to appear before him at Jalandhar. Ultimately the Assessing Officer could not ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination by the assessee. The Assessing Officer has expressed her inability to produce the witness at Jalandhar. The assessee again requested the Assessing Officer to produce the witness for cross examination, but no such steps were taken by the Assessing Officer to ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination. [Para 20]

■

A perusal of the record would suggest that there are two sets of evidence available with the Assessing Officer. On the one hand, he has an information transmitted by the Investigation Wing exhibiting the fact that certain concerns of Bhanwar (Mumbai) and Rajendra were engaged in providing accommodation entries to various beneficiaries. The list of all those companies/firms are mentioned in that report. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee has made purchases from three concerns. In the second set of evidence is the material submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer. This set contains audited accounts of the assessee, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers, namely PAN, VAT, TIN, CST numbers. [Para 21]

■

The assessee has produced quantitative details, which were verifiable and also tallied. For example, if 100 kgs. of raw material is being purchased, then sales also represent those 100 kgs. or unsold items are reflected in the closing stock. [Para 22]

■

The short question is, whether on the basis of the information collected from the back of the assessee from a third party, its purchases could be doubted and disallowance of expenditure is to be made. [Para 23]

■

The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Odeon Builders (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 64/266 Taxman 461/418 ITR 315, had held that disallowance based on third party information gathered by the Investigation wing of the Department without independent verification of the Assessing Officer cannot be made. In other words, the information transmitted by the DIT (Investigation) was a material to ignite assessment machinery in motion but it cannot be treated as gospel truth for disallowing the claim of the assessee without independent cross verification of those information by the Assessing Officer. [Para 24]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits -  Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether in every case of application of section 68, nature and source of sum found credited in books of account of assessee has to be examined first - Held, yes - Assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O' - Assessing Officer carried deep investigations through survey and searches at premises of parties where from assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills in respect of export of diamonds - He, therefore, held that purchases were bogus and, therefore, there was no question of any sale or export and, accordingly, treated credit entries appearing in books of account of assessee as in-genuine and made addition under section 68 - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order - It was found from records that lower authorities had not examined nature of credit entries and also had not provided a reasonable opportunity to assessee to explain those credit entries - Whether without examining above important aspects and without recording a proper finding thereon, it could be said that provision of section 68 had not been properly applied - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 2001-02, the assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O'. The Assessing Officer carried out deep investigations through survey and searches at the premises of the parties where from the assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that the alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills. Further, it was found that M/s. 'V' was owned by one 'G'. The income-tax records of 'V' showed that it had filed some return at Surat but he was also not found at the address given in the return. Further, as per the recorded statement of above parties it was found that above concern was giving entries and sale bills to accommodate people who were showing export of diamonds. In the case of M/s. 'O' the revenue carried a survey and recorded statement of its proprietor 'S', wherein he stated that head office of the concern was at Surat. However, when a survey was carried out, the above premises was found to be locked. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that 'S' had made a false statement. He, therefore, concluded that the alleged purchases were bogus and, therefore, the transaction of export of diamond was not believable. He, therefore, treated the credit entries appearing in the books of account of the assessee as unexplained and assessed the same in its the hands under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: It is now a settled-law that for explaining cash credits the assessee has to establish the following three things :

(i )

Genuineness of the credit entry,

(ii )

Identity of the creditors, and

(iii)

The creditworthiness of the creditor.

After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order,

, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21] With respect to one-to-one mapping therefore only criteria is the sale of carats of the diamond. Assessee has shown that number of carats purchased from the three entities is 585.88 carats and the sale of the diamond is also 585.88 carats. The amount of purchases recorded is 6.27 crores whereas the sale of the same diamond is shown at 6.71 crores. With respect to purchases from RA Distributors Private Limited, the assessee has purchased 496.88 carats and identical carats were sold. The purchase price of these diamonds is Rs. 5.39 crores and the sale is Rs. 5.79 crores. With respect to the purchases from three different entities the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that assessee has purchased from these parties Rs. 5.29 crores, 6.97 crores and Rs. 7.40 crores out of which the Assessing Officer has doubted only Rs. 2.49 crore, 2.19 crores and Rs. 1.58 crores. The total purchases affected by the parties are also having identical billing narration. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly decided that there is a one-to-one mapping available from purchases which are considered as alleged bogus purchases by the Assessing Officer and corresponding sales. Further, it has been held that there is no connection established by the Assessing Officer with respect to purchases from these three parties by the assessee with the alleged bogus purchases recorded in the investigation wing information as well as the charge sheet filed by the enforcement directorate. The Assessing Officer has also not challenged that assessee has not maintain proper books of account including purchase and register, since register, stock register and day-to-day bank book. No specific defect or irregularity was recorded by the Assessing Officer. With respect to the gross profit computed by the assessee from bogus sales is based on the number of carats purchased by the assessee and the same number of carats sold by the assessee. With respect to purchases from three different entities, the Commissioner (Appeals) has computed gross profit of Rs. 44.49 Lacs and purchases from 'R' gross profit is computed at Rs. 40.72 lakhs. Thus, the average gross profit earned by the assessee on total purchases of Rs. 11.66 crores; assessee has earned gross profit of Rs. 85.21 lakhs, which is 6.81 per cent. Gross profit as per the regular books of account is 6.73 per cent. Thus, no infirmity can be found in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) whereas assessee has shown higher gross profit from alleged bogus purchases compared to its regular transaction. [Para 22]

In case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be the sufficient compliance; therefore, the assessee cannot be further burdened to show the colour and number of diamonds. When bills of purchases from other parties and from the same parties where part of the purchase consideration is accepted as genuine, no such details are available in the sale bill, there was no reason to deviate from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals).[Para 23]

In view of the above facts, it is found that the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly considered that the purchases from these parties is genuine when part of purchases from the same parties is not disputed, even otherwise, even if it is held that the purchases from these parties are bogus, then also, the proper course would be to determine the profit arising from the purchases by looking at corresponding sales and what amount of gross profit is earned on alleged bogus purchases. If the alleged bogus purchases show gross profit higher than the regular gross profit shown by the assessee, no further addition is required to be made in the hands of the assessee. The logic behind this is that sale is already accounted for on the credit side of the profit and loss account. If the purchases are to be removed, the corresponding sale is also required to be removed from the profit and loss account, sales is higher than the purchases in rupees terms, therefore, the addition would be only required to be made to the extent of lower gross profit on alleged bogus purchases then the regular gross profit. This also takes the care of the argument that no proof of delivery of goods purchased are shown by the assessee, similarly, the sales are also bogus. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that amount invested in acquiring the bogus purchases should also be considered as an addition, because the only addition is disallowance of bogus purchases, no further addition is warranted. In view of this, the ground of appeal of the Assessing Officer are dismissed. [Para 24]

HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Cash purchases)  - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee, engaged in diamond trading, filed return of income - Reassessment was initiated under section 148 - During a search at premises of M/s. REPL, software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found - Based on this, it was alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL - Assessee submitted that it purchased diamonds from REPL through banking channels, exported goods, and offered income to tax, supported by invoices and stock records - AO, relying solely on third-party software, treated cash purchases as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - Assessee sought copies of corroborative material and statement of authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided - Whether since addition rested solely on alleged recovery of software during search action on M/s. REPL, which according to AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales, and said material was not supplied to assessee and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted, impugned addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

Insofar as the merits of the impugned addition are concerned, the addition rests solely on the alleged recovery of a software during the search action on M/s. REPL, which according to the AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales. The said material was not supplied to the appellant and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted. The observation by the CIT(A) that no opportunity of cross-examination was claimed is factually incorrect. The reply dated 05.04.2023 filed by the appellant before the AO shows that the appellant sought a copy of the statement of the authorized person of M/s. REPL and the corroborative material to support the allegation of cash paid by the appellant to M/s. REPL against purchase of diamonds, as well as the opportunity to cross-examine. [Para 13]

■

It is settled that if the AO proposes to rely on any material for making the impugned addition, the same must be supplied to the assessee and an opportunity of cross-examination must be granted wherever claimed. Failure in this regard is a breach of the principles of natural justice. The appellant cannot be expected to establish a negative. The onus to disprove arises only when material is brought on record and appropriate opportunity is granted to the assessee to challenge it. The matter would depend upon facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case there was failure on the part of the AO to supply the corroborative material and to grant opportunity of hearing and, therefore, the impugned addition cannot be sustained. [Para 14]

■

As the ground raised on merits is accepted, it is not necessary to deal with the additional ground raised. [Para 15]

■

It is also the case of revenue that the Assessing Officer has made independent enquiries also by issuing notices under section 133(6) to the seven parties which reveal that the notices were returned unserved by the postal authorities with remarks 'not known', 'left', 'unclaimed', etc. The aforesaid two aspects have formed the basis for the Assessing Officer to treat the purchases of Rs. 37 lakhs from the said seven parties as bogus transactions. [Para 7] The assessee asserted before the Assessing Officer that he has effected purchase of goods from the said parties and further resold it to various parties and without effecting such purchases, sales were not possible. He furnished copies of purchase bills, evidence of having made payments by account payee cheques, copies of bank statements, etc. Most importantly, the assessee pointed out to the Assessing Officer that if any of the depositions made by the said parties is to be used against him, copies of the same be furnished, so that he can avail the opportunity of cross-examining each of them. All these submissions of the assessee have been set to naught by the Assessing Officer by merely referring to the aspect of information having been received from the DGIT, Mumbai and the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) to the parties. In the assessment order other than the generalised observation about information having been received from DGIT, Mumbai, there is no reference to any specific material or details in this regard. The entire factual matrix brings out that leave alone confronting the assessee with the specific material, the assessment order itself does not record any specifics about the material on which the reliance has been placed by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, on facts, such an addition is susceptible to deletion. [Para 8]

Another aspect is the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6). In fact, non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) by itself cannot be a conclusive proof that transactions with the parties are bogus because there was enough material before the Assessing Officer to show that payments have been made to the said parties through banking channels. It required further collection of evidence by the Assessing Officer to prove the bogus nature of such transactions. The assessee has pointed to the Assessing Officer that he was maintaining day-to-day stock record, wherein all purchases are entered as 'inward' and sales are recorded as 'outward'. He had enclosed copies of account of the said parties appearing in his account books, copies of purchase invoices, copies of bank statement for payment to the parties, etc. Under these circumstances, having regard to the material on record, it is not possible to uphold the charge of Assessing Officer that the purchases from the seven parties are bogus. [Para 8.1]

Section 69C prescribes that where in any financial year an assessee has incurred any expenditure and he offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation offered by him is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year. In the context of the application of section 69C what is of importance is that either there is no explanation about the 'source of such expenditure' or that the explanation offered is not found satisfactory. The underlying emphasis is on the explanation in relation to the 'source of such expenditure'. The Assessing Officer has invoked section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases as unexplained. So, however, the assessee has demonstrated that the payments for such purchases have been made through account payee cheques for which there is no repudiation by the Assessing Officer thereby implying that the source of expenditure stands explained. In fact, the case of Assessing Officer is that the purchase transactions are 'only accommodation entries and not really purchases', thereby implying that the assessee has not incurred such expenditure. To hold the transactions as mere accommodation entries and not real purchases is quite different from saying that the sources of expenditure for the purchases from the seven parties have not been explained in the context of section 69C. Therefore, invoking of section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases stated to have been made from the seven parties as unexplained expenditure is on a wrong footing. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the orders of lower authorities deserved to be set aside. [Para 10]

He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

On the complete appreciation of the facts and also touchstone of human probabilities, the story of sale of gold bars appears to be a smokescreen while real objective was to introduce undisclosed income into banking system by way of deposit of cash in bank accounts. On the perusal of the documents which are on record it is crystal clear that the assessee was not having adequate infrastructure to handle such huge transactions in gold bars and had no experience to handle turnover in gold bars of such a huge magnitude, rather if the theory of assessee is accepted as to the sale and purchase of gold bars, then by not disclosing the names of ultimate buyers of gold who have allegedly bought gold through assessee, the assessee has in fact facilitated introduction of the undisclosed money of his buyers into the bank accounts of the assessee and its conversion into gold bars without disclosing their identity which also prevented end use of gold bars to be monitored. [Para 10]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. It is stated by the assessee that there is no onus on the assessee under any law to reveal the identity of buyers who allegedly bought gold bars from the assessee, this argument is fallacious as the amount of cash allegedly received from unknown buyers of gold bars stood deposited in the bank account of the assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor.

HELD: Applicability of section 69 to assessee's case

• It is an admitted position that names of each of the seller were given by the assessee to the Assessing Officer, since otherwise he could not have compiled the list giving the details of such disallowance as an annexure to the assessment order. In the nature of trade of the assessee, it may not always be possible to get the address of all its customers. Even if customers give their address, there is no means available to the assessee to ensure that such addresses were right.

• The assessee, in the nature of its trade, cannot insist for an identification process akin to Know Your Customer (KYC) rules applied by banks. There is no such mandatory requirement in the business of jewellery to maintain any records in line with KYC rules of bank. In fact, a prudent businessman might not insist on such rigorous identification process since insistence on such conditions will be to the detriment of his business. Just for the reason that purchases effected from certain parties did not carry full address, a disallowance ought not have been made. Admittedly, such purchases were recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also shown in its stock. [Para 14]

• In view of above, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting impugned addition.[Para 15]

The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

The inquiries conducted in that behalf and the material facts about the comparability of S’s flats and inquiries in that respect were not confronted to the assessee at the assessment stage, so as to controvert the same. Time gap of 15 months was significantly long; fact about direct booking of flats from builders and purchase from third-party also had very important effect on the price of the flat. Only explanation given by the lower authorities, that there was a recessionary time and subsequent flats might have been sold at a lesser figure, was a general and sweeping statement, which could not be used against the assessee. There were other flat buyers, who could have also been examined, particularly those who booked the flats from the builders at early stage. That comparability at the most could create a suspicion which could not be made a basis of addition. Therefore, the addition of Rs. 50 lakhs, as made by the Assessing Officer and confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), could not be sustained and the same should be deleted. There was no dispute between the Members of the Division Bench on the following issues :

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: ■ The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

The sale of shares of KAFL which was dematerialized in Demat account has taken place through recognised stock exchange and assessee received money through banking channel. So, the assessee has explained the nature and source of the money with supporting documents and thus has discharged the onus casted upon him by producing the relevant documents, accordingly, the question of treating the said gain as unexplained cash credit under section 68 cannot arise unless the Assessing Officer is able to find fault/infirmity with the same. The source of the receipt of the amount has been explained and the transaction in respect of which the said amount has been received by assessee has not been cancelled by the stock exchange/SEBI. So, it is difficult to countenance the action of the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) in the aforesaid facts and circumstances explained. [Para 13]

Even assuming that the brokers may have done some manipulation then also the assessee cannot be held liable for the illegal action of the brokers when the entire transactions have been carried out through banking channels duly recorded in the Demat accounts with a Government depository and traded on the stock exchange unless specific evidence emerges that the assessee was in hand in gloves with the broker for committing the unscrupulous activity to launder his own money in the guise of LTCG. [Para 14]

There was also nothing on record which could suggest that the assessee gave his own cash and got cheque from the alleged brokers/buyers. The assessment refers also to some third party statement of one SD which was admittedly recorded behind the back of the assessee and the assessee has neither been allowed to cross examine this person by the assessee nor the statement of SD furnished to assessee, so the statements even if adverse against the assessee cannot be relied upon by the Assessing Officer to draw adverse inference against the assessee and in the light of the documents to substantiate the claim of LTCG, which has not been found fault with by the Assessing Officer. [Para 15]

For the reasons given in the case the action of the Commissioner (Appeals)/Assessing Officer cannot be accepted, since the scrip of KAFL cannot be held to be bogus; and based on the finding of fact supra which are supported by documents which have not been adversely commented upon by Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals), the appeals of the assessee are inclined to be allowed and the Assessing Officer is directed to allow the claim of LTCG on sale of scrips of KAFL in respect of all the assessees. On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

was given by cheques to such persons had come back to the assessee in the form of cash. Thus, Commissioner (Appeals) restricted disallowance out of bogus purchases to 10 per cent of such purchases and directed Assessing Officer to disallow 10 per cent of alleged bogus purchases being the profit from purchases made from parties during the year under consideration.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal to the High Court: HELD: Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

headnotes.text: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Jewellery) - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee availed of benefit under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme (VDIS) and declared items, which were mostly of jewellery, namely, gold and diamonds - Subsequently, assessee sold away jewellery declared by them under VDIS - Assessing Officer doubted genuinity of sale of diamonds - He thus treated amount shown as sale proceeds of diamonds as unexplained cash credit - Tribunal, however, deleted said addition - It was noted that not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds was furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed - Moreover, bank accounts of purchasers were verified and demand drafts issued to assessee towards consideration corresponded to entries in bank accounts - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, mere fact that on certain occasions, assessee did not proceed to Surat, could not be a factor to disbelieve transactions in question - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had paid commission to four entities on export of diamond and had furnished all relevant details in respect of said commission alongwith details of service tax collected thereon, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure as non-genuine and bogus

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]  Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer received information from investigation wing that assessee had debited expenses in form of commission from four different parties - Enquiries were conducted and found that all 4 companies had same address and they were not available on addresses mentioned in income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises - Based on said information, Assessing Officer disallowed commission expenses claimed by assessee - It was noted that all four entities were assessed by same Assessing Officer and commission income shown by them was accepted - It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was engaged in import and exports of diamond - A search under section 132 was conducted upon 'SG' group to which assessee belonged - During search operation, it transpired that assessee had received accommodation entries in respect of several purchases from other business concern of its group - Accordingly, Assessing Officer made additions to income of assessee on account of such bogus purchases - It was noted that notices under section 133(6) issued to suppliers did not elicit any response and none of suppliers was found at given addresses - Assessee also failed to produce any of suppliers to confirm purchase transactions - Therefore, basic onus to establish genuineness of purchases remained un-discharged - However, at same time, assessee was in possession of purchase invoices and payment to suppliers was made through banking channels - Ledger confirmation as well as PAN of suppliers was also placed on record - Import as well as exports was certified by custom authorities - Further, complete quantitative tally of stock was provided along with correlation of purchases with corresponding sales - There could be no sale without actual purchase of material keeping in mind fact that assessee was engaged in trading activities - Therefore, it was a fit case for estimation of profit element embedded in these purchase transactions to plug possible leakage of revenue - Whether, on facts, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in restricting addition at rate of 6 per cent on account of such bogus purchases - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee failed to produce any of suppliers to confirm transactions of purchases shown by it, however, at same time, assessee was in possession of purchase invoices and ledger confirmation as well as PAN of suppliers was also placed on record and payment to suppliers was made through banking channels, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in restricting addition at rate of 6 per cent on account of bogus purchases   INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed expenditure on account of labour charges paid by it for conversion of rough diamonds into polished diamond, since said payment was made through account payee cheques after deduction of tax at source and there was no concrete material before Assessing Officer to disallow such labour charges paid by assessee, impugned disallowance of said expenditure by Assessing Officer was unjustified
