The income based on the books of account of ‘V’ was accepted in his case under the Act which included the said transaction. [Para 25]

Similarly, ‘V’ being the registered dealer under the BST and CST Act had filed the returns under those Acts, duly disclosing the said transaction with the assessee much before the date of survey. [Para 26] The observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that since ‘V’ was denying the explanation given at the time of survey, it was upon him to explain the cash deposits in his bank accounts and the lack of closing stock was not convincing. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The two statements were conflicting and as to for which statement he said ‘remained’, was not known. It would be more logical, if it was so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000, which was confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. [Para 27]

The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. [Para 28]

The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath, recorded by the Assessing Officer, ‘V’ claiming that while he knew ‘S’, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, could not raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs.10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as ‘hawala’ transaction in the statement given to the department. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. [Para 30]

It was true that at the time of survey, it was not the case of ‘V’ that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants, but the fact remained that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee was concerned throughout. [Para 31]

Large amounts of cash were deposited in various bank accounts of ‘D’ on various dates by ‘R’, but there was no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there was no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32]

The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee submitted his return of income which, inter alia, included capital gains on sale of gold and jewellery. He availed the benefit of Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 and declared gold and diamond and necessary certificate under the said Scheme was issued by the Commissioner. Later, the assessee sold the gold and diamonds separately to ‘A’ and ‘S’, respectively. The sale of gold was accepted as genuine by the Assessing Officer, while the sale of diamonds to ‘S’ was not accepted as genuine and entire sale value thereof was added under section 68 by the Assessing Officer treating the same as unexplained credit. Accordingly, assessment was completed. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer did not accept the reply of the assessee and by taking view that the assessee had not provided the details of purchases and the names of the parties and had also not produced the persons to whom sales made with documents showing the colour and size of diamonds made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to the income of the assessee on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought the same for taxation at the rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer by holding that the assessee had to prove the nature and source of deposit with three conditions as per provisions of section 68 and the assessee could not explain the nature and source of aforesaid amount of Rs. 29.66 lakhs.

On appeal to Tribunal:

As stated in earlier para, some diamond studded jewellery have been purchased during this year. The difference in weight can be reconciled only after the diamonds are valued by an approved diamond valuer."

According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order, as under :

■

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

For the assessment year 2001-02, the assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O'. The Assessing Officer carried out deep investigations through survey and searches at the premises of the parties where from the assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that the alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills. Further, it was found that M/s. 'V' was owned by one 'G'. The income-tax records of 'V' showed that it had filed some return at Surat but he was also not found at the address given in the return. Further, as per the recorded statement of above parties it was found that above concern was giving entries and sale bills to accommodate people who were showing export of diamonds. In the case of M/s. 'O' the revenue carried a survey and recorded statement of its proprietor 'S', wherein he stated that head office of the concern was at Surat. However, when a survey was carried out, the above premises was found to be locked. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that 'S' had made a false statement. He, therefore, concluded that the alleged purchases were bogus and, therefore, the transaction of export of diamond was not believable. He, therefore, treated the credit entries appearing in the books of account of the assessee as unexplained and assessed the same in its the hands under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of retail sales of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited certain amount in specified bank notes to the bank account. The case was selected for scrutiny to verify the source for cash deposited and certain details were called for.

■

The assessee submitted that it had deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers and had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period and demonstrated that the cash deposited in bank was out of sales proceeds of stock on hand.

■

The Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee and observed that cash sales entered in the cash book and sales register were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by the assessee company merely to build an explanation for the cash deposits in to the bank accounts and made addition of total of cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the assessee had explained the sources of cash deposits as cash sales received on 08-11-2016 against the sales and the assessee also produced the sale bills and books of accounts and that when there was sufficient stock to effect the sales and no defect had been found in the stock as well as the sales and purchases and since, the assessee has already admitted the sales as revenue receipt, there was no case for considering cash deposit as not explained and adding the same and deleted the addition.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order,

For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. On revenue's appeal:

held.text:
■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. ■ The Tribunal duly considered the facts and circumstances of the case. The Tribunal noticed from the assessment order that the AO has proceeded to hold the sales of the assessee to be bogus, primarily on account of the fact that the figures of purchases and sales in the period immediately prior to demonetization were at wide variance with the figures of purchases and sales in the corresponding period of the previous year and also at variance with the figures of the previous months in the present financial year. The AO also noted that the purchases on the basis of which the sales were made were effected from certain sister concerns and that too, only upto the period of demonetization. He could not find any nexus between the purchase and the payment made to the persons from whom the purchase had been made and from the same he came to the conclusion that a channel of purchase and sale was created just to give colour to unexplained cash deposit under the garb of sale and for this the VAT return had been utilized as a tool. In consideration of these findings, the Tribunal observes that a departure in trading patterns cannot in itself be a ground to make an addition by holding such departure to be bogus. It can at best be a ground for further investigation to determine the reason for such departure and if the assessee is unable to prove that the enhanced figures were genuine, then only could the credits purported to be made on account of such sales be brought to tax under the provisions of section 68. However, before section 68 could be invoked, the AO was obliged to demonstrate with evidence as to why the explanation furnished by the assessee for cash sales in that particular period were not acceptable. Such evidence could be the fact that the assessee did not have the inventory to make the sale that it claimed, or that the assessee had not made corresponding purchases which stood subsequently effected by way of sales. Unless the AO could find sufficient material to disturb the trading results declared by the assessee in the audited accounts, he would not be at liberty to regard the explanation offered by the assessee for the said cash deposits as unexplained. The Tribunal noticed that in the instant case, the AO had voiced suspicion that the purchases had been shown to have been made from sisterconcerns only so as to create a channel of purchase and sales to explain the deposit of money. He comes to this conclusion on account of the fact that he was unable to relate payment for such purchases to the actual purchases made. The Tribunal again notes that the suspicion could only be a starting point for further investigation and the purchase of goods on credit cannot in itself be a ground to reject the genuineness of the purchase. The Tribunal further notes from the assessee's submission that the AO had issued notices under section 133(6), but could not find anything adverse in this regard. On the contrary, the Tribunal notes from the paper book filed by the assessee that the assessee had inventories amounting to Rs. 4.61 crores as on the first day of the accounting year and that the assessee is able to explain an opening stock of worth Rs.4.41 crores as on 1-10-2016 as per the perpetual inventory method, prepared on the basis of its VAT returns filed upto September, 2016, which the Tribunal notes had been filed on 20-10-2016 i.e. before the date of demonetization. In the circumstances, there do not appear to be any reasons to question the sales made by the assessee in the month of October, 2016 were not due till later, out of those stocks or even in November, 2016 out of the residual stocks that remained on 31-10-2016 and purchases made during the period. The AO has pointed out that there was possibility for manipulation in sales on account of the fact that the VAT returns for the month of October, 2016 but the Tribunal notes that even if that were so, it would not change the nature of the receipt from being realization of sales of stocks that was available unless it could be demonstrated that such sales were not made or that the stock to make such sales was not available. No credence can be given to the AO's views that such sales were shown only with a view to deposit cash during demonetization and the stocks were later on actually sold outside the books of accounts as no such evidence has been brought on record by the AO to back up this suspicion. The Tribunal is therefore in agreement with the decision of the ITAT Chennai Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. Viswa and Devji Diamonds (P.) Ltd. [2025] 171 taxmann.com 474 (Chennai - Trib.) wherein the ITAT Chennai Bench has held that if no defect could be pointed out in the books of accounts and the cash deposited had been stated to be made out of sales, since the assessee had discharged the burden of proving the source of cash deposited in the bank, the impugned addition was fit to be deleted

If the alleged bogus purchases show gross profit higher than the regular gross profit shown by the assessee, no further addition is required to be made in the hands of the assessee. The logic behind this is that sale is already accounted for on the credit side of the profit and loss account. If the purchases are to be removed, the corresponding sale is also required to be removed from the profit and loss account, sales is higher than the purchases in rupees terms, therefore, the addition would be only required to be made to the extent of lower gross profit on alleged bogus purchases then the regular gross profit. This also takes the care of the argument that no proof of delivery of goods purchased are shown by the assessee, similarly, the sales are also bogus. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that amount invested in acquiring the bogus purchases should also be considered as an addition, because the only addition is disallowance of bogus purchases, no further addition is warranted. In view of this, the ground of appeal of the Assessing Officer are dismissed. [Para 24]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. All these submissions of the assessee have been set to naught by the Assessing Officer by merely referring to the aspect of information having been received from the DGIT, Mumbai and the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) to the parties. In the assessment order other than the generalised observation about information having been received from DGIT, Mumbai, there is no reference to any specific material or details in this regard. The entire factual matrix brings out that leave alone confronting the assessee with the specific material, the assessment order itself does not record any specifics about the material on which the reliance has been placed by the Assessing Officer. Another aspect is the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6). In fact, non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) by itself cannot be a conclusive proof that transactions with the parties are bogus because there was enough material before the Assessing Officer to show that payments have been made to the said parties through banking channels. It required further collection of evidence by the Assessing Officer to prove the bogus nature of such transactions. The assessee has pointed to the Assessing Officer that he was maintaining day-to-day stock record, wherein all purchases are entered as 'inward' and sales are recorded as 'outward'. He had enclosed copies of account of the said parties appearing in his account books, copies of purchase invoices, copies of bank statement for payment to the parties, etc. Under these circumstances, having regard to the material on record, it is not possible to uphold the charge of Assessing Officer that the purchases from the seven parties are bogus. Section 69C prescribes that where in any financial year an assessee has incurred any expenditure and he offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation offered by him is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year. In the context of the application of section 69C what is of importance is that either there is no explanation about the 'source of such expenditure' or that the explanation offered is not found satisfactory. The underlying emphasis is on the explanation in relation to the 'source of such expenditure'. The Assessing Officer has invoked section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases as unexplained. So, however, the assessee has demonstrated that the payments for such purchases have been made through account payee cheques for which there is no repudiation by the Assessing Officer thereby implying that the source of expenditure stands explained. In fact, the case of Assessing Officer is that the purchase transactions are 'only accommodation entries and not really purchases', thereby implying that the assessee has not incurred such expenditure. To hold the transactions as mere accommodation entries and not real purchases is quite different from saying that the sources of expenditure for the purchases from the seven parties have not been explained in the context of section 69C. Therefore, invoking of section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases stated to have been made from the seven parties as unexplained expenditure is on a wrong footing. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the orders of lower authorities deserved to be set aside. [Para 10]

The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. The certificate issued by the revenue under the VDIS, 1997 to the effect that the assessee had diamond jewellery weighing 65.75 carats continued to be valid and subsisting and no proceedings had been initiated by the revenue till relevant time to cancel the certificate. [Para 12]

When the assessee claimed that the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 had been sold to T for Rs. 10,35,562, the same was accepted in the original assessment. However, in the reassessment order, the claim was disbelieved mainly by relying on the statement of 'T' recorded on 31-3-2000, wherein he had stated that the transactions recorded in his books were hawala transactions. It was further held that the above statement was corroborated by the non-availability of the diamond jewellery allegedly sold by the assessee to T and the bank accounts of T showed that he had received cash before issuing cheques to various parties including the assessee. [Para 13]

T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

It was seen from records that the Assessing Officer had come to the conclusion that the amount of Rs. 66.90 lakhs found credited in the bank account of the assessee was unexplained credit simply on the ground that the assessee was not able to produce the broker before him for examination and basing on the statement of the assessee recorded under section 131, and the purchase price was paid by the assessee in eight instalments spreading over a period of two months, but the assessee had produced the share certificate issued by 'C' for acquisition of 3,50,000 equity shares. The 'C' was a public limited company where public were substantially interested. Its shares were listed in the Ahmedabad Stock Exchange. The said company was regularly filing statutory return as required under the Companies Act, 1956. If the Assessing Officer really doubted the genuineness of transaction, he ought to have obtained the list of shareholders coupled with the holding of the said shareholders together with the share certificate numbers and folio numbers of the shares held by each shareholder. This was cogent evidence, which went to the root of the matter to find as to the genuineness of the purchase and sale of shares by the assessee, but this was not done by the Assessing Officer though he had abundant powers under section 131. The Assessing Officer had also not written to the stock exchange of Ahmedabad as to the trading of those shares by the said broker in the stock exchange. In the absence of all these material facts, it could never be said that the transactions of purchase and sale conducted by the assessee through broker were not genuine. More so, in the presence of letter communicated by the broker giving the details of shares purchased and sold on behalf of the assessee, mentioning therein the commission charged by him as well as proceeds available with him for purchase of shares as well as realization of sale proceeds and crediting the same to the bank account of the assessee. Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

With respect to one-to-one mapping therefore only criteria is the sale of carats of the diamond. Assessee has shown that number of carats purchased from the three entities is 585.88 carats and the sale of the diamond is also 585.88 carats. The amount of purchases recorded is 6.27 crores whereas the sale of the same diamond is shown at 6.71 crores. With respect to purchases from RA Distributors Private Limited, the assessee has purchased 496.88 carats and identical carats were sold. The purchase price of these diamonds is Rs. 5.39 crores and the sale is Rs. 5.79 crores. With respect to the purchases from three different entities the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that assessee has purchased from these parties Rs. 5.29 crores, 6.97 crores and Rs. 7.40 crores out of which the Assessing Officer has doubted only Rs. 2.49 crore, 2.19 crores and Rs. 1.58 crores. The total purchases affected by the parties are also having identical billing narration. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly decided that there is a one-to-one mapping available from purchases which are considered as alleged bogus purchases by the Assessing Officer and corresponding sales. Further, it has been held that there is no connection established by the Assessing Officer with respect to purchases from these three parties by the assessee with the alleged bogus purchases recorded in the investigation wing information as well as the charge sheet filed by the enforcement directorate. The Assessing Officer has also not challenged that assessee has not maintain proper books of account including purchase and register, since register, stock register and day-to-day bank book. No specific defect or irregularity was recorded by the Assessing Officer. With respect to the gross profit computed by the assessee from bogus sales is based on the number of carats purchased by the assessee and the same number of carats sold by the assessee. With respect to purchases from three different entities, the Commissioner (Appeals) has computed gross profit of Rs. 44.49 Lacs and purchases from 'R' gross profit is computed at Rs. 40.72 lakhs. Thus, the average gross profit earned by the assessee on total purchases of Rs. 11.66 crores; assessee has earned gross profit of Rs. 85.21 lakhs, which is 6.81 per cent. Gross profit as per the regular books of account is 6.73 per cent. Thus, no infirmity can be found in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) whereas assessee has shown higher gross profit from alleged bogus purchases compared to its regular transaction. [Para 22]

In case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be the sufficient compliance; therefore, the assessee cannot be further burdened to show the colour and number of diamonds. When bills of purchases from other parties and from the same parties where part of the purchase consideration is accepted as genuine, no such details are available in the sale bill, there was no reason to deviate from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals).[Para 23]

The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

In aforesaid circumstances, it was to be held that the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessees' claim. [Para 7]

There is no evidence on record that any cash amount was paid back by assessee to VDT. The possession of loose diamonds by assessee is proved by assessee's declaration under VDIS. As such, considering all the facts and circumstances of the case together with the legal position, we find no justification for holding the sale of loose diamonds by assessee to M/s. Dhananjay Diamonds as bogus order as a mere paper transaction and not genuine, and in turn for making/sustaining addition. We, therefore, delete the addition.

In the result, assessee's appeal No. 7963/Mum./2003 is allowed.

Now we take up ITA No. 7845/Mum./2003 being appeal by assessee named Smt. Sampat Devi. We will decide the appeal considering only the revised grounds of appeal. Revised ground No. 1 disputes the reopening of assessment but, the same has not been pressed before us by the learned Authorised Representative of assessee during arguments and so the same is dismissed accordingly.

Revised ground Nos. 2(i) and (ii) dispute the addition of Rs. 10,43,595 made/sustained by treating the sale of loose diamonds weighing 65.90 carats by assessee to M/s. Dhananjay Diamonds, proprietary concern of VDT as bogus. Both the rival representatives have relied on their same contentions as relied by them on similar issue in the case of Mohanlal R. Daga, in ITA No. 7963/Mum./2003, as discussed by us above, submitting that the facts of both the cases are identical.

facts. Unless there was some evidence in support of the claim that the money reached back to the assessee, it could not be held that the finding arrived at by the revenue authorities was the right one. Suspicion alone, however, strong was not sufficient. It was true that the Assessing Officer clearly established the modus operandi in this line of business. But unless there was some evidence against the assessee, however, weak, the decision had to go in the assessee’s favour. As regard the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee made purchases to the tune of Rs. 5,30,87,813, there was not an iota of evidence, except the reasoning of the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee made purchases by making cash payments. Not even a single question was put to any of the parties from whom the statements were recorded by the Assessing Officer, as to whether the payment made by the assessee by cheque was withdrawn and paid back to the assessee. In the absence of any other evidence on facts, the reasoning of the Assessing Officer that the assessee made the cash purchases could not be accepted. In view of the above facts, the further addition made to the income of the assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) did not survive. In view of the above, it was also held that there was no material to recompute the profits for the purpose of deduction under section 80HHC.

Since there was no basis for making any addition on account of cash purchases, the excess peak investment worked out by the Commissioner (Appeals) automatically did not survive.

There was no case for the revenue that the assessee was not maintaining books of account. The purchases were recorded in the books of account. Payments were made by cheque to the immediate purchasers. They accepted and confirmed the sale. To hold otherwise, there should be some evidence in the possession of the revenue. Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of evidence and that alone cannot be the criteria for deciding the matter.

Though search was conducted during the period under consideration, yet nothing incriminating was found during the search action. There was no evidence to show that the money had come back to the assessee or claim of the payment was bogus. In such circumstances, for the subsequent period to hold that the entire purchase was bogus was a conclusion that was very difficult to arrive at. Another reasoning of the Assessing Officer to come to the conclusion that the assessee had not actually purchased the diamonds from the immediate suppliers was that their suppliers from Surat had no capacity and even if they had the capacity, there was no evidence that they transported it to Mumbai. According to the Assessing Officer, the diamonds worth crores of Rupees, if they claimed to have transported these diamonds should have been insured and the mode of transportation or at least the details of tickets, etc. of the persons who brought diamonds should have been mentioned. No question had been put to immediate suppliers of the assessee whether they purchased the material from the open market other than the parties who said to have supplied them from Surat. Therefore, the proposition that in the absence of insurance, mode of transportation, etc. the claim that the diamonds came from Surat could not be accepted, was not a sound conclusion arrived at. It was true that the profit shown by the assessee was extremely high. But, then, no similar cases of export had been mentioned anywhere by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals) to discredit the assessee’s claim of higher profit. Export of the assessee was accepted by the Customs Department, which showed that the export of diamonds could not be doubted.

The results of the inquiry made by the Assessing Officer with the third parties and the reliance placed by the assessee that no opportunity was provided to the assessee, had not much relevance. Summons issued were received by these parties. They confirmed the sales. Payment made by cheque was confirmed. The only reasoning of the Assessing Officer to disallow assessee’s claim was that subsequently these parties withdrew the amount reflected in their accounts by cash and disappeared. But there was no evidence to show that the money had come back to the assessee. Further, the reasoning of the Assessing Officer, as confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), was that there was no evidence to show that the material had been transported from Surat to Mumbai. The third parties were not the parties who sold to the assessee directly. Surat parties claimed that they had delivered the goods to the sellers from whom assessee made purchases. Therefore, this point also could not be strictly taken against the assessee.

Hence, the order of the revenue authorities were liable to be set aside as there was no evidence on record to show that the payments made by the assessee had come back to the assessee, except the modus operandi said to be prevalent in this line of business.

Further, there was no evidence to show that the assessee had made purchases on payment of cash, because the payment was made by the assessee by cheques, which was also reflected in the books of account of the purchasers as well as of the assessee.

In the result the appeal was to be allowed.

In the present case, on the basis that the assessee has deposited cash amounting to Rs. 12.25 lakhs, during the demonetization period in his bank account, the Assessing Officer made the addition by treating the same as unexplained money under section 69A. On the other hand, it is the plea of the assessee that the amount deposited in cash in the bank account during the demonetization period was received by him from his customers to whom he had earlier granted loans against the gold ornaments. As per the assessee, against such gold ornaments, he took loans from the Federal Bank and earns interest income from the customers. In order to support the submission that the assessee availed gold loans from Federal Bank, the assessee has placed on record the statement of its bank account maintained with Federal Bank for the period 13-9-2015 to 13-9-2019. From the perusal of the bank statement, it is evident that the same pertains to 'Fast Track Gold Loan/Gold Loan' availed by the assessee from the Federal Bank and the loan disbursements were made to the assessee from time-to-time. As per the assessee, the amount received from the Federal Bank against the gold ornaments was given as a loan by him to his customers against the gold ornaments. The assessee has also placed on record the list of his customers to whom loans were given against the gold ornaments, which were repaid in cash. From the perusal of the list, it is found that apart from providing the name and address of the customers, the assessee has also provided the PAN details of all these 23 customers. From the perusal of these details, it is further found that these loans were given to the customers as early as 4-5-2016 and as late as 8-11-2016. It is further found that, except in two cases where the loan was repaid on 30-8-2016, the rest of the 21 customers repaid the loan during the demonetization period. It is found that though the assessee furnished all these documents before the lower authorities, however, none of these documents were rejected, nor despite the availability of the information regarding the customers, any verification was made by the Assessing Officer from them. [Para 9]

■

Further, as regards the findings of the lower authorities that the assessee was not authorized to accept the repayment made by the customers in cash in Specified Bank Notes after 8-11-2016, it is found that merely for the reason that there is a violation of certain notifications/GO issued by the Government in transacting with Specified Bank Notes, the genuine explanation offered by the assessee towards the source of cash deposit cannot be rejected, unless the Assessing Officer makes out the case that the assessee has deposited unaccounted cash into bank account in Specified Bank Notes. [Para 10]

■

Therefore, having carefully perused the documentary evidence filed by the assessee, it is viewed that the assessee has duly explained the source of cash deposited by him in his bank account during the demonetization period, and same cannot be treated as unexplained money under section 69A. Accordingly, the impugned addition of Rs. 12.25 lakhs made by the Assessing Officer, being the cash deposits in the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A, is deleted. [Para 11]

The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

As regards the first and second statements of VDT, the same having been recorded not during the proceedings pertaining to the assessee, but during survey in the case of VDT, the copies of the same having not been supplied to the assessee prior to assessment and supplied only as attached with the assessment order and opportunity for cross-examining VDT in respect of those statements having not been accorded to the assessee, the same could not be read/used against the assessee. The question of the assessee's self asking for cross examination of VDT in respect of those two statements, dated 30/31-3-2000 did not arise when the copies of the same had not been supplied to the assessee before making assessment. Besides, it is the basic principle of law that without affording opportunity of cross-examination, a statement recorded at the back of the assessee will not partake of the nature of evidence against the assessee and cannot be read/used against the assessee. Even apart, the said statements had been retracted by VDT vide his letter dated 4-4-2000. In the said retraction VDT had mentioned that those statements were given by him as directed by the department and he was under a state of total confusion. He had also mentioned in the said retraction letter that he had made the purchases, correctly issued bills, accounted for in his books and also furnished to the Sales-tax Department. He had supported the purchase of 71 carats of diamonds from the assessee by his affidavit and statement dated 25-10-2002 recorded by the Assessing Officer when he made his attendance before the Assessing Officer in response to the summons issued to him by the Assessing Officer during assessment proceedings pertaining to the present assessee. The sale of diamonds by the present assessee to VDT was also supported by VDT's purchase bill; the payments had been made by VDT to the assessee by account payee cheques and the same was corroborated by bank statement. That transaction of sale of 71 carats of loose diamonds by the assessee to VDT had already been accepted in the assessee's original assessment under section 143(3). There was no evidence on record that any cash amount was paid back by the assessee to VDT. The possession of loose diamonds by the assessee was proved by the assessee's declaration under VDIS. As such, there was no justification for holding the sale of loose diamonds by the assessee to 'DD' as bogus sale or as a mere paper transaction and not genuine, and in turn for making/sustaining addition. The addition of Rs. 11,18,250 made in the income of the assessee was, therefore, liable to be deleted.

P.K. Pardia for the Appellant. P.S.S. Reddy for the Respondent.

ORDER - S.R. CHAUHAN, JUDICIAL MEMBER - ITA No. 7845/Mum./2003 and 7963/Mum./2003 are appeals by assessee namely Smt. Sampat Devi M. Daga and Mohanlal R. Daga respectively for asst. yr. 1998-99 and are directed against two separate orders of CIT(A), Mumbai each dated 26th Sept., 2003.

We have heard the arguments of both sides and have also perused the records.

The facts, in brief, are that Mohanlal R. Daga, assessee in ITA No. 7963/Mum./2003 is carrying on the business of corrugated rolls and boxes. He had made a voluntary disclosure under VDIS 1997 disclosing 71 carats of loose diamonds along with other gold ornaments and the disclosure was accepted by the CIT. The assessee showed the sale of above diamonds weighing 71 carats and of gold ornaments claiming long-term capital gain/loss in the return for asst. yr. 1998-99 filed on 29th Oct., 1998. The original assessment was made on 25th Jan., 2001 under section 143(3).

The nature of business of the assessee is not disputed that he is engaged in the wholesale and retail business of gold and silver ornaments. It is also not in dispute that in this line of business sale of jewellery in cash is normal trade practice. The books of assessee are audited by the independent Chartered Accountant and copy of audit report and statement of profit and loss account is filed by the assessee. It is noted from the record that the case of the assessee was taken up for scrutiny assessment under section 143(3) on the basis of CASS and desired information by the Assessing Officer were submitted by the assessee from time-to-time. After completion of assessment the Assessing Officer vide his order assessed the income of the assessee by making a single addition of Rs. 80 lakh out of the total cash deposited being the demonetized currency for an amount of Rs. 84 lakh. The assessee is selling the jewellery in cash in past year also and the assessee in his submission explained that in fact in the year under consideration the overall sales as per cent to total sales has reduced. [Para 9]

The said sum is picked as unexplained as the assessee has deposited a sum of Rs. 84 lakhs being the demonetized currency in the bank account considering the sales shown by the assessee as not genuine. Out of total sales of Rs. 1.86 crores made in the year under consideration only a sum of Rs. 80 lakh not considered as genuine. The only reasons that was advanced that the details of the buyers showing complete name, address and phone were not verifiable. The sales shown by the assessee is supported by the following documents which were not doubted by Assessing Officer :

(a)

Bill wise detail in respect of cash sales during the period from 03-11-2016 to 8-11-2016, along with the sales sills. (b) Copy of the monthly summary of stock register. (c) Copy of sales register from the books of account of assessee for the relevant previous year. (d) Copy of cash book for the relevant previous year. (e) Copies of VAT return filed by the assessee, for the year under consideration. (f) Tax Audit Report Audited Financial Statements. [Para 9.1]

The assessee by selling the goods in cash did not violate any provision of the Income-tax Act and even the. Assessing Officer has not mentioned any of the law provision to disbelieve the sales so made by the assessee. All the sales made by the assessee is supported by a commercial invoice duly complied with the value added tax (VAT) provision and the related VAT is also paid by the assessee. The invoices issued is also reported in VAT return filed and the sales has been accepted by the VAT authority without any adverse remark and in fact even the Assessing Officer has not made any adverse remark on the sales register and cash book submitted by the assessee to support the contentions of having been sold the goods/jewellery in cash. [Para 9.2]

The Assessing Officer accepted the opening stock, purchase, as well as the closing stock at the year-end to be genuine and correct. It is also worthwhile to mention that the Assessing Officer has not rejected the books of account of the assessee by invoking the provisions of section 145(3) and even there is no whisper in the order about any defects in the books of account. The Assessing Officer has not brought any material on record to establish that the sale bills were bogus or any evidences indicating that sales were bogus. The Assessing Officer is wrong in not accepting the declared cash sales as not verifiable which are recorded in books of account which were found to be correct and complete. It was also noted that the assessee has undertaken cash sales of Rs. 1.86 crores. Out of the total cash sales, cash sales amounting to Rs. 80 lakhs has been found to be non-genuine and added under section 68. Explanation offered to substantiate the cash sales has been arbitrarily rejected without holding that the sales is duly recorded in the books and is also supported by the various records produced in the assessment proceedings. [Para 9.5]

Respectfully following the consistent view and after considering the factual matrix of the cash on hand the addition made cannot be sustained and therefore, the addition of Rs. 80 lakhs made under section 68 is vacated as the same cannot be made without rejecting the books of account of the assessee regularly maintained by the assessee and the said cash deposited is duly supported by the entries passed in the books of account and part of the sale accepted by the Assessing Officer. [Para 9.8]

The sales shown by the assessee had been accepted by VAT/Sales Tax Department, the book result shown by the assessee were in the same line as had been accepted by the Department in the preceding years, the cash sales made by the assessee had been credited in the books of account and reduction in the stock has not been doubted, even during the course of search just after the closing of the year under consideration, neither excess nor shortage of stock was found in the stock register maintained by the assessee, the identity of the purchasers to whom cash sales had been made was disclosed in the sale bills where the name, address and PAN was mentioned. It is also not a case that there was sudden spurt in the sale only in the month of October 2016 as the chart furnished by the assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) clearly revealed that the cash sales were on higher side in another months of different preceding years. The Assessing Officer made the addition on the basis of difference in the cash sales from 1-10-2016 to 29-10-2016, only on this basis that the said difference was there in the computer and the pen-drive found from the residential premises of the part time accountant of the assessee but no opportunity to cross examine the said accountant was given to the assessee and moreover, no specific defect was pointed out in the proper books of account maintained by the assessee in the regular course of business and nothing is brought on record to substantiate that the sales from 1-10-2016 to 29-10-2016 were not made, out of the existing stock available with the assessee. In the instant case the assessee explained that the exhibitions were held in every year and the sales were normally higher in certain month and that in the month of October 2016 the cash sales was on the higher side as lots of festivals like Diwali, Dhanteras, Bhaiya Duj and Karwa Chauth etc. fell in that period. The said explanation cannot be brushed aside considering the trend of the society in India wherein people make the purchases of jewellery during the festive season. [Para 10.3]

In the instant case also the assessee was maintaining complete stock tally, the sales were recorded in the regular books of account and the amount was deposited in the bank account out of the sale proceeds, therefore, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified.[Para 10.5]

The Assessing Officer made the addition on the basis of the statement of 'N', the then part time accountant of the assessee but no opportunity to cross examine to rebut the statement made by 'N' was allowed to the assessee and moreover nothing was brought on record to substantiate that cash obtained by the assessee from the sales which reduced the stock of the assessee was utilized elsewhere and that the cash sales made during the month of October 2016 were in the line of the cash sales in earlier years and was equal to the sales in the Month of July 2016, therefore, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified. [Para 10.7]

Further, sales made by the assessee to cover the cash deposited in the bank post-demonetization, was sufficient source of the cash deposited i.e.; the sales from the existing stock available with the assessee and was well explained, therefore, the addition made by the Assessing Officer and sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified. [Para 10.9]

Furthermore, the opening stock, purchases & sales and closing stock, declared by the assessee has not been doubted, the sales were made by the assessee out of the opening stock and purchases and the resultant closing stock has been accepted, the sales had not been disturbed either by the Assessing Officer or by the sales tax/VAT Department and even there was no difference in the quantum figures of the stock at the time of search on 12-4-2017, therefore, the sales made by the assessee out of the existing stock were sufficient to explain the deposit of cash (obtained from realization of the sales) in the bank account and cannot be treated as undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 10.11]

The contention of the departmental representative that the books of account, computer floppies and other evidences relating to purchase of diamonds by ‘S’ could not be verified on the pretext that these were washed away in floods in the heart of Surat and that the purchaser could not retrieve the same, was contrary to the facts and evidence on record. ‘S’ co-operated in all enquiries of the Department. The payments were made by DDs from Mumbai. The facts that the assessee himself removed the diamonds at his own risk and that the payments were received a month after handing over of the diamonds which was again a risk taken by the assessee, could not be a ground to hold that the transactions of sale of diamonds were not genuine. This had been demonstrated by the assessee with documentary evidence. In respect of huge deposits of amounts in the bank account of ‘S’, the assessee could not be called upon to comment on the same as the department ought to have examined ‘S’ as summons under section 131 was issued. The Supreme Court in CIT v. Noorjahan (P.K.) (Smt.) [1999] 237 ITR 570/ 103 Taxman 382 , held that the discretion postulated in section 69 before making the addition has to be judiciously exercised. The provisions of section 68 are in pari materia with section 69. Therefore, before making an addition under section 68, the Assessing Officer has to exercise his discretion judiciously. In the instant case, in spite of the facts pointing in the direction of genuineness and identity of ‘S’ and their creditworthiness not being in doubt, the addition had been made on presumptions, surmises and suspicions and, therefore, the judgment of the Supreme Court (supra ) applied to the facts of the instant case. Therefore, the Assessing Officer had erred in making the addition under section 68. The case laws relied on by the departmental representative were all distinguishable on facts and did not apply to the facts of the assessee’s case. [Paras 40 & 41]

In view of the above, the Assessing Officer was not justified in treating the transaction of sale of diamonds with ‘S’ as not being genuine and, therefore, erred in adding the impugned amount under section 68. Therefore, addition was to be deleted. [Para 44]
