Swiss Legal Position: Reliance on Stolen Information

Till 2019, a total of 628 cases of HSBC Bank, Geneva, were reported accounting for undisclosed income of INR 8,465 crores were brought to tax. Out of these, over 208 cases were found to be "non-actionable because of no balances in account's information, non-residents, not traceable, an amount taxable in some other hand."

On administrative assistance relating to tax matters, on July 17, 2018 [decision no. 2C_648/2017], Swiss Supreme Court ('SSC') rendered a decision concerning stolen data. The court categorically distinguished its decision from an earlier decision dated March 17, 2017 on the same subject matter.

The decision rendered by the SSC on March 17, 2017 was based on the 'principle of good faith' as envisaged under the Swiss Criminal law, violation of which is a criminal offence. The court applied the principle and concluded that Swiss Federal Tax Administration ('FTA') cannot provide administrative assistance for any request made by foreign tax authorities based on the theft of data.

The subsequent decision of the SSC dated July 17, 2018, ruled that exchange of information based on stolen information will not per se be in violation of the 'principle of good faith' as contemplated under Article 7 of the Swiss Tax Administrative Assistance Act ('STAA'). The principle may defer basis the facts and circumstances of each case.

The exchange of stolen information would constitute violation if there were an explicit arrangement between India and Switzerland to not use the stolen data. As per SSC, there was no explicit declaration or assurance given by the Indian Tax Authorities to not use the stolen data and therefore, Indian Tax Authorities could use the said information.

The theory on administrative tax assistance was also considered in yet another decision of Swiss Supreme Court rendered on July 26, 2019, which makes it easier for foreign tax authorities to submit a general request for obtaining information without having to demonstrate concrete indication of alleged tax transgressions by account holders at Swiss banks.

For administrative tax assistance, the most crucial requirement is to depict that the request made by the tax authorities is for 'foreseeable relevance' and not for 'speculative requests' which are prohibited. With this premise, the tax authorities will be able to put in broad requests without having to showcase alleged tax transgressions.

17. Reopening of cases of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi is valid as they failed to disclose shares allotted in excess of FMV: HC

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

As a corollary, when the figures reported in the mentioned column are substantial, and the following instances are present, the auditor should exercise heightened vigilance to ensure the authenticity of the transactions:

(a)

Taxable Products: If the products purchased are taxable under GST, it raises the significance of these transactions and warrants closer scrutiny.

(b)

Cash Payments: Payments made in cash can increase the risk of irregularities or inaccuracies in reporting, and therefore, require careful examination.

(c)

Absence of TDS: Transactions not subjected to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) can potentially indicate a need for closer inspection, as TDS is a common regulatory requirement for certain types of payments.

(d)

Internal Documentation: Transactions primarily supported by internal vouchers, bills, or purchase notes, as opposed to external invoices or receipts, may necessitate a more thorough examination to verify their legitimacy.

If the auditor encounters difficulties in forming a conclusive opinion based on the data provided by the assessee, it is essential to include appropriate comments in the main report. These comments should clearly convey an concerns or uncertainties regarding the reported transactions, ensuring transparency and clarity in the audit process.

Expenses covered under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM):

In case of expenditures that were subjected to tax on reverse charge basis, we may encounter with two issues-

(a)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by a person registered under GST but issuing RCM invoices;

(b)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by an unregistered person where the assessee pays tax under RCM on voluntary basis.

In the first scenario, the expenditure under the said category ought to be reported under column 5 of clause 44 i.e., "Relating to other registered entities".

In the second scenario, the expenditure under the said category should be reported under column 7 i.e., Expenditure relating to entities not registered under GST".

VI. The Human Dimension of Compliance Beyond statutes and audits lies the behavioural aspect of compliance. Gold's emotional significance in India often translates into informal holdings within families. Many citizens view gold as a private inheritance rather than a financial instrument. This cultural mindset complicates formal disclosure.

Legal practitioners and policymakers must recognise this human element. Compliance should be accompanied by public education, awareness campaigns, and accessible disclosure mechanisms. Incentivising legitimate investment through Sovereign Gold Bonds, Exchange-Traded Funds, and regulated exchanges can help channel informal wealth into transparent avenues.

VII. Policy Recommendations

A. For Corporates and Financial Institutions

1.

Conduct comprehensive due diligence on all counterparties in domestic and international gold trade.

2.

Implement real-time monitoring systems and periodic AML training for compliance officers.

3.

Use standard benchmarks like LBMA and MCX for valuation to ensure transparency.

4.

Maintain transfer-pricing documentation for all inter-company trades.

5.

Employ blockchain or digital traceability tools to create tamper-proof audit trails.

6.

Report all cross-border transactions accurately under FEMA and PMLA requirements.

B. For Regulators and Policymakers

1.

Integrate data platforms across the ED, FIU, RBI, and Customs for seamless information flow.

2.

Issue clear valuation norms to reduce disputes and improve tax certainty.

3.

Rationalise import duties and GST rates to discourage smuggling and promote legal trade.

Enforce uniform standards for digital gold and tokenised assets.

5.

Strengthen cooperation with international agencies through MLATs and automatic information exchange.

VIII. Conclusion

Gold's brilliance today reflects both opportunity and risk. Its ascent in 2025 is not merely a market story but a mirror of geopolitical shifts and economic uncertainty. For India and other emerging economies, gold remains integral to cultural identity and financial security, yet its regulation defines the boundary between prosperity and peril.

The legal framework, which spans the Income-tax Act, PMLA, GAAR, FEMA, and Benami laws, offers a strong foundation. What is needed is harmonisation, technology-led enforcement, and a compliance culture that values integrity as much as investment.

When transparency governs trade, and law guides wealth, gold evolves from a shadowed asset into a symbol of lawful prosperity. The real value of gold lies not in its karats but in the clarity of the systems that sustain it.

A transparent, accountable, and globally aligned gold economy will not only safeguard national interests but also strengthen India's position as a credible participant in the international financial order.

Though the wilful attempt to evade tax or any other offence under the Income Tax Act is not a scheduled offense under the PMLA, in the context of Income Declaration of Scheme, 2016 or otherwise, any disclosure of income or property could attract the provisions of PMLA, if the property is as defined u/s. 2(v) of the PMLA and the same is sourced out of proceeds of crime as defined u/s. 2(u) of the PMLA.

[However, CBDT Circular No. 17/2016 dated 20.05.16 clarified that, the IDS 2016 incorporates the provisions of section 138 of the Income-tax Act relating to disclosure of information in respect of assessees. Therefore, the information in respect of declaration made shall be kept confidential as in the case of return of income filed by assessees.]

Judicial update

Recently, Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in Rajmandir Estates (P.) Ltd. v. Pr. CIT [2016] 386 ITR 162/240 Taxman 306/70 taxmann.com 124, had an occasion to deal with the issue of validity of reopening of assessment by CIT u/s. 263, in the backdrop of possible money-laundering.

The CIT in his order dated 22.03.13 passed under Section 263 opined that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went undetected due to lack of requisite enquiry and non-application of mind. He entertained the belief "that unaccounted money is laundered as clean share capital by creating a façade of paper work, routing the money through several bank accounts and getting it the seal of statutory approval by getting the case reopened u/s.147 suo motu. Accordingly he concluded that assessment order passed u/s. 143(3)/147 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. He, therefore, set aside the same and issued directions for a thorough enquiry.

Hon'ble High Court in its elaborate order after referring to the PMLA and observing various facets and evidences of possible money laundering under the peculiar facts of the case upheld the order of CIT u/s. 263 in following words:

"We have indicated above the pieces of evidence which go to show that the Commissioner had reasons to entertain the belief that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went unnoticed because the assessing officer did not hold requisite investigation except for calling for the records. ……. The fact that the assessing officer did not apply his mind to those pieces of evidence would be evident from the assessment order itself.

The question for consideration is whether in the presence of materials discussed above the Commissioner was justified in treating the assessment order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. That question in the facts and circumstances has to be answered in the affirmative."

It is important to note that, Hon'ble High Court distinguished some of the Supreme Court precedents cited by the appellant to support his case inter alia on the ground that The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 was not there on the statute at that point of time. Therefore, though offences under the Income Tax act, 1961 per se are not scheduled offences for the purpose of PMLA, nevertheless assessing officer can proceed in assessment or CIT can direct further investigation in order to verify possibility of income/assets added or declared u/s. 68, 69, 69A etc. of the IT act being sourced out of proceeds of crime as defined u/s. 2(u) of the PMLA, so that further action under PMLA, if necessary, can be taken.

Conclusion

It has to be kept in view that India has a problem of black economy, which is unacounted and many a time the holders of black money also launder the black money in order to acquire legitimate assets. Legal or illegal income which evades tax and illegal income that comes within the exempted taxation slab constitute the unreported Gross Domestic Product or black economy. Laundering the black money and laundering proceeds of crime are two different issues, although there is frequent overlap between the two. While laundering black money is to be handled through taxation laws or similar laws, the laundering of proceeds of crime is to be handled through special anti-money-laundering laws. [Dr. M. C. Mehanathan in his commentary on the Law of Prevention of Money Laundering in India published by Lexis Nexis (2014 edition)]

13. Review and Contemporary Analysis

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act has become one of the most important economic laws in India’s regulatory system. Over the years, it has strengthened the government’s ability to trace illegal money, investigate financial frauds, recover public assets, and tackle organized economic offences. Enforcement actions against banking scams, shell companies, Ponzi schemes, cyber frauds, and cross-border laundering networks have played a major role in protecting investors, financial institutions, and the broader economy.

Recent data released by the Enforcement Directorate shows the increasing scale of enforcement under the PMLA. As of March 2026, the ED had registered more than 8,800 ECIRs, issued over 3,500 provisional attachment orders, and attached assets worth nearly ₹2.36 lakh crore. During the financial year 2025–26 alone, attachments reportedly crossed ₹81,000 crore, marking a sharp rise compared to previous years.

These enforcement measures have also produced significant economic benefits. Official figures indicate that assets worth more than ₹63,000 crore have either been returned or steps have been taken to return them to banks, investors, financial institutions, and homebuyers affected by large-scale frauds. India has also strengthened international cooperation in tracing illegal financial flows and fugitive offenders. At the prosecution stage, nearly 2,400 complaints have been filed before Special Courts under the PMLA. Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee. Assessee submitted a bill in respect of purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges. However, AO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee. Held once the identity of the diamond jewellery found during the course of search had been accepted as explainable from the purchase voucher and labour charges bill produced by the assessee at the time of search as well as during the course of regular assessment proceedings, the addition of the difference could be made by the AO only by establishing the fact that the value stated in the purchase invoice was fictitious. The burden clearly lay upon the department to prove that the value shown in the purchase invoice was not the real value. The department had not brought any material whatever on records to prove that the value of such diamonds embedded in the diamond jewellery at the time of its purchase in the month of July 1981 was understated in the purchase invoices. Such a burden was required to be discharged by the department by bringing clinching and conclusive evidence on record. The AO had not even examined the jeweller from whom these diamonds were purchased. The assessee had successfully discharged the initial burden of proving the source of acquisition of aforesaid diamond jewellery by producing the aforesaid bills at the time of search. Off-market deals in shares

Since purchase and sale of shares outside floor of Stock Exchange is not an unlawful activity, it was not possible to hold that off-market transactions reported by assessee were quite sham. Since books of account maintained by assessee clearly reflected purchase of those shares and since evidence on record fully established that assessee had purchased shares and had sold shares, sale proceeds of shares stood explained by assessee and hence addition in question was unjustified - Mukesh R. Marolia v. Addl. CIT [2006] 6 SOT 247 (Mum.).

Assessee made certain off-market transactions in shares through two stock brokers who were members of Calcutta Stock Exchange (CSE). In relevant assessment year assessee's return was selected for scrutiny. Assessee submitted all required documents relating to said transactions. However, Assessing Officer held that said transactions were not genuine as CSE had denied transactions of one of aforesaid brokers through its online trading mechanism. Therefore, Assessing Officer made additions, treating cash credits of assessee as unexplained under section 68. Since in instant case assessee had offered capital gains to tax from sale of shares in off-market transaction and moreover, respective stock brokers had confirmed said transaction, in such circumstances, Assessing Officer was not justified in making addition under section 68. - Acchyalal Shaw v. ITO [2009] 30 SOT 44 (Kol.)(URO).

Unless the recipient has proved the genuineness thereof, the gift can very well be treated to be an accommodation entry of the assessee's own money, which is not disclosed for the purpose of taxation [Tirath Ram Gupta v. Instances in which explanation as to source of investments were held to be satisfactory

The following are some of the instances in which the explanation offered by the assessee was held to be satisfactory:

Where as a part of memorandum of understanding between group companies, certain shares of a group company was transferred to assessee at cost and all these investments were recorded in books of account and it was not case of Revenue that assessee had paid any amount in excess of what was recorded in books and apparent consideration was not real consideration, no addition was sustainable under section 69. - Rupee Finance & Management (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 22 SOT 174 (Mum.)

Note : Even if it was a case of apparent consideration not being the real consideration, section 69B and not section 69 will be attracted.

Where assessee was in Government service for 39 years and after retirement he had received retiremental benefits in cash and had been receiving pension since year 1996 and Revenue had not found any investment elsewhere, except in purchase of jeep, it could be concluded that assessee was having sufficient funds to purchase jeep from savings of salary as well as pension and amount received on retirement and impugned addition was to be deleted - Nagarmal Sharma v. ITO [2009] 30 SOT 4 (Jodh.)(URO)

Where cash found during course of search was duly explained by assessee as belonging to its various firms/companies and cash in hands of firms/companies were duly explained as having been withdrawn from their bank accounts, addition not justified - CIT v. Sanjay Raj Shobha [2010] 2 DTL ONLINE 290 (Delhi)

Where property-in-question was bought and later on sold by assessee's son and investment was duly reflected in accounts of son, no addition on account of unexplained investment could be made in hands of assessee, even though receipt was in assessee's name. - Hafiz Mohammad v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 298 ITR 315 (Raj.)

Where assessee in order to demonstrate that it had made addition to fixed asset contended that such assets had duly been reflected in audited accounts and produced evidence to show enhanced production capacity, enhanced power charges, enhanced electric load and term loan obtained by assessee for expansion purpose, addition on account of unexplained investment was not justified-Victoria Foods (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 3 ITR (Trib.) 35 (Delhi)

Where assessee a non-resident had substantial Non-Resident Non-Repatriable (NRNR), Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR), and NRSB deposits, as assessee had brought money into India through proper banking channel, it could be said that onus on assessee under section 69 stood discharged and, therefore, it was not taxable in India under section 5(2)(b). - Smt. Susila Ramasamy v. Asstt. CIT [2010] 37 SOT 146 (Chennai)

Where it was seen from records that assessee had advanced amount in question to his HUF for making payments to 'A' and that HUF had fully repaid loan in subsequent years, CIT(A) rightly concluded that property belonged to HUF and, therefore, no addition in respect of said property could be made to assessee's income. - Asstt. Loose papers - Investigation could not have been directed in case of high public functionaries on basis of legally inadmissible evidence in form of loose papers. In this case, raids were conducted on the two business groups and incriminating materials in form of random sheets and loose papers, computer prints, hard disk, pen drives etc. were found. Question arose as to whether a case was made out on the basis of above materials, to constitute Special Investigation Team (SIT) and direct investigation against the various functionaries/officers and further monitor the same. It was held that the department had no evidence to prove that the entries in these loose papers and electronic data were kept regularly during the course of business of concerned business house. Thus, these detailed documents recovered by the authorities had no evidentiary values and they could not have been relied on to direct registration of the FIR and investigation in case of high public functionaries occupying important offices. Further, the materials in question were not only irrelevant but were also legally inadmissible u/s 34 of the Evidence Act [Common Cause (A Registered Society) v. UOI [2017] 77 taxmann.com 245/245 Taxman 214 (SC)].

Sworn statement of assessee - Where assessee himself stated in sworn statement during search and seizure about his undisclosed income, same was to be levied tax on basis of admission without scrutinizing documents [B. Kishore Kumar v. DCIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 449/[2015] 229 Taxman 614 (Mad.), SLP dismissed inB. Kishore Kumar v. DCIT [2015] 62 taxmann.com 215/234 Taxman 771 (SC)].

In the absence of any corroborative evidence, addition could not be made to assessee's income in respect of confessional statement made under the Maharashtra Central Organised Crime Act, 1999, that he paid certain undisclosed amount to assessee [CIT v. Jagdishprasad Mohanlal Joshi [2018] 99 taxmann.com 287 (Bom.), SLP dismissed inCIT v. Jagdishprasad Mohanlal Joshi [2018] 99 taxmann.com 288/259 Taxman 342 (SC)].

IDENTITY OF THE PERSON PAN card - The word 'identity' meant the condition or fact of a person or thing being that specified unique person or thing. Mere production of Permanent Account Number (PAN) or assessment particulars does not establish the identity of a person. The identification of a person includes the place of work, the staff and the fact that it was actually carrying on business and further recognition of the said company/individual in the eyes of public. PAN cannot be blindly and without consideration of surrounding circumstances treated as sufficiently disclosing the identity of the individual [CIT v. N. R. Portfolio (P.) Ltd. [2014] 42 taxmann.com 339/222 Taxman 157 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

Banking transaction - The very fact that all the transactions were entered into between the parties through account-payee cheques makes the question of identity of creditors fall into oblivion and it becomes absolutely irrelevant [Addl. CIT v. Bahri Bros. (P.) Ltd. [1985] 22 Taxman 3 (Pat.)].

In case of shareholders - If the shareholders exist then, possibly, no further enquiry need be made. But if the AO finds that the alleged shareholders do not exist then, in effect, it would mean that there is no valid issuance of share capital. Shares cannot be issued in the name of non-existing persons. If the shareholders are identified and it is established that they have invested money in the purchase of shares, then the amount received by the company would be regarded as a capital receipt but if the assessee offers no explanation at all or the explanation offered is not satisfactory, then the provisions of section 68 may be invoked [CIT v. Sophia Finance Ltd. [1993] 70 Taxman 69 (Delhi - FB)].

CREDITWORTHINESS OF THE PERSON

Earning capacity - Creditworthiness of the donor would depend upon the income and earning of the donor and whether and did he have necessary funds. Rarely one finds a poor man giving gifts to a rich and powerful, out of natural love and affection [Pawan Kumar Aggarwal v. ITO [2015] 60 taxmann.com 133 = [2015] 234 Taxman 144 (Delhi)].

Payment by cheque, etc. - Creditworthiness is not proved by showing issue and receipt of a cheque or by furnishing a copy of statement of bank account, when circumstances requires that there should be some more evidence of positive nature to show that the subscribers had made genuine investment or had acted as angel investors after due diligence or for personal reasons. There should be some positive evidence to show the nature and resources of the share subscribers [CIT v. Nipun Builders & Developers [2013] 30 taxmann.com 292/214 Taxman 429 (Delhi)].

When payment by cheque did not establish the creditworthiness of the lender, mere examination of the pass book or the bank statement or the letter of confirmation or the balance sheet of the lender was not enough [CIT v. Maithan International [2015] 56 taxmann.com 283/231 Taxman 381 (Cal.)].

Justice cannot be delivered in a mechanical manner. In other words, what we see on the records available before us, sometime we have to travel beyond it after ignoring the same. Furthermore, while delivering the justice, we have to ensure in this process that culprits should only be punished and no innocent should be castigated. An innocent person should not suffer for the wrongdoings of the other parties. In the case on hand, admittedly there was no evidence available on record suggesting that the assessee or his broker was involved in the rigging up of the price of the script of M/s Shree Nath Commercial & Finance Ltd. | If an 'unexplained investment' is 'undisclosed asset located outside India', the same will be taxed under the Black Money (Undisclosed Income & Assets) Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 (BM Act), not u/s 69 read with section 115BBE(1) in the year of detection. It will also entail penalty and prosecution under that Act. Investments covered u/s 69 are those made by the assessee, not by any other person such as his father/mother. If investment made by assessee, it will be covered u/s 69 even if it stands in some other person's name. Basis of invoking section 69 is assessee made investments, not ownership. Unlike section 68, section 69 applies regardless of assessee maintains books of account or not. Assessee bound to justify the source of investments made by him either by showing the entry in the books of account, if any, maintained by him for any source of income. If no entry in books or he does not maintain books, then he is bound to offer satisfactory explanation to AO as to the nature and source of the investments. Obligation to offer satisfactory explanation is on the assessee, not on his legal heirs or any other person. Jewellery disclosed in Wealth Tax Return before the date of search has been held not 'unexplained investment'. As per CBDT's Instruction No.1916 dated 11-5-1994, in the case of a wealth-tax assessee, gold jewellery and ornaments found in excess of the gross weight declared in the wealth-tax return only need to be seized. The Finance Act, 2015 has repealed the Wealth-tax Act,1957. So, it is no longer possible to file WT returns. By way of analogy, it can be said that disclosure of any investment in Schedule AL of ITR forms would achieve the same effect. CBDT needs to clarify this. As per CBDT's Instruction No.1916 dated 11-5-1994, in the case of a person not assessed to wealth-tax gold jewellery and ornaments to the extent of 500 gms. per married lady 250 gms per unmarried lady and 100 gms. per male member of the family, need not be seized. So, gold jewellery and ornaments to this extent is not unexplained investment. Explanation of nature and source furnished by assessee should be a factual explanation and not a mere legal argument. If assessee is able to partly explain the source and nature of investments by way of entry in his books of account or otherwise, then section 69B shall apply and not section 69. See Para 2.12/Para 2.13 as regards voluntary disclosure of unexplained investments under section 69. Unexplained investments made by the assessee in the name of benamidars will be covered under section 69 as well as the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (PBPT Act). This would mean tax and penalty under the Act as well as confiscation and prosecution under the PBPT Act. Unexplained investments in assessee's name made where he is the benamidar will not be taxed under section 69 as assessee's income as investments have not been made by the assessee but by the beneficial owner. The investment would be liable for confiscation under Benami Act and both the benamidar-assessee and beneficial owner will be liable for prosecution under the Benami Act. It is quite possible that the investment may be taxed u/s 69 in the hands of beneficial owner. |

12.0

Overview of section 69

Section 69 constitutionally valid [Para 12.1]

Unaccounted and unexplained investments [Para 12.2]

Interpretation of 'investments' [Para 12.3]

Investments which are 'undisclosed foreign assets' will be taxed under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 ('the BM Act') and not under section 69 [Para

-tax provisions, it can only be a currency token, bank notes or other circulating medium in general use, which has the representative value. Therefore, the currency notes on the day when they were found to be in possession of the assessee should have had the representative value, namely, it could be tendered as a money, which has intrinsic value [CIT v. Andhra Pradesh Yarn Combines (P.) Ltd. [2006] 153 Taxman 121 (Kar.)]. Bitumen, not a 'valuable article' – Bitumen is not a valuable article in the context of s. 69A [D.N. Singh v. CIT [2023] 150 taxmann.com 301/293 Taxman 550/454 ITR 595 (SC), setting aside D.N. Singh v. CIT [2010] 324 ITR 304 (Patna)].

'Income' has wider meaning - The expression 'income', as used in section 69A, has wide meaning which meant anything which came in or resulted in gain [Chuharmal v. CIT [1988] 38 Taxman 190 (SC)].

Receipt by assessee's agent - Assessee could not escape liability u/s 69A by merely pleading that amount in question was not received by him rather it was received by his agent [Mahesh Kumar Agarwal v. Asstt. CIT [2019] 104 taxmann.com 254 (Pat.)].

Burden of proof - The burden is not on the department to prove that the assessee is the owner of the amount found in the possession of the assessee [CIT v. K. T. M. S. Mohamood [1997] 92 Taxman 169 (Mad.)]. Where there were unaccounted sale transactions, onus was on assessee to show that unaccounted investment in purchases was out of accounted stock, and it could not be presumed that unaccounted sales must have been made from accounted purchases [CIT v. Ajay Kapoor [2013] 36 taxmann.com 513/219 Taxman 42 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

TAXABILITY

Burden of proof not discharged - Where wrist watches were found in the possession of a person, and that person did not adduce any evidence, far less discharged the onus, of proving that wrist watches did not belong to him, the value of the wrist watches could be treated as the income of the assessee [Chuharmal v. CIT [1988] 38 Taxman 190 (SC)].

Where assessee was managing a firm which collected deposits from public, but there was no evidence regarding registration and genuineness of firm and assessee could not explain source of deposits, nor could assessee establish that such deposits did not belong to him, addition of such deposits as assessee's unexplained investments was justified [CIT v. K. Chinnathamban [2007] 162 Taxman 459 (SC)].

Where assessee failed to justify his stand that there was no unaccounted sale as indicated in seized documents, addition made on basis of seized documents was justified [CIT v. S. Rudramuniyappa [2015] 64 taxmann.com 411 (Kar.), SLP dismissed inS. Rudramuniyappa v. CIT [2016] 75 taxmann.com 241/243 Taxman 353 (SC)].

No entry in books of account - Where amount surrendered during survey was not reflected in books of account and no source from where it was derived was declared by assessee, it was assessable as deemed income of assessee u/s 69A [Kim Pharma (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2013] 35 taxmann.com 456/216 Taxman 153 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Family transaction - Where certain amount was transferred from parents' bank account to assessee's bank account, there being transfer of funds inter se between family members, no addition could be made to assessee's income u/s 69A in respect of the aforesaid amount [CIT v. Palwinder Pal Singh [2012] 17 taxmann.com 17/204 Taxman 55 (Mag.) (P&H)]. Also see, CIT v. Meghjibhai Popatbhai Virani [2013] 35 taxmann.com 100/217 Taxman 35 (Mag.) (Guj.).

Gifts - Where assessee received gifts from two persons on behalf of his daughters on occasion of their marriage since said gifts were made by demand drafts and genuineness of same was confirmed by bank in which person making gifts had their accounts, impugned addition made u/s 69A was to be set aside [CIT v. Jawahar Lal Oswal [2016] 67 taxmann.com 168/238 Taxman 225 (P&H)].

's books had been prepared on basis of bills and vouchers and there was no allegation that either purchase of raw-material or production was found unrecorded, mere fact that there was some variation during few months in electricity consumption could not be a basis for making addition on account of unaccounted production and gross profit on unaccounted sales [CIT v. Paras Agro Products [2014] 42 taxmann.com 411/222 Taxman 60 (Mag.) (Guj.)]. Profit element is to be taxed - When undisclosed purchases are discovered in course of assessment, it is only profit embedded in said transactions which can be added to total income u/s 69C [PCIT v. Subarna Rice Mill [2018] 96 taxmann.com 286/257 Taxman 509 (Cal.), SLP dismissed inPCIT v. Subarna Rice Mill [2020] 114 taxmann.com 572/269 Taxman 565 (SC)]. Also see, PCIT v. Jakharia Fabric (P.) Ltd. [2020] 118 taxmann.com 406/274 Taxman 52 (Bom.).

No double taxation - Once 'on money' was considered as revenue receipt and addition to income was made, then any expenditure out of such money could not be treated as unexplained expenditure, doing so would amount to double addition [CIT v. Golani Brothers [2017] 85 taxmann.com 355/250 Taxman 446 (Bom.)].

Deemed income not to be allowable as deductible expenditure - Proviso to section 69C inserted w.e.f. 1-4-1999 does not apply retrospectively. The deemed income (where the source of the expenditure is not explained) cannot be allowed as a deduction under any head of income [P. Ram Gopal Varma v. DCIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 106/[2014] 220 Taxman 84 (Mag.) (AP)].

Where assessee had not incurred any expenditure in relevant FY on purchase of plot, Tribunal had rightly deleted disallowance of pro rata cost on sale of part of plot holding that proviso to section 69C could also not have been invoked [CIT v. Chandulal Sadhuram Khemani [2015] 53 taxmann.com 293 (Bom.)].

onus is required to be placed on such companies besides the general onus to establish identity and creditworthiness of creditor and genuineness of transaction. This additional onus, needs to be placed on such companies to also prove the source of money in the hands of such shareholder or persons making payment towards issue of shares before such sum is accepted as genuine credit. If the company fails to discharge the additional onus, the sum shall be treated as income of the company and added to its income". The judicial pronouncements referred in the Memorandum, inter alia, include:

♦ CIT v. Lovely Exports (P.) Ltd. [2008] 216 CTR 195 (SC)

The onus cast upon the assessee company was discharged upon disclosure of the names and particulars of the alleged bogus shareholders. It was for the Department to conduct its own enquiry thereafter and additions if any may be made in the hands of the shareholders.

♦ CIT v. Steller Investment Ltd. [2001] 115 Taxman 99 (SC)

Even if subscribers to the capital are not genuine, the amount received by the company as share capital could not be assessed in the hands of the company itself. Such amounts should be considered for assessment in the hands of persons who are alleged to have really advanced the money.

♦ CIT v. Divine Leasing & Finance Ltd. [2007] 158 Taxman 440 (Delhi) - Delhi High Court held that the amount of share application money received by a Company from alleged bogus shareholders could not be regarded as undisclosed income u/s 68 when the assessee furnished details regarding shareholders. If the names of the alleged bogus shareholders are given to the AO, then the Department is free to proceed to reopen their individual assessments in accordance with law. The Supreme Court upheld this view.

♦ CIT v. STL Extrusion (P.) Ltd. [2011] 333 ITR 269/ 11 taxmann.com 125 (MP)

Where assessee had duly discharged its onus by furnishing names, age, address, date of filing application of share, number of shares of each subscriber, the AO was not justified in making addition u/s 68.

♦ CIT v. Arunananda Textiles (P.) Ltd. [2011] 203 Taxman 32 (Mag.)/ 15 taxmann.com 226 (Kar.)

It was not for the assessee to place material before the Assessing Officer about creditworthiness of the shareholders. Once the company had given the addresses of the shareholders and their identity was not in dispute, it was for the Assessing Officer to make further inquiry with the investors about their capacity to invest the amount in shares.

♦ CIT v. Dwarkadhish Investment (P.) Ltd. [2010] 194 Taxman 43/[2011] 330 ITR 298 (Delhi)

Once the assessee proves the identity of creditors/share applicants, by either furnishing their PAN or income-tax assessment numbers, and shows genuineness of transaction by showing money in his books either by account payee cheque or by draft or by any other mode, onus of proof would shift to revenue.

♦ CIT v. Creative World Telefilms Ltd. [2011] 203 Taxman 36/ 333 ITR 100/ 15 taxmann.com 183 (Bom.)

Once documents like PAN card, bank account details or details from the bankers were given by the assessee, onus shifts upon the Assessing Officer and it is on him to reach the shareholders. The Assessing Officer could not burden the assessee merely on the ground that summons issued to the investors were returned back with the endorsement not traceable.

The decisions were based on a settled legal position, applicable to any 'cash credit', like, loans, deposits, advances, share capital or others, that:

♦ Primary onus is on assessee;

♦ an assessee does not have to establish source of source;

♦ if primary onus is discharged, burden shifts to Tax Department;

♦ AO needs to discharge his burden and reach an objective satisfaction;

♦ AO has a discretion to assess cash credits;

♦ in a given case the amount can be assessed in the hands of investor/lender under other applicable provisions of law, like, section 69.

15.2.3 Salient features of the first proviso

♦ If a closely held company (that is, a company in which public are not substantially interested),

♦ Credits any sum (consisting of share application money, share capital, share premium or any such amount by whatever name called) in its books of account to a resident person,

♦ Explanation about the credit, in terms of section 68 (without considering proviso, as inserted) would not be deemed to be satisfactory, unless:

- Person in whose name such credit is recorded offers an explanation about the nature and the source of such credit; and

- Explanation by such person is to the satisfaction of AO,

♦ The amount so received would be treated as unexplained cash credit and accordingly included in its income.

16.2

Trigger for section 69B

Trigger for section 69B is not possession of some valuable article. Trigger for section 69B is that:

assessee has made any investment or is found to be the owner of any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article and such bullion, jewellery or valuable article in the financial year in question;

the amount expended by him on the investment or on the acquisition of money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article exceeds the amount recorded in the books of account maintained by the assessee; and

the assessee offers no explanation as to such excess amount or the explanation offered by him is not satisfactory in the opinion of the AO

Section 69B is attracted such excess amount is not satisfactorily explained as to source either by way of entry in books of account maintained for any source of income or otherwise as having been met out of tax-paid income of past years or out of tax-free incomes or out of non-taxable capital receipts such as loans/deposits. If entire expenditure is not satisfactorily explained by way of entry in books of account for any source of income or otherwise, then section 69 or section 69A (as the case may be) shall apply and not section 69B.

Where there was a clear admission by assessee firm that excess stock found during survey was added in its stock register but no corresponding entry was passed in books of account, it could be considered that investment in such stock was made out of undisclosed source, thus, addition was to be made under section 69B in respect of such excess stock [SVS Oil Mills v. ACIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 388 (Madras)]

rewritten_query: Can genuine diamond purchases made through banking channels be treated as unexplained expenditure only because the stock was later sold for cash to buyers whose identities could not be verified?

case_summary.text: INCOME TAX: Where assessee, diamond trader, imported diamonds and purchases were executed through banking channels and in compliance with statutory provisions, furthermore sine purchases were accepted as genuine with proper supporting documents, expenditure on such purchases could not be treated as unexplained merely because sales were made in cash or buyers could not be fully identified, and thus, disallowance under section 69C was unjustified

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales,

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected,

IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

INCOME TAX: Where assessee engaged in diamond trading was alleged to have made bogus purchases from two entities based on third party investigation, but furnished all purchase and sales records, payment proofs and export documents correlating purchases with export sales and sales were not doubted, entire purchases could not be disallowed and only profit element relating to disputed purchases could be added to income.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization period and claimed that same arose out of cash sales of jewellery, since other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT and books of account of assessee were accepted by AO, said deposits could not be said to be unexplained cash deposit

INCOME TAX : Where assessee received loan from various creditors who had sold their old jewellery to jewellers and gave loan to assessee out of said sale consideration, and assessee had disclosed name of jewellers to whom jewellery was sold and also established mode of payment through banking channel and further no inquiry was made from jeweller to whom jewellery was sold by creditors,

Additions u/s 69C deleted as genuine diamond purchases can't be disallowed merely due to cash sales: HC

INCOME TAX: Where assessee’s long-term capital gains from sale of diamonds were supported by declaration under IDS, 2016 and valid holding period, additions under sections 68 and 69C treating sale proceeds and alleged commission as unexplained were unsustainable and liable to be deleted.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of trading in bullion and jewellery, deposited cash in its bank accounts during demonetisation period, since assessee had successfully explained source of such cash deposits as sales/advances duly recorded in its books of account and comparative sales data dispelled allegation of abnormal cash sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating same as unexplained cash credits under section 68

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery, claimed that cash deposited in bank account during demonetization period pertained to sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers, since assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences, impugned addition made under section 69A, read with section 115BBE treating cash sales as bogus was to be deleted

INCOME TAX: Where assessees claimed exemption under section 10(38) on LTCG from sale of shares alleged to be penny stock scrips, but transactions were through stock exchange, supported by Demat records and banking channels, and revenue failed to establish any direct evidence of assessees' conscious involvement or nexus with brokers, entry providers or share-rigging activities, additions made as unexplained money were unsustainable and liable to be deleted

IT: Where neither huge cash in hand over Rs. 20 lakhs was substantiated by wealth-tax return of other documentary proof nor photocopies of shares purchased or share numbers were furnished, impugned transaction could not be held to be genuine and explained
High value shown in stock statement sent to banks couldn't be held as unexplained investment
Disallowance on alleged bogus diamond purchases restricted to profit element as sales and documentation undisputed:ITAT

INCOME TAX : Where assessee duly proved genuineness of sale transaction by bringing on record contract notes of sale and purchase, bank statement of broker and demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, Assessing Officer was not justified in bringing to tax capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit

IT : Value of diamond jewellery received by assessee from family members and partners only for exhibition and covered under VDIS could not be added to assessee's income as unexplained investment in jewellery

INCOME TAX : Where assessee was trading in diamonds and Assessing Officer made disallowance at rate of 100 per cent of purchases made by assessee on account of unexplained purchases being accommodation entries, in view of judicial precedent on identical issue disallowance at rate of 6 per cent of disputed purchases would be sufficient to meet possibility of revenue leakage
Share application money can’t be deemed as unexplained if identity and creditworthiness of applicants are proved
IT : Where transaction of sale of shares at stock exchange through demat account could not be proved to be bogus, capital gain arising therefrom could not be added as unexplained income

INCOME TAX : Where assessee sold shares through stock exchange, paid STT, disclosed transaction in return, held shares in demat account and routed payments through banks, addition of sale proceeds as unexplained cash credit based solely on generalized penny-stock investigation findings without direct nexus to assessee's involvement was arbitrary and liable to be deleted

INCOME TAX : Where assessee duly proved genuineness of sale transaction by bringing on record contract notes of sale and purchase, bank statement of broker and demat account showing transfer in and out of shares, Assessing Officer was not justified in bringing to tax capital gain arising from sale of shares as unexplained cash credit.
Receipt of share application money via banking channel couldn't be held as unexplained

INCOME TAX : Where two entities from whom assessee made purchases were found to be bogus but assessee had shown from its audited books of account, stock statement as well as material receipt register that it could not have sold equivalent quantum of diamond jewellery without these two purchases, addition on account of bogus purchases was to be restricted to 3 per cent of total purchases

INCOME TAX : Where assessee had furnished various details including bank payment details for purchase of shares, subsequent consolidation statement and also contract notes for sale of shares through stock exchange and proved genuineness of transactions of purchase and sale of shares of company SCL as an ordinary investor, addition made by Assessing Officer treating sale consideration received for sale of shares as unexplained money was to be deleted

INCOME TAX :Where assessee had sold goods and deposited cash in bank during demonetization period and part of said cash was deposited in SBN and remaining part of cash was directly deposited into bank account by seller, though SBN, since same had not been received by assessee directly and same was received by bank which was permitted till 31st December to be received by bank, said amount could not be considered as unexplained money in hands of assessee

INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer made an addition in respect of sale proceeds of shares as unexplained cash credit under section 68, since shares were purchased by assessee on floor of stock exchange and not from broker, payment was made through banking channel, deliverables were taken in DEMAT account where shares remained for more than one year, contract notes were issued and shares were also sold on stock exchange, Tribunal had rightly deleted impugned addition

INCOME TAX : Where during search conducted at premises of one S, gold jewellery which was to be received by assessee as consignee was seized, since payment for purchasing said gold was made through banking channels and purchases were duly accounted for in books of account of assessee, no additions could be made for unaccounted investment with respect to said gold jewellery and same was to be released in favour of assessee

Addition for unexplained cash payment on jewellery purchase unsustainable as no incriminating evidence found in search: ITAT

digest.text:
HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

On second appeal :

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. FACT: The assessees were dealers in diamonds. Each of the assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997. The said declarations were accepted by the Department and a certificate was issued to the respective assessees under the VDIS, 1997. The assessees claimed to have sold the jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 in the year relevant to the assessment year 1998-99 and offered to tax the capital gains arising from the respective sales. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessees on the ground that the persons to whom the jewellery was sold had stated in their statements that the transactions were not genuine and, although, later on the statements were retracted and affidavits were filed on oath to effect that the transactions were genuine, but the transactions were not proved. Challenging the aforesaid orders, appeals were filed and ultimately the Tribunal allowed the claim of the assessees and deleted the additions.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

In aforesaid circumstances, it was to be held that the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessees' claim. [Para 7]

It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32] The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

Under the provisions of section 68, if the explanation with regard to nature and source of deposit is found unsatisfactory, only then, the amount so credited may be added as income. In the instant case, there was no evidence of any ‘hawala’ transaction. [Para 37]

The fact that ‘V’ admitted that his son was the proprietor of ‘R’ and that he had no experience of the diamonds trade and the business was handled by him and his son was nowhere connected with ‘R’ personally, was not a determinative factor of the issue that the transaction by the assessee with ‘V’ or ‘D’ was not genuine. [Para 38]

In view of the conflicting statements of ‘V’, and the absence of any material on record justifying the alleged ‘hawala’ in one of his statements contrary to his first statement on the day of survey itself accepting the transaction to be true, even the validity of reopening could not be upheld. [Para 39]

In the instant case, the assessee had himself given a statement of genuine business transaction initially and three more times thereafter by way of letter, affidavit and a subsequent statement under section 131 explaining the circumstance for giving a contrary statement on 31-3-2000. The transaction was recorded in the books of ‘V’ which were all through with the department much before the survey in the case of ‘V’. The assessee had given the reasons and in any case the statement dated 31-3-2000 was not specific to the transaction with the assessee and transaction with the assessee was stated to be true in subsequent statements and supported by books and bills issued for the sale of diamonds. Therefore, the statement, which accorded with the other facts on record, like existence of diamond as declared and accepted under VDIS, bills of sales, entries in books, payment by account-payee cheque, should be accepted. [Para 42]

In those facts and circumstances, the appeal of the assessee was to be allowed. [Para 48]

The whole controversy can also be seen from the another angle, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases to the tune of Rs. 48.78 crores during the subject assessment year as the payments for these purchases were stated to be made out of cash deposited in bank accounts out of so-called cash sales of gold made by the assessee of which identity of the buyers was not revealed by the assessee. Thus, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit in the bank account and consequently sources of incurring expenditure by way of purchases claimed by the assessee in its profit and loss account of Rs. 48.78 crores could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee and onus cast under section 69C was not satisfied which would make amount covered by such expenditure represented by purchases of gold bars to be deemed income of the assessee under the deeming fiction of section 69C. The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. Thus, revenue succeeds on this ground while the assessee fails on this issue in their respective appeals. [Para 10]

Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]  Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - FACT: The assessee-company was engaged in the business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds. It filed its return of income for the relevant assessment year declaring it's total income.

Subsequently information was received from Investigation wing that assessee-company had made bogus payment to 'R' and 'RS' which were paper companies without having any business activities. These companies were engaged in providing accommodation entries or sending bogus foreign remittances to entities based in Hong Kong and UAE in guise of bogus import purchases. Further information was received from investigation directorate Mumbai that an action under section 133A was carried out wherein it was found that assessee had debited expenses in the form of commission from four different parties. The enquiries were conducted and found that all the 4 companies have the same address and they were not available on the addresses mentioned in the income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises. Based on the above information, the Assessing Officer made additions on account of (i) bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods and (ii) bogus commission payment made by assessee during the year under consideration.
