On revenue's appeal:

HELD: Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section 69A, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained Moneys (Demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery - During demonetization period, assessee deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers in its bank account - Assessing Officer observed that cash sales were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by assessee company merely to build an explanation for cash deposits in to bank account and made an addition of total cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE - Assessee furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for relevant period and cash sales made by assessee had been credited in books of account and, thus, assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences - Further, no defect had been pointed out in books of account of assessee - When sale had been offered to tax, adding same again would amount to double taxation - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving source of cash deposited in bank, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of retail sales of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited certain amount in specified bank notes to the bank account. The case was selected for scrutiny to verify the source for cash deposited and certain details were called for.

■

The assessee submitted that it had deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers and had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period and demonstrated that the cash deposited in bank was out of sales proceeds of stock on hand.

■

The Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee and observed that cash sales entered in the cash book and sales register were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by the assessee company merely to build an explanation for the cash deposits in to the bank accounts and made addition of total of cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the assessee had explained the sources of cash deposits as cash sales received on 08-11-2016 against the sales and the assessee also produced the sale bills and books of accounts and that when there was sufficient stock to effect the sales and no defect had been found in the stock as well as the sales and purchases and since, the assessee has already admitted the sales as revenue receipt, there was no case for considering cash deposit as not explained and adding the same and deleted the addition.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The fact with regard to the impugned dispute are that the assessee has deposited a sum in specified bank notes during demonetization period to the bank account. In response to notice under section 142(1), the assessee had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period. The stock moved out of the books on account of sales made by the assessee has been established from stock registers. The VAT returns and annual audit report under TNVAT Act for the relevant period reflected such sales which have been accepted by the VAT authorities. The assessee has maintained proper books of account which are subjected to tax audit under section 44AB. The assessee also maintained quantitative details of the stock of Gems, Gold and Diamond separately and furnished before the lower authorities, which have not been rejected. The books of account of the assessee have been accepted by the lower authorities while framing the assessment and not rejected by pointing out any defects. [Para 8]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32] As regards the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998, the assessee had stated in response to a question that he was at Surat on most of the dates and not necessarily on all the dates. In view of the fact that preceding the date of 15-3-1998, there was sales of diamonds on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 24-1-1998 of other family members of the assessee, sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998 was to be accepted as genuine. [Para 33]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 25-3-1998 after perusal of statement and rejoinder of the assessee, it was found that Rs. 5,00,000 was not drawn on 25-3-1998 but was credited to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and it was a transfer entry on 25-3-1998 from the bank account of ‘H’ in State Bank of India to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and, therefore, the contention of the revenue that the assessee was at Hyderabad on 25-3-1998 was not correct. [Para 34]

As regards letters filed by the departmental representative, it was to be held that these were internal correspondence between the Income-tax Department at Surat and at Hyderabad which were never put to the assessee. None of these letters, which were in the form of general statements, pertained to ‘S’ with whom the assessee had transactions. A specific reference to letter dated 5-3-2001 showed that the Dy. Commissioner, Surat, clearly mentioned that the jurisdiction qua ‘S’ lay with Mumbai office and not Surat and, therefore, nothing turned on this correspondence. As for the postal remark that the letter addressed to ‘S’ at Surat was returned, it was to be held that the correct address of ‘S’ at the time was at Mumbai and not at Surat and the letter was, therefore, returned ‘unserved’. Nothing turned on this issue as far as the genuineness of the transaction was concerned. [Para 35]

The contention of the departmental representative that the books of account, computer floppies and other evidences relating to purchase of diamonds by ‘S’ could not be verified on the pretext that these were washed away in floods in the heart of Surat and that the purchaser could not retrieve the same, was contrary to the facts and evidence on record. ‘S’ co-operated in all enquiries of the Department. The transaction was confirmed by ‘S’ in response to summons under section 131. The purchase of diamonds was reflected in the stock register maintained by ‘S’. The payments were made by DDs from Mumbai. The facts that the assessee himself removed the diamonds at his own risk and that the payments were received a month after handing over of the diamonds which was again a risk taken by the assessee, could not be a ground to hold that the transactions of sale of diamonds were not genuine. The initials placed on the business purchase invoices of ‘N’ Textiles, in which the assessee was a partner, were the dates meant for payment and the endorsements were made earlier. This had been demonstrated by the assessee with documentary evidence. In respect of huge deposits of amounts in the bank account of ‘S’, the assessee could not be called upon to comment on the same as the department ought to have examined ‘S’ as summons under section 131 was issued. The proceedings thereafter had not been placed before the Tribunal by the revenue. [Para 37]

Thus, the identity of ‘S’ Jeweller, genuineness of the transaction and creditworthiness of ‘S’ Jeweller had been amply established by the assessee. [Paras 37 & 38]

As stated in earlier para, some diamond studded jewellery have been purchased during this year. The difference in weight can be reconciled only after the diamonds are valued by an approved diamond valuer."

The specific items which the assessee had clearly identified as purchased by her are as under : After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order, as under :

issuing cheques to various parties including the assessee. [Para 13]

T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14] In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

Assuming the revenue was right in its contention that the sale did not involve actual delivery of diamond jewellery, then unless it was established that the assessee had passed on his undisclosed income to T, it could not be said that the amount received by the assessee from T represented the undisclosed income of the assessee. Neither T in his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 had stated that the assessee had given the cash amount to T nor in the reassessment proceedings the Assessing Officer had gathered any evidence to that effect. Perusal of the reassessment order showed that the Assessing Officer had not made any efforts to link that the cash received and deposited by T in his bank account was, in fact, paid by the assessee. In those circumstances, in the absence of any cogent evidence brought on record, the decision of the Tribunal in holding that the Assessing Officer had failed to establish the nexus between the cash amount deposited in the bank account of T was attributable to the cheque issued by T in favour of the assessee could not be faulted. [Para 18]

In the instant case, cash credits were not introduced in the accounts of the assessee. From the fact that the cash credits were introduced in the accounts of T, it could not be inferred that the said cash belonged to the assessee. The assessee was not under any obligation to prove the cash credits in the accounts of 'T'. The assessee had proved that he was in possession of the diamond jewellery which was duly declared and certified under the VDIS, 1997. He had proved the identity of the person to whom the said diamond jewellery was sold, his creditworthiness and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from the sale of the diamond jewellery. [Para 19]

The sale transaction of diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 between the assessee and T had been accepted by the Sales Tax Authorities and the assessments made them had attained finality. In any event, in the facts of the instant case, the view taken by the Tribunal that the retracted statement of T was corroborated by the pay-in-slips/cash deposits in the bank account of T and the non-availability of the jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee to T was a reasonable and possible view. [Para 20]

Therefore, the appeal filed by the revenue was without any merit and was liable to be dismissed. [Para 21]

HEADNOTE: Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading in bullion and jewellery. During demonetization, the assessee had deposited a significant amount of cash in its bank accounts. The assessee explained that the cash deposits were out of cash advances received from customers against cash sales of jewellery/bullion.

■

The Assessing Officer rejected the assessee’s explanation and treated the amount of cash deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68, read with section 115BBE, and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The entire case of the revenue is built upon the basis of suspicion regarding the sales booked by the assessee prior to the start of demonetization period. The Assessing Officer has rejected the books of account merely because there was a spike in cash advances on three dates. However, the comparative data furnished by the assessee clearly dispels this suspicion. A perusal of the chart reveals that the cash sales in the year under consideration were in fact significantly lower than the preceding year. When the assessee has demonstrated that in the previous year, during the corresponding period, the cash sales were much higher, the allegation of ‘abnormal’ sales during the demonetization period falls flat. The data furnished by the assessee shows that the assessee’s total sales as well as cash sales during the year under consideration including the relevant demonetization period were comparatively very less than the preceding financial year. This data shows that the assessee’s cash sales were not abnormal during the relevant period and Assessing Officer’s suspicion of cash sales is not based on any reliable material. [Para 11]

■

Further, the Assessing Officer has not pointed out any discrepancy in the stock register, and the assessee was evidently possessed of the requisite stock to effect the impugned sales. It is a matter of record that the purchases have been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income. The notices issued under section 133(6) were largely complied with, and the mere fact that one party went into bankruptcy does not make the entire purchases bogus. Though the Assessing Officer has doubted the purchases, it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had not debited the amount of purchases from its books or that the assessee had made purchases out of its unexplained income. Once the purchases are accepted and the stock is not disputed, the sales flowing out of such stock cannot be treated as non-genuine. The sales have been recorded in the books of account and the profit arising therefrom has been offered to tax. Therefore, the entire receipts from the corresponding sales cannot be treated as unaccounted income of the assessee; only the profit element embedded in such sales can be taxed, which the assessee has duly offered for taxation. Taxing the gross receipts again under section 68 would amount to double taxation of the same amount. [Para 12]

■

Even, at the most, it can be alleged, though not proved, by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had made certain sales and accepted SBN/demonetized currency during the relevant period. Even assuming so, the assessee may have breached or violated the relevant circular/notification of the RBI/Demonetization Scheme, however, even then it cannot be held a case of income from unexplained sources. [Para 14]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-HUF filed its return of income for assessment year 1998-99 and declared long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds - Assessee submitted that said diamonds had been declared under voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced VDIS certificate issued by Commissioner - Assessee further submitted that sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts and was deposited in savings bank account of assessee and he also placed before Assessing Officer confirmation letters from buyers of diamonds; sale invoices; copy of extract of bank account and valuation report of diamonds - Assessing Officer, however, found that (i) main activity of purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries; (ii) demand drafts were purchased by depositing equivalent amounts of cash in bank account; (iii) assessee travelled to Surat alone in unreserved compartment carrying diamonds and stayed in dharamshala under a fictitious name; (iv) 'G' who was connected with purchasing parties in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between - In view of said details Assessing Officer concluded that assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold diamonds to Surat based parties and he, accordingly, rejected claim of capital gains of assessee and made addition under section 68 - Whether since diamonds were declared in VDIS which was supported through certificate issued by Commissioner and further, buyers had confirmed to have purchased diamonds and sale invoices; copy of bank account giving full description and details had been placed on record, which were not controverted by Assessing Officer, it could be said that there was a strong presumption in favour of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes

assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor. Thus, these so-called proceeds of cash sales deposited in bank accounts of the assessee are cash credits appearing in the books of account of the assessee sources of which are not satisfactorily explained by the assessee keeping in view detailed factual matrix of the case and onus cast under section 68 on the assessee is not fulfilled. The genuineness of these cash receipts could not be satisfactorily proved by the assessee as there is no third party evidences to substantiate the authenticity of these cash deposits as no details of the said persons to whom cash sales were allegedly made by the assessee was revealed by the assessee. It is incomprehensible and unacceptable that the assessee having issued cash sales invoices of average value of around Rs.3 crores per single invoice in majority of case and at the same time the assessee is claiming that the name of the said alleged buyers of gold bars is not known to the assessee rather it is the assessee who is actively concealing the identity of these so-called buyers of gold bars. It is incomprehensible keeping in view factual matrix of the case that the assessee have extended credit of Rs. 27.55 crores to its so-called buyers of gold bars out of sale of gold bars of Rs. 48.99 crores concluded in April 2005 as the said amount of Rs. 27.55 crores was realized in the months of May, June, July and August 2005 which does not inspire confidence. The genuineness of the business of gold bars carried on by the assessee of such huge magnitude keeping in view background of the assessee based on material on record and infrastructure facilities maintained by the assessee as well no experience in this field itself cast serious shadow of doubt on the genuineness of said business carried on by the assessee. The onus was on the assessee to prove genuineness of the business of gold bars conducted by the assessee. Provisions of section 68 is a special provisions and is a deeming provision which cast obligation on the assessee to satisfactorily explain the cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee by revealing identity, creditworthiness of the creditor and genuineness of the transaction which has not been fulfilled by the assessee and burden cast on the assessee is not fulfilled by the assessee in the instant case as detailed above.

The assessee failed to satisfactorily explain the sources of these cash deposits in bank accounts of the assessee which are in the nature of cash credits in the books of account /bank accounts of the assessee, which is stated to be from cash sales of gold bar wherein identity of the buyers is not revealed by the assessee and is a devise used to convert undisclosed income/money into gold bars without disclosure of the identity of depositor of cash in bank accounts, and thus burden cast on the assessee under section 68 did not stood discharged and the said cash credit will be deemed to be income of the assessee from the undisclosed income chargeable to tax within deeming fiction of section 68, which in the instant case it is held this issue against the assessee and in favour of revenue based on factual matrix of the case detailed above.

The whole controversy can also be seen from the another angle, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases to the tune of Rs. 48.78 crores during the subject assessment year as the payments for these purchases were stated to be made out of cash deposited in bank accounts out of so-called cash sales of gold made by the assessee of which identity of the buyers was not revealed by the assessee.

Further, payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel - He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances - Whether in light of factual context and balance of probabilities, issue would be adjudicated in favour of assessee, and disallowances made on this count were to be cancelled - FACT: The assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery. Pursuant to a search conducted at the premises of the assessee the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N'.

The assessee contended that the allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer had ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties were placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. Further, the payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances.

The Assessing Officer was however, dissatisfied with the documentary evidences filed to support the purchases made from these two parties, and treated same as bogus and made addition.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition on account of bogus purchases.

On second appeal:

HELD: As noted above, the assessee contends that the allegation towards bogus purchases is wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contends that the Assessing Officer has ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties are placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. The payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. It is also the contention of the assessee that both the parties from whom the assessee has made purchases are existing parties and such parties have independently filed their confirmation with regard to the supplies made by such parties to the assessee and mere non-attendance per se after a lapse of time could not be viewed adversely.[Para 9.1]

Having regard to the nature of business, i.e. trade in bullion, where stocks are identifiable and the price is also governed by market forces with little scope for manipulations; the purchases duly accounted for; the transaction of only 2 parties doubted despite extensive enquiry on 122 parties etc. there was potency in the plea of bonafides. There can be variety of reasons for non-attendence by unrelated third parties and it is not always within the domain of assessee to enforce attendance of third parties. Nothing adverse need to be imputed in such circumstances, more so, where the payments have been made through banking channel. [Para 9.1.1]

HEADNOTE: Section 69, read with sections 40A(3) and 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee a trader in diamonds and VCD rights, declared that during previous year it had earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on purchases and sales of diamonds - Assessing Officer noted that profit earned by assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher as in assessee’s line of business normally profit was 6 per cent; that all parties from whom assessee made purchases, on examination, had confirmed transactions but none of them could reply satisfactorily about amount of credit given; that though all suppliers to assessee’s sellers were based at Surat, none of those parties were traceable and that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to assessee - Accordingly, Assessing Officer concluded that assessee made purchases of diamonds from open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC - Assessing Officer further held that assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and, accordingly, worked out peak credit; treated same as assessee’s unexplained investment and added same to income of assessee - Assessing Officer also while computing deduction under section 80HHC rejected purchases declared by assessee and fixed same at higher amount - Assessing Officer also made an addition to income of assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of cash purchases - Commissioner (Appeals) increased unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds - He also upheld addition made by Assessing Officer under section 40A(3) - Whether since no comparative case was brought on record to substantiate that in line of assessee’s business normally profit was 6 per cent, view of revenue that profit earned by assessee was high could not be subscribed with - Held, yes - Whether since parties from whom assessee had purchased goods had confirmed transaction and also in response to notice under section 131 had appeared, fact that they were not existing at given address could not be reason for rejection of their confirmation - Held, yes - Whether since there was no evidence to show that money which seller parties withdrew reached back to assessee, finding arrived at by revenue authorities in that regard was not right one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes

HEADNOTE: II. Section 69A,  read with section 158BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Block period 1-4-1995 to 13-9-2001 - Diamond was found in business premises of assessee - Only after several months, assessee explained that diamond stock was received on approval basis from an entity - Proprietor of said entity stated that said transactions were only by way of accommodation for which he received commission equivalent to tax paid by him - No receipt or encashment slip was made available by assessee - Whether assessee failed to discharge burden cast upon him to explain diamonds in his possession - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition made on account of unexplained diamonds was sustainable - Held, yes [Para 14][In favour of revenue]

FACT: In course of search and seizure, the department found 338 carats of diamonds from the business premises of the assessee. He explained several months after the search action was conducted that diamond stock was received on approval basis from an entity.

Statement was made by the proprietor of the entity to the effect that said transactions were only by way of accommodation entries for which he received commission equivalent to tax paid by him. Statement made was shown to the assessee who chose not to cross-examine the proprietor. The assessee rather modified his earlier statement made to the effect of availability of quantity of diamonds. The revenue sought copy of the entrustment slip for the alleged receipt of diamonds but same was said to be unavailable with the assessee.

The Assessing Officer held that neither the transaction nor the explanation tendered was bona fide. Accordingly, a sum of Rs. 67.75 lakhs was added as an undisclosed income.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal, the Tribunal reversed the order of the Assessing Officer on the ground that addition was made solely on the basis of statements made by the proprietor of the entity and since the statement was not shown to the assessee and an opportunity of cross-examination was not afforded, the addition was liable to be deleted.

On appeal before the High Court by the revenue.

HELD: The sequence of facts as narrated would make it clear that the explanations tendered by the assessee have been made several months after the time of search. This, coupled with the fact that primary documents such as the entrustment slips have not been produced, lead to a belief that the explanation tendered is a mere after thought. The statement of the proprietor of BE who confirms that the transaction was not bona fide, but an accommodation for commission. No opportunity has been sought to cross examine the proprietor and in any event, this aspect of the matter is merely incidental and in addition to the overwhelming evidence already available to disprove the version of events adduced by the assessee. The totality of circumstances support the conclusion that the assessee has failed to discharge the burden cast upon him to explain the diamonds in his possession. [Para 14]

The order of the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted the aforesaid sequence as elaborated, in confirming the addition. The assessee appears to have, retracted the sworn statements. The retraction has not been accepted on the ground that it is made after inordinate delay and is not supported by any material contrary to the facts set out in the sworn statements. That view is endorsed. [Para 15]

In any event, the statements of 'M' and 'H', proprietor of BM are, but one spoke in the entire wheel and the totality of the events that transpired have to be taken into consideration. Viewed in this light, the conclusion of the Tribunal on this account is unsustainable. [Para 18]

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) accepted the assessee's cash-flow statement and records, noted that the audited books, purchases, sales and VAT returns had not been rejected or found non-genuine, held that the deposits stood explained as arising from recorded sales and that taxing them again would result in double taxation, and accordingly deleted the addition of Rs. 2.64 crores.

■

On revenue’s appeal to the Tribunal

HELD: ■ The Tribunal duly considered the facts and circumstances of the case. The Tribunal noticed from the assessment order that the AO has proceeded to hold the sales of the assessee to be bogus, primarily on account of the fact that the figures of purchases and sales in the period immediately prior to demonetization were at wide variance with the figures of purchases and sales in the corresponding period of the previous year and also at variance with the figures of the previous months in the present financial year. The AO also noted that the purchases on the basis of which the sales were made were effected from certain sister concerns and that too, only upto the period of demonetization. He could not find any nexus between the purchase and the payment made to the persons from whom the purchase had been made and from the same he came to the conclusion that a channel of purchase and sale was created just to give colour to unexplained cash deposit under the garb of sale and for this the VAT return had been utilized as a tool. In consideration of these findings, the Tribunal observes that a departure in trading patterns cannot in itself be a ground to make an addition by holding such departure to be bogus. It can at best be a ground for further investigation to determine the reason for such departure and if the assessee is unable to prove that the enhanced figures were genuine, then only could the credits purported to be made on account of such sales be brought to tax under the provisions of section 68. However, before section 68 could be invoked, the AO was obliged to demonstrate with evidence as to why the explanation furnished by the assessee for cash sales in that particular period were not acceptable. Such evidence could be the fact that the assessee did not have the inventory to make the sale that it claimed, or that the assessee had not made corresponding purchases which stood subsequently effected by way of sales. Unless the AO could find sufficient material to disturb the trading results declared by the assessee in the audited accounts, he would not be at liberty to regard the explanation offered by the assessee for the said cash deposits as unexplained. The Tribunal noticed that in the instant case, the AO had voiced suspicion that the purchases had been shown to have been made from sisterconcerns only so as to create a channel of purchase and sales to explain the deposit of money. He comes to this conclusion on account of the fact that he was unable to relate payment for such purchases to the actual purchases made. The Tribunal again notes that the suspicion could only be a starting point for further investigation and the purchase of goods on credit cannot in itself be a ground to reject the genuineness of the purchase. The Tribunal further notes from the assessee's submission that the AO had issued notices under section 133(6), but could not find anything adverse in this regard. On the contrary, the Tribunal notes from the paper book filed by the assessee that the assessee had inventories amounting to Rs. 4.61 crores as on the first day of the accounting year and that the assessee is able to explain an opening stock of worth Rs.4.41 crores as on 1-10-2016 as per the perpetual inventory method, prepared on the basis of its VAT returns filed upto September, 2016, which the Tribunal notes had been filed on 20-10-2016 i.e. before the date of demonetization. In the circumstances, there do not appear to be any reasons to question the sales made by the assessee in the month of October, 2016 were not due till later, out of those stocks or even in November, 2016 out of the residual stocks that remained on 31-10-2016 and purchases made during the period. The AO has pointed out that there was possibility for manipulation in sales on account of the fact that the VAT returns for the month of October, 2016 but the Tribunal notes that even if that were so, it would not change the nature of the receipt from being realization of sales of stocks that was available unless it could be demonstrated that such sales were not made or that the stock to make such sales was not available. No credence can be given to the AO's views that such sales were shown only with a view to deposit cash during demonetization and the stocks were later on actually sold outside the books of accounts as no such evidence has been brought on record by the AO to back up this suspicion. The Tribunal is therefore in agreement with the decision of the ITAT Chennai Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. Viswa and Devji Diamonds (P.) Ltd. [2025] 171 taxmann.com 474 (Chennai - Trib.) wherein the ITAT Chennai Bench has held that if no defect could be pointed out in the books of accounts and the cash deposited had been stated to be made out of sales, since the assessee had discharged the burden of proving the source of cash deposited in the bank, the impugned addition was fit to be deleted

HEADNOTE: Section  69C,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing, buying and selling of jewellery - During relevant assessment year, assessee had entered into transactions with five parties - Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in books of assessee - Assessing Officer further presumed that assessee had earned additional gross profit by procuring diamonds from grey market and accordingly made addition being 8 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases -  Commissioner  (Appeals) restricted profit estimation to 3 per cent - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating detailed evidences filed by assessee including quantitative details, purchase and sales registers, bank statements, confirmations, sales-tax registration, and income-tax returns of supplier parties, came to conclusion that sales and closing stock figures were duly accepted by Assessing Officer - Commissioner (Appeals) further observed that without corresponding purchases, assessee could not have affected sales - Thus, only profit element embedded in such alleged purchases could be brought to tax, not entire purchase value - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly restricted addition to 3 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases was fair, reasonable and in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of manufacturing, buying, and selling jewellery. During relevant assessment year, the assessee had entered into transactions with five parties.

■

The Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated the entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in the books of the assessee

■

The Assessing Officer further presumed that the assessee had earned additional gross profit at the rate of 8 per cent by procuring diamonds from the grey market, and accordingly made an addition of certain amount being 8 per cent of the alleged non-genuine purchases.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) restricted the profit estimation from 8 per cent to 3 per cent, thereby partly allowing the appeal of the assessee.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Investigation Wing that diamonds shown by the assessee as purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14 were bogus. Accordingly, he made an addition in the hands of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ A perusal of the record would suggest that the assessee is engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. It has been maintaining its proper books of account. The accounts were duly audited. The assessee has filed its return of income on the strength of those accounts. When the Assessing Officer has confronted the assessee for explaining its position with regard to certain purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14. The assessee has submitted copy of the audited balance-sheet, Profit & Loss account along with auditor’s report, the complete stock tally of the ornaments. It has also filed copy of the stock register exhibiting opening stock, purchase, sales and closing stock. The assessee thereafter filed purchase bills issued by Daksh Diamonds, Jewel Diamonds and Nazar Impex in the respective years. The assessee has made the payments to its suppliers through banking channel. The seller of the diamonds was having PAN, VAT, TIN and CST no. Those details were submitted by the assessee to the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings. The assessee had made request that the person, who has disclosed from its back that he was engaged in providing bogus entries, then, such a person be subject to cross examination. The Assessing Officer had issued summons under section 131 to Bhanwar Lal Jain for appearance, he never appeared. The assessee thereafter brought it to the notice of the Assessing Officer that a perusal of the statement given by Bhanwar Lal Jain would suggest that he has not specifically taken the name of assessee disclosing therein that the assessee has availed accommodation entries. The information disclosed by him is a general nature whereby he disclosed that he controls 68 firms mentioned therein and such firms were engaged in providing accommodation entry. It is not specific whether such firm has specifically provided accommodation entry to the assessee or not. The assessee further produced details of the sales made by it. [Para 19]

■

It is also pertinent to note that in assessment year 2013-14, the assessee has requested that Sanjay Chaudhary managing the affairs of Nazar Impex be produced for cross examination. The Assessing Officer has issued the summons for the appearance of Sanjay Chaudhary before the Assessing Officer. However, he has expressed his inability to appear before him at Jalandhar. Ultimately the Assessing Officer could not ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination by the assessee. The Assessing Officer has expressed her inability to produce the witness at Jalandhar. The assessee again requested the Assessing Officer to produce the witness for cross examination, but no such steps were taken by the Assessing Officer to ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination. [Para 20]

■

A perusal of the record would suggest that there are two sets of evidence available with the Assessing Officer. On the one hand, he has an information transmitted by the Investigation Wing exhibiting the fact that certain concerns of Bhanwar (Mumbai) and Rajendra were engaged in providing accommodation entries to various beneficiaries. The list of all those companies/firms are mentioned in that report. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee has made purchases from three concerns. In the second set of evidence is the material submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer. This set contains audited accounts of the assessee, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers, namely PAN, VAT, TIN, CST numbers. [Para 21]

■

The assessee has produced quantitative details, which were verifiable and also tallied. For example, if 100 kgs. of raw material is being purchased, then sales also represent those 100 kgs. or unsold items are reflected in the closing stock. [Para 22]

■

The short question is, whether on the basis of the information collected from the back of the assessee from a third party, its purchases could be doubted and disallowance of expenditure is to be made. [Para 23]

■

The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Odeon Builders (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 64/266 Taxman 461/418 ITR 315, had held that disallowance based on third party information gathered by the Investigation wing of the Department without independent verification of the Assessing Officer cannot be made. In other words, the information transmitted by the DIT (Investigation) was a material to ignite assessment machinery in motion but it cannot be treated as gospel truth for disallowing the claim of the assessee without independent cross verification of those information by the Assessing Officer. [Para 24]

■

HEADNOTE: Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits -  Assessment year 2001-02 - Whether in every case of application of section 68, nature and source of sum found credited in books of account of assessee has to be examined first - Held, yes - Assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O' - Assessing Officer carried deep investigations through survey and searches at premises of parties where from assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills in respect of export of diamonds - He, therefore, held that purchases were bogus and, therefore, there was no question of any sale or export and, accordingly, treated credit entries appearing in books of account of assessee as in-genuine and made addition under section 68 - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld said order - It was found from records that lower authorities had not examined nature of credit entries and also had not provided a reasonable opportunity to assessee to explain those credit entries - Whether without examining above important aspects and without recording a proper finding thereon, it could be said that provision of section 68 had not been properly applied - Held, yes

FACT: For the assessment year 2001-02, the assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O'. The Assessing Officer carried out deep investigations through survey and searches at the premises of the parties where from the assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that the alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills. Further, it was found that M/s. 'V' was owned by one 'G'. The income-tax records of 'V' showed that it had filed some return at Surat but he was also not found at the address given in the return. Further, as per the recorded statement of above parties it was found that above concern was giving entries and sale bills to accommodate people who were showing export of diamonds. In the case of M/s. 'O' the revenue carried a survey and recorded statement of its proprietor 'S', wherein he stated that head office of the concern was at Surat. However, when a survey was carried out, the above premises was found to be locked. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that 'S' had made a false statement. He, therefore, concluded that the alleged purchases were bogus and, therefore, the transaction of export of diamond was not believable. He, therefore, treated the credit entries appearing in the books of account of the assessee as unexplained and assessed the same in its the hands under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

HELD: It is now a settled-law that for explaining cash credits the assessee has to establish the following three things :

(i )

Genuineness of the credit entry,

(ii )

Identity of the creditors, and

(iii)

The creditworthiness of the creditor.

After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order,

, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21] With respect to one-to-one mapping therefore only criteria is the sale of carats of the diamond. Assessee has shown that number of carats purchased from the three entities is 585.88 carats and the sale of the diamond is also 585.88 carats. The amount of purchases recorded is 6.27 crores whereas the sale of the same diamond is shown at 6.71 crores. With respect to purchases from RA Distributors Private Limited, the assessee has purchased 496.88 carats and identical carats were sold. The purchase price of these diamonds is Rs. 5.39 crores and the sale is Rs. 5.79 crores. With respect to the purchases from three different entities the Commissioner (Appeals) has noted that assessee has purchased from these parties Rs. 5.29 crores, 6.97 crores and Rs. 7.40 crores out of which the Assessing Officer has doubted only Rs. 2.49 crore, 2.19 crores and Rs. 1.58 crores. The total purchases affected by the parties are also having identical billing narration. Thus, the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly decided that there is a one-to-one mapping available from purchases which are considered as alleged bogus purchases by the Assessing Officer and corresponding sales. Further, it has been held that there is no connection established by the Assessing Officer with respect to purchases from these three parties by the assessee with the alleged bogus purchases recorded in the investigation wing information as well as the charge sheet filed by the enforcement directorate. The Assessing Officer has also not challenged that assessee has not maintain proper books of account including purchase and register, since register, stock register and day-to-day bank book. No specific defect or irregularity was recorded by the Assessing Officer. With respect to the gross profit computed by the assessee from bogus sales is based on the number of carats purchased by the assessee and the same number of carats sold by the assessee. With respect to purchases from three different entities, the Commissioner (Appeals) has computed gross profit of Rs. 44.49 Lacs and purchases from 'R' gross profit is computed at Rs. 40.72 lakhs. Thus, the average gross profit earned by the assessee on total purchases of Rs. 11.66 crores; assessee has earned gross profit of Rs. 85.21 lakhs, which is 6.81 per cent. Gross profit as per the regular books of account is 6.73 per cent. Thus, no infirmity can be found in the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) whereas assessee has shown higher gross profit from alleged bogus purchases compared to its regular transaction. [Para 22]

In case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be the sufficient compliance; therefore, the assessee cannot be further burdened to show the colour and number of diamonds. When bills of purchases from other parties and from the same parties where part of the purchase consideration is accepted as genuine, no such details are available in the sale bill, there was no reason to deviate from the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals).[Para 23]

In view of the above facts, it is found that the Commissioner (Appeals) has correctly considered that the purchases from these parties is genuine when part of purchases from the same parties is not disputed, even otherwise, even if it is held that the purchases from these parties are bogus, then also, the proper course would be to determine the profit arising from the purchases by looking at corresponding sales and what amount of gross profit is earned on alleged bogus purchases. If the alleged bogus purchases show gross profit higher than the regular gross profit shown by the assessee, no further addition is required to be made in the hands of the assessee. The logic behind this is that sale is already accounted for on the credit side of the profit and loss account. If the purchases are to be removed, the corresponding sale is also required to be removed from the profit and loss account, sales is higher than the purchases in rupees terms, therefore, the addition would be only required to be made to the extent of lower gross profit on alleged bogus purchases then the regular gross profit. This also takes the care of the argument that no proof of delivery of goods purchased are shown by the assessee, similarly, the sales are also bogus. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that amount invested in acquiring the bogus purchases should also be considered as an addition, because the only addition is disallowance of bogus purchases, no further addition is warranted. In view of this, the ground of appeal of the Assessing Officer are dismissed. [Para 24]

HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Cash purchases)  - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee, engaged in diamond trading, filed return of income - Reassessment was initiated under section 148 - During a search at premises of M/s. REPL, software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found - Based on this, it was alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL - Assessee submitted that it purchased diamonds from REPL through banking channels, exported goods, and offered income to tax, supported by invoices and stock records - AO, relying solely on third-party software, treated cash purchases as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - Assessee sought copies of corroborative material and statement of authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided - Whether since addition rested solely on alleged recovery of software during search action on M/s. REPL, which according to AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales, and said material was not supplied to assessee and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted, impugned addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

Insofar as the merits of the impugned addition are concerned, the addition rests solely on the alleged recovery of a software during the search action on M/s. REPL, which according to the AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales. The said material was not supplied to the appellant and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted. The observation by the CIT(A) that no opportunity of cross-examination was claimed is factually incorrect. The reply dated 05.04.2023 filed by the appellant before the AO shows that the appellant sought a copy of the statement of the authorized person of M/s. REPL and the corroborative material to support the allegation of cash paid by the appellant to M/s. REPL against purchase of diamonds, as well as the opportunity to cross-examine. [Para 13]

■

It is settled that if the AO proposes to rely on any material for making the impugned addition, the same must be supplied to the assessee and an opportunity of cross-examination must be granted wherever claimed. Failure in this regard is a breach of the principles of natural justice. The appellant cannot be expected to establish a negative. The onus to disprove arises only when material is brought on record and appropriate opportunity is granted to the assessee to challenge it. The matter would depend upon facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case there was failure on the part of the AO to supply the corroborative material and to grant opportunity of hearing and, therefore, the impugned addition cannot be sustained. [Para 14]

■

As the ground raised on merits is accepted, it is not necessary to deal with the additional ground raised. [Para 15]

■

It is also the case of revenue that the Assessing Officer has made independent enquiries also by issuing notices under section 133(6) to the seven parties which reveal that the notices were returned unserved by the postal authorities with remarks 'not known', 'left', 'unclaimed', etc. The aforesaid two aspects have formed the basis for the Assessing Officer to treat the purchases of Rs. 37 lakhs from the said seven parties as bogus transactions. [Para 7] The assessee asserted before the Assessing Officer that he has effected purchase of goods from the said parties and further resold it to various parties and without effecting such purchases, sales were not possible. He furnished copies of purchase bills, evidence of having made payments by account payee cheques, copies of bank statements, etc. Most importantly, the assessee pointed out to the Assessing Officer that if any of the depositions made by the said parties is to be used against him, copies of the same be furnished, so that he can avail the opportunity of cross-examining each of them. All these submissions of the assessee have been set to naught by the Assessing Officer by merely referring to the aspect of information having been received from the DGIT, Mumbai and the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) to the parties. In the assessment order other than the generalised observation about information having been received from DGIT, Mumbai, there is no reference to any specific material or details in this regard. The entire factual matrix brings out that leave alone confronting the assessee with the specific material, the assessment order itself does not record any specifics about the material on which the reliance has been placed by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, on facts, such an addition is susceptible to deletion. [Para 8]

Another aspect is the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6). In fact, non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) by itself cannot be a conclusive proof that transactions with the parties are bogus because there was enough material before the Assessing Officer to show that payments have been made to the said parties through banking channels. It required further collection of evidence by the Assessing Officer to prove the bogus nature of such transactions. The assessee has pointed to the Assessing Officer that he was maintaining day-to-day stock record, wherein all purchases are entered as 'inward' and sales are recorded as 'outward'. He had enclosed copies of account of the said parties appearing in his account books, copies of purchase invoices, copies of bank statement for payment to the parties, etc. Under these circumstances, having regard to the material on record, it is not possible to uphold the charge of Assessing Officer that the purchases from the seven parties are bogus. [Para 8.1]

Section 69C prescribes that where in any financial year an assessee has incurred any expenditure and he offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation offered by him is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year. In the context of the application of section 69C what is of importance is that either there is no explanation about the 'source of such expenditure' or that the explanation offered is not found satisfactory. The underlying emphasis is on the explanation in relation to the 'source of such expenditure'. The Assessing Officer has invoked section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases as unexplained. So, however, the assessee has demonstrated that the payments for such purchases have been made through account payee cheques for which there is no repudiation by the Assessing Officer thereby implying that the source of expenditure stands explained. In fact, the case of Assessing Officer is that the purchase transactions are 'only accommodation entries and not really purchases', thereby implying that the assessee has not incurred such expenditure. To hold the transactions as mere accommodation entries and not real purchases is quite different from saying that the sources of expenditure for the purchases from the seven parties have not been explained in the context of section 69C. Therefore, invoking of section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases stated to have been made from the seven parties as unexplained expenditure is on a wrong footing. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the orders of lower authorities deserved to be set aside. [Para 10]

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. [Para 13]

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]
