On the complete appreciation of the facts and also touchstone of human probabilities, the story of sale of gold bars appears to be a smokescreen while real objective was to introduce undisclosed income into banking system by way of deposit of cash in bank accounts. On the perusal of the documents which are on record it is crystal clear that the assessee was not having adequate infrastructure to handle such huge transactions in gold bars and had no experience to handle turnover in gold bars of such a huge magnitude, rather if the theory of assessee is accepted as to the sale and purchase of gold bars, then by not disclosing the names of ultimate buyers of gold who have allegedly bought gold through assessee, the assessee has in fact facilitated introduction of the undisclosed money of his buyers into the bank accounts of the assessee and its conversion into gold bars without disclosing their identity which also prevented end use of gold bars to be monitored. [Para 10]

Now coming back to the controversy in hand, it is observed that the assessee has allegedly made sales of gold bars to the tune of Rs. 49.17 Crores during the impugned assessment year wherein sale proceeds have been stated to have been received in cash from undisclosed buyers which has been deposited by the assessee in the bank account of the assessee and hence sources of these cash deposit could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee although the same is stated to be cash received on account of cash sales of gold bars to undisclosed buyers. Thus, if the story of the assessee is to be believed then he had acted in a manner to facilitate conversion of undisclosed money of undisclosed persons to enable them to convert their undisclosed money into safe havens of gold bar at his own perils which got further aggravated by a consistent adamant and unacceptable stand of the assessee in not revealing the names of buyers of the gold bars by stating that the details of these buyers who have paid in cash for gold bar are not known to the assessee which stand of the assessee also prevented authorities below to make enquiry against these holders of undisclosed money leading to escapement of income in the hands of such undisclosed buyers due to the adamant stand of the assessee in not revealing the identities of the said undisclosed buyers , and the assessee is acting in a manner to shield these unidentified persons for which the assessee itself is to be blame for his own agonies. It is settled proposition that the Court will assist those who come to Court with clean hands and Court will not help those whose own hands are dirty. At this stage it is important to refer to provisions of sections 106 and 114(g) of the Indian Evidence Act,1872. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. It is stated by the assessee that there is no onus on the assessee under any law to reveal the identity of buyers who allegedly bought gold bars from the assessee, this argument is fallacious as the amount of cash allegedly received from unknown buyers of gold bars stood deposited in the bank account of the assessee and are cash credits appearing in books of account of the assessee and the assessee has to fulfil three ingredients requirements as are mandated under section 68 before the said cash credits can be accepted viz. identity of the creditors, creditworthiness of the creditors and genuineness of the cash credits . Thus, to say that no burden lay on the assessee to fulfil all the three ingredient requirements stated above before is accepted wherein one of the ingredient requirement is to establish identity of the creditor.

HELD: Applicability of section 69 to assessee's case

• It is an admitted position that names of each of the seller were given by the assessee to the Assessing Officer, since otherwise he could not have compiled the list giving the details of such disallowance as an annexure to the assessment order. In the nature of trade of the assessee, it may not always be possible to get the address of all its customers. Even if customers give their address, there is no means available to the assessee to ensure that such addresses were right.

• The assessee, in the nature of its trade, cannot insist for an identification process akin to Know Your Customer (KYC) rules applied by banks. There is no such mandatory requirement in the business of jewellery to maintain any records in line with KYC rules of bank. In fact, a prudent businessman might not insist on such rigorous identification process since insistence on such conditions will be to the detriment of his business. Just for the reason that purchases effected from certain parties did not carry full address, a disallowance ought not have been made. Admittedly, such purchases were recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also shown in its stock. [Para 14]

• In view of above, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in deleting impugned addition.[Para 15]

one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

Similarly, the fact regarding ‘S’ having purchased flats in June, 1999 from a third-party also had not been denied. The inquiries conducted in that behalf and the material facts about the comparability of S’s flats and inquiries in that respect were not confronted to the assessee at the assessment stage, so as to controvert the same. Time gap of 15 months was significantly long; fact about direct booking of flats from builders and purchase from third-party also had very important effect on the price of the flat. Only explanation given by the lower authorities, that there was a recessionary time and subsequent flats might have been sold at a lesser figure, was a general and sweeping statement, which could not be used against the assessee. There were other flat buyers, who could have also been examined, particularly those who booked the flats from the builders at early stage. That comparability at the most could create a suspicion which could not be made a basis of addition. Therefore, comparative purchase instance of ‘S’ could not be made a basis for addition in the hands of the assessee. Therefore, the addition of Rs. 50 lakhs, as made by the Assessing Officer and confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), could not be sustained and the same should be deleted. There was no dispute between the Members of the Division Bench on the following issues :

1.The addition of Rs. 3,65,000 made on account of cash found during search was unsustainable in view of uncontroverted explanation given by the assessee therefor.

2.The addition of Rs. 4,00,900 made on account of diamond jewellery seized from the bank lockers was unwarranted when acquisition of same was supported by purchase vouchers and payments for purchase were duly reflected in regular books of account.

3.The claim of depreciation could not be assessed under Chapter XIV-B when the same was already allowed under section 143(3) proceedings.

4.The addition made on account of credit written back in the books of account could not be sustained when no specific seized document was referred to as basis for making that addition.

5.The addition made on account of bank deposits was unsustainable as the same was not made on the basis of any seized document.

6.The addition made on account of bifurcation of income which was offered as undisclosed income for the block period, would qualify for set off against the other undis- closed income resulting from unexplained investment.

7.The addition made on account of payment remitted for interior decoration of flat purchased by the assessee could not be sustained, as said payment was made out of amount withdrawn from bank.

8.The addition made on account of prize money and remuneration received by the assessee from the organi-zers of the Miss World Competition on her being crowned as Miss World was not warranted in the block assessment, when same had been properly dealt with in regular books of account.

9.The addition of certain amount made for the reason that the assessee had credited that amount in her capital account under the head transfer from ‘C’ bank, was unsustainable.

10.The addition made on account of bonus, interest and other receipts received by the assessee from the organizers of Miss World Competition was required to be deleted when issue was covered in the regular assessment and same was not supported by any seized material.

11.Where amount of remittance from foreign bank account to the assessee’s account had escaped assessment, said amount was rightly assessed in the block period as undisclosed income.

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: ■ The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

The sale of shares of KAFL which was dematerialized in Demat account has taken place through recognised stock exchange and assessee received money through banking channel. So, the assessee has explained the nature and source of the money with supporting documents and thus has discharged the onus casted upon him by producing the relevant documents, accordingly, the question of treating the said gain as unexplained cash credit under section 68 cannot arise unless the Assessing Officer is able to find fault/infirmity with the same. Therefore, the Assessing Officer opined although, the assessee had furnished name and address of the purported parties, however assessee had not furnished confirmation from even single person. He thus, held that assessee had failed to discharge initial onus and treated said deposits as unexplained cash credit and brought same to tax under section 68 read with section 115 BBE.

HEADNOTE: Section  68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Demonetization) - Assessment year  2017-18 - During demonetization period, assessee-jeweller deposited huge amount in three bank accounts - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had suddenly made cash sales to unidentifiable small customers during period from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - He, therefore, made addition under section 68 on account of such unexplained cash credit (sales) - It was noted that business of assessee was an expanding business and sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over years - Assessee had furnished before Assessing Officer month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and movement in stock position - Details of stock, purchases and sales that had been submitted by assessee before Assessing Officer had not been questioned or doubted in any manner by Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee had presented evidence of available stock and depletion of said stock on account of sales and Assessing Officer had not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of receipts on account of sale of that stock were unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 was made out - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, engaged in jewellery business, filed its return of income.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that during the demonetization period, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 3.80 crores in three bank accounts. He further noted that the assessee had made total sales of Rs. 49.99 crores during the financial year 2016-17 and the total cash sales during the year amounted to Rs. 4.94 crores. However, of the total cash sales, the assessee had made cash sales of Rs. 3.68 crores in October, 2016 and of Rs. 37.25 lakhs uptil 8.11.2016 i.e. in the period between 1.10.2016 to 8.11.2016, the assessee had suddenly made cash sales to the tune of Rs. 4.05 crores to unidentifiable small customers.He held that the assessee had not satisfactorily explained the credit of Rs. 3.68 crores recorded as cash sales in his books during the period 1.10.2016 to 30.10.2016, he held the same to be unexplained under section 68

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the Assessing Officer had not established that the assessee had accumulated cash in its books which was deposited on 10-11-2016. The assumptions made on the basis of comparison of sales figures of earlier years were not foolproof, as similar or higher sales had been made by the assessee in following financial year and the refusal to accept the sales shown by the assessee was not on account of any independent enquiry but only on the basis of assumptions/interpretations made by the Assessing Officer while comparing results of earlier years.

■

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition of Rs. 2.98 crores on account of unexplained cash deposit.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

Thus, Commissioner (Appeals) restricted disallowance out of bogus purchases to 10 per cent of such purchases and directed Assessing Officer to disallow 10 per cent of alleged bogus purchases being the profit from purchases made from parties during the year under consideration.

On second appeal, the Tribunal upheld the order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals).

On revenue's appeal to the High Court: HELD: Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

headnotes.text: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Jewellery) - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee availed of benefit under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme (VDIS) and declared items, which were mostly of jewellery, namely, gold and diamonds - Subsequently, assessee sold away jewellery declared by them under VDIS - Assessing Officer doubted genuinity of sale of diamonds - He thus treated amount shown as sale proceeds of diamonds as unexplained cash credit - Tribunal, however, deleted said addition - It was noted that not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds was furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed - Moreover, bank accounts of purchasers were verified and demand drafts issued to assessee towards consideration corresponded to entries in bank accounts - Whether in aforesaid circumstances, mere fact that on certain occasions, assessee did not proceed to Surat, could not be a factor to disbelieve transactions in question - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in deleting addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]IT : Where in support of sale of diamonds not only particulars of persons who purchased diamonds were furnished but also manner of payment was disclosed, impugned addition made under section 68 in respect of sale proceeds of diamonds was to be set aside

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in export of diamonds, made purchares of diamonds from certain parties and in support of such purchases furnished details like ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties and bank statements showing payment made to parties and had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases, and sales, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating purchases of diamonds in question as bogus  INCOME TAX : Where assessee had paid commission to four entities on export of diamond and had furnished all relevant details in respect of said commission alongwith details of service tax collected thereon, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure as non-genuine and bogus

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases made by assessee from various parties without supply of actual goods - On appeal, Commissioner (Appeals) noted that assessee had submitted evidences with respect to ledger accounts of transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of assessee showing payment made to parties - Assessee had also shown mapping of corresponding purchases and sales - Department however argued that one-to-one mapping shown by assessee was not correct for reason that in purchase bills of these parties there was no narration with respect to quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as colour etc. - Whether in case of Diamond trade, carrat wise stock maintenance would be sufficient compliance and therefore, assessee could not be further burdened to show colour and number of diamonds - Held, yes - Whether therefore, it could not be said that in purchase bills assessee should have mentioned this details as that was not trade practice - Held, yes - Whether in view of above facts, Commissioner (Appeals) had correctly considered that purchases from these parties was genuine when part of purchases from same parties was not disputed - Held, yes [Paras 21, 23 and 24] [In favour of assessee]  Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee-company was engaged in business of trading, manufacturing, import and export of diamonds - Assessing Officer received information from investigation wing that assessee had debited expenses in form of commission from four different parties - Enquiries were conducted and found that all 4 companies had same address and they were not available on addresses mentioned in income tax return and no business activity was being carried out from those premises - Based on said information, Assessing Officer disallowed commission expenses claimed by assessee - It was noted that all four entities were assessed by same Assessing Officer and commission income shown by them was accepted - It was further, noted that commission had been paid on export of diamond stating details of exports made by assessee, respective commission and details of service tax collected thereon and assessee had also produced details of other commission expenditure incurred by assessee which were also identical - Whether in view of above facts, there was no reason to treat commission expenditure in question as non-genuine and bogus - Held, yes [Para 26] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was engaged in import and exports of diamond - A search under section 132 was conducted upon 'SG' group to which assessee belonged - During search operation, it transpired that assessee had received accommodation entries in respect of several purchases from other business concern of its group - Accordingly, Assessing Officer made additions to income of assessee on account of such bogus purchases - It was noted that notices under section 133(6) issued to suppliers did not elicit any response and none of suppliers was found at given addresses - Assessee also failed to produce any of suppliers to confirm purchase transactions - Therefore, basic onus to establish genuineness of purchases remained un-discharged - However, at same time, assessee was in possession of purchase invoices and payment to suppliers was made through banking channels - Ledger confirmation as well as PAN of suppliers was also placed on record - Import as well as exports was certified by custom authorities - Further, complete quantitative tally of stock was provided along with correlation of purchases with corresponding sales - There could be no sale without actual purchase of material keeping in mind fact that assessee was engaged in trading activities - Therefore, it was a fit case for estimation of profit element embedded in these purchase transactions to plug possible leakage of revenue - Whether, on facts, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in restricting addition at rate of 6 per cent on account of such bogus purchases - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee failed to produce any of suppliers to confirm transactions of purchases shown by it, however, at same time, assessee was in possession of purchase invoices and ledger confirmation as well as PAN of suppliers was also placed on record and payment to suppliers was made through banking channels, Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in restricting addition at rate of 6 per cent on account of bogus purchases   INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed expenditure on account of labour charges paid by it for conversion of rough diamonds into polished diamond, since said payment was made through account payee cheques after deduction of tax at source and there was no concrete material before Assessing Officer to disallow such labour charges paid by assessee, impugned disallowance of said expenditure by Assessing Officer was unjustified

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading of gold  diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. - Assessing Officer on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three parties were bogus - Accordingly, he made an addition - It was observed that assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers - Further, information gathered by Investigation Wing was based upon statements of persons who were managing affairs of assessee’s suppliers, however, these witnesses were not subject to cross examination - Whether, on facts, said purchases could not be treated as bogus and, therefore, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 26] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer had made an addition in hands of assessee on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three concerns were bogus purchases, since assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers etc., such purchases could not be treated as bogus

Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained money -  Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessees were dealers in diamonds - Each of assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 - Said declaration was accepted by Department and a certificate was issued to respective assessees under VDIS, 1997 - During relevant assessment year, assessees sold jewellery declared under VDIS, 1997 and offered to tax capital gains arising from respective sales - Assessing Officer disallowed assessees’ claim holding that sales transactions were not genuine - Tribunal, however, allowed assessees’ claim - Whether since identity of purchasers had been established and amounts received from purchasers had also been accounted for, in absence of any material to contrary it was to be concluded that transactions were genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in allowing assessee’s claim - Held, yes

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2007-08 and 2013-14 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading of gold  diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. - Assessing Officer on basis of information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds purchased by assessee from three parties were bogus - Accordingly, he made an addition - It was observed that assessee had provided all necessary details of its audited accounts, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers - Further, information gathered by Investigation Wing was based upon statements of persons who were managing affairs of assessee’s suppliers, however, these witnesses were not subject to cross examination - Whether, on facts, said purchases could not be treated as bogus and, therefore, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 20, 21 and 26] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - In course of assessment, Assessing Officer made addition in respect of bogus purchase of diamond from 'M' - In order to prove genuineness of purchases, assessee filed details like receipt notes, payment vouchers, retail invoice and bank statement in which payments were cleared - Commissioner (Appeals) taking into consideration material on record, deleted addition made by Assessing Officer - Whether on facts, impugned order passed by Commissioner (Appeals) did not require any interference - Held, yes [Para 6][In favour of assessee]

Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessment year  2010-11  - Assessee, a partnership firm engaged in manufacturing and trading of cut and polished diamonds, filed its return declaring income of Rs. 4.74 lakhs - Case was reopened under section 148 based on Investigation Wing information following search/survey in Bhawarlal Jain group, alleging accommodation purchase entries from Mohit Enterprises and Nice Diamonds aggregating to Rs. 46.46 lakhs - In response, assessee furnished purchase bills, stock register, sales and purchase registers, bank statements evidencing payments through banking channels, export invoices and shipping bills, and bank realisation advices, and correlated impugned purchases to export sales with proceeds realised through banking channels - Assessing Officer, emphasizing modus operandi of Bhawarlal Jain syndicate and terming documentation unilateral, treated purchases from two parties as bogus and disallowed 100% of Rs. 46.46 lakhs, completing assessment under section 144, without pointing out discrepancies in evidences filed or disputing sales - Whether since it is an admitted position that sales had not been doubted and without purchases, there cannot be any sales, no adverse inference could be made insofar as export of diamonds were concerned for which all documentary evidences were placed on record - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition was to be restricted to profit element, i.e., difference in gross profit on undisputed purchases and disputed purchases - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 7.2] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Assessment year 2004-05 - Assessee was a legal heir of 'W' - During relevant assessment year, assessee filed his return showing loss arising from sale of diamond jewellery belonging to 'W' - In order to prove genuineness of sales transactions, assessee produced sale invoices and submitted that sale consideration had been received through account payee cheques - Assessing Officer rejected documentary evidence furnished by assessee and concluded that no such sale of jewellery took place - He thus treated amount of sales deposited in bank as income from unexplained sources - Tribunal confirmed order of Assessing Officer - It was apparent from records that nothing had been disclosed in respect of jewellery in assessee's wealth tax returns - Moreover, evidence which had been produced was of recent origin in form of sale invoice or report of valuer but initial onus placed upon assessee was not discharged by providing unimpeachable evidence - Whether on facts, assessee failed to prove that sales transactions in question were genuine and, therefore, impugned addition made by Tribunal was to be upheld - Held, yes [Para 7] [In favour of revenue]IT : Where assessee, a legal heir of 'W', declared certain loss arising from sale of jewellery belonging to 'W', in view of fact that nothing had been disclosed in respect of said jewellery in Wealth tax return, sale in question being bogus, sale amount deposited in bank was to be treated as assessee's income from unexplained sources

Section  69C,  read with section  145,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases)  - Assessment year  2013-14  - Assessee was engaged in business of manufacturing, buying and selling of jewellery - During relevant assessment year, assessee had entered into transactions with five parties - Assessing Officer held that these five parties were linked to one B group, identified as accommodation entry providers, and thus, treated entire transactions as non-genuine purchases in books of assessee - Assessing Officer further presumed that assessee had earned additional gross profit by procuring diamonds from grey market and accordingly made addition being 8 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases -  Commissioner  (Appeals) restricted profit estimation to 3 per cent - It was noted that Commissioner (Appeals) after appreciating detailed evidences filed by assessee including quantitative details, purchase and sales registers, bank statements, confirmations, sales-tax registration, and income-tax returns of supplier parties, came to conclusion that sales and closing stock figures were duly accepted by Assessing Officer - Commissioner (Appeals) further observed that without corresponding purchases, assessee could not have affected sales - Thus, only profit element embedded in such alleged purchases could be brought to tax, not entire purchase value - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) rightly restricted addition to 3 per cent of alleged non-genuine purchases was fair, reasonable and in accordance with law - Held, yes [Para 5] [In favour of assessee]

Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Cash purchases)  - Assessment year  2019-20  - Assessee, engaged in diamond trading, filed return of income - Reassessment was initiated under section 148 - During a search at premises of M/s. REPL, software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found - Based on this, it was alleged that assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL - Assessee submitted that it purchased diamonds from REPL through banking channels, exported goods, and offered income to tax, supported by invoices and stock records - AO, relying solely on third-party software, treated cash purchases as unexplained expenditure under section 69C - Assessee sought copies of corroborative material and statement of authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided - Whether since addition rested solely on alleged recovery of software during search action on M/s. REPL, which according to AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales, and said material was not supplied to assessee and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted, impugned addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 69C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years 2011-12, 2012-13 and 2014-15 - Assessee was engaged in trading and manufacture of silver, gold, diamonds, stones and its jewellery - During assessment, Assessing Officer made addition on account of bogus purchases - Commissioner (Appeals) observed that though two entities were found to be bogus, assessee had, in fact, purchased diamonds which were used for purpose of making diamond jewellery and, therefore, sale of such diamond jewellery had been accepted by Assessing Officer - He further observed that assessee had shown from its audited books of account, stock statement as well as material receipt register that it could not have sold equivalent quantum of diamond jewellery without these two purchases - He, therefore, found it reasonable to disallow 3 per cent of total purchases from bogus Hawala concerns and reduced addition - Tribunal confirmed view of Commissioner (Appeals) - Whether once purchases are accepted, difference between inflated and actual price of purchases would be required to be disallowed and as to what would be extent of difference would be a matter of estimate - Held, yes - Whether estimate made by two appellate authorities did not warrant interference as, even otherwise, whether estimate should be at a particular sum or at a different sum, can never be an issue of law - Held, yes [Para 4.8] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section 69A,  read with section 158BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Block period 1-4-1995 to 13-9-2001 - Diamond was found in business premises of assessee - Only after several months, assessee explained that diamond stock was received on approval basis from an entity - Proprietor of said entity stated that said transactions were only by way of accommodation for which he received commission equivalent to tax paid by him - No receipt or encashment slip was made available by assessee - Whether assessee failed to discharge burden cast upon him to explain diamonds in his possession - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition made on account of unexplained diamonds was sustainable - Held, yes [Para 14][In favour of revenue]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessee-HUF filed its return of income for assessment year 1998-99 and declared long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds - Assessee submitted that said diamonds had been declared under voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced VDIS certificate issued by Commissioner - Assessee further submitted that sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts and was deposited in savings bank account of assessee and he also placed before Assessing Officer confirmation letters from buyers of diamonds; sale invoices; copy of extract of bank account and valuation report of diamonds - Assessing Officer, however, found that (i) main activity of purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries; (ii) demand drafts were purchased by depositing equivalent amounts of cash in bank account; (iii) assessee travelled to Surat alone in unreserved compartment carrying diamonds and stayed in dharamshala under a fictitious name; (iv) 'G' who was connected with purchasing parties in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between - In view of said details Assessing Officer concluded that assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold diamonds to Surat based parties and he, accordingly, rejected claim of capital gains of assessee and made addition under section 68 - Whether since diamonds were declared in VDIS which was supported through certificate issued by Commissioner and further, buyers had confirmed to have purchased diamonds and sale invoices; copy of bank account giving full description and details had been placed on record, which were not controverted by Assessing Officer, it could be said that there was a strong presumption in favour of assessee - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, merely because assessee travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying diamonds, it would not affect transaction which was otherwise duly supported by documentary evidence - Held, yes - Whether, moreover, since assessee had not been given an opportunity to cross-examine 'G' and there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that assessee was accommodated by him in any manner, his statement could not be taken into consideration, and, hence, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether provisions of section 68 are in pari materia with section 69 and, therefore, before making an addition under section 68, Assessing Officer has to exercise his discretion judiciously - Held, yes - Assessee sold gold and diamond separately and same was shown in its return - However, Assessing Officer did not accept sale of diamond as genuine and added it towards assessee’s income as unexplained credit - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving that sale transaction in diamonds was genuine and creditworthiness of purchasers had been proved beyond doubt, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating transaction as not being genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, addition under section 68 was to be deleted - Held, yes

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected however in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposit) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading of diamonds - Assessing Officer having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 assessee made cash deposit in various bank accounts asked assessee to furnish details of cash deposits - Assessee filed a reply stating that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, cash deposit in banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs - Assessing Officer did not accept reply of assessee and made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought same for taxation at rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE - Whether when purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected, component of sales in cash could not be rejected - Held, yes - Whether in order to avoid possibility of revenue leakage, 10 per cent of disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet ends of justice - Held, yes - Whether since substantial part of addition was deleted, addition sustained would not be liable to tax at enhanced rate under section 115BBE - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 12] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 69, read with sections 40A(3) and 80HHC of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments - Assessment year 2001-02 - Assessee a trader in diamonds and VCD rights, declared that during previous year it had earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on purchases and sales of diamonds - Assessing Officer noted that profit earned by assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher as in assessee’s line of business normally profit was 6 per cent; that all parties from whom assessee made purchases, on examination, had confirmed transactions but none of them could reply satisfactorily about amount of credit given; that though all suppliers to assessee’s sellers were based at Surat, none of those parties were traceable and that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to assessee - Accordingly, Assessing Officer concluded that assessee made purchases of diamonds from open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC - Assessing Officer further held that assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and, accordingly, worked out peak credit; treated same as assessee’s unexplained investment and added same to income of assessee - Assessing Officer also while computing deduction under section 80HHC rejected purchases declared by assessee and fixed same at higher amount - Assessing Officer also made an addition to income of assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of cash purchases - Commissioner (Appeals) increased unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds - He also upheld addition made by Assessing Officer under section 40A(3) - Whether since no comparative case was brought on record to substantiate that in line of assessee’s business normally profit was 6 per cent, view of revenue that profit earned by assessee was high could not be subscribed with - Held, yes - Whether since parties from whom assessee had purchased goods had confirmed transaction and also in response to notice under section 131 had appeared, fact that they were not existing at given address could not be reason for rejection of their confirmation - Held, yes - Whether since there was no evidence to show that money which seller parties withdrew reached back to assessee, finding arrived at by revenue authorities in that regard was not right one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes

Section 69A, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained Moneys (Demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in trading business of gold and diamond jewellery - During demonetization period, assessee deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers in its bank account - Assessing Officer observed that cash sales were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by assessee company merely to build an explanation for cash deposits in to bank account and made an addition of total cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE - Assessee furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for relevant period and cash sales made by assessee had been credited in books of account and, thus, assessee's claim was backed up by relevant evidences - Further, no defect had been pointed out in books of account of assessee - When sale had been offered to tax, adding same again would amount to double taxation - Whether since assessee had discharged burden of proving source of cash deposited in bank, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 68, read with section 153A, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Unexplained cash deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Certain cash was deposited during post-demonetisation in account of assessee, engaged in resale of jewellery, diamond etc. - Assessing Officer observed that there were two sets of books of account, i.e., one in computer of accountant and another in pen drive of accountant with different sales figures for October 2016 and assessee having failed to furnish documentary evidence regarding source of cash deposits in its bank accounts, addition was made to income of assessee - However, it was found that assessee was maintaining complete stock tally, sales were recorded in regular books of account and amounts were deposited in bank account out of sale proceeds - Nothing was brought on record to substantiate that cash obtained by assessee from sales which reduced stock of assessee was utilized elsewhere - Cash sales made during month of October, 2016 were in line of cash sales in earlier years and equal to sales in month of July, 2016 - Opening stock, purchases and sales and closing stock, declared by assessee were not doubted - Cash deposited post-demonetization by assessee was out of cash sales which had been accepted by Sales Tax/VAT Department and not doubted by Assessing Officer - There was sufficient stock available with assessee to make cash sales - Whether therefore, sales made by assessee out of existing stock were sufficient to explain deposit of cash (obtained from realization of sales) in bank account and could not have been treated as undisclosed income of assessee and accordingly, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was not justified - Held, yes [Paras 10.5, 10.7, 10.9, 10.11 and 10.13] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where cash deposited post-demonetization by assessee was out of cash sales which had been accepted by Sales Tax/VAT Department and not doubted by Assessing Officer and there was sufficient stock available with assessee to make cash sales, sales made by assessee out of existing stock were sufficient to explain deposit of cash (obtained from realization of sales) in bank account and, thus, cash deposits could not have been treated as undisclosed income of assessee  INCOME TAX : Where difference between valuation shown by assessee and estimated by Departmental Valuation Officer was less than 10 per cent, Assessing Officer was not justified in substantiating valuation determined by Departmental Valuation Officer for cost shown by assessee and therefore, addition made by Assessing Officer on account of difference in valuation as determined by DVO and as shown by assessee in its regular books of account was to be deleted

Section  68,  read with section  115BBE,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash Credit (Demonetisation)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - Assessee engaged in trading of bullion and jewellery deposited cash during demonetisation period and explained same as arising from sales/advances duly recorded in books of account - Assessing Officer treated deposits as unexplained cash credits under section 68 read with section 115BBE and treated the same as income from undisclosed sources - It was noted that assessee had demonstrated that in previous year, during corresponding period, cash sales were much higher, allegation of "abnormal" sales during demonetization period fell flat - Further, Assessing Officer had not pointed out any discrepancy in stock register, and assessee was evidently possessed of requisite stock to effect impugned sales - It was a matter of record that purchases had been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income - Whether since assessee had successfully explained source of cash deposits as sales/advances which were duly recorded in books of account and suspicion of Assessing Officer regarding genuineness of sales was not supported by any concrete evidence and was contradicted by comparative sales data, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 11 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading in gold and jewellery - During demonetization, assessee had deposited substantial amount of cash in his bank accounts - Assessee claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers for gold scheme - Assessing Officer treated cash receipts as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to prove genuineness of credits found in his bank account - It was noted that assessee had filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there was no discrepancy in books of account - Further, assessee had reported sales made before date of demonetization to GST authorities - Whether since assessee received trade advances in cash and same had been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68 - Held, yes - Whether furthermore assessee had furnished name and address of customers from whom it had received cash for sale of jewellery and law did not mandate assessee to collect PAN details of persons, if sale value of jewellery did not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs, assessee had satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of persons and thus, additions under section 68 was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 13, 14 and 15] [In favour of assessee]

X. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  104  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained moneys (Bullion)  - Assessment year  2023-24  - During search, a rough slip was found and confronted to assessee - In statement under section 132(4), assessee stated purchase of two gold coins of 100 grams each, admitted to have paid Rs.5 lakhs in cash to jewellers with balance of about Rs.11.50 lakhs pending - He explained source of Rs.5 lakhs as withdrawal from capital account in M/s Kalta Liquors and later furnished purchase bill and evidence that balance was paid through banking channels - Whether since assessee furnished ample evidences during course of assessment proceedings to substantiate its stand, this addition could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and rule 114B of the Income-tax Rules, 1962 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee was engaged in business of trading in gold and jewellery - During demonetization, assessee had deposited substantial amount of cash in his bank accounts - Assessee claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers for gold scheme - Assessing Officer treated cash receipts as unexplained cash credit under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to prove genuineness of credits found in his bank account - It was noted that assessee had filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there was no discrepancy in books of account - Further, assessee had reported sales made before date of demonetization to GST authorities - Whether since assessee received trade advances in cash and same had been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68 - Held, yes - Whether furthermore assessee had furnished name and address of customers from whom it had received cash for sale of jewellery and law did not mandate assessee to collect PAN details of persons, if sale value of jewellery did not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs, assessee had satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of persons and thus, additions under section 68 was unwarranted - Held, yes [Paras 13, 14 and 15] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee during demonetization deposited substantial amount of cash in banks and claimed that source for cash deposits was out of advance received from customers which were subsequently converted into sales of jewellery, since said trade advances were subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, said trade advance could not be examined in light of provisions of section 68

Section 69C, read with section 147, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years  2011-12  and 2012-13 - Assessing Officer received information from Investigation Wing that RJ and its related concerns provided accommodation entries of sales of diamonds etc. and assessee was one of beneficiaries - Assessing Officer on basis of said information reopened assessment - He held that purchases made from two parties were unverifiable and were bogus purchases for purpose of reducing its profits - Accordingly, he disallowed 100 per cent of such bogus purchases - Whether where assessee was under cloud of obtaining bogus purchases bills, Assessing Officer should primarily first verify, whether purchase quantity corresponding to bogus purchase bills was entered in day to day stock register;
