if not, then 100 per cent amount of bogus bills was liable for disallowance - Held, yes - Whether where, sales by an assessee corresponding to bogus purchases were verified, then only presumption was that assessee must have purchased goods in cash from grey market and supplied to sales parties - Held, yes - Whether in such cases, it was to be seen from day to day stock register, as when goods had arrived in warehouse or godown of assessee and date of entry in warehouse or godown was deemed to be date of cash purchase by assessee and assessee must have paid cash for purchase of goods from grey market, but source of which, assessee was required to explain - Held, yes - Whether further it needs to be examined when assessee had made payment through cheque in respect of bogus purchases debited in books of account, it could be presumed that assessee must have received cash back from those parties and same could have been utilized for funding purchase of goods in cash for supplying to sales parties - Held, yes - Whether in such a situation, availability of unexplained cash in hands of assessee need to be examined and wherever no cash was available with assessee for such purchase, addition for unexplained cash purchases also need to be considered - Held, yes - Whether thus, matter was to be remanded to Assessing Officer to examine stock inventory of purchases and sales, date of payments debited in bank account for corresponding purchases - Held, yes [Paras 7, 7.2 and 7.3] [Matter remanded]

I. Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Purchase) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery - Pursuant to a search conducted at premises of assessee Assessing Officer found that assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N' and accordingly, made addition - Assessee contended that allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law as Assessing Officer had ignored overwhelming factual evidences - Confirmations of both parties were placed on record and purchases made from these parties had entered in stock register and corresponding sales had not been disputed by revenue authorities - Further, payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel - He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances - Whether in light of factual context and balance of probabilities, issue would be adjudicated in favour of assessee, and disallowances made on this count were to be cancelled - Held, yes [Para 9.1.2] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee had made purchase from two parties, since confirmations of both parties were placed on record and purchases made from these parties had entered in stock register and corresponding sales had not been disputed by revenue authorities and payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel, Assessing Officer was not justified in treating said purchase as bogus and making addition  INCOME TAX : Where pursuant to a search conducted at assessee-firm's branch office, unaccounted cash of Rs. 3 crore was found and Assessing Officer taxed it as unexplained based on partner's statements, since assessee clarified that its main office maintained proper books of account, and moreover, partners' statements were taken under dubious circumstances and retracted later, assessee could not be blamed for towering failure of search team to keep main office out of purview of search action and, therefore, addition on account of unexplained cash was to be deleted  INCOME TAX : Where stock found in search emanated from stock register detailing pattern of inward and outward stock and resultant stock in hand at a given point of time, there was no justifiable reason to treat such stock found to be unexplained

I. Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Purchase) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery - Pursuant to a search conducted at premises of assessee Assessing Officer found that assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N' and accordingly, made addition - Assessee contended that allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law as Assessing Officer had ignored overwhelming factual evidences - Confirmations of both parties were placed on record and purchases made from these parties had entered in stock register and corresponding sales had not been disputed by revenue authorities - Further, payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel - He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances - Whether in light of factual context and balance of probabilities, issue would be adjudicated in favour of assessee, and disallowances made on this count were to be cancelled - Held, yes [Para 9.1.2] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Cash) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Pursuant to a search conducted at branch office of business premises of assessee-firm, unaccounted cash amounting to Rs. 3 crore were found and seized - On being inquired about source of cash found in course of search, assessee pointed out that aforesaid cash of Rs. 3 crore was accumulated out of cash sales affected during immediately preceeding period between 5-9-2014 to 21-9-2014 prior to search - Assessing Officer on basis of statement of partners of firm who stated that firm did not maintain books of account invoked provisions of section 69A read with section 115BBE to tax cash as unexplained - It was noted that branch office was searched, not main establishment, and partner statements were extracted under questionable circumstances, and subsequently retracted - Whether where stock so purchased and corresponding sales were duly recorded in stock book and stock stand tallied without any perceptible discrepancy in stock qua cash sales made, source of cash found was to be regarded as sufficiently explained and hence could not be treated as unexplained money under section 69A - Held, yes - Whether further, assessee could not be blamed for towering failure of search team to keep main office out of purview of search action and it was rather inexplicable that only a branch office was covered under search and a statement of partner was regarded as gospel truth despite visible lack of business activities, attendant work force, books, records etc. - Held, yes -Whether benefit of doubt, in peculiar circumstances, thus need to go in favour of assessee and therefore, action of revenue authorities to make additions towards unexplained cash sales under section 69A being without any sound basis deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 9.2.3, 9.2.6 and 9.2.7] [In favour of assessee]  III. Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Stock) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Commissioner (Appeals) attempted to increase assessed income based on unaccounted bullion stock found during a search, primarily relying on a discredited statement from a partner - However, assessee maintained that stock was properly recorded in their books of account and stock register - Whether where stock found in search emanated from stock register detailing pattern of inward and outward stock and resultant stock in hand at a given point of time, there was no justifiable reason to treat such stock found to be unexplained - Held, yes - Whether further since statement of partners stood discredited and rendered unreliable by chain of events such as recorded in odd hours and without any books and without taking cognizance of bank entries; retraction of such statement without much delay etc., thus, there was hardly any justification in enhancement action of Commissioner (Appeals) - Held yes [Para 9.5.2] [In favour of assessee]   Circulars and Notifications : Instruction F.No.286/2/2003-IT (In), dated 10-3-2003

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments (Illustrations) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee in regard to purchase of jewellery during year stated that her relative purchased said jewellery for a function using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his agricultural income and savings - Whether since onus to prove genuineness of transaction, creditworthiness and identity lay with assessee and it was to be discharged with reasonable explanation which had not been put forward unequivocally by assessee and bill was also in name of assessee, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69 - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed that purchase of jewellery during year was made by her relative using her PAN as relative did not have PAN and payment was made in cash by relative out of his savings, since onus to prove genuineness of transaction lay with assessee which had not been discharged, lower authorities had rightly treated amount of cash jewellery purchase as undisclosed investment under section 69  INCOME TAX : Where assessee stated that during year she jointly purchased an immovable property along with a party and sale amount toward her share was paid by aforesaid party and it was given as interest free loan outstanding as loan as on date, since assessee had not furnished statement of affairs of aforesaid party to prove that she was a debtor in his books, Commissioner (Appeals) had rightly considered aforesaid amount as assessee's income from other sources

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus labour charges) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee was engaged in import and exports of diamond - Assessee claimed expenditure towards labour charges paid by it for conversion of rough diamond into polished diamonds - Assessing Officer disallowed same on ground that assessee booked bogus labour expenditure - It was noted that conversion of rough diamonds into polished diamond by assessee would certainly require certain labour / job work - Payment to labour contractor was made through account payee cheques after deduction of tax at source - There was no concrete material before Assessing Officer to disallow labour charges incurred by assessee - Whether, on facts, impugned disallowance of expenditure merely on basis of suspicion or doubt was unjustified and same could not be sustained - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]

II. Section  69A  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained moneys (Purchase of Jewellery)  - Assessment year  2017-18  - In course of search and seizure operation, a pair of diamond bangles purchased from FI was found during search in case of assessee - Departmental valuer valued one bangle at Rs. 7.76 lakhs and left out other - Assessee in a statement under section 132(4) stated that pair of bangles was purchased for a consideration of Rs. 8.72 lakhs and also furnished supporting evidence by way of purchase bill - He further stated that other bangle left out by Departmental valuer was valued by another registered valuer at Rs. 4.39 lakhs and, hence, value of two bangles would work out to Rs. 8.78 lakhs, which was more or less equal to invoice value - However, Assessing Officer relying upon statement of an employee of FI added back an amount of Rs. 8.62 lakhs, being amount allegedly paid in cash over and above invoice value - Whether addition made to income of assessee under section 69A solely relying upon statement of a third party was not sustainable, more so, when assessee denied of having paid any cash - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition so made was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 15 and 16] [In favour of assessee]

Section  68,  read with section  69C,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Sale of diamonds)  - Assessment year  2020-21  - Assessing Officer also made addition of about Rs. 14.88 lakhs under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure at 0.18 per cent of sale consideration - It was noted that Tribunal in case of assessee’s family member on identical issue had held that existence of rough diamonds could not be doubted having regard to declaration of same under IDS, 2016 having been accepted by Pr. CIT, coupled with payment of due taxes - Tribunal further held that gain on sale of diamonds was assessable as long-term capital gain since entire holding period of diamonds, including that of previous owner, was to be considered in view of Explanation 1(i)(b) to section 2(42A) - Accordingly, addition under section 68 was deleted - Whether, following said decision, additions made under section 68 on account of sale of diamonds and consequential addition under section 69C towards alleged commission expenditure were to be deleted - Held, yes. [Para 7] [In favour of assessee]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Accommodation entry) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee company was engaged in business of manufacturing and trading in precious stones and jewelry - A survey under section 133A was conducted upon assessee - Subsequent to survey, statement of a director of assessee was recorded in which he stated that assessee had provided only bill entries and there was no actual transaction of purchase and sale - On basis of same, Assessing Officer concluded that assessee was engaged in activity of issuing accommodation bills for purchase and sale of diamonds coupled with acting as dummy for importers and, accordingly, made additions under section 68 - It was noted that on verification of documents and other materials on record Tribunal was satisfied that assessee was mainly engaged in import of diamonds and further sales in local markets to exporters - Import of diamonds by assessee was done through custom authorities and through regular banking channels in India - All transactions relating to purchase and sales were made through account payee cheques and that there was not a single transaction by way of cash - Parties to transactions were reputed in trade - Sales were made to reputed exporters who were assessed to tax and their identities were known to department besides they were registered under State tax laws - Tribunal had further noted that assessee had discharged onus of proving transactions as genuine by furnishing relevant documents such as copies of bank statements, ledger copies of various purchases, purchase invoices, daily stock register, etc. - It also noted that survey party did not find any incriminating evidence and material that could establish stand taken by Assessing Officer - On such basis Tribunal recorded a clear finding of fact that assessee was not engaged in issuing accommodation bills and acting as a dummy for importing diamond bills - Whether merely a statement of director of assessee that too recorded after 25 days of survey could not be a basis for making any addition to income without further supporting or corroborative evidence - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, impugned addition made under section to income of assessee was unjustified - Held, yes [Para 14] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX: Where Assessing Officer made additions to income of assessee on account of bogus purchase and sale transactions merely on basis of statement of a director of assessee that assessee had provided only bill entries and there was no such actual transaction, since assessee discharged onus of proving its transactions of sale and purchase as genuine by furnishing relevant documents and revenue had not found any incriminating evidence that could establish stand of Assessing Officer, impugned addition was unjustified

Section 68, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Unexplained money) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account during period of demonetization - He contended that same were proceeds of cash sales - Assessing Officer observed that assessee failed to explain source of such huge cash deposit - He thereby invoked provision of section 145(3) and rejected book results - Further, he did not consider sales to tune of Rs. 37.96 lakhs out of cash deposited by assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016 and made addition under section 68 on account of same - It was noted that in support of sales so made, assessee submitted all invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of persons to whom cash sales were made - On this information Assessing Officer had not made any independent inquiry - He considered part of sales as genuine and on same set of records, part of sales were not considered as genuine - This pick  chose approach was not correct on same set of evidence - Assessee had maintained all records that sales were duly reflected in VAT return and also in books of accounts of assessee - Further, Assessing Officer had not given required notice before rejection of book results, as required under law - Also profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales - Whether, on facts, Assessing Officer was not justified in rejecting books of account by invoking provisions of section 145(3) and further impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was also liable to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 13 and 14] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of gold and diamond jewellery deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs during demonetization period in his bank accounts and claimed that said cash was proceeds of cash sales, since assessee furnished all sales invoices with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of person to whom cash sales were made, such sales could not be considered as unexplained money and that too when profit derived from those sales proceeds was already taxed as part of sales

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits - Assessment year 1998-99 - Whether under provisions of section 68, if explanation with regard to nature and source of cash credit is found unsatisfactory, only then, amount so credited may be added as income - Held, yes - On basis of survey conducted in business premises of ‘V’, wherein ‘V’ had given statement that all transactions of purchase and sale of diamonds appearing in profit and loss account of his proprietary concern ‘D’ were ‘fictitious’ transactions, assessment of assessee was reopened as on scrutiny of records, it was noticed that assessee had credited certain amount in his capital account, source of which was claimed to be sale of diamonds declared under VDIS, 1997 to ‘D’ - Though in his statement, recorded under section 131, ‘V’ retracted from his statement given during course of survey by stating that purchases made by him were true and were totally accounted for in books of account, yet Assessing Officer, relied on earlier statement of ‘V’ and added that amount as assessee’s income under section 68 - Commissioner (Appeals) upheld additions - Whether since diamonds were declared by assessee under VDIS, they were sold under sale bills to ‘D’ who was identified person and had confirmed transaction, source of payment was bank account of purchaser, and there was no 
 material on record to show that source of that money was assessee, it could be said that source of amount found credited in assessee’s books stood explained and, therefore, it could not be said to be income of assessee, in any circumstances, under section 68 - Held, yes

Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment years  2009-10 and 2012-13 - Assessee was engaged in business of import, processing, trading and export of diamond - During assessment proceedings, Assessing Officer on basis of information received from Investigation Wing, Mumbai, regarding accommodation entries provided by 'BJ Group' concluded that assessee failed to prove genuineness of purchases and made an addition of 100 per cent of alleged bogus purchases - On appeal, Tribunal sustained addition at rate of 6 per cent - Whether since in several matters arising out of transactions with said 'BJ Group', Tax Appeals of Department had been dismissed where, Tribunal had assessed disallowance at 6 per cent, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order - Held, yes [Para 6] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in business of import, processing, trading and export of diamond, failed to prove genuineness of purchases from certain parties and Tribunal had assessed disallowance at 6 per cent, no question of law arose from Tribunal's order in present case

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Demonetization deposits)  - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee-company was engagd in business of trading in gold, diamond jewellery etc. - During search and survey conducted on premises of assessee, huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced - Initially MD of assessee claimed that said amount was received as advances of less than Rs. 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of gold bullion on date of annoucement of demonetization of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes - Assessee initially accepted such income and agreed to deposit taxes as per Scheme Pradhan Mantri Garib Kalyan Yojana, 2016 - However, later on it contradicted with earlier statement and contended that amount so deposited was received from NS, owner of ALG, and invoices were issued in names supplied by a third party - It was noted that invoices issued by assessee were bogus and even 12 customers whose documents were given by assessee to prove their identity, had denied to have given their advances for purchase of gold from assessee - It was furhter noted that assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization - As per report of CFSL and Forensic Analysis of Computers and Software installed therein it could be cleary seen that system was shut down on 8-11- 2016 at 18:45:34 and it was again logged on 9-11-2016 at 09:20:32 - However, receipts recovered from premises of assessee clearly showed that they were issued/printed after demonetization notification and more particularly, after 9-11-2016, indicating that demonetized notes (SBNs) were accepted contrary to RBI notification - Thus, in absence of availabilty of gold with assessee, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers - It was further noted that bank account of assessee in which alleged amount was deposited was only opened on 10-11-2016 and as per notification assessee could not deposit more than Rs. 50,000 in its account till KYC was completed - Therefore, disability of assessee to deposit more than Rs. 50,000 as per notification would entail disability of its delegate/agent and thus its contention that deposits were made by third party could not be accepted - Whether any unexplained amount credited in books of assessee shall be deemed to be of assessee if explanation of assessee was not satisfactory or was against preponderance of probabilty and evidence on record and hence, Assessing Officer was justified in making additions under section 68 treatings deposits of SBNs found in its bank account as unexplained credit in hands of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 70 to 77] [In favour of revenue]INCOME TAX : Where during search and survey operation conducted on premises of assessee-company huge deposits were found in its bank account after demonetization was announced and assessee claimed source of said deposit receipt of advances of less than Rs 2 lakhs from 2153 customers for purchase of bullions, since assessee had no/negligible ‘stock-in-trade’ of gold as on 8-11-2016 and no orders were place on 8-11-2016 and 9-1-2016 after announcement of demonetization, it was difficult to infer that there was a sale agreement between assessee and annonymous buyers and therefore, impugned additions made under section 68 treating deposit of demonetized notes as unexplained credit was justified

Section 69 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investments - Assessment year 1982-83 - During search under section 132, department recovered diamond ornament at premises of assessee - Assessee submitted a bill in respect or purchase of diamond and bill for labour charges - However, ITO got these items valued from Departmental Valuer and added difference in value in total income of assessee - Whether by producing purchase bill and labour charges bill, assessee discharged his burden of explanation and, thus, addition could not be made merely on ground that purchase invoice was fictitious - Held, yes

IV. Section 158BB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Block assessment in search cases - Undisclosed income, computation of - Block period 1991-92 to 9-8-2000 - Whether where various members of assessee’s family had disclosed diamonds under VDIS, 1997, which was accepted by department and same were later sold and sale proceeds of said diamonds was deposited in bank accounts of family members from which assessee had received loan which was duly reflected in regular return, in said circumstances, it could be said that deposits remained fully explained in hands of assessee and further sale of diamonds could not be treated as bogus - Held, yes - Whether therefore, no addition could be made in hands of assessee - Held, yes

Section  68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Cash credit (Demonetization) - Assessment year  2017-18 - During demonetization period, assessee-jeweller deposited huge amount in three bank accounts - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had suddenly made cash sales to unidentifiable small customers during period from 1-10-2016 to 8-11-2016 - He, therefore, made addition under section 68 on account of such unexplained cash credit (sales) - It was noted that business of assessee was an expanding business and sales had not abnormally increased in one particular month but was showing a constant trend of increasing over years - Assessee had furnished before Assessing Officer month wise details of purchases and sales made after that date and movement in stock position - Details of stock, purchases and sales that had been submitted by assessee before Assessing Officer had not been questioned or doubted in any manner by Assessing Officer - Whether since assessee had presented evidence of available stock and depletion of said stock on account of sales and Assessing Officer had not carried out any enquiry to show that any portion of receipts on account of sale of that stock were unexplained by such sales, no case for addition under section 68 was made out - Held, yes [Para 10] [In favour of assessee]

I. Section 28(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business loss/deductions - Allowable as (Embezzlement of stock) - Assessment year 2011-12 - Assessee carrying on business of gold and diamond jewellery claimed loss in respect of embezzlement of stock by an employee and others - Lower authorities disallowed claim of embezzlement - Whether since FIR had been filed by assessee quantifying details of embezzlement of theft and police had confirmed said FIR and assessee had also filed all relevant documents to prove that there was an actual embezzlement, loss claimed by assessee deserved to be allowed - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 7] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Bogus purchases) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessing Officer treated entire purchases made by assessee from two parties as bogus purchases and added amount to assessee's income invoking section 69C - Whether since assessee had filed details of purchases made from aforesaid parties and corresponding quantity of sales made, entire purchases could not have been added - Held, yes - Whether further source of purchases was from books, addition could not have been made under section 69C - Held, yes - Whether only gross profit rate of 3 per cent was to be applied over and above gross profit rate declared by assessee on bogus purchases - Held, yes [Para 11] [Partly in favour of assessee]

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposits post demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization - Assessee claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration - Assessing Officer made addition under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format, and thus, claim made by assessee remained unexplained - Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed order of Assessing Officer on ground that assessee made sale transaction below Rs. 2 lakhs and cash sales during demonetization was 90.59 per cent of cash sales for entire period of next financial year - It was noted that other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT - Also Assessing Officer without examining any parties to whom goods were sold by assessee concluded that sales were not genuine - Whether since Assessing Officer accepted books of account of assessee and entries in books of account were matched, there would be no case to make additions - Held, yes - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) committed error in upholding addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization period and claimed that same arose out of cash sales of jewellery, since other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT and books of account of assessee were accepted by AO, said deposits could not be said to be unexplained cash deposit

Section 68, read with section 115BBE, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Bank deposits post demonetization) - Assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee deposited substantial amount of cash in bank during demonetization - Assessee claimed that said cash arose out of cash sales of jewellery made during year under consideration - Assessing Officer made addition under section 68 on ground that assessee had failed to provide item-wise stock statement to show item-wise quantities as well as their corresponding amount in month-wise format, and thus, claim made by assessee remained unexplained - Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed order of Assessing Officer on ground that assessee made sale transaction below Rs. 2 lakhs and cash sales during demonetization was 90.59 per cent of cash sales for entire period of next financial year - It was noted that other wing of Government had already accepted sale transaction under VAT - Also Assessing Officer without examining any parties to whom goods were sold by assessee concluded that sales were not genuine - Whether since Assessing Officer accepted books of account of assessee and entries in books of account were matched, there would be no case to make additions - Held, yes - Whether thus, Commissioner (Appeals) committed error in upholding addition made by Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 23] [In favour of assessee]

Section 69, read with section 153C, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained investment (Jewellery) - Assessment year 2018-19 - During search conducted at premises of one S it was found that a consignor, one P Ltd. dispatched a package containing gold jewellery weighing 524.500 gms which was to be received by assessee as consignee - Said gold jewellery was seized - Assessing Officer initiated proceedings under section 153C and made additions in assessee's income for seized value of gold jewellary by treating same as unaccounted investment - It was noted that assessee purchased said gold from one P Ltd. for which payment was made through banking channels and purchases were duly accounted for in books of account of assessee - Whether thus, said purchases could not be termed as unaccounted investments and seized gold jewellery was to be released in favour of assessee - Held, yes [Paras 10 and 11] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where during search conducted at premises of one S, gold jewellery which was to be received by assessee as consignee was seized, since payment for purchasing said gold was made through banking channels and purchases were duly accounted for in books of account of assessee, no additions could be made for unaccounted investment with respect to said gold jewellery and same was to be released in favour of assessee

I. Section 69C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Investment in flat) - Assessment year 2010-11 - Assessee purchased a flat for Rs. 60 lakhs and paid stamp duty of Rs. 2.82 lakhs along with an unrelated party - Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 32.82 lakhs as unexplained investment of assessee - Commissioner (Appeals) deleted same on ground that respective sale consideration was transferred from bank account of unrelated party without any cash deposits by assessee and unrelated party was able to prove source of investment in purchase of flat - Whether since revenue authorities had not brought any material on record to show that findings recorded by Commissioner (Appeals) were incorrect, addition made by Assessing Officer was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 9] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee purchased a flat along with an unrelated party and respective sale consideration was transferred from bank account of unrelated party without any cash deposits by assessee and unrelated party was able to prove source of investment in purchase of flat, Assessing Officer was not justified in making addition under section 69C in hands of assessee  INCOME TAX : Where assessee denied in making alleged investment in transactions in Gold Futures Contracts in MCX exchange and trading made by assessee resulted in loss and copy of ledger account provided by MCX was never given to assessee for his rebuttal, AO was not justified in making addition of alleged investment as undisclosed investment in hands of assessee

Section 68 read with section 147 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Purchase) - Assessment year 2012-13 - Assessee, engaged in sarafi business and metal trading, faced reopening under section 147 for Assessment Year 2012-13 based on information from investigation wing regarding accommodation entries in diamond trading - It was alleged that assessee purchased diamonds from a company involved in such entries and sold them to other entities - Assessing Officer added entire purchase amount to assessee's income by treating same as bogus purchases- It was noted that director of said company had given a statement about providing accommodation entries, but later retracted it, however, this retraction was not considered by tax authorities - Furthermore, assessee had received payments from two separate entities for diamonds sold, which suggested that purchases were genuine and that indicated that assessee had indeed purchased diamonds, which were then sold to other entities - Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by assessee with regard to sale and purchase of goods and all 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which had been purchased - Whether in view of above facts, Assessing Officer was not justified in adding entire purchase amount to assessee's income by treating same as bogus purchases - Held, yes [Paras 10,11 and 12] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in sarafi business, purchased diamonds from a company and sold them to other entities, since assessee had received payments from separate entities for diamonds sold, which suggested that purchases were genuine, transaction could not be treated as bogus

I. Section 69A, read with section 158BC, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Jewellery) - Block period 1-4-1995 to 13-9-2001 - During search over 5 kgs gold was seized from business premises of assessee - Assessee explained that gold was received for manufacturing jewellery - However, difference between time of receipt of gold for manufacturing and date for accounting of same as well as retention of gold with assessee for more than one and half years till time of its return was unexplainable - Assessee could not produce even basic documents such as receipt vouchers - Whether burden on assessee to tender credible and bona fide explanation was not discharged - Held, yes - Whether addition of unexplained gold was sustainable - Held, yes [Para 8] [In favour of revenue]IT: Difference in time of more than one and half years from date of receipt of gold and date of returning jewellery manufactured being unexplained and receipt vouchers being not produced, addition of unexplained gold to assessee's income was sustainable  IT: Where diamond stock shown to have been received by assessee from an entity was, in fact, done through accommodation entry for which said entity received commission equivalent to tax paid by it, addition made on account of undisclosed income was sustainable  IT: Where additions were based only on returns filed by wife of assessee as well as various other entities and were not relatable to seized materials, such additions pursuant to search and seizure were to be deleted  IT: Where addition was arising from a difference in valuation vis-à-vis assessee and departmental valuer and was not relatable to search material, same was to be deleted

Section 68, read with section 10(38), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Share dealings) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee purchased shares of a company - During relevant year, assessee sold said shares which resulted in substantial amount of LTCG in a short span and claimed same as exempt - Assessing Officer treated said capital gains as bogus receipts under section 68 on ground that assessee made unrealistic non-taxable capital gains on a very small investment that too in a short period of just 17 months by indulging in transactions of penny stocks - It was noted that assessee purchased said shares in cash and not through banking channels and said shares were held in pool account of broker for 17 months - Also on perusal of assessee's Demat account it was observed that shares were credited in assesses account after a period of 17 months just before date of sale - Whether thus, impugned transactions could not be said to be genuine and Assessing Officer was justified in treating LTCG as undisclosed income under section 68 - Held, yes [Paras 17 to 20] [In favour of revenue]  Section 69C, read with section 10(38), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained expenditure (Commission) - Assessment year 2014-15 - Assessee purchased shares of a company - During relevant year, assessee earned LTCG on sale of said shares - Assessing Officer treated capital gains as bogus receipts under section 68 on ground that assessee made unrealistic non-taxable capital gains on a very small investment that too in a short period of just 17 months by indulging in transactions of penny stocks - Consequently, Assessing Officer made additions on account of estimated brokerage cost incurred by assessee out of undisclosed sources - Whether since transactions with respect to sale of shares could not be said to be genuine, Assessing Officer was justified in making addition with respect to commission by holding that same was incurred to arrange bogus LTCG - Held, yes [Para 21] [In favour of revenue]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credit (Jewellery) - Assessment year 2013-14 - Assessee had received loan from various related parties - Said creditors sold their old jewellery to jewellers and had given loan to assessee out of said sale consideration - Assessing Officer treated said loan as unexplained cash credit under section 68 in hands of assessee - Tribunal deleted addition made under section 68 - It was noted that assessee had disclosed name of jewellers to whom jewellery was sold by creditors of assessee - It also established mode of payment through banking channel - Furthermore, no inquiry was made from jeweller to whom creditors had sold jewellery - Whether since, existence of deposit made by creditors to assessee was not in dispute and no credible/tangible material was brought on record by Assessing Officer which would have led to any satisfaction or finding that transaction was not genuine, impugned addition under section 68 was to be deleted - Held, yes [Paras 5 and 6] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee received loan from various creditors who sold their old jewellery and gave loan to assessee out of sale consideration, since assessee had disclosed name of jewellers to whom jewellery was sold and also established mode of payment through banking channel, and moreover existence of deposits made to assessee by creditors was not in dispute, impugned addition under section 68 with respect to loan could not be sustained

facts.text:
■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

V’ for the sale on 20-1-1998 and were produced to the department. [Para 24]

The income based on the books of account of ‘V’ was accepted in his case under the Act which included the said transaction. [Para 25]

Similarly, ‘V’ being the registered dealer under the BST and CST Act had filed the returns under those Acts, duly disclosing the said transaction with the assessee much before the date of survey. [Para 26] The observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that since ‘V’ was denying the explanation given at the time of survey, it was upon him to explain the cash deposits in his bank accounts and the lack of closing stock was not convincing. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The two statements were conflicting and as to for which statement he said ‘remained’, was not known. It would be more logical, if it was so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000, which was confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. [Para 27]

The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. [Para 28]

The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath, recorded by the Assessing Officer, ‘V’ claiming that while he knew ‘S’, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, could not raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs.10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as ‘hawala’ transaction in the statement given to the department. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. [Para 30]

It was true that at the time of survey, it was not the case of ‘V’ that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants, but the fact remained that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee was concerned throughout. [Para 31]

Large amounts of cash were deposited in various bank accounts of ‘D’ on various dates by ‘R’, but there was no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there was no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32]

The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee submitted his return of income which, inter alia, included capital gains on sale of gold and jewellery. He availed the benefit of Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 and declared gold and diamond and necessary certificate under the said Scheme was issued by the Commissioner. Later, the assessee sold the gold and diamonds separately to ‘A’ and ‘S’, respectively. The sale of gold was accepted as genuine by the Assessing Officer, while the sale of diamonds to ‘S’ was not accepted as genuine and entire sale value thereof was added under section 68 by the Assessing Officer treating the same as unexplained credit. Accordingly, assessment was completed. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer did not accept the reply of the assessee and by taking view that the assessee had not provided the details of purchases and the names of the parties and had also not produced the persons to whom sales made with documents showing the colour and size of diamonds made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to the income of the assessee on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought the same for taxation at the rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer by holding that the assessee had to prove the nature and source of deposit with three conditions as per provisions of section 68 and the assessee could not explain the nature and source of aforesaid amount of Rs. 29.66 lakhs.

On appeal to Tribunal:

As stated in earlier para, some diamond studded jewellery have been purchased during this year. The difference in weight can be reconciled only after the diamonds are valued by an approved diamond valuer."

According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order, as under :

■

The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

For the assessment year 2001-02, the assessee-company claimed to have exported diamonds, which were shown to have been purchased from two parties, viz., M/s. 'V' and M/s. 'O'. The Assessing Officer carried out deep investigations through survey and searches at the premises of the parties where from the assessee had claimed to have purchased diamonds for export and found that the alleged sellers were running a racket of arranging for Hawala entries of import and export and of providing bogus bills. Further, it was found that M/s. 'V' was owned by one 'G'. The income-tax records of 'V' showed that it had filed some return at Surat but he was also not found at the address given in the return. Further, as per the recorded statement of above parties it was found that above concern was giving entries and sale bills to accommodate people who were showing export of diamonds. In the case of M/s. 'O' the revenue carried a survey and recorded statement of its proprietor 'S', wherein he stated that head office of the concern was at Surat. However, when a survey was carried out, the above premises was found to be locked. The Assessing Officer, therefore, concluded that 'S' had made a false statement. He, therefore, concluded that the alleged purchases were bogus and, therefore, the transaction of export of diamond was not believable. He, therefore, treated the credit entries appearing in the books of account of the assessee as unexplained and assessed the same in its the hands under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal :

■

The assessee-company was engaged in business of retail sales of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited certain amount in specified bank notes to the bank account. The case was selected for scrutiny to verify the source for cash deposited and certain details were called for.

■

The assessee submitted that it had deposited cash out of sale proceeds of gold and diamond jewellery collected from its customers and had furnished cash book, sales register, purchase register, bank statements along with stock registers for the relevant period and demonstrated that the cash deposited in bank was out of sales proceeds of stock on hand.

■

The Assessing Officer was not satisfied with the explanation furnished by the assessee and observed that cash sales entered in the cash book and sales register were bogus as cash sales were created fictitiously by the assessee company merely to build an explanation for the cash deposits in to the bank accounts and made addition of total of cash deposits to tax under section 69A, read with section 115BBE.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) noted that the assessee had explained the sources of cash deposits as cash sales received on 08-11-2016 against the sales and the assessee also produced the sale bills and books of accounts and that when there was sufficient stock to effect the sales and no defect had been found in the stock as well as the sales and purchases and since, the assessee has already admitted the sales as revenue receipt, there was no case for considering cash deposit as not explained and adding the same and deleted the addition.

■

On the revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

After exchange of letters in respect of gold jewellery and diamonds which we have extracted above, the Assessing Officer drew inference that the assessee has failed to explain satisfactorily the sources of gold jewellery and diamonds. According to the Assessing Officer, the unexplained gold jewellery and diamonds was to the tune of Rs. 27,86,400 which was treated as undisclosed income of the block period. The details which are worked out by the Assessing Officer at page 7 of the assessment order,

For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998, the assessee had stated in response to a question that he was at Surat on most of the dates and not necessarily on all the dates. In view of the fact that preceding the date of 15-3-1998, there was sales of diamonds on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 24-1-1998 of other family members of the assessee, sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998 was to be accepted as genuine. [Para 33]

As regards the sale of diamonds on 25-3-1998 after perusal of statement and rejoinder of the assessee, it was found that Rs. 5,00,000 was not drawn on 25-3-1998 but was credited to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and it was a transfer entry on 25-3-1998 from the bank account of ‘H’ in State Bank of India to the bank account of ‘N’ Textiles and, therefore, the contention of the revenue that the assessee was at Hyderabad on 25-3-1998 was not correct. [Para 34]

■ The Tribunal duly considered the facts and circumstances of the case. The Tribunal noticed from the assessment order that the AO has proceeded to hold the sales of the assessee to be bogus, primarily on account of the fact that the figures of purchases and sales in the period immediately prior to demonetization were at wide variance with the figures of purchases and sales in the corresponding period of the previous year and also at variance with the figures of the previous months in the present financial year. The AO also noted that the purchases on the basis of which the sales were made were effected from certain sister concerns and that too, only upto the period of demonetization. He could not find any nexus between the purchase and the payment made to the persons from whom the purchase had been made and from the same he came to the conclusion that a channel of purchase and sale was created just to give colour to unexplained cash deposit under the garb of sale and for this the VAT return had been utilized as a tool. In consideration of these findings, the Tribunal observes that a departure in trading patterns cannot in itself be a ground to make an addition by holding such departure to be bogus. It can at best be a ground for further investigation to determine the reason for such departure and if the assessee is unable to prove that the enhanced figures were genuine, then only could the credits purported to be made on account of such sales be brought to tax under the provisions of section 68. However, before section 68 could be invoked, the AO was obliged to demonstrate with evidence as to why the explanation furnished by the assessee for cash sales in that particular period were not acceptable. Such evidence could be the fact that the assessee did not have the inventory to make the sale that it claimed, or that the assessee had not made corresponding purchases which stood subsequently effected by way of sales. Unless the AO could find sufficient material to disturb the trading results declared by the assessee in the audited accounts, he would not be at liberty to regard the explanation offered by the assessee for the said cash deposits as unexplained. The Tribunal noticed that in the instant case, the AO had voiced suspicion that the purchases had been shown to have been made from sisterconcerns only so as to create a channel of purchase and sales to explain the deposit of money. He comes to this conclusion on account of the fact that he was unable to relate payment for such purchases to the actual purchases made. The Tribunal again notes that the suspicion could only be a starting point for further investigation and the purchase of goods on credit cannot in itself be a ground to reject the genuineness of the purchase. The Tribunal further notes from the assessee's submission that the AO had issued notices under section 133(6), but could not find anything adverse in this regard. On the contrary, the Tribunal notes from the paper book filed by the assessee that the assessee had inventories amounting to Rs. 4.61 crores as on the first day of the accounting year and that the assessee is able to explain an opening stock of worth Rs.4.41 crores as on 1-10-2016 as per the perpetual inventory method, prepared on the basis of its VAT returns filed upto September, 2016, which the Tribunal notes had been filed on 20-10-2016 i.e. before the date of demonetization. In the circumstances, there do not appear to be any reasons to question the sales made by the assessee in the month of October, 2016 were not due till later, out of those stocks or even in November, 2016 out of the residual stocks that remained on 31-10-2016 and purchases made during the period. The AO has pointed out that there was possibility for manipulation in sales on account of the fact that the VAT returns for the month of October, 2016 but the Tribunal notes that even if that were so, it would not change the nature of the receipt from being realization of sales of stocks that was available unless it could be demonstrated that such sales were not made or that the stock to make such sales was not available. No credence can be given to the AO's views that such sales were shown only with a view to deposit cash during demonetization and the stocks were later on actually sold outside the books of accounts as no such evidence has been brought on record by the AO to back up this suspicion. The Tribunal is therefore in agreement with the decision of the ITAT Chennai Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. Viswa and Devji Diamonds (P.) Ltd. [2025] 171 taxmann.com 474 (Chennai - Trib.) wherein the ITAT Chennai Bench has held that if no defect could be pointed out in the books of accounts and the cash deposited had been stated to be made out of sales, since the assessee had discharged the burden of proving the source of cash deposited in the bank, the impugned addition was fit to be deleted

If the alleged bogus purchases show gross profit higher than the regular gross profit shown by the assessee, no further addition is required to be made in the hands of the assessee. The logic behind this is that sale is already accounted for on the credit side of the profit and loss account. If the purchases are to be removed, the corresponding sale is also required to be removed from the profit and loss account, sales is higher than the purchases in rupees terms, therefore, the addition would be only required to be made to the extent of lower gross profit on alleged bogus purchases then the regular gross profit. This also takes the care of the argument that no proof of delivery of goods purchased are shown by the assessee, similarly, the sales are also bogus. It is not the case of the Assessing Officer that amount invested in acquiring the bogus purchases should also be considered as an addition, because the only addition is disallowance of bogus purchases, no further addition is warranted. In view of this, the ground of appeal of the Assessing Officer are dismissed. [Para 24]
