Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor. Gold trading entities often use complex cross-border arrangements for warehousing and invoicing. Such structures, if devoid of economic substance, can be recharacterised by tax authorities. The growing collaboration between Indian regulators and international counterparts has made tax arbitrage more difficult to conceal.

C. Money Laundering and the PMLA Framework

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) forms the backbone of India's anti-money-laundering regime. Jewellers, refiners, and bullion dealers are designated as reporting entities. They must verify customer identity, maintain records, and report suspicious transactions exceeding Rs. 10 lakh to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-IND).

The Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India [2022] 140 taxmann.com 610 (SC) upheld the constitutional validity of the PMLA, emphasising its deterrent role. Non-compliance now attracts criminal prosecution, with attachment and confiscation of assets linked to proceeds of crime.

Gold, due to its liquidity and global mobility, remains a preferred medium for layering and integration in money-laundering chains. Enforcement agencies have therefore prioritised the bullion trade in their investigative strategies.

D. Benami and Black-Money Legislation

The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, as amended in 2016, prohibits holding gold or other assets in another person's name. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ganpati Dealcom Pvt Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 389/289 Taxman 177/447 ITR 108 clarified that the 2016 amendments are prospective, giving enforcement agencies clear timelines for action.

The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 criminalises undisclosed offshore holdings, including gold kept in foreign vaults or nominee accounts. Residents must report such assets in Schedule FA of their tax returns or face penalties and imprisonment.

E. Customs and FEMA Compliance

Gold imports and exports are regulated under the Customs Act, 1962 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA). Importers must obtain authorisation from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) and route payments through authorised banking channels.

Under-invoicing and over-invoicing are treated as contraventions under both Customs and FEMA. Such activities may trigger proceedings under Section 111 of the Customs Act and attract compounding penalties under FEMA.

IV. Cross-Border Trade and International Coordination

A. The FATF and Global Standards

The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has repeatedly identified the gold trade as a high-risk sector for money laundering and terror financing. Its 2024 evaluation called upon member countries to expand reporting obligations and enhance beneficial ownership transparency. India, through the Asia-Pacific Group on Money Laundering, is implementing these standards across its financial institutions and bullion exchanges.

B. OECD and Transfer-Pricing Guidelines

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) mandates country-by-country reporting for multinational enterprises engaged in commodities trading. Gold refiners and trading houses must justify pricing models and inter-company margins. The Central Board of Direct Taxes has aligned domestic rules with OECD recommendations to ensure consistency in valuation.

C. Information Sharing and Treaties

India's participation in the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and multiple Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) enables exchange of financial information with more than 100 countries. This allows regulators to trace offshore holdings and identify beneficial owners of foreign gold accounts.

Under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) framework, Indian institutions also report US-linked gold-backed assets, ensuring reciprocity in disclosure.

D. Digital Gold and New-Age Risks

Digital gold platforms have transformed retail investment. While convenient, they raise jurisdictional and compliance questions because the underlying bullion is often stored overseas. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) are now evaluating mechanisms to regulate digital gold and tokenised bullion under a unified compliance regime.

Proper regulation is critical to prevent misuse of digital assets for cross-border transfer or concealment.

V. Corporate Governance and Enforcement Trends

Corporate scandals involving misreporting of gold inventories and false collateral declarations have drawn scrutiny under the Companies Act, 2013. Section 447 defines such manipulation as fraud, punishable by imprisonment and fines.

Investigations today employ digital forensics, audit analytics, and blockchain tracing to verify authenticity of gold-backed financial products. Collaboration among the Enforcement Directorate, Income Tax Department, Customs, and FIUhas improved substantially.

India's cooperation with foreign regulators, especially in the UAE and Singapore, facilitates tracing of assets and repatriation of proceeds of crime. The country's growing adherence to FATF and OECD frameworks enhances its credibility in global financial governance.

From the plain reading of the above section 68, it is abundantly clear that the essential and mandatory pre-requisite for making an addition under this section is that the unexplained sum must be found credited in the books of an assessee maintained by him for any previous year. Presumptions in inter-connected transactions:

7. There may be several inter-connected transactions in the conversion of tainted money into untainted money. It is possible that during the course of investigation only one transaction is proved to be involved in money laundering process. Therefore, Section 23 of the PMLA provides that, where money laundering process involves two or more interconnected transactions and one or more such inter-connected transactions are proved to be involved in money laundering, then for the purposes of adjudication or confiscation or for the trial of offence of money laundering, it shall, unless otherwise proved to the satisfaction of the adjudicating authority, or the Special Court, be presumed that the remaining transactions form part of such inter-connected transactions.

Burden of proof:

8. Several persons, including professionals, may be involved in processing of the proceeds of crime for converting it into untainted money. The ultimate beneficiary of the proceeds of crime in the untainted form may be made the prime accused and all those persons who had knowledge or who were involved may also be made co-accused. There may be other persons who may be charged for abatement, but that cannot be under PMLA as no such provision exists in this Act. The charge of abatement/conspiracy can be brought under Section 120B of IPC. Therefore, where a person is charged with the offence of money laundering under section 3, then as per Section 24 of the PMLA, the Authority or Court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering: and, in the case of any other person (who is not charged u/s 3of PMLA) the Authority or Court may presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering. The use of the word "may" in this Section provides a discretion to the Court, whether to cast burden on the accused to prove his innocence. Thus, Section 24 casts the burden of proving that alleged proceeds of crime are not involved in money laundering, on the accused charged u/s 3 of PMLA. However, this does not relieve the prosecution of making specific (and not a vague and omnibus) allegation or charge, supported by substantive evidence that money involved in laundering is earned from or through a scheduled offence and, therefore, are proceeds of crime. Once a charge is made, the accused has to establish that investment (assets or properties) alleged to be out of tainted money, are, in fact, acquired legitimately by lawful means. This can be proved on a standard of preponderance of probability.

While investigating the case under PMLA, the director, additional director, Joint director, deputy director or assistant director of the Directorate of Enforcement have the power to summon, under section 11(2) & section 50(3) of the PMLA, any person whose attendance he considers necessary for giving evidence or for producing any records. All the persons so summoned are bound to attend in person or through authorized agents, as such officer may direct, and the persons so summoned are bound to state the truth of the subject in respect of which they are examined or their statement is recorded and to produce such documents as may be required by such officer who also has power under Section 50(1) to take affidavits on oath with respect to discovery of facts. From section 50 it follows that an accused person can also be summoned, an affidavit on oath can be taken from him and he can be compelled to state the truth, disclose the facts and thus practically incriminate himself. The question remains open as to whether there is violation of constitutional rights under Article 20(3) of the Constitution.

Cash Transaction

The above mechanism is useful for transactions made through banking channels, but for cash transactions, it is near to impossible to catch them as the cash system works in the same fashion as 'hawala' works. The word 'hawala' is a local version of the English word 'reference'; this system works only on a reference basis. An anonymous person cannot go directly to the 'hawala' dealer for transfer of money between cities or countries. A reference from some known person is required. These dealers are not maintaining any written record; once a transaction is completed, the record is erased. Even if any record is found during the course of the survey or search, nothing can be made out of these jotted entries. Generally, these transactions are very smooth. Trust and risk are primary conditions. So dealing with cash crypto is almost like dealing with 'hawala' transactions. No separate provisions of the law are applicable, and no special expertise is required to crack these transactions. Traditional hawala methods were mainly operating through two methods. Firstly, the quantum of money of the sender and receiver should be the same. The second method is 'under-invoicing or over-invoicing' of import and export bills as required. But transfer through crypto is not based on any such conditions, the money can be sent unilaterally. So the emphasis is required only on those transactions which are done through banking channels.

Major Challenge

The main danger of cryptocurrencies is the convenience of transferring money to offshore places. A person can buy crypto in cash in India and transfer it to some person living abroad. That person would sell it and receive money in the local currency. Same as in the case of international debit or credit cards, where the deposits are made in one country in local currency, but ATM withdrawals can be made in any country. But these transactions contain heavy transaction fees, which is not there in the case of crypto. 24. Payment of advance salary to defeat purpose of demonetisation won't come under purview of benami transaction

[G. Bahadur v. ACIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 179 (PBPTA - AT)]

The appellant was employed in a College run by a Trust. He received Rs. 50 thousand as advance salary from the said trust. The appellant deposited entire amount in his bank account, which was subsequently withdrawn by him and used for own purposes.

The Initiating Officer (IO) assumed that Chairman of trust had forced employees to distribute, deposit and retain their own money in demonetized currency in guise of loan received, which had to be repaid after some time in new currency. Thus, IO held chairman of college as beneficial owner and appellant as benamidar and passed order provisionally attaching bank account of appellant.

The Appellate Tribunal held in favour of appellant as under:

Every cash transaction couldn't be termed as a 'benami' transaction. As per section 2(9) of Benami Act the following twin conditions are needed to be satisfied to construe any transaction as benami: (1) the property being held by a person who has not provided the consideration, (2) the property is held by that person for the immediate or future benefit, direct or indirect of the person who has provided the said consideration.

The characteristic of a 'benami' transaction is that there must be a mere lending of name without any intention to benefit the person in whose name it is made, i.e., a mere name lender. The mischiefs sought to be punished by the Act are only such transactions which have a name lending element without deriving any benefit therein, i.e., 'benami' transactions.

The transaction where cash was paid to person in lieu of a future promise couldn't be a 'benami' transaction, as there was no lending of name. There could be no 'benami' transaction if the future benefit was due from the person who was also the holder of property.

The impugned order was not sustainable as it intended to punish the appellants for wanting to defeat the purpose of demonetization and was beyond the purview of the Act.

CONCLUDING OBSERVATION AND SUGGESTIONS Based on the above observation, it can be stated that the introduction of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 was a much-needed step for the prosecution of fugitive economic offenders. This Act is a tailor-made specific statute that deals with a typical form of white collar crime which constitutes a huge chunk of economic offences in the country. It can also be stated that there are various unique features in this statute. This brings out various positive points that the legislators have tried to implement through this Act. The Act provides for time-bound prosecution of the offenders of economic crimes. To ensure this, the Act is formulated in such a way that there is no delay in the trial and other judicial proceedings. The distinctive feature of this Act is the attachment and confiscation of different types of properties that are not acquired by legal means. Such attachment and confiscation are based on the United Nations Convention against Corruption. Thus it can be said from the above observation and analysis that this legislation is drafted keeping in mind the speedy trial and recovery of monetary value in question. The above provisions of the Act are closely associated with the nature of offenses that the country has faced in the past few years. Economic offenses of grave nature affect the country's GDP and become a hurdle in the path of progress of the economy. Therefore such accused who are declared as fugitive economic offenders under the Act must be brought to justice so that the sanctity of the rule of law is maintained. This will also ensure the removal of the block in the path of the country's economic progress. This legislation was the need of the time and the Central Government has been successful in bringing out a law that deals with all major aspects of offices whose offenders have turned fugitive and are trying to avoid prosecution. The powers granted to the authority and the designated officers are wider in nature as compared to previous money laundering and economic offenses legislations.

On one hand where the government's move towards tackling such nature of offenses is being appreciated, on the other hand, the implementation of the said Act is also put to question with several lacunas. The lacuna lies in the fact that as per Section 4 of the Act, a person is straightway declared as a fugitive if sufficient evidence is against him. It also observes that imbalanced power is granted to the special court and nodal agency for conducting search and seizure and attaching the property of the accused. The law is subject to proper judicial review from the higher courts to be perfectly implantable since it violates basic human rights and laws of natural justice prima facie on its implementation. The pre-confiscation of the property of the accused before the conviction of the offence violated the basic principle of criminal law which states that every person is to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Thus, it is important to note that this legislation should go under judicial review by the appropriate court. To make the implementation of the law more effective, the Central Government needs to bring amendments as per the rule of law observing the principles of natural justice, the right to free and fair trial, and in consonance with the fundamental rights provisions of the Indian Constitution. The Act is a much-needed step to recover and prevent economic offenses of modern times and will prove a milestone shortly if implemented and executed with due care.

In today's world, financial fraud instances are on the rise, and with advancements in technology, fraudsters are smarter to contrive new ways to carry out their nefarious schemes. Money laundering is one of these crimes that has been exploiting businesses for a long time. Criminals have devised alternate methods for concealing the source of money obtained unlawfully. Money laundering is a significant concern for financial institutions and Fintech firms. Placement, layering, and integration are the three stages of money laundering. The most difficult yet vital of these is placement. Most of the evidence that could aid in tracking the funds is destroyed during this stage. The funds are then layered in the second stage, which means they are given a frame that makes them appear legitimate. The funds are brought back into the legal economy during the last step of integration. Several bank accounts from different jurisdictions are used during the layering stage. Multiple account transfers obstruct tracking and circumvent value constraints. Authorities should be unable to track the origins of incriminated monies during the integration stage.

Given the recent significant surge in money laundering cases, firms anticipate an upsurge in the future as well. Regulatory authorities are functioning to prevent money laundering globally. Every company must follow the Financial Actions Task Force's rules (FATF) recommendations to combat Money Laundering cases that intend to protect enterprises from many sorts of illegal activities, particularly money laundering. Furthermore, the guidelines have highlighted specific actions that can assist businesses in detecting money laundering. FATF recommends these acts as red flags, making money laundering detection simpler.

If resources are valuable, fraudsters will try taking advantage of them. Gold and diamonds perfect for money laundering

Recently there have been several gold-related financial crime cases. According to the United States "Financial Action Task Force," criminals prefer to launder money through global gold and diamond markets because they offer predictable profits, participants deal mostly in cash, tracing transactions is complex, and gold and diamonds are easier to transport.

Many case studies have crammed how drug traffickers accept diamonds or gold as payment for drugs, smugglers convert gold into common unidentifiable objects like belt buckles, corrupt payments, bribes, and illegal gold and diamond mining to fund terrorism avoiding taxes. In most cases, Shell companies are established as a front business for illicit trades. Money laundering and shell companies share an old camaraderie, and in most cases of reported money laundering and smuggling, shell companies have played a significant role. This is prevalent worldwide. Shell companies are the entities that generally have no physical presence otherwise than an address and generate no or little economic value. They can be formed for legitimate purposes, too; yet, they have become a common tool for money laundering due to their ability to hide ownership and mask the financial details.

Money laundering occurs in a variety of ways. For example, someone might form a shell company to trade precious metals and use the shell company's name and bank account to receive the sale proceeds. Apart from this, the schemes involving magnified valuations of precious metals or stones due to a lack of expert valuation knowledge are also widespread. In such cases, the owner of a stone usually hires a third party to help evaluate the stone. The valuer doing the valuation often provides a deceptive report to the seller by claiming the stone to be of low value per carat. The stone's market worth may be high, but due to the seller's lack of knowledge, it will be presented to the seller at a marginally lower price.

Though FATF provides recommendations on Anti-Money Laundering practices, specific regulations to combat money laundering using precious metals and jewels have been provided by the "Kimberley Process," which was formed in 2003 and today has 56 participants from 82 nations. (The EU's 27 member states are counted as single participants.) The certification process oversees the requirements and provisions, such as creating national conflict legislation, commitment to transparency, statistical data exchange, prohibition of diamond trade with non-members, and provision of conflict-free certification for shipments. However, some nations are not Kimberley Process participants, and this is a big issue in the possibility of illicit trade involving stones from those countries.

Much more can be written about the issues likely to emerge consequent to the decision to demonetize the high denomination notes on the basis of present situation. The inconvenience that the common man is suffering because of unpreparedness of the Govt. to meet the resultant problems is un-excusable. 10.2 Also, demonetization is only one way for tackling black money problem. People do not generate black money to keep it idle in chests at home. They churn it out to add more money by investments in real estate, gold/silver jewellery, precious stones, investments in India and abroad and in many other ways, including its use in political funding. Hence, tackling in parts the problem of black money is likely to be counterproductive. Consolidated effort in this direction is needed. Measures like demonetization inconvenience merely the small traders and common man across the country. Hence, simultaneous efforts are necessary to check investments in aforesaid avenues. Further, measures will have to be thought of to dis-incentivise fresh generation of black money and clean up the political funding and keep check on the finances of political parties. All parties must be, through law, made to mandatorily declare their monthly receipts and expenditure, which must be open to public scrutiny and vetted by the Election Commission. TAXMANN ADVISORY AND RESEARCH TEAM (INCOME TAX)

Introduction

1. Demonetization has encouraged people to shift towards digital mode of payment while making financial transactions. By adopting digital mode of payment, no financial transactions would remain undisclosed and Consequently, an enhanced turnover of business might get reflected in the books of account.

Under the circumstances, an apprehension has been caused that increased turnover in the current year may lead to reopening of earlier years' cases causing undue harassment to taxpayers.

Thus, CBDT and CBEC (vide Circular No. 40/2016 and Circular No. 137/155/2012-Service tax) have advised tax officials not to re-open past assessments in income-tax and indirect tax cases only because increased turnover is reflected in books of account of business on account of increased use of digital means of payment.

2. Points to be considered for interpreting such circulars:

It would be incorrect to construe the above Circulars as giving any amnesty to tax-evaders.

The above circulars do not say that any spurt in turnover reported in books of account of businesses of current financial year (and consequently in their ITRs or indirect tax returns) is not need to be explained.

The Circulars do not give businessmen a license to show their accumulated black money in the form of demonetized notes as current year's turnover and get away scot-free without any interest or penalty and by paying normal tax for current year. If such a license is given by the circulars, the proposed PMGKY Scheme and proposed amendments to section115BBE of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and proposed new section 271AAC of that Act would be redundant.

The two circulars clarify the following points which is mere re-iteration of the existing law:

Suppose any business reported Rs.1cr to Rs.1.5 cr as its turnover in service tax and VAT in last 5 years. If the business reports a turnover of Rs.5 cr in financial year 2016-17, then it is natural for any tax official to suspect that increased turnover;

However, such suspicion alone is not sufficient to entail reopening of past assessments in income-tax and well as service tax/customs;

The Circulars do not take away the powers of tax officials to make inquiries into the sudden spurt in reported turnover;

If the results of enquiries yield information which can form basis of "reason to believe" escapement of turnover/income in the past periods, the assessments can be reopened.

The Circulars are innocuous and merely caution tax officials to adopt systematic approach under the law to enquire into sudden jumps and reopen past assessment only if enquiry throws up reason to believe that past turnovers/incomes escaped assessment. Sudden jump in turnover may give reason to suspect that turnover/income had escaped assessment in past years. But that suspicion should not lead to reopening of past assessments without making necessary inquiries and verification regarding causes of the sudden increase.

Huge increase in reported turnover can be due to genuine reasons as well as due to book-keeping sophistry.

3. Examples of genuine reasons for increased turnover due to increased use of digital means of payments:–

(1)

Credit cards offer EMI terms on purchases made through credit cards. This may have resulted in increase in sales. So, a business which was selling only on cash basis may experience a jump in turnover on account of this reason.

(2)

Impolitic purchases through plastic cards

(3)

Special cash back schemes of mobile wallets/debit cards/credit cards.

(4)

Expansion of facility of service provider/increase in manpower enabling him to service more customers.

4. Comments

Increased turnover reflected in books of accounts may also be due to past unaccounted money now shown in current year's books as current year's turnover and thereafter these notes are banked.

Whatever be the reasons, taxpayers can (and should be) asked to explain the huge increase in current period's turnover. If they are able to explain the same by valid reasons and also show corresponding increase in stocks and purchases (or expansion in size of facilities/manpower), then their explanation will be believed and past assessments will not be reopened. If they cannot explain the sudden increase in reported turnover, they can always declare their huge unexplained cash/bank deposits in proposed PMGKY Scheme and pay 49.9% tax and deposit 25% in PMGKY deposit (no interest; 4 years lock-in). If they declare their unaccounted cash/bank deposits in PMGKY, then obviously, there would be no question of reopening their past assessments of income-tax or indirect taxes. If they do not declare in PMGKY and opt to show it as current year's turnover, then they should be able to justify it.

Abstract

Gold has regained prominence as a universal store of value amid rising geopolitical uncertainty, inflation, and distrust in fiat currencies. Its surge to record highs in 2025 reflects both legitimate economic behaviour and increasing compliance challenges. This article analyses how global gold dynamics intersect with taxation, money-laundering laws, and white-collar crime, particularly within India's regulatory ecosystem. It also examines cross-border trade complexities, enforcement coordination, and the evolving standards of global financial governance. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for policymakers and corporate stakeholders to balance economic opportunity with legal responsibility.

Keywords: Gold, Taxation, Compliance, PMLA, FATF, GAAR, Cross-Border Trade, Corporate Governance, White-Collar Crime

I. Research Objective and Context

Gold remains more than a commodity. It is an emotion, a financial anchor, and a barometer of public confidence. In 2025, its value has soared not only because of market mechanics but also due to geopolitical tension and financial distrust. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the legal, tax, and compliance implications of gold's renewed prominence in the global economy.

The research aims to:

1.

Examine the global and Indian gold market trends shaping 2025.

2.

Analyse the legal and regulatory architecture governing taxation, anti-money-laundering, and cross-border transactions.

3.

Identify vulnerabilities that enable gold to be used for white-collar crime.

4.

Recommend policy and governance strategies that uphold transparency and accountability without impeding legitimate trade.

Gold's unique attributes such as liquidity, anonymity, and universal acceptance make it both an asset of stability and a tool of concealment. Understanding this duality is essential for designing laws that protect integrity while enabling commerce.

II. The Global Gold Surge: Economics, Emotion and Law

A. Price Trends and Market Forces

According to Reuters and the World Gold Council, gold prices in 2025 have risen nearly 50 percent year-on-year, reaching around US $3,950 per ounce internationally and crossing Rs. 1,25,000 per 10 grams in India. This dramatic rise stems from persistent inflation, high global debt, and growing investor preference for tangible assets.

Central banks across Asia and the Middle East have purchased record quantities of gold to diversify reserves. Goldman Sachs has forecast prices could approach US $4,900 per ounce by 2026 if inflation remains elevated and interest rates stabilise.

This global pattern underscores gold's transformation from a passive store of value into a geopolitical hedge. It reflects both market sentiment and institutional strategy.

B. India's Domestic Context

India's relationship with gold is historical and deeply cultural. Demand peaks during festivals and marriage seasons, creating a recurring impact on trade balances. India imports nearly all its gold, which has implications for the current account deficit and currency stability.

High import duties and fluctuating exchange rates have incentivised smuggling and under-invoicing. In March 2025, the government discontinued parts of the Gold Monetisation Scheme to limit fiscal exposure. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has since reported a notable increase in illegal inflows through land and maritime borders.

C. Geopolitical Context

Gold's rally cannot be separated from the global political landscape. The continuing Russia–Ukraine conflict, instability in the Middle East, and trade tensions between the United States and China have disrupted global supply chains. Sanctions against Russian bullion refineries have redirected trade to Asian hubs such as Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

As trade flows realign, enforcement agencies must address differing compliance standards among jurisdictions. Some free-trade zones have become conduits for gold trading with limited regulatory oversight, increasing risks of mis-invoicing and money laundering.

III. Legal Framework Governing Gold and Financial Compliance

A. Income-Tax and Disclosure Laws

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, unexplained gold holdings can be taxed as income under Sections 69 and 69B. High-net-worth individuals and corporations are required to declare gold holdings accurately to avoid reassessment and penalty.

Cross-border transactions in gold attract transfer-pricing scrutiny under Section 92F. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued guidelines requiring documentation that justifies arm's-length pricing.

Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor.

Judicial Review of Demonetization in 2016

On January 2, 2023, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India [2023] 146 taxmann.com 36 upheld the Central Government's decision to demonetise currency notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1,000 denominations. The Constitution Bench, led by Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, inter-alia, held that demonetization was proportionate to the Union's stated objectives and was implemented reasonably.

The Petitioners before the Apex Court had contended that demonetization could only be initiated on the RBI's Central Board recommendation, highlighting a lack of evidence of deliberation and consultation between the Union and the RBI. They further argued that, under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act 1934, which allows the Central Government to declare that "any series of bank notes of any denomination shall cease to be legal tender" after a recommendation from the Central Board of RBI, the Union could only announce demonetization for a specific series, not all notes. This, they claimed, significantly impacted the economy, as 86% of circulating currency was in demonetized notes.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court deemed it an Executive's economic policy, immune to reversal as judicial review did not apply to economic policy decisions. The Hon'ble Bench accepted the Government's claim of consultation with the RBI prior to demonetization, asserting a reasonable connection between the Government and the RBI in implementing the measure.

Consequently, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that demonetization did not violate the "Doctrine of Proportionality" asserting that the demonetization process involved deliberation, and application of mind, and lacked procedural flaws.

In hindsight, when the Hon'ble Apex Court rendered its verdict, the question of the Constitutionality of demonetization seemed moot. The deed was done, and the repercussions were evident. With over 99% of the currency returned within the stipulated deadline, the dust had settled and possibly little was left to reverse or rectify.

9. Technological Challenges in Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement

9.1 Crypto currency and Decentralized Finance

Modern laundering systems increasingly rely upon:

• decentralized exchanges,

• privacy coins,

• peer-to-peer transfers,

• offshore wallets,

• mixers and tumblers,

• cross-chain bridges.

Traditional banking-based AML systems are often ineffective against decentralized financial ecosystems.

9.2 Trade-Based Money Laundering

Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) remains one of the least detected forms of financial crime. (Hanson, 2025)

Methods include:

• over-invoicing,

• under-invoicing,

• phantom shipments,

• duplicate invoicing,

• false declarations.

India presently lacks sophisticated, integrated trade data analytics capable of real-time anomaly detection. (Trade Intelligence & Analytics (TIA) Portal - A New Integrated Platform for India’s Trade Insights, 2025)

9.3 Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership Concealment

Complex ownership structures spread across tax havens continue to conceal beneficial ownership through:

• nominee directors,

• layered subsidiaries,

• offshore trusts,

• shell corporations.

The absence of centralized beneficial ownership intelligence weakens financial investigations. (Beneficial Ownership Transparency: The Missing Link in AML Investigations, 2024)

banks. Countries with less stringent banking laws become tax-haven for the criminals, who by striking an understanding with the bank officials, deposit the crime proceeds in bank accounts and discreetly purchase some property with that money.

Electronic transfer has further facilitated criminal organizations in swift and almost risk-free transfer of funds between countries. With increased automation in banking and financial systems, there is lesser face-to-face contact between the customers and the bank officials. As a result, the chances of smelling a suspicious transaction turn remote. The actual modus operandi of money-laundering activity can be divided into 3 stages, viz., introduction, conversion and merger. The three stages are described as follows :

Initially the launderer introduces the criminal proceeds into the banking system. This can be done in more than one way; the most common being by disintegrating the proceeds into smaller sums which bear lesser chances of arousing suspicion. Alternatively, the launderer may transfer funds in various accounts in different locations through a number of financial instruments of smaller denomination.

The next stage is of conversion, which is achieved by making a series transactions, with a view to distance the final application of proceeds from their original source. The basic objective is to camouflage the source by multiplicity of transactions so that it becomes more difficult to find trail of the criminal source. This is done simply by serial transfer of funds from one account to another, either physically or electronically. The objective is better served, if the various accounts are spread over different countries. At times, the transfer of funds may be disguised as payment for goods or services.

The last stage is merger of proceeds into the mainstream economy under disguise of a legitimate transaction such as investment in immovable property, or in establishment of a business, or in buying expensive items or luxuries.

Banks, thus, become an integral part of transactions of money-laundering, intentionally or more often unintentionally. The law on prevention of money-laundering has, therefore, assigned a major role for banks in fulfilling the international endeavour.

Assessing Authorities' Stand in OCM/Demonetisation Assessment Cases concerning Assesses' Claims of Cash deposits being made out of Cash Sales in Business

5. In the cases of persons engaged in business and maintaining books of accounts, the most common and natural explanation and justification for the cash deposits being made by them in the post demonetisation period has been cash sales being made by them in their businesses.

The assessing authorities, in majority of the OCM assessment cases, have declined to accept the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made out of cash sales of business in post demonetisation period and have made huge income-tax demands under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in the regular assessment orders in such OCM/demonetisation cases. The most common arguments and contentions being made by the assessing authorities in rejecting the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made by the assessees out of their cash sales in business post demonetisation period are discussed as under:

i.

Since w.e.f. 8.11.2016 midnight, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes (SBNs) were declared invalid and were not to be considered as legal tender, therefore, for the assesses carrying on business, booking of cash sales and accepting such SBNs for transacting business transactions, during post demonetisation period, was prohibited.

ii.

The money measurement concept of accounting underlines the fact that in accounting and economics generally, every recorded event or transaction is measured in terms of money, i.e., the local currency monetary unit of measure. Since the SBNs were just a piece of papers and they bear no value on 9th November 2016 or after, as Central Government, the guarantor, had withdrawn its guarantee and hence, the receipt of these SBNs can't be journalized in books of account. Therefore, the transactions made in SBNs on or after 9th November 2016 cannot be entered into cash books.

iii.

Therefore, if the assessee has received any SBN notes after 09.11.2016 on account of any monetary transactions and utilizes the same for making cash deposits into the bank account, then the credit of the same into the books of accounts is not to be considered as valid and has to be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act and brought to tax.

In some other cases, where the cash deposits have been explained by the assessees as pertaining to cash sales being made by them prior to the demonetisation period, the assessing authorities have again rejected the genuineness and authenticity of such claims believing that the assessees might have backdated the cash sales just before the demonetisation period so as to reflect cash in hand as on 8.11.2016 consisting of banned notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000, which they have deposited in their bank accounts post demonetisation.

Swiss Legal Position: Reliance on Stolen Information

Till 2019, a total of 628 cases of HSBC Bank, Geneva, were reported accounting for undisclosed income of INR 8,465 crores were brought to tax. Out of these, over 208 cases were found to be "non-actionable because of no balances in account's information, non-residents, not traceable, an amount taxable in some other hand."

On administrative assistance relating to tax matters, on July 17, 2018 [decision no. 2C_648/2017], Swiss Supreme Court ('SSC') rendered a decision concerning stolen data. The court categorically distinguished its decision from an earlier decision dated March 17, 2017 on the same subject matter.

The decision rendered by the SSC on March 17, 2017 was based on the 'principle of good faith' as envisaged under the Swiss Criminal law, violation of which is a criminal offence. The court applied the principle and concluded that Swiss Federal Tax Administration ('FTA') cannot provide administrative assistance for any request made by foreign tax authorities based on the theft of data.

The subsequent decision of the SSC dated July 17, 2018, ruled that exchange of information based on stolen information will not per se be in violation of the 'principle of good faith' as contemplated under Article 7 of the Swiss Tax Administrative Assistance Act ('STAA'). The principle may defer basis the facts and circumstances of each case.

The exchange of stolen information would constitute violation if there were an explicit arrangement between India and Switzerland to not use the stolen data. As per SSC, there was no explicit declaration or assurance given by the Indian Tax Authorities to not use the stolen data and therefore, Indian Tax Authorities could use the said information.

The theory on administrative tax assistance was also considered in yet another decision of Swiss Supreme Court rendered on July 26, 2019, which makes it easier for foreign tax authorities to submit a general request for obtaining information without having to demonstrate concrete indication of alleged tax transgressions by account holders at Swiss banks.

For administrative tax assistance, the most crucial requirement is to depict that the request made by the tax authorities is for 'foreseeable relevance' and not for 'speculative requests' which are prohibited. With this premise, the tax authorities will be able to put in broad requests without having to showcase alleged tax transgressions.

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

VI. The Human Dimension of Compliance Beyond statutes and audits lies the behavioural aspect of compliance. Gold's emotional significance in India often translates into informal holdings within families. Many citizens view gold as a private inheritance rather than a financial instrument. This cultural mindset complicates formal disclosure.

Legal practitioners and policymakers must recognise this human element. Compliance should be accompanied by public education, awareness campaigns, and accessible disclosure mechanisms. Incentivising legitimate investment through Sovereign Gold Bonds, Exchange-Traded Funds, and regulated exchanges can help channel informal wealth into transparent avenues.

A. For Corporates and Financial Institutions

1.

Conduct comprehensive due diligence on all counterparties in domestic and international gold trade.

2.

Implement real-time monitoring systems and periodic AML training for compliance officers.

3.

Use standard benchmarks like LBMA and MCX for valuation to ensure transparency.

Maintain transfer-pricing documentation for all inter-company trades.

5.

Employ blockchain or digital traceability tools to create tamper-proof audit trails.

Report all cross-border transactions accurately under FEMA and PMLA requirements.

1.

Integrate data platforms across the ED, FIU, RBI, and Customs for seamless information flow.

VIII. Conclusion

Gold's brilliance today reflects both opportunity and risk. Its ascent in 2025 is not merely a market story but a mirror of geopolitical shifts and economic uncertainty. For India and other emerging economies, gold remains integral to cultural identity and financial security, yet its regulation defines the boundary between prosperity and peril.

The legal framework, which spans the Income-tax Act, PMLA, GAAR, FEMA, and Benami laws, offers a strong foundation. What is needed is harmonisation, technology-led enforcement, and a compliance culture that values integrity as much as investment.

When transparency governs trade, and law guides wealth, gold evolves from a shadowed asset into a symbol of lawful prosperity. The real value of gold lies not in its karats but in the clarity of the systems that sustain it.

A transparent, accountable, and globally aligned gold economy will not only safeguard national interests but also strengthen India's position as a credible participant in the international financial order.

[Part C of the Schedule to PMLA] and can give rise to proceedings under the PMLA. Judicial update

Recently, Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in Rajmandir Estates (P.) Ltd. v. Pr. CIT [2016] 386 ITR 162/240 Taxman 306/70 taxmann.com 124, had an occasion to deal with the issue of validity of reopening of assessment by CIT u/s. 263, in the backdrop of possible money-laundering.

The CIT in his order dated 22.03.13 passed under Section 263 opined that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went undetected due to lack of requisite enquiry and non-application of mind. He entertained the belief "that unaccounted money is laundered as clean share capital by creating a façade of paper work, routing the money through several bank accounts and getting it the seal of statutory approval by getting the case reopened u/s.147 suo motu. Accordingly he concluded that assessment order passed u/s. 143(3)/147 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. He, therefore, set aside the same and issued directions for a thorough enquiry.

Hon'ble High Court in its elaborate order after referring to the PMLA and observing various facets and evidences of possible money laundering under the peculiar facts of the case upheld the order of CIT u/s. 263 in following words:

"We have indicated above the pieces of evidence which go to show that the Commissioner had reasons to entertain the belief that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went unnoticed because the assessing officer did not hold requisite investigation except for calling for the records. ……. The fact that the assessing officer did not apply his mind to those pieces of evidence would be evident from the assessment order itself.

The question for consideration is whether in the presence of materials discussed above the Commissioner was justified in treating the assessment order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. That question in the facts and circumstances has to be answered in the affirmative."

It is important to note that, Hon'ble High Court distinguished some of the Supreme Court precedents cited by the appellant to support his case inter alia on the ground that The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 was not there on the statute at that point of time. Therefore, though offences under the Income Tax act, 1961 per se are not scheduled offences for the purpose of PMLA, nevertheless assessing officer can proceed in assessment or CIT can direct further investigation in order to verify possibility of income/assets added or declared u/s. 68, 69, 69A etc. of the IT act being sourced out of proceeds of crime as defined u/s. 2(u) of the PMLA, so that further action under PMLA, if necessary, can be taken.

Conclusion

It has to be kept in view that India has a problem of black economy, which is unacounted and many a time the holders of black money also launder the black money in order to acquire legitimate assets. Legal or illegal income which evades tax and illegal income that comes within the exempted taxation slab constitute the unreported Gross Domestic Product or black economy. Laundering the black money and laundering proceeds of crime are two different issues, although there is frequent overlap between the two. While laundering black money is to be handled through taxation laws or similar laws, the laundering of proceeds of crime is to be handled through special anti-money-laundering laws. [Dr. M. C. Mehanathan in his commentary on the Law of Prevention of Money Laundering in India published by Lexis Nexis (2014 edition)]

13. Review and Contemporary Analysis

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act has become one of the most important economic laws in India’s regulatory system. Over the years, it has strengthened the government’s ability to trace illegal money, investigate financial frauds, recover public assets, and tackle organized economic offences. Enforcement actions against banking scams, shell companies, Ponzi schemes, cyber frauds, and cross-border laundering networks have played a major role in protecting investors, financial institutions, and the broader economy.

Recent data released by the Enforcement Directorate shows the increasing scale of enforcement under the PMLA. As of March 2026, the ED had registered more than 8,800 ECIRs, issued over 3,500 provisional attachment orders, and attached assets worth nearly ₹2.36 lakh crore. During the financial year 2025–26 alone, attachments reportedly crossed ₹81,000 crore, marking a sharp rise compared to previous years.

These enforcement measures have also produced significant economic benefits. Official figures indicate that assets worth more than ₹63,000 crore have either been returned or steps have been taken to return them to banks, investors, financial institutions, and homebuyers affected by large-scale frauds. India has also strengthened international cooperation in tracing illegal financial flows and fugitive offenders. At the prosecution stage, nearly 2,400 complaints have been filed before Special Courts under the PMLA. Value of investments deemed to be income

In section 68, it is the amount credited in books and unexplained which is deemed to be income while in section 69C it is amount of unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be income. In section 69, it is the value of undisclosed/unexplained investments which shall be deemed to be income. Thus, while sections 68 and 69C involve no valuation issues, section 69 involves valuation issues. Section 142A of the Act empowers AO to refer the matter to the Valuation Officer.

Assessee made certain off-market transactions in shares through two stock brokers who were members of Calcutta Stock Exchange (CSE). Therefore, Assessing Officer made additions, treating cash credits of assessee as unexplained under section 68. Pahuja v. ITAT [2015] 54 taxmann.com 258/229 Taxman 252 (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. Y. M. Singla [2014] 50 taxmann.com 410/[2015] 228 Taxman 90 (Mag.) (P&H), SLP dismissed inY. M. Singla v. CIT [2015] 56 taxmann.com 17/230 Taxman 270 (SC).

Where, in order to prove genuineness of gift, the assessee had only filed an affidavit and copies of cheques and pay orders but did not file any of documents such as copy of proof of income of donor, copy of bank account of donor from where withdrawals were made along with proof of his identity, Tribunal rightly concluded that transaction of gift was sham [Seema Anil Modani v. ITO [2013] 40 taxmann.com 456/[2014] 220 Taxman 167 (Mag.) (Guj.)].

Mere declaration that gift was made out of love and affection in case of donor and donee being strangers is not sufficient [Pawan Kumar Aggarwal v. ITO [2015] 60 taxmann.com 133/234 Taxman 144 (Delhi)].

Foreign gifts - NRI gift from a stranger was neither genuine nor valid. Further it has been held that NRI gift could not be accepted as genuine unless the assessee was able to prove natural love and affection and financial capacity of the donor [Lal Chand Kalra v. CIT [1981] 22 CTR (P&H) 135; Smt. Rajrani Gupta v. DCIT [2012] 27 taxmann.com 235/211 Taxman 346 (Bom.)]. Also see, CIT v. Udham Singh & Sons [2014] 42 taxmann.com 192/222 Taxman 155 (Mag.) (P&H).

Once income of donor as per his return of income had not been disbelieved by assessing authority, then payment of meagre amount of Rs. 10 lakhs by him should not be doubted, merely because entire transcript of NRE account was not furnished [CIT v. S. K. Jain [2013] 31 taxmann.com 390/214 Taxman 10 (All.)].

A gift by a close relative through banking channels along with copy of cheque and acknowledgement of filing return in USA by him is not an unexplained gift [CIT v. Hatish Ramanlal Patel [2013] 35 taxmann.com 16/217 Taxman 26 (Guj.)].

Share application form is not an unimpeachable document, but a corroborative document - The mere filing of share application is not enough as the said application is not an unimpeachable document and does not on its own prove the genuineness or authenticity of the transaction. It can at best be treated as a corroborative document and cannot on its own be treated as sufficient for cross-verification of the transaction [CIT v. N. Tarika Properties Investment (P.) Ltd. [2013] 40 taxmann.com 525/[2014] 221 Taxman 14 (Delhi), SLP dismissed inN. Tarika Properties Investment (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2014] 51 taxmann.com 387/227 Taxman 373 (SC)].

17.7

No additions u/s 69C for purchases paid through banking channels and evidenced by delivery challans, purchase bills etc.

Where assessee-proprietor, engaged in resale of industrial goods, made payments through banking channels towards certain purchases and furnished evidences in form of delivery challans, purchase bills etc. relating to same, Tribunal was justified in holding that assessee had discharged initial burden or onus of providing details of parties and, thus, case did not fall within ambit of section 69C. [Principal Commissioner of Income-tax v. Jagdish Thakkar [2022] 145 taxmann.com 414 (Bombay)]

Where Assessing Officer having noticed that assessee had shown in account books purchases of milk made from farmers in cash and it failed to provide contact number of farmers made addition of said amount to assessee's income under section 69C and Tribunal deleted addition holding that entire source of purchases was duly recorded in account books, as Tribunal returned findings of facts based on material on record, there was no substance in appeal. [Principal Commissioner of Income-tax (Central)-2 v. Param Dairy Ltd. [2022] 139 taxmann.com 546 (Delhi)]

UF) v. Asstt. CIT [2015] 61 taxmann.com 274 (Mad.)].

Where documents found during survey established that assessee was in possession of assets over and above assets declared in books of account against which surrender was made, retraction made by assessee after more than 3 months would not absolve assessee from its liability [Gurdev Agro Engineers v. CIT [2017] 80 taxmann.com 148 (P&H)]. Cross-examination - Additions held not sustainable on the basis of statements of persons who were not allowed to be cross examined by the assessee [CIT v. Indrajit Singh Suri [2013] 33 taxmann.com 281/215 Taxman 581 (Guj.)].

Discrepancies in valuation of stock - If there was actual discrepancy in the stocks hypothecated to the bank and that shown in the accounts, for which the assessee failed to explain by any acceptable explanation or material, no exception could be taken to the addition made by the authorities [Century Foams (P). Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 82 Taxman 575 (All.)]. Also see, Smt. Shakuntla Thukral v. CIT [2014] 52 taxmann.com 86/[2015] 230 Taxman 166 (P&H).

Where there was difference between the value of stock shown in accounts and the value disclosed to the bank, and the Tribunal's finding was that the AO had not been able to point out any discrepancy in the quantity of stock hypothecated to the bank and the quantity of stock as per books of account, on the face of such finding, even if there was some difference in the valuation of the said quantity of the stock in the balance-sheet, as against the valuation shown in the bank, it could not be said to be resulting into any income from undisclosed sources coming to the assessee capable of being added to its income [CIT v. Laxmi Engineering Industries [2009] 308 ITR 279 (Raj.)].

Where assessee had not maintained stock register and AO, on verification of records of assessee, found certain excess stock of bearings, he was justified in making addition on account of that as unexplained investment, since it was obligatory for assessee to maintain stock register so that one was able to ascertain actual position of stock lying with the assessee in which he was trading [Sanjay v. CIT [2006] 154 Taxman 101 (MP)].

Where nature and source of excess stock found during search was not specifically identifiable from profits which had accumulated from earlier years, AO was justified in holding that said excess stock was not undisclosed investment of assessee [PCIT v. Deccan Jewellera (P.) Ltd. [2021] 132 taxmann.com 73/283 Taxman 578 (AP), SLP notice issued inPCIT v. Deccan Tobacco Company [2022] 137 taxmann.com 470/286 Taxman 558 (SC)].

Documents to be examined by AO - Where a diary recovered during search at assessee's premises revealed a list of persons and various amounts mentioned against their names, said amounts could not be treated as assessee's unexplained investment when affidavits of aforesaid persons were not examined by AO [CIT v. ITAT [2012] 19 taxmann.com 61/206 Taxman 60 (Chhattisgarh)].

Estimation of value - It is only when, on the basis of material available on record, AO forms an opinion that provisions of section 69/69A/69B would apply to assessee's case, he can resort to section 142A for estimating value of such investment or expenditure. However, AO cannot call for report of valuer u/s 142A merely to determine whether there has been any unexplained investment or expenditure [Me & Mummy Hospital v. Asstt. CIT [2014] 45 taxmann.com 248/224 Taxman 65 (Mag.) (Guj.)].

Addition held not justified on the basis of project report which showed the estimated figures and did not prove that undisclosed investment was made by the assessee [CIT v. Vinayak Plasto Chem (P.) Ltd. [2014] 42 taxmann.com 43/221 Taxman 439 (Raj.)]. Also see, CIT v. Vatika Landbase (P.) Ltd. [2016] 67 taxmann.com 372/238 Taxman 448 (Delhi).

Loose slips - Where assessee purchased certain land at a consideration as shown in sale deed executed therefor and, subsequently, certain notes on loose sheets allegedly written by assessee, were found and seized by revenue during a search operation, Tribunal's finding that reliance could not be placed on those loose sheets and vendor's contradictory statements could not be relied on, was finding of fact [CIT v. P. V. Kalyanasundaram [2007] 164 Taxman 78 (SC)].

4.71

Cash deposits made by assessee during demonetisation period stood explained by availability of cash balance in its books

Where entire cash deposits made by assessee during demonetization period in Specified Bank Notes stood properly explained by availability of cash balance in its books, no addition thereon could be made under section 68 [Jet Freight Logistics Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-tax Appeal (NFAC) [2023] 146 taxmann.com 349 (Mumbai - Trib.)] Where assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 45 lacs in cash into bank account during demonetization period since deposit had been made from cash balance available in account books, there was no question of treating same as unexplained cash deposit [R.S. Diamonds India (P.) Ltd. v. ACIT [2022] 145 taxmann.com 545 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

Commissioner of Income-tax 16(2), Mumbai [2018] 100 taxmann.com 43 (Mumbai - Trib.)

Where High Court upheld Tribunal's order deleting addition in respect of undisclosed sales of flats on ground that sale was in fact carried out by developer and sale proceeds never came into possession of assessee, SLP filed against said decision was to be dismissed- Commissioner of Income-tax v. Sadiq Sheikh [2018] 100 taxmann.com 10 (SC) During search operation, assessee, in his statement, surrendered Rs.18 crores on account of investment made in purchase of jewellery, precious stones and Rs. 6 crores as cash in hand duly shown in books of account. Rs. 7 crores were surrendered in stipulation that details of same would be given in due course of time. However, no incriminating materials or documents had been brought on record for said amount of Rs. 7 crores. Since no assets of Rs. 7 crores were found by authorities, nor such assets were identified or declared by assessee, it could be inferred that no such assets actually existed and the Tribunal was right in holding that addition in respect of Rs. 7 crores was not based on any evidence - Commissioner of Income-tax v. Dilbagh Rai Arora [2019] 104 taxmann.com 371 (Allahabad)

Where excess jewellery found during search proceedings belonged to partners of assessee-jewellery firm, no addition was to be made in hands of firm treating same as firm's undisclosed income- Sri. Kavitha Jewellers v. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax, Special Investigation Circle [2019] 104 taxmann.com 445 (Madras)

12.16

When ornaments seized not considered unexplained [CBDT's Instruction No. 1916, dated 11-5-1994]

As per CBDT's Instruction No.1916 dated 11-5-1994, in the case of a person not assessed to wealth-tax gold jewellery and ornaments to the extent of 500 gms. per married lady 250 gms per unmarried lady and 100 gms. per male member of the family, need not be seized. So, gold jewellery and ornaments to this extent is not unexplained investment.

Unless Revenue shows anything to contrary, it is to be presumed that source of jewellery to the extent stated in CBDT Instruction No. 1916, dated 11-5-1994 stands explained [N. Roja v. ACIT, Central Circle-1 [2020] 117 taxmann.com 90 (Cuttack - Trib.)] If acquisition of jewellery is explained with proof, said quantity to be allowed separately over and above weight of jewellery allowed in CBDT Instruction No. 1916, dated 11-5-1994 [Ram Prakash Mahawar v. Deputy Commissioner of Income-tax, Central Circle Alvar (Raj.)[2020] 115 taxmann.com 241 (Jaipur - Trib.)]

The following judicial rulings may also be noted:

In view of instruction issued by Board that while making addition on account of unexplained investment in jewellery, at least, a credit of 500 grams per married lady and 250 grams for unmarried girl should be given - Rajendra C. Shah v. Jt. CIT [2007] 158 Taxman 170 (Mum.) (Mag.).

Since assessee's daughter-in-law and married daughters were in possession of gold jewellery, which was much below CBDT's prescribed limit of 500 grams, no addition could be sustained on that account - Dy. CIT v. Arjun Dass Kalwani [2006] 101 ITD 337 (Jodh.).

Where in search of assessee's premises, out of 770 gms. found, purchase of gold ornaments of 115 gms. could not be satisfactorily explained, while remaining 655 gms. Stood explained on account of fact that assessee's wife was having ornaments of her own, brought as marriage gift from her parents and also by fact that assessee and his children received them on various occasions by way of gifts and in view of fact that gold ornaments of 342 gms. belonging to wife was much below limit of 500 gms. indicated in CBDT's Instruction dated 11-5-1994, additions in this respect could not be sustained in assessee's hands. Similarly, in view of CBDT's Instruction, addition in respect of ornaments of 313 gms. attributed to assessee and his children would also be unwarranted as the benefit of doubt was to be given to the assessee up to 300 gms. at the rate of 100 gms. per male member of the family. - ITO v. Manilal. S. Dave [2001] 117 Taxman 23 (Ahd.) (Mag.)

Where certain jewellery and documents concerning their purchase were found from assessee's possession during search, merely on ground that premises was occupied jointly by assessee, his sons, their spouses and children, assessee could not claim that jewellery belonged to ladies and not to him. - K.P. Agarwal v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 117 TTJ (Agra) (TM) 1

Collecting jewellery of 906.900 gms. by a woman in a married life of 25 years in form of stree dhan or on other occasions is not abnormal and therefore, Assessing Officer was unjustified in treating only 400 gms. as 'reasonable' and treating remaining jewellery as 'unexplained'. Therefore, addition made was to be deleted. - Ashok Chaddha v. ITO [2011] 14 taxmann.com 57/202 Taxman 395 (Delhi)

As per Instruction No. 3/2017, dated 21-2-2017, housewife having no business income would not be questioned if bank deposits made by her during demonetization were found to be less than Rs. 2.50 lakhs [Smt. Uma Agrawal v. Income-tax Officer-1(3), Gwalior M.P [2021] 127 taxmann.com 735 (Agra - Trib.)]

The assessee is in the business of diamond trade and such stock was part of the business affair of the company. Therefore, since income declared is in the nature of business income, the same is not taxable under any of the section referred above and accordingly section 115BBE has no application in case." Section 115BBE does not apply to business receipts/business turnover. Where AO had accepted after confronting the assessee with facts that undisclosed amount of assessee in his bank account was undisclosed business receipts/turnover and made additions applying @ 4% net profit margin on the amount, section 115BBE would not be attracted and revisionary order under section 263 directing AO to apply section 115BBE cannot be sustained. Only probability and likelihood to find error in assessment order is not permitted under section 263, Commissioner ought to find out specific error in assessment order [Abdul Hamid v. Income-tax Officer [2020] 117 taxmann.com 986 (Gauhati - Trib.)]

In Principal Commissioner of Income Tax, 20, Delhi v. Akshit Kumar [2021] 124 taxmann.com 123 (Delhi), it was held that where quantum figure and opening stock was accepted in previous years during scrutiny assessments, receipt from sales made by assessee proprietary concern out of its opening stock could not be treated as unexplained income to be taxed as 'income from other sources'.

Where nature and source of excess stock found during search was not specifically identifiable from profits which had accumulated from earlier years, AO was justified in holding that said excess stock was not undisclosed investment of assessee and no case of perversity or lack of enquiry on part of Assessing Officer was made out so as to render his decision erroneous under Explanation 2 to section 263. In the present cases, explanations have been offered by the assessees that excess stock was a result of suppression of profits from business over the years and is a part of the overall stock found. In ITA Nos. 9 & 14 of 2021, the assessees concerned gave further clarification that the excess stock had been admitted in Schedule 'L' under the heading, 'other operating income' under the head "Profits and Gains of the Business" in Part A of the Return filed for the relevant Assessment Year. Hence, the excess stock could not have been treated as 'undisclosed investment' under section 69 of the Act. [PCIT v. Deccan Jewellers (P.) Ltd. [2021] 132 taxmann.com 73 (AP)]

AO can't make additions u/s 69A on a hypothetical basis without carrying out enquiry to find out more details. Where assessee sold several flats during year and pursuant to search, a letter addressed to one DS showed that DS paid Rs. 57.73 lakhs towards purchase of flat, whereas agreement value with reference to same was Rs. 49.18 lakhs and Assessing Officer multiplied difference in sale price to number of flats sold and made additions under section 69A, Tribunal having accepted assessee's explanation that initially said flat was negotiated for a sum of Rs. 59.34 lakhs, however, later booking was cancelled and thereafter it was sold at Rs. 49.18 lakhs to DS, entire additions having been made by Assessing Officer without enquiry on hypothetical basis, Tribunal had not committed any perversity or applied incorrect principles to given facts to set aside additions so made [PCIT v. Nexus Builders and Developers (P.) Ltd. [2022] 134 taxmann.com 82 (Bom.)]

Where AO made addition under section 68 on account of huge cash amount deposited by assessee-jeweller in its bank account post demone-tization, since assessee had explained source of said cash deposits as sales of jewellery, produced sale bills and admitted same as revenue receipt as well as offered it to tax and assessee also represented outgo of stocks which was matching with sales, impugned addition was to be deleted [ACIT v. Hirapanna Jewellers [2021] 128 taxmann.com 291 (Visakhapatnam - Trib.)]

Where assessee-builder received certain on-money receipts from buyers of flats, since nature and source of same being duly accepted by Assessing Officer in remand report, same would construe only as business receipt and not as cash credit under section 68 [Dy. CIT v. Adarsh Industrial Estate (P.) Ltd. [2021] 130 taxmann.com 142 (Mum. - Trib.)]

Where assessee was not an individual but a partnership firm whose only source of income was business income, undisclosed income embedded in undisclosed business transactions would not attract section 115BBE. However, undisclosed income attributable to excess cash from other sources would attract section 115BBE [Saaras Agro Industries v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax [2022] 143 taxmann.com 319 (Indore - Trib.)]
