12.60

Jewellery seized already declared in WT returns

If jewellery in question had been shown in wealth-tax return filed before date of search, it could not be treated as unexplained investment in gold jewellery-Mahadev Prasad Agarwal v. CIT [2004] 136 Taxman 211 (Raj.)

Where assessee declared 3659 gms. of jewellery in her WT returns and only 953 gms. found in search and assessee explained that she had given 2706 gms. to her husband who sold them to meet his obligations, AO was justified in taxing capital gains from sale of jewellery. But in the absence of any material that indicated that 2706 gms. have been again purchased, AO not justified in treating value of 2706 gms. as unexplained investments and the addition deserves to be deleted. - CIT v. Smt. V. Prema [2007] 163 Taxman 726 (Mad.)

12.10

Instances in which explanation as to source of investments were held to be satisfactory

The following are some of the instances in which the explanation offered by the assessee was held to be satisfactory:

Where as a part of memorandum of understanding between group companies, certain shares of a group company was transferred to assessee at cost and all these investments were recorded in books of account and it was not case of Revenue that assessee had paid any amount in excess of what was recorded in books and apparent consideration was not real consideration, no addition was sustainable under section 69. - Rupee Finance & Management (P.) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 22 SOT 174 (Mum.)

Note : Even if it was a case of apparent consideration not being the real consideration, section 69B and not section 69 will be attracted.

Where assessee was in Government service for 39 years and after retirement he had received retiremental benefits in cash and had been receiving pension since year 1996 and Revenue had not found any investment elsewhere, except in purchase of jeep, it could be concluded that assessee was having sufficient funds to purchase jeep from savings of salary as well as pension and amount received on retirement and impugned addition was to be deleted - Nagarmal Sharma v. ITO [2009] 30 SOT 4 (Jodh.)(URO)

Where cash found during course of search was duly explained by assessee as belonging to its various firms/companies and cash in hands of firms/companies were duly explained as having been withdrawn from their bank accounts, addition not justified - CIT v. Sanjay Raj Shobha [2010] 2 DTL ONLINE 290 (Delhi)

Where property-in-question was bought and later on sold by assessee's son and investment was duly reflected in accounts of son, no addition on account of unexplained investment could be made in hands of assessee, even though receipt was in assessee's name. - Hafiz Mohammad v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 298 ITR 315 (Raj.)

Where assessee in order to demonstrate that it had made addition to fixed asset contended that such assets had duly been reflected in audited accounts and produced evidence to show enhanced production capacity, enhanced power charges, enhanced electric load and term loan obtained by assessee for expansion purpose, addition on account of unexplained investment was not justified-Victoria Foods (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2010] 3 ITR (Trib.) 35 (Delhi)

Where assessee a non-resident had substantial Non-Resident Non-Repatriable (NRNR), Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR), and NRSB deposits, as assessee had brought money into India through proper banking channel, it could be said that onus on assessee under section 69 stood discharged and, therefore, it was not taxable in India under section 5(2)(b). - Smt. Susila Ramasamy v. Asstt. CIT [2010] 37 SOT 146 (Chennai)

Where it was seen from records that assessee had advanced amount in question to his HUF for making payments to 'A' and that HUF had fully repaid loan in subsequent years, CIT(A) rightly concluded that property belonged to HUF and, therefore, no addition in respect of said property could be made to assessee's income. - Asstt. CIT v. Rakesh S. Agrawal [2010] 36 SOT 148 (Ahd.)

Since assessee had explained that stamp duty was paid by him out of advance amount as reflected in balance sheet and only accounting adjustment remained to be made, in such situation without bringing any adverse material on record, Assessing Officer was not justified in making addition. - Om Prakash Joshi v. ITO [2009] 34 SOT 33 (Jodh.) (URO)

Satisfaction of Assessing Officer himself is of prime importance while making assessment of an income and these duties cannot be performed by substituting satisfaction of someone else (for example, satisfaction of sales tax department). Where Assessing Officer had made addition merely on basis of observations made by Sales-tax Department and had not conducted any independent enquiries for making addition and moreover assessee had discharged primary onus cast on him by showing purchase in books of account, payment by way of account payee cheque, and producing vouchers of sales of goods, in such circumstances, alleged purchase could not be considered as bogus and addition made in said respect was to be deleted. - ITO v. Permanand [2008] 25 SOT 11 (Jodh.) (URO)

(Guj.).

Gifts - Where assessee received gifts from two persons on behalf of his daughters on occasion of their marriage since said gifts were made by demand drafts and genuineness of same was confirmed by bank in which person making gifts had their accounts, impugned addition made u/s 69A was to be set aside [CIT v. Jawahar Lal Oswal [2016] 67 taxmann.com 168/238 Taxman 225 (P&H)]. Jewellery - Collecting jewellery of 906 grams by a woman in a married life of 25 years in the form of stree dhan or on other occasions such as child birth, etc., is not abnormal and, hence, addition of 506 grams by the AO is unjustified [Ashok Chaddha v. ITO [2011] 14 taxmann.com 57/202 Taxman 395 (Delhi)]. Also see, CIT v. Prafulbhai @ Rohitbhai J. Shah [2013] 33 taxmann.com 147/215 Taxman 86 (Mag.) (Guj.); CIT v. Ghanshyam Das Johri [2014] 41 taxmann.com 295 (All.); CIT v. Satya Narain Patni [2014] 46 taxmann.com 440/224 Taxman 312 (Raj.).

Money belongs to third parties - Where amount received by assessee via pay orders in its bank account did not belong to him and assessee was only a conduit through whom amounts were floated and said amount was added to income of its beneficiary, no addition could be made to income of assessee [CIT v. Anoop Jain [2019] 112 taxmann.com 355/[2020] 268 Taxman 427 (Delhi)].

Lack of documentary evidence - Amount received by assessee on maturity of certain policies by cheque could not be treated as unexplained moneys u/s 69A merely because assessee could not furnish necessary information before AO due to some unavoidable circumstances [CIT v. Sonia Dhillon [2012] 21 taxmann.com 107/207 Taxman 67 (Mag.) (P&H)]. Also see, CIT v. Jeet Construction Co. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 526 (All.), SLP dismissed inCIT v. Jeet Construction Co. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 527/278 Taxman 293 (SC).

Where there was neither trace of creditor nor any document evidencing loan terms or any special relationship between parties on account whereof huge loan of Rs. 30 lakhs could be given without demand of any interest, such loan recorded in assessee's books of account was to be added to income of assessee u/s 69A [Namdev Arora v. CIT [2016] 72 taxmann.com 124/241 Taxman 303 (P&H)].

Loose papers - Investigation could not have been directed in case of high public functionaries on basis of legally inadmissible evidence in form of loose papers. In this case, raids were conducted on the two business groups and incriminating materials in form of random sheets and loose papers, computer prints, hard disk, pen drives etc. were found. Question arose as to whether a case was made out on the basis of above materials, to constitute Special Investigation Team (SIT) and direct investigation against the various functionaries/officers and further monitor the same. It was held that the department had no evidence to prove that the entries in these loose papers and electronic data were kept regularly during the course of business of concerned business house. Thus, these detailed documents recovered by the authorities had no evidentiary values and they could not have been relied on to direct registration of the FIR and investigation in case of high public functionaries occupying important offices. Further, the materials in question were not only irrelevant but were also legally inadmissible u/s 34 of the Evidence Act [Common Cause (A Registered Society) v. UOI [2017] 77 taxmann.com 245/245 Taxman 214 (SC)].

IDENTITY OF THE PERSON PAN card - The word 'identity' meant the condition or fact of a person or thing being that specified unique person or thing. Mere production of Permanent Account Number (PAN) or assessment particulars does not establish the identity of a person. The identification of a person includes the place of work, the staff and the fact that it was actually carrying on business and further recognition of the said company/individual in the eyes of public. PAN cannot be blindly and without consideration of surrounding circumstances treated as sufficiently disclosing the identity of the individual [CIT v. N. R. Portfolio (P.) Ltd. [2014] 42 taxmann.com 339/222 Taxman 157 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

Banking transaction - The very fact that all the transactions were entered into between the parties through account-payee cheques makes the question of identity of creditors fall into oblivion and it becomes absolutely irrelevant [Addl. CIT v. Bahri Bros. (P.) Ltd. [1985] 22 Taxman 3 (Pat.)].

In case of shareholders - If the shareholders exist then, possibly, no further enquiry need be made. But if the AO finds that the alleged shareholders do not exist then, in effect, it would mean that there is no valid issuance of share capital. Shares cannot be issued in the name of non-existing persons. If the shareholders are identified and it is established that they have invested money in the purchase of shares, then the amount received by the company would be regarded as a capital receipt but if the assessee offers no explanation at all or the explanation offered is not satisfactory, then the provisions of section 68 may be invoked [CIT v. Sophia Finance Ltd. [1993] 70 Taxman 69 (Delhi - FB)].

CREDITWORTHINESS OF THE PERSON

Earning capacity - Creditworthiness of the donor would depend upon the income and earning of the donor and whether and did he have necessary funds. Rarely one finds a poor man giving gifts to a rich and powerful, out of natural love and affection [Pawan Kumar Aggarwal v. ITO [2015] 60 taxmann.com 133 = [2015] 234 Taxman 144 (Delhi)].

Payment by cheque, etc. - Creditworthiness is not proved by showing issue and receipt of a cheque or by furnishing a copy of statement of bank account, when circumstances requires that there should be some more evidence of positive nature to show that the subscribers had made genuine investment or had acted as angel investors after due diligence or for personal reasons. There should be some positive evidence to show the nature and resources of the share subscribers [CIT v. Nipun Builders & Developers [2013] 30 taxmann.com 292/214 Taxman 429 (Delhi)].

When payment by cheque did not establish the creditworthiness of the lender, mere examination of the pass book or the bank statement or the letter of confirmation or the balance sheet of the lender was not enough [CIT v. Maithan International [2015] 56 taxmann.com 283/231 Taxman 381 (Cal.)].

Income-tax assessee - When the cash creditor is an income-tax assessee, it cannot be said that he is not a man of means [Kamal Motors v. CIT [2003] 131 Taxman 155 (Raj.)].

Deposits from tenants - In regard to deposit from tenants, it is sufficient if the assessee proves the identity of the tenant and the genuineness of the transaction under which the deposit is made. It will not be necessary for the assessee to prove the capacity of the tenant to make the deposit/advance [CIT v. Nevendram Ahuja [2007] 290 ITR 453 (MP)].

GENUINENESS OF THE TRANSACTION

Burden of proof - The burden of proving genuineness of a transaction of receipt of income by him from a claimed source, particularly income on the basis of which exemption of tax is claimed, is on the assessee. The said burden can be discharged by him either by leading evidence or from the circumstances on record. In absence of positive evidence of the assessee, the AO, by applying test of human probabilities can draw an inference of money being undisclosed income of the assessee [CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1969] 72 ITR 807 (SC); CIT v. Daulat Ram Rawatmull [1973] 87 ITR 349 (SC)].

In such factual scenario, the Assessing Officers as well as the CIT(A) have adopted an inferential process which is a process which would be followed by a reasonable and prudent person. The Assessing Officers and the CIT(A) have culled out proximate facts in each of the cases, took into consideration the surrounding circumstances which came to light after the investigation, assessed the conduct of the assessee, took note of the proximity of the time between the buy and sale operations and also the sudden and steep rise of the price of the shares of the companies when the general market trend was admittedly recessive and thereafter arrived at a conclusion which in our opinion is a proper conclusion and in the absence of any satisfactory explanation by the assessee, the Assessing Officers were bound to make addition under Section 68 of the Act.

In the post-demonetization period persons having old currency notes from unexplained sources have deposited the same in the accounts of other persons including fictitious persons for withdrawing the same in new currency later for their use. Now the controversy also arises whether a person who genuinely purchases the shares at a low price and sold at high price, therefore, he enjoyed the windfall from such scripts, can he be disallowed the benefit of tax exemption provided under section 10(38) of the Act in a situation where it is established that the share price of the company was rigged up to extend the benefit to certain parties. Justice cannot be delivered in a mechanical manner. In other words, what we see on the records available before us, sometime we have to travel beyond it after ignoring the same. Furthermore, while delivering the justice, we have to ensure in this process that culprits should only be punished and no innocent should be castigated. An innocent person should not suffer for the wrongdoings of the other parties. In the case on hand, admittedly there was no evidence available on record suggesting that the assessee or his broker was involved in the rigging up of the price of the script of M/s Shree Nath Commercial & Finance Ltd. Thus, it appears that the assessee acted in the given facts and circumstances in good-faith.

Where assessee claimed exemption under section 10(38) towards long-term capital gains (LTCG) earned on sale of shares of AGL and furnished various documentary evidence in form of copies of contract notes, demat account, details of share transactions etc., onus casted upon assessee in terms of section 68 was discharged and, therefore, impugned addition made against alleged bogus LTCG was to be deleted. [Jatinder Kumar Jain v. Income-tax Officer [2022] 142 taxmann.com 234 (Chandigarh - Trib.)

quantity details etc. [Para 12.75]

CIT(A) cannot enhance addition made by AO u/s 69 without giving notice of enhancement/show cause notice to the assessee [Para 12.76]

Additions to plant and machinery made by assessee evidenced by purchase bills [Para 12.77]

Addition not justified as assessee submitted that cash was deposited out of sale proceeds of potatoes by producing balance sheet, P&L etc. [Para 12.78] When assessee can claim Peak credit and Telescoping reliefs in respect of additions [Para 12.79]

No additions in respect of Jewellery seized where payment for the same was made through banking channels and the same was duly accounted in books [Para 12.79A]

Difference in amount of investment as shown in fixed asset schedule and balance sheet [Para 12.80]

Ready Reckoner of possible legal consequences of investments depending on source and nature of income & Manner of investment of income [SeePara 12.85]

15.52

Gold jewellery found during search explained as belonging to mother who was residing with assessee

In view of CBDT Instruction No. 1916 of 11-5-1994, where gold jewellery was found during search at residential premises of assessee's husband which belonged to assessee's mother, since mother was residing with assessee and assessee was her only daughter, mother would be considered family member and said jewellery would not be treated as unexplained investment. [Muppavarapu Kavitha v. Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax [2022] 142 taxmann.com 250 (Visakhapatnam - Trib.)]

UNEXPLAINED INVESTMENTS UNDER SECTION 69

| SALIENT FEATURES/ACTION POINTS |
| --- |
| If an 'unexplained investment' is 'undisclosed asset located outside India', the same will be taxed under the Black Money (Undisclosed Income & Assets) Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 (BM Act), not u/s 69 read with section 115BBE(1) in the year of detection. It will also entail penalty and prosecution under that Act. Investments covered u/s 69 are those made by the assessee, not by any other person such as his father/mother. If investment made by assessee, it will be covered u/s 69 even if it stands in some other person's name. Basis of invoking section 69 is assessee made investments, not ownership. Unlike section 68, section 69 applies regardless of assessee maintains books of account or not. Assessee bound to justify the source of investments made by him either by showing the entry in the books of account, if any, maintained by him for any source of income. If no entry in books or he does not maintain books, then he is bound to offer satisfactory explanation to AO as to the nature and source of the investments. Obligation to offer satisfactory explanation is on the assessee, not on his legal heirs or any other person. Jewellery disclosed in Wealth Tax Return before the date of search has been held not 'unexplained investment'. As per CBDT's Instruction No.1916 dated 11-5-1994, in the case of a wealth-tax assessee, gold jewellery and ornaments found in excess of the gross weight declared in the wealth-tax return only need to be seized. The Finance Act, 2015 has repealed the Wealth-tax Act,1957. So, it is no longer possible to file WT returns. By way of analogy, it can be said that disclosure of any investment in Schedule AL of ITR forms would achieve the same effect. CBDT needs to clarify this. As per CBDT's Instruction No.1916 dated 11-5-1994, in the case of a person not assessed to wealth-tax gold jewellery and ornaments to the extent of 500 gms. per married lady 250 gms per unmarried lady and 100 gms. per male member of the family, need not be seized. So, gold jewellery and ornaments to this extent is not unexplained investment. Explanation of nature and source furnished by assessee should be a factual explanation and not a mere legal argument. If assessee is able to partly explain the source and nature of investments by way of entry in his books of account or otherwise, then section 69B shall apply and not section 69. See Para 2.12/Para 2.13 as regards voluntary disclosure of unexplained investments under section 69. Unexplained investments made by the assessee in the name of benamidars will be covered under section 69 as well as the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988 (PBPT Act). This would mean tax and penalty under the Act as well as confiscation and prosecution under the PBPT Act. Unexplained investments in assessee's name made where he is the benamidar will not be taxed under section 69 as assessee's income as investments have not been made by the assessee but by the beneficial owner. The investment would be liable for confiscation under Benami Act and both the benamidar-assessee and beneficial owner will be liable for prosecution under the Benami Act. It is quite possible that the investment may be taxed u/s 69 in the hands of beneficial owner. |

12.0

Overview of section 69

Section 69 constitutionally valid [Para 12.1]

Unaccounted and unexplained investments [Para 12.2]

Interpretation of 'investments' [Para 12.3]

Investments which are 'undisclosed foreign assets' will be taxed under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, 2015 ('the BM Act') and not under section 69 [Para

-tax provisions, it can only be a currency token, bank notes or other circulating medium in general use, which has the representative value. Therefore, the currency notes on the day when they were found to be in possession of the assessee should have had the representative value, namely, it could be tendered as a money, which has intrinsic value [CIT v. Andhra Pradesh Yarn Combines (P.) Ltd. [2006] 153 Taxman 121 (Kar.)]. Bitumen, not a 'valuable article' – Bitumen is not a valuable article in the context of s. 69A [D.N. Singh v. CIT [2023] 150 taxmann.com 301/293 Taxman 550/454 ITR 595 (SC), setting aside D.N. Singh v. CIT [2010] 324 ITR 304 (Patna)].

'Income' has wider meaning - The expression 'income', as used in section 69A, has wide meaning which meant anything which came in or resulted in gain [Chuharmal v. CIT [1988] 38 Taxman 190 (SC)].

Receipt by assessee's agent - Assessee could not escape liability u/s 69A by merely pleading that amount in question was not received by him rather it was received by his agent [Mahesh Kumar Agarwal v. Asstt. CIT [2019] 104 taxmann.com 254 (Pat.)].

Burden of proof - The burden is not on the department to prove that the assessee is the owner of the amount found in the possession of the assessee [CIT v. K. T. M. S. Mohamood [1997] 92 Taxman 169 (Mad.)]. Where there were unaccounted sale transactions, onus was on assessee to show that unaccounted investment in purchases was out of accounted stock, and it could not be presumed that unaccounted sales must have been made from accounted purchases [CIT v. Ajay Kapoor [2013] 36 taxmann.com 513/219 Taxman 42 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

TAXABILITY

Burden of proof not discharged - Where wrist watches were found in the possession of a person, and that person did not adduce any evidence, far less discharged the onus, of proving that wrist watches did not belong to him, the value of the wrist watches could be treated as the income of the assessee [Chuharmal v. CIT [1988] 38 Taxman 190 (SC)].

Where assessee was managing a firm which collected deposits from public, but there was no evidence regarding registration and genuineness of firm and assessee could not explain source of deposits, nor could assessee establish that such deposits did not belong to him, addition of such deposits as assessee's unexplained investments was justified [CIT v. K. Chinnathamban [2007] 162 Taxman 459 (SC)].

Where assessee failed to justify his stand that there was no unaccounted sale as indicated in seized documents, addition made on basis of seized documents was justified [CIT v. S. Rudramuniyappa [2015] 64 taxmann.com 411 (Kar.), SLP dismissed inS. Rudramuniyappa v. CIT [2016] 75 taxmann.com 241/243 Taxman 353 (SC)].

No entry in books of account - Where amount surrendered during survey was not reflected in books of account and no source from where it was derived was declared by assessee, it was assessable as deemed income of assessee u/s 69A [Kim Pharma (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [2013] 35 taxmann.com 456/216 Taxman 153 (Mag.) (P&H)].

Family transaction - Where certain amount was transferred from parents' bank account to assessee's bank account, there being transfer of funds inter se between family members, no addition could be made to assessee's income u/s 69A in respect of the aforesaid amount [CIT v. Palwinder Pal Singh [2012] 17 taxmann.com 17/204 Taxman 55 (Mag.) (P&H)]. Also see, CIT v. Meghjibhai Popatbhai Virani [2013] 35 taxmann.com 100/217 Taxman 35 (Mag.) (Guj.).

Gifts - Where assessee received gifts from two persons on behalf of his daughters on occasion of their marriage since said gifts were made by demand drafts and genuineness of same was confirmed by bank in which person making gifts had their accounts, impugned addition made u/s 69A was to be set aside [CIT v. Jawahar Lal Oswal [2016] 67 taxmann.com 168/238 Taxman 225 (P&H)].

's books had been prepared on basis of bills and vouchers and there was no allegation that either purchase of raw-material or production was found unrecorded, mere fact that there was some variation during few months in electricity consumption could not be a basis for making addition on account of unaccounted production and gross profit on unaccounted sales [CIT v. Paras Agro Products [2014] 42 taxmann.com 411/222 Taxman 60 (Mag.) (Guj.)]. Profit element is to be taxed - When undisclosed purchases are discovered in course of assessment, it is only profit embedded in said transactions which can be added to total income u/s 69C [PCIT v. Subarna Rice Mill [2018] 96 taxmann.com 286/257 Taxman 509 (Cal.), SLP dismissed inPCIT v. Subarna Rice Mill [2020] 114 taxmann.com 572/269 Taxman 565 (SC)]. Also see, PCIT v. Jakharia Fabric (P.) Ltd. [2020] 118 taxmann.com 406/274 Taxman 52 (Bom.).

No double taxation - Once 'on money' was considered as revenue receipt and addition to income was made, then any expenditure out of such money could not be treated as unexplained expenditure, doing so would amount to double addition [CIT v. Golani Brothers [2017] 85 taxmann.com 355/250 Taxman 446 (Bom.)].

Deemed income not to be allowable as deductible expenditure - Proviso to section 69C inserted w.e.f. 1-4-1999 does not apply retrospectively. The deemed income (where the source of the expenditure is not explained) cannot be allowed as a deduction under any head of income [P. Ram Gopal Varma v. DCIT [2013] 40 taxmann.com 106/[2014] 220 Taxman 84 (Mag.) (AP)].

Where assessee had not incurred any expenditure in relevant FY on purchase of plot, Tribunal had rightly deleted disallowance of pro rata cost on sale of part of plot holding that proviso to section 69C could also not have been invoked [CIT v. Chandulal Sadhuram Khemani [2015] 53 taxmann.com 293 (Bom.)].

onus is required to be placed on such companies besides the general onus to establish identity and creditworthiness of creditor and genuineness of transaction. This additional onus, needs to be placed on such companies to also prove the source of money in the hands of such shareholder or persons making payment towards issue of shares before such sum is accepted as genuine credit. If the company fails to discharge the additional onus, the sum shall be treated as income of the company and added to its income". The judicial pronouncements referred in the Memorandum, inter alia, include:

♦ CIT v. Lovely Exports (P.) Ltd. [2008] 216 CTR 195 (SC)

The onus cast upon the assessee company was discharged upon disclosure of the names and particulars of the alleged bogus shareholders. It was for the Department to conduct its own enquiry thereafter and additions if any may be made in the hands of the shareholders.

♦ CIT v. Steller Investment Ltd. [2001] 115 Taxman 99 (SC)

Even if subscribers to the capital are not genuine, the amount received by the company as share capital could not be assessed in the hands of the company itself. Such amounts should be considered for assessment in the hands of persons who are alleged to have really advanced the money.

♦ CIT v. Divine Leasing & Finance Ltd. [2007] 158 Taxman 440 (Delhi) - Delhi High Court held that the amount of share application money received by a Company from alleged bogus shareholders could not be regarded as undisclosed income u/s 68 when the assessee furnished details regarding shareholders. If the names of the alleged bogus shareholders are given to the AO, then the Department is free to proceed to reopen their individual assessments in accordance with law. The Supreme Court upheld this view.

♦ CIT v. STL Extrusion (P.) Ltd. [2011] 333 ITR 269/ 11 taxmann.com 125 (MP)

Where assessee had duly discharged its onus by furnishing names, age, address, date of filing application of share, number of shares of each subscriber, the AO was not justified in making addition u/s 68.

♦ CIT v. Arunananda Textiles (P.) Ltd. [2011] 203 Taxman 32 (Mag.)/ 15 taxmann.com 226 (Kar.)

It was not for the assessee to place material before the Assessing Officer about creditworthiness of the shareholders. Once the company had given the addresses of the shareholders and their identity was not in dispute, it was for the Assessing Officer to make further inquiry with the investors about their capacity to invest the amount in shares.

♦ CIT v. Dwarkadhish Investment (P.) Ltd. [2010] 194 Taxman 43/[2011] 330 ITR 298 (Delhi)

Once the assessee proves the identity of creditors/share applicants, by either furnishing their PAN or income-tax assessment numbers, and shows genuineness of transaction by showing money in his books either by account payee cheque or by draft or by any other mode, onus of proof would shift to revenue.

♦ CIT v. Creative World Telefilms Ltd. [2011] 203 Taxman 36/ 333 ITR 100/ 15 taxmann.com 183 (Bom.)

Once documents like PAN card, bank account details or details from the bankers were given by the assessee, onus shifts upon the Assessing Officer and it is on him to reach the shareholders. The Assessing Officer could not burden the assessee merely on the ground that summons issued to the investors were returned back with the endorsement not traceable.

The decisions were based on a settled legal position, applicable to any 'cash credit', like, loans, deposits, advances, share capital or others, that:

♦ Primary onus is on assessee;

♦ an assessee does not have to establish source of source;

♦ if primary onus is discharged, burden shifts to Tax Department;

♦ AO needs to discharge his burden and reach an objective satisfaction;

♦ AO has a discretion to assess cash credits;

♦ in a given case the amount can be assessed in the hands of investor/lender under other applicable provisions of law, like, section 69.

15.2.3 Salient features of the first proviso

♦ If a closely held company (that is, a company in which public are not substantially interested),

♦ Credits any sum (consisting of share application money, share capital, share premium or any such amount by whatever name called) in its books of account to a resident person,

♦ Explanation about the credit, in terms of section 68 (without considering proviso, as inserted) would not be deemed to be satisfactory, unless:

- Person in whose name such credit is recorded offers an explanation about the nature and the source of such credit; and

- Explanation by such person is to the satisfaction of AO,

♦ The amount so received would be treated as unexplained cash credit and accordingly included in its income.

16.2

Trigger for section 69B

Trigger for section 69B is not possession of some valuable article. Trigger for section 69B is that:

assessee has made any investment or is found to be the owner of any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article and such bullion, jewellery or valuable article in the financial year in question;

the amount expended by him on the investment or on the acquisition of money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article exceeds the amount recorded in the books of account maintained by the assessee; and

the assessee offers no explanation as to such excess amount or the explanation offered by him is not satisfactory in the opinion of the AO

Section 69B is attracted such excess amount is not satisfactorily explained as to source either by way of entry in books of account maintained for any source of income or otherwise as having been met out of tax-paid income of past years or out of tax-free incomes or out of non-taxable capital receipts such as loans/deposits. If entire expenditure is not satisfactorily explained by way of entry in books of account for any source of income or otherwise, then section 69 or section 69A (as the case may be) shall apply and not section 69B.

Where there was a clear admission by assessee firm that excess stock found during survey was added in its stock register but no corresponding entry was passed in books of account, it could be considered that investment in such stock was made out of undisclosed source, thus, addition was to be made under section 69B in respect of such excess stock [SVS Oil Mills v. ACIT [2020] 113 taxmann.com 388 (Madras)]

merged.text: INCOME TAX: Where assessee, diamond trader, imported diamonds and purchases were executed through banking channels and in compliance with statutory provisions, furthermore sine purchases were accepted as genuine with proper supporting documents, expenditure on such purchases could not be treated as unexplained merely because sales were made in cash or buyers could not be fully identified, and thus, disallowance under section 69C was unjustified

HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 / Section  105  of the Income-tax Act, 2025 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessee, a diamond trader, imported diamonds in accordance with Customs Act and other applicable laws - Assessing Officer noted that assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales aggregating to Rs. 97 crores - He thus, opined that since source of purchase was cash received from these sales, purchases amounting to Rs. 97.13 crores (being amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under section 69C - It was noted that assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores - Whether since purchases had been accepted to be genuine and those purchases had been executed through proper documents and banking channels, its source could not be said to be unexplained - Held, yes -Whether if an assessee was allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there was no non-compliance of any statutory provision, purchase could not be disallowed - Held, yes - Whether best case, which Assessing Officer could frame against assessee was that identity of buyers was not known or persons to whom sales were made were not verifiable, but that by itself did not fall foul to any of statutory provisions - Held, yes - Whether thus, impugned addition made under section 69C on account of cash sales was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 12] [In favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of dealing in diamonds. The assessee imported diamonds from various countries in accordance with the provisions of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law.

■

The Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had issued 6,358 cash sale bills of less than Rs. 2 lakhs each aggregating to Rs. 97 crores. He, thus, treated the corresponding purchase expenditure of Rs. 97 crores as unexplained on the ground that the source of expenditure was cash from these retail sales and disallowed the purchase expenditure.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition made under section 69C.

■

On appeal, the Tribunal upheld the deletion noting that all purchases were made through banking channels after payment of customs duties and were supported by purchase and import documents.

■

On appeal to the High Court :

HELD: ■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. In any event, the assessee had an opening stock of Rs. 114.62 crores and had imported diamonds worth Rs. 97 crores. Meaning thereby, he has sold the diamonds, which he had purchased obviously for business reasons. The best case, which the Assessing Officer can frame against the assessee was that identity of the sellers is not known or the persons to whom sales were made is not verifiable, but that by itself does not fall foul to any of the statutory provisions. [Para 12]

■

Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

1. All these appeals involve common facts and propose identical questions of law, for which we are deciding them by a common order. For the purpose of clarity and convenience, facts of ITA No. 675/2025 are however, being taken into consideration.

He submitted that simply because the invoices were issued to the retailers and the sales were made in cash, which cash from time to time was deposited in the bank, it does not mean that the deposits were unexplained and hence, the source of purchase was not properly explained.

10. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

11. Both the Appellant Authorities namely the CIT(A) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the AO has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under Section 69C of the Act of 1961. Not only the Appellate Authority even the AO himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine.

■

Both the Appellant Authorities namely the Commissioner (Appeals) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the Assessing Officer has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under section 69C. Not only the Appellate Authority even the Assessing Officer himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine. [Para 11]

■

When the purchases have been accepted to be genuine and those purchases have been executed through proper documents and banking channels, how its source can be said to be unexplained. The Assessing Officer’s stand that the money in bank accounts had come through the cash deposited out of retail sale is unexplained, is misconceived. If an assessee is allowed or permitted to sell goods in cash and there is no non-compliance of any statutory provision, the purchase cannot be disallowed. Therefore, hardly any substance and merit is found in the present appeals. The appeals are, therefore, dismissed. [Para 13]

The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The issues involved in the present appeal are squarely covered by the decision of the coordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of family member of assessee,Shashi Kant Chaurasia v. DCIT in ITA Nos.3844 & 3845/Del/2023,dated 20-1-2025. The findings of the ITAT in case of Shashi Kant Chaurasia (supra), which are squarely applicable to the case of the assessee, are summarized hereunder:

(i) The coordinate Bench held that the existence of rough diamonds cannot be doubted having regard to the declaration of the same in IDS, 2016 being accepted by the Pr. CIT, coupled with the fact that the assessee had paid due taxes thereon. The Tribunal held that the IDS declaration is to be treated as conclusive proof of matters contained therein and is binding on all the parties including regulatory authorities. The Tribunal held that such declaration cannot be doubted by the revenue in the light of the sovereign commitment given by the Government of India;

(ii) The coordinate Bench held that cutting, polishing, etc., of the rough diamonds by the job workers in Surat cannot be doubted having regard to the contemporaneous evidence placed on record including ITRs, proof of actual payments, confirmations, etc. of the job workers and particularly the confirmations/responses directly filed by the parties in response to invoices issued under section 133(6);

(iii) The genuineness of sale of diamonds was upheld by the coordinate Bench having regard to – (a) uncontroverted evidence including invoices, confirmation directly filed by the parties, ledger accounts, stock registers, bank statements, ITRs, etc.: and (b) the diamonds being received as gift and kept in lockers, as confirmed by the family members in the various statements recorded;

(iv) The coordinate Bench rejected the allegation of the revenue that the sale of diamonds is not genuine in light of the fact that the parties have directly responded to the Assessing Officer by furnishing direct reply/evidences in response to notices issued under section 133(6) and furnished documents such as confirming purchases of diamond/ledger accounts with information of quantity and weight, stock registers, sale registers, list of sundry debtors, copy of ITR’s computation, tax audit. financial statement, bank statement, etc.;

, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

On second appeal :

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

It would be more logical, if they were so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000 which is confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. 28. The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000 retracting his statement was not given on oath is of no consequence as it is supporting to earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002 though we agree that between these contradictory statements, those made under oath will have greater value. It is a fact that VDT has retracted his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it is without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock has nothing to do with that, because it is the department who claims that the money had been given by the assessee.

29. The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath recorded by the Assessing Officer, VDT claiming that while he knew Saxena, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, cannot raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs. 10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as hawala transaction in the statement given to the Income-tax Department. The acknowledgement of Saxena as a business associate and then to delink the present transaction from those transactions does not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one.

30. The claim of the assessee that VDT was in fact the witness of the department cannot be accepted as it is the department who is relying upon his statement to allege that what is apparent is not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remains with the department and does not shift to the assessee.

31. It is true that at the time of survey it was not the case of VDT that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants but the fact remains that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee is concerned throughout.

32. Large amounts of cash deposited in various bank accounts of Dhananjay Diamonds on various dates by Ratnakar, but there is no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there is no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It may be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another the payment to the assessee has been made but how the assessee is responsible for that. Nothing is on record that money was given by the assessee.

33. The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS, they were sold to Dhananjay, payment was received by account payee cheques. In these circumstances how it can be a cash credit the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person who paid it is identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment is the bank account of the payer, it is stated to be consideration for sale of diamond, there is no material on record that source of that money is the assessee or it was given for any services have been rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In these circumstances it cannot be said to be the income of the assessee by any circumstance much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 of the Act as applied by the revenue authorities. In my opinion the source is satisfactorily explained by the assessee.

V’ for the sale on 20-1-1998 and were produced to the department. [Para 24]

The income based on the books of account of ‘V’ was accepted in his case under the Act which included the said transaction. [Para 25]

Similarly, ‘V’ being the registered dealer under the BST and CST Act had filed the returns under those Acts, duly disclosing the said transaction with the assessee much before the date of survey. [Para 26] The observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that since ‘V’ was denying the explanation given at the time of survey, it was upon him to explain the cash deposits in his bank accounts and the lack of closing stock was not convincing. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The two statements were conflicting and as to for which statement he said ‘remained’, was not known. It would be more logical, if it was so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000, which was confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. [Para 27]

The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. [Para 28]

The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath, recorded by the Assessing Officer, ‘V’ claiming that while he knew ‘S’, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, could not raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs.10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as ‘hawala’ transaction in the statement given to the department. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. [Para 30]

It was true that at the time of survey, it was not the case of ‘V’ that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants, but the fact remained that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee was concerned throughout. [Para 31]

Large amounts of cash were deposited in various bank accounts of ‘D’ on various dates by ‘R’, but there was no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there was no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32]

The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

HEADNOTE: Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained money -  Assessment year 1998-99 - Assessees were dealers in diamonds - Each of assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997 - Said declaration was accepted by Department and a certificate was issued to respective assessees under VDIS, 1997 - During relevant assessment year, assessees sold jewellery declared under VDIS, 1997 and offered to tax capital gains arising from respective sales - Assessing Officer disallowed assessees’ claim holding that sales transactions were not genuine - Tribunal, however, allowed assessees’ claim - Whether since identity of purchasers had been established and amounts received from purchasers had also been accounted for, in absence of any material to contrary it was to be concluded that transactions were genuine - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, Tribunal was justified in allowing assessee’s claim - Held, yes

FACT: The assessees were dealers in diamonds. Each of the assessees had declared certain diamond jewellery under the Voluntary Disclosure of Income Scheme, 1997. The said declarations were accepted by the Department and a certificate was issued to the respective assessees under the VDIS, 1997. The assessees claimed to have sold the jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 in the year relevant to the assessment year 1998-99 and offered to tax the capital gains arising from the respective sales. The Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of the assessees on the ground that the persons to whom the jewellery was sold had stated in their statements that the transactions were not genuine and, although, later on the statements were retracted and affidavits were filed on oath to effect that the transactions were genuine, but the transactions were not proved. Challenging the aforesaid orders, appeals were filed and ultimately the Tribunal allowed the claim of the assessees and deleted the additions.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

In aforesaid circumstances, it was to be held that the Tribunal was justified in allowing the assessees' claim. [Para 7]

HEADNOTE: Section  69C  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Unexplained expenditure (Purchases)  - Assessment year  2010-11  - Assessee, a partnership firm engaged in manufacturing and trading of cut and polished diamonds, filed its return declaring income of Rs. 4.74 lakhs - Case was reopened under section 148 based on Investigation Wing information following search/survey in Bhawarlal Jain group, alleging accommodation purchase entries from Mohit Enterprises and Nice Diamonds aggregating to Rs. 46.46 lakhs - In response, assessee furnished purchase bills, stock register, sales and purchase registers, bank statements evidencing payments through banking channels, export invoices and shipping bills, and bank realisation advices, and correlated impugned purchases to export sales with proceeds realised through banking channels - Assessing Officer, emphasizing modus operandi of Bhawarlal Jain syndicate and terming documentation unilateral, treated purchases from two parties as bogus and disallowed 100% of Rs. 46.46 lakhs, completing assessment under section 144, without pointing out discrepancies in evidences filed or disputing sales - Whether since it is an admitted position that sales had not been doubted and without purchases, there cannot be any sales, no adverse inference could be made insofar as export of diamonds were concerned for which all documentary evidences were placed on record - Held, yes - Whether therefore, addition was to be restricted to profit element, i.e., difference in gross profit on undisputed purchases and disputed purchases - Held, yes [Paras 7 and 7.2] [Partly in favour of assessee]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in manufacturing and trading of cut and polished diamonds, filed its return declaring income of about Rs. 4.74 lakhs. The case was reopened under section 148 based on Investigation Wing information following search/survey in the Bhawarlal Jain group, alleging accommodation purchase entries from Mohit Enterprises and Nice Diamonds aggregating to about Rs. 46.46 lakhs.

■

In response, the assessee furnished purchase bills, stock register, sales and purchase registers, bank statements evidencing payments through banking channels, export invoices and shipping bills, and bank realisation advices, and correlated the impugned purchases to export sales to SR Exports (HK) Ltd. and Lotus Gems BVBA with proceeds realised through banking channels.

■

The Assessing Officer, emphasizing the modus operandi of the Bhawarlal Jain syndicate and terming the documentation unilateral, treated the purchases from the two parties as bogus and disallowed 100% of about Rs. 46.46 lakhs, completing the assessment under section 144, without pointing out discrepancies in the evidences filed or disputing the sales.

■

In first appeal, the assessee reiterated that disallowance could not be made merely on third-party statements without corroboration and highlighted that sales were not doubted. The Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the full disallowance.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

The Tribunal considered the material on record and the judicial precedents relied upon by both the parties. Admittedly, it is a fact on record that assessee has made detailed submissions along with corroborative documentary evidences to establish the genuineness of the purchases made by it, which have been alleged to be bogus by the Assessing Officer. The details of documents furnished by the assessee to support the contentions made is listed below: i. Stock Register along with Sale & Purchase Register for Assessment Year 2010-11 ii. Purchase bill of Nice Diamonds along with its corresponding subsequent Export Sale invoice & Shipping Bill to SR Exports HK Ltd. iii. Purchase bill of Mohit Enterprises along with its corresponding subsequent Export Sale invoice & Shipping Bill to Lotus Gems BVBA. iv. Bank statements showing payment made towards the purchases from Mohit Enterprises and Nice Diamonds & Payments received for corresponding export sales made from SR Exports HK Ltd. v. Copy of Bank Realisation advice for export receipt from SR Exports HK Ltd. vi. Copy of Bank Realisation advice for export receipt from Lotus Gems BVBA along with Copy of Bank Statement highlighting the said receipt. [Para 6]

■

In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

29. We have considered the submissions of both sides and perused the relevant record available with us and perused the paper books filed by both sides. We are of the considered opinion that the sum of Rs. 51,92,750 representing the sale of diamonds to Shukra Jewellers, Surat, cannot be sustained for the reasons stated below. 30. It is an admitted fact that the appellant had declared gold and jewellery under the VDIS 1997 and it was accepted by the Department by issue of necessary certificate in accordance with the said scheme. It is also a fact that the gold and diamonds were sold separately. It is also an admitted fact that the sale of gold which was separated from the diamonds was made for Rs. 4,59,979 at Hyderabad and this sale has been accepted. The fact remains that the diamonds were separated. As regards the sale of diamonds to Shukra Jewellers, Surat, we find from the material evidence placed before us that the identity of the party has been established, the transaction is genuine and the creditworthiness of Shukra Jewellers has been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of M/s. Shukra Jewellers which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by Shukra Jewellers and sent to the appellant which were credited in the appellant’s bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. As regards the credits in the bank account of Shukra Jewellers, we agree with the submission of the learned authorised representative of the appellant that it is not the duty of the appellant to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of Shukra Jewellers. The appellant cannot establish the source of the source. The decision of the Honourable Madras High Court in S. Hastimal’s case (supra) also supports this view of the appellant.

31. As regards the appellant’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, the Revenue has relied on the credit card statement of Standard Chartered Bank and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 to hold that on these dates the appellant was at Hyderabad and, therefore, he could not have been at Surat on the aforesaid dates. In this connection, we accept the submission of the learned authorised representative of the appellant that credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 cannot be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the appellant and were never put to the appellant for rebuttal, as held by the Honourable Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram’s case (supra).

32. Notwithstanding the above, we hold that although the Revenue claims that the appellant was in Orchid Restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence has been brought on record to show that the appellant was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. We have also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad is an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 in the last paragraph of his order and the travel time from Mumbai at Surat is 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the appellant was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted is not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the learned authorised representative of the appellant that the appellant was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 has also equal force to support that the appellant was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night.

33. As regards the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998, we find that the appellant had stated in response to question No. 128 (page 71 of the appellant’s paper book) that he was at Surat on most of the dates and not necessarily on all the dates. In view of the fact that preceding the date of 15-3-1998, there were sales of diamonds on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 24-1-1998 of other family members of the appellant, we accept the plea of the appellant that the sale of diamonds on 15-3-1998 was genuine.

The Accountant Member discussed the matter in detail and held that the facts stated by VDT and statement on oath were sufficient enough to cause doubt in the mind of the Assessing Officer about the genuineness of the explanation offered by the assessee to explain the nature and source of cash credit. He then examined the case of the assessee in the light of the aforesaid four differences and held that the said decision in the case of Mohanlal R. He accordingly held that a look at the whole sequence of events, it was quite clear as to how the things were managed in the present case. Entries in cash book were passed for the purchase of old gold and diamond from the customers by debiting the purchase account and crediting cash initially. At the end of the day, cash account was debited and concerned parties account was credited as contra. Therefore, as per the assessee, these were all contra entries passed in the cash book for showing credit purchase. There was no outflow of cash at all. Again as per assessee, when sales were effected to such customers, cash account was first debited and credit given to sales account. Again at the end of the day, parties accounts were debited and cash account was credited as contra. Result was that credit balances in customers accounts for purchases, were effaced through the subsequent sales. There was no actual cash flow but the A.O. misunderstood the transactions.

8. CIT (Appeals) went through the cash book and day book as also stock register. CIT (Appeals) noted that at no point of time there were any cash payments effected by the assessee. Transactions were reflected in the cash book and ledger account for the purchases and sales as contras. CIT (Appeals) also verified two of the items included in the annexure to the assessment order and concluded that the customers referred therein had effected purchase of jewellery from assessee and sale of old ornaments were only exchange transactions. Settled amount was only for the difference. He thus held that there was no outflow of cash and there was no justification for invoking Section 40A(3) of the Act. Nevertheless, he sustained an addition of Rs. 3,54,375/- for old gold purchase and Rs. 8,12,905/- for diamond purchase for a reason that these amounts were not supported by necessary vouchers. Thus except for a sum of Rs. 11,67,280/-, all additions made under Section 40A(3) was deleted.

9. As for the disallowance of Rs. 58,62,020/- made by the A.O. considering some purchases as not genuine, CIT (Appeals) was of the opinion that in the nature of trade of the assessee, customers might not always be willing to give complete address. According to him, assessee had furnished all possible details of the customers who had sold the old jewellery and diamonds to the assessee. All the purchases were recorded in the stock register. Physical stock of such diamonds were taken into account for calculating the closing stock. He was of the opinion that just for a reason that address of certain parties were not available, an addition could not have been made. He thus deleted the disallowance of Rs. 58,62,020/- also.

10. Now before us, learned D.R. strongly assailing the order of CIT (Appeals), submitted that assessee had produced fresh evidence before CIT (Appeals) in the nature of stock register, bills and vouchers which were not made available before the Assessing Officer. As per the learned D.R., where on the same day itself, assessee had adjusted sales with credit purchase, it could be true that there could be no cash transaction for applying Section 40A(3) of the Act. However, in assessee's case, sales were effected in a number of cases on a date subsequent to date of purchase of old gold and diamonds and assessee also could not establish a one-to-one match between old gold purchase and sale of jewellery at a later date to the same parties. He submitted that assessee had produced fresh evidence before CIT (Appeals) and the matter required a re-visit by the Assessing Officer. Insofar as disallowance for purchase were concerned, learned D.R. submitted that assessee could not give address of the customers from whom it had effected the purchases and therefore, A.O. had no opportunity for verifying the claim of such purchases.

Assessing Officer held, the statement of the assessee is that it is not the duty of the assessee to verify from where the purchase party procures goods and a mere failure of a sub-creditor cannot in the absence of clinching evidence be treated as income of the assessee derived from undisclosed sources.
