INCOME TAX: Where assessee engaged in diamond trading was alleged to have made bogus purchases from two entities based on third party investigation, but furnished all purchase and sales records, payment proofs and export documents correlating purchases with export sales and sales were not doubted, entire purchases could not be disallowed and only profit element relating to disputed purchases could be added to income.

It is also the case of revenue that the Assessing Officer has made independent enquiries also by issuing notices under section 133(6) to the seven parties which reveal that the notices were returned unserved by the postal authorities with remarks 'not known', 'left', 'unclaimed', etc. The aforesaid two aspects have formed the basis for the Assessing Officer to treat the purchases of Rs. 37 lakhs from the said seven parties as bogus transactions. [Para 7] The assessee asserted before the Assessing Officer that he has effected purchase of goods from the said parties and further resold it to various parties and without effecting such purchases, sales were not possible. He furnished copies of purchase bills, evidence of having made payments by account payee cheques, copies of bank statements, etc. Most importantly, the assessee pointed out to the Assessing Officer that if any of the depositions made by the said parties is to be used against him, copies of the same be furnished, so that he can avail the opportunity of cross-examining each of them. All these submissions of the assessee have been set to naught by the Assessing Officer by merely referring to the aspect of information having been received from the DGIT, Mumbai and the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) to the parties. In the assessment order other than the generalised observation about information having been received from DGIT, Mumbai, there is no reference to any specific material or details in this regard. The entire factual matrix brings out that leave alone confronting the assessee with the specific material, the assessment order itself does not record any specifics about the material on which the reliance has been placed by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, on facts, such an addition is susceptible to deletion. [Para 8]

Another aspect is the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6). In fact, non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) by itself cannot be a conclusive proof that transactions with the parties are bogus because there was enough material before the Assessing Officer to show that payments have been made to the said parties through banking channels. It required further collection of evidence by the Assessing Officer to prove the bogus nature of such transactions. The assessee has pointed to the Assessing Officer that he was maintaining day-to-day stock record, wherein all purchases are entered as 'inward' and sales are recorded as 'outward'. He had enclosed copies of account of the said parties appearing in his account books, copies of purchase invoices, copies of bank statement for payment to the parties, etc. Under these circumstances, having regard to the material on record, it is not possible to uphold the charge of Assessing Officer that the purchases from the seven parties are bogus. [Para 8.1]

Section 69C prescribes that where in any financial year an assessee has incurred any expenditure and he offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation offered by him is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year. In the context of the application of section 69C what is of importance is that either there is no explanation about the 'source of such expenditure' or that the explanation offered is not found satisfactory. The underlying emphasis is on the explanation in relation to the 'source of such expenditure'. The Assessing Officer has invoked section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases as unexplained. So, however, the assessee has demonstrated that the payments for such purchases have been made through account payee cheques for which there is no repudiation by the Assessing Officer thereby implying that the source of expenditure stands explained. In fact, the case of Assessing Officer is that the purchase transactions are 'only accommodation entries and not really purchases', thereby implying that the assessee has not incurred such expenditure. To hold the transactions as mere accommodation entries and not real purchases is quite different from saying that the sources of expenditure for the purchases from the seven parties have not been explained in the context of section 69C. Therefore, invoking of section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases stated to have been made from the seven parties as unexplained expenditure is on a wrong footing. [Para 9]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery. During demonetization period, the assessee deposited cash of Rs. 50 lakhs in his bank account. The assessee contended that cash deposits were proceeds of the cash sales and were supported by the sales invoices reflected in the books of account, which were audited.

■ The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee failed to explain the source of huge cash deposited of Rs. 50 lakhs on a single day which was considered as colourable device of the assessee trying to explain the source of the huge cash deposited in the bank account which was in fact the income of the assessee from undisclosed sources and not from the actual sale made. He considered that cash sale shown during October and till 8th November, 2015 as this period of year 2015 and 2016 covered most of big festivals/auspicious occasions like deepawali, marriages, etc and such festivals/ occasions fell in these two FYs also during October and November and further allowing thereon weightage on account of overall inflation, changes in price of diamond/ gold etc. at the rate of 5 percent. The assessee’s sale in October 2015 was Rs. 21.13 lakhs and from 1st November to 8th November 2016 same was Rs. 2.56 lakhs totaling to Rs. 23.69 lakhs, hence, this way the cash earned by the assessee out of genuine cash sale was worked out at Rs. 24.88 lakhs after allowing weightage of 5 percent over last year turnover shown during this period and thereby the Assessing Officer did not consider the sales to the tune of Rs. 37.95 lakhs out of the cash deposited by the assessee between 01.10.2016 to 13.11.2016. He, thus, invoked the provision of section 145(3) and rejected the book results. He further made addition for an amount of Rs. 37.96 lakhs as unexplained cash deposits under section 68.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the Assessing Officer.

On appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: ■

The broad issue raised before this Tribunal is as to whether the cash sales recorded and supported by the sale invoice be considered as unexplained money and that too when the profit derived from those sales proceeds is already taxed as part of sales. The bench notes that on 13-11-2016 i.e. after the five days of the demonetization, the assessee deposited a sum of Rs. 50 lakhs in the bank account. The assessee claimed before the lower authority that the said cash deposit was derived from the sale proceeds i.e., received on account of the sales made by the assessee. In support of the sales so made, the assessee submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, names, addresses and telephone numbers of the person to whom the cash sales was made and that cash collected from them had been deposited into the bank account. The assessee also submitted the comparison of sales and cash deposited into the bank account with last year for each month. From that, the assessee submitted that for the financial year 2014-15 cash deposited was for an amount of Rs. 1.26 crores whereas in the year under consideration i.e. 2015-16 cash deposited was Rs. 1.30 crores thereby increasing trend of Rs. 4.10 lakhs only and that too not abnormal. [Para 13]

■

The bench notes that on the one hand the Assessing Officer noted the submission of the assessee where in it was written that the assessee has submitted all the invoice with complete year cash book, name, address and telephone number of the person to whom the cash sales was made whereas contended that the assessee has not submitted the contact details of those purchasers this is contrary to the facts. At the time of hearing of the appeal, the revenue did not controvert said aspect argued by the assessee. As regards the signature on the invoice when the sale is supported by the invoice, there is no necessity to obtain the signature of the purchaser of goods. In support of the cash sales, the assessee also submitted that the assessee has maintained all the records that sales are duly reflected in the VAT return and also in the books of account. Thus, the Assessing Officer could not make an addition on ill-founded assumption and presumption and without understanding and appreciating the books of account. The Assessing Officer simply mentioned about the invocation of section 145(3), but the mandatory notice was not given mentioning the defects in the books of account based on the provision of section 145. [Para 13]

For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. Section 106 of the 1872 Act stipulates that burden of proving fact which is especially within the knowledge of any person is on that person. Similarly section 114(g) of the 1872 Act stipulates that the evidence which could be and is not produces would , if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it. The assessee in the instant appeal has withheld the details and identity of the buyers of gold bars for which the assessee is to be blamed and presumption is drawn against the assessee as it cannot be accepted that such a huge sales averaging more than Rs 3 crores executed per one sale invoice in majority of cases by the assessee to persons whose details are not known to the assessee rather the assessee is deliberately withholding such details at his own peril and is clearly hit by sections 106 and 114(g) of the 1872 Act and presumption is drawn against the assessee that either the assessee has introduced his own undisclosed income into the bank accounts of the assessee or if the story of the assessee is believed has facilitated introduction of undisclosed money of the undisclosed buyers of gold and its conversion into gold without revealing identity of the buyers. HELD: Applicability of section 69 to assessee's case

• It is an admitted position that names of each of the seller were given by the assessee to the Assessing Officer, since otherwise he could not have compiled the list giving the details of such disallowance as an annexure to the assessment order. In the nature of trade of the assessee, it may not always be possible to get the address of all its customers. Even if customers give their address, there is no means available to the assessee to ensure that such addresses were right.

• The assessee, in the nature of its trade, cannot insist for an identification process akin to Know Your Customer (KYC) rules applied by banks. There is no such mandatory requirement in the business of jewellery to maintain any records in line with KYC rules of bank. In fact, a prudent businessman might not insist on such rigorous identification process since insistence on such conditions will be to the detriment of his business. Just for the reason that purchases effected from certain parties did not carry full address, a disallowance ought not have been made. Admittedly, such purchases were recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also shown in its stock. [Para 14]

The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. It is also the case of revenue that the Assessing Officer has made independent enquiries also by issuing notices under section 133(6) to the seven parties which reveal that the notices were returned unserved by the postal authorities with remarks 'not known', 'left', 'unclaimed', etc. The aforesaid two aspects have formed the basis for the Assessing Officer to treat the purchases of Rs. 37 lakhs from the said seven parties as bogus transactions. [Para 7]

The assessee asserted before the Assessing Officer that he has effected purchase of goods from the said parties and further resold it to various parties and without effecting such purchases, sales were not possible. He furnished copies of purchase bills, evidence of having made payments by account payee cheques, copies of bank statements, etc. Most importantly, the assessee pointed out to the Assessing Officer that if any of the depositions made by the said parties is to be used against him, copies of the same be furnished, so that he can avail the opportunity of cross-examining each of them. All these submissions of the assessee have been set to naught by the Assessing Officer by merely referring to the aspect of information having been received from the DGIT, Mumbai and the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) to the parties. In the assessment order other than the generalised observation about information having been received from DGIT, Mumbai, there is no reference to any specific material or details in this regard. The entire factual matrix brings out that leave alone confronting the assessee with the specific material, the assessment order itself does not record any specifics about the material on which the reliance has been placed by the Assessing Officer. Therefore, on facts, such an addition is susceptible to deletion. [Para 8]

Another aspect is the non-service of notices issued under section 133(6). In fact, non-service of notices issued under section 133(6) by itself cannot be a conclusive proof that transactions with the parties are bogus because there was enough material before the Assessing Officer to show that payments have been made to the said parties through banking channels. It required further collection of evidence by the Assessing Officer to prove the bogus nature of such transactions. The assessee has pointed to the Assessing Officer that he was maintaining day-to-day stock record, wherein all purchases are entered as 'inward' and sales are recorded as 'outward'. He had enclosed copies of account of the said parties appearing in his account books, copies of purchase invoices, copies of bank statement for payment to the parties, etc. Under these circumstances, having regard to the material on record, it is not possible to uphold the charge of Assessing Officer that the purchases from the seven parties are bogus. [Para 8.1]

Section 69C prescribes that where in any financial year an assessee has incurred any expenditure and he offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof, or the explanation offered by him is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer, then the amount covered by such expenditure or part thereof may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year. In the context of the application of section 69C what is of importance is that either there is no explanation about the 'source of such expenditure' or that the explanation offered is not found satisfactory. The underlying emphasis is on the explanation in relation to the 'source of such expenditure'. The Assessing Officer has invoked section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases as unexplained. So, however, the assessee has demonstrated that the payments for such purchases have been made through account payee cheques for which there is no repudiation by the Assessing Officer thereby implying that the source of expenditure stands explained. In fact, the case of Assessing Officer is that the purchase transactions are 'only accommodation entries and not really purchases', thereby implying that the assessee has not incurred such expenditure. To hold the transactions as mere accommodation entries and not real purchases is quite different from saying that the sources of expenditure for the purchases from the seven parties have not been explained in the context of section 69C. Therefore, invoking of section 69C to treat the expenditure on purchases stated to have been made from the seven parties as unexplained expenditure is on a wrong footing. [Para 9]

In view of the aforesaid, the orders of lower authorities deserved to be set aside. [Para 10]

A perusal of the record would suggest that the assessee is engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. It has been maintaining its proper books of account. The accounts were duly audited. The assessee has filed its return of income on the strength of those accounts. When the Assessing Officer has confronted the assessee for explaining its position with regard to certain purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14. The assessee has submitted copy of the audited balance-sheet, Profit & Loss account along with auditor’s report, the complete stock tally of the ornaments. It has also filed copy of the stock register exhibiting opening stock, purchase, sales and closing stock. The assessee thereafter filed purchase bills issued by Daksh Diamonds, Jewel Diamonds and Nazar Impex in the respective years. The assessee has made the payments to its suppliers through banking channel. The seller of the diamonds was having PAN, VAT, TIN and CST no. Those details were submitted by the assessee to the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings. The assessee had made request that the person, who has disclosed from its back that he was engaged in providing bogus entries, then, such a person be subject to cross examination. The Assessing Officer had issued summons under section 131 to Bhanwar Lal Jain for appearance, he never appeared. The assessee thereafter brought it to the notice of the Assessing Officer that a perusal of the statement given by Bhanwar Lal Jain would suggest that he has not specifically taken the name of assessee disclosing therein that the assessee has availed accommodation entries. The information disclosed by him is a general nature whereby he disclosed that he controls 68 firms mentioned therein and such firms were engaged in providing accommodation entry. It is not specific whether such firm has specifically provided accommodation entry to the assessee or not. The assessee further produced details of the sales made by it. [Para 19]

The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Odeon Builders (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 64/266 Taxman 461/418 ITR 315, had held that disallowance based on third party information gathered by the Investigation wing of the Department without independent verification of the Assessing Officer cannot be made. In other words, the information transmitted by the DIT (Investigation) was a material to ignite assessment machinery in motion but it cannot be treated as gospel truth for disallowing the claim of the assessee without independent cross verification of those information by the Assessing Officer. one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. The Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 40A(3). He also held that the provisions of sections 69B and 69C were applicable to the instant case.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

[Para 37] Coming to the support derived from the comparable case of ‘S’, the fact, that the assessee agreed to purchase the flat in March, 1998 directly from the builder at booking stage, had not been denied. Similarly, the fact regarding ‘S’ having purchased flats in June, 1999 from a third-party also had not been denied. The inquiries conducted in that behalf and the material facts about the comparability of S’s flats and inquiries in that respect were not confronted to the assessee at the assessment stage, so as to controvert the same. Time gap of 15 months was significantly long; fact about direct booking of flats from builders and purchase from third-party also had very important effect on the price of the flat. Only explanation given by the lower authorities, that there was a recessionary time and subsequent flats might have been sold at a lesser figure, was a general and sweeping statement, which could not be used against the assessee. There were other flat buyers, who could have also been examined, particularly those who booked the flats from the builders at early stage. That comparability at the most could create a suspicion which could not be made a basis of addition. Therefore, comparative purchase instance of ‘S’ could not be made a basis for addition in the hands of the assessee. Therefore, the addition of Rs. 50 lakhs, as made by the Assessing Officer and confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), could not be sustained and the same should be deleted. Since the addition had been made as unexplained cash credit, it was necessary to examine the case in the light of the provisions of section 68. [Para 21]

Under section 68, if the explanation with regard to nature and source of deposit is found unsatisfactory, only then the amount so credited may be treated as income. [Para 22] The revenue had failed to substantiate its claim that the silver utensils did not exist, neither transported from Kolkata to Delhi nor sold to Delhi merchants and the alleged sale proceeds was nothing but an accommodation entry. As a matter of fact, the Assessing Officer, in the remand report, had finally accepted that the silver utensils were properly disclosed, and transported by trucks as evidenced by consignment notes and, the same was delivered at Delhi which was also confirmed by the consignees and there was no direct evidence to show that the jewellers of Delhi had given accommodation entries to the assessee. Besides that, the Assessing Officer while disallowing the long-term capital loss on sale of such silver utensils had accepted that such loss was loss on sale of personal effects. Therefore, the assessee had discharged his burden that the silver utensils were disclosed under the VDIS, 1997, transported by trucks and sold at Delhi, and that the sale proceeds were obtained through banking channels and disclosed in the books of account. Therefore, the assessee had proved the identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of the transactions in terms of section 68 and, therefore, the addition made by the Assessing Officer was not sustainable in law and, accordingly, the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) in deleting the same was to be upheld. 71,221 from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd and sold the diamonds to two entities, M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd.

■

The Assessing Officer made an addition of Rs. 3,51,71,221 to the total income of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the CIT(A) deleted the addition.

■

On revenue’s appeal :

HELD: ■ The undisputable facts emanate from the records are that Shri Deepak Babel has given a statement on 05.08.2018 about the nature of accommodation entries provided and retracted the same on 28.03.2018 before the Revenue Authorities. This fact has not been considered by the Assessing Officer or mentioned anywhere in the proceedings taken up by the Revenue Authorities. Further, it is an undisputable fact that the assessee has received amounts from two entities, namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., against the diamonds sold. It cannot be expected that these two entities have paid amounts to the assessee without receiving any goods – whether it be diamonds or otherwise. Hence, such diamonds have been duly purchased from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. Even if the argument is considered, there were certain goods which were purchased by the assessee for Rs.3.53 crores which in turn have been sold to two entities at Rs.3.56 crores, then this leads to a situation where the Revenue has accepted the sales and, as a natural corollary, there have been purchases - whether from M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. But, in a situation where the corresponding sales have been accepted, it cannot be said that there were no purchases. [Para 10]

■

In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. In case both the purchase and sales have been treated as bogus, then the difference amount of Rs.2,81,914/- is to be treated as the amount earned by the assessee after receiving the money from two parties namely M/s. Isabelle Tours N Travels and M/s. Shreeji Overseas (I) Pvt. Ltd., and sending it to a third party namely M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. In that way, the assessee is acted as a conduit for transferring money through his account. The Revenue has failed to undertake any inquiry to prove that the assessee is operating as a conduit for transfer of money to various persons. The Revenue has also not disputed that the sales parties were bogus to buttress the arguments that the assessee is acting as a conduit for transfer of money.

■

The Assessing Officer has held that the assessee has inflated the purchases by taking accommodation entries to reduce the legitimate tax liability (para 4.5 of the AO). If that is the case, the contention of the Assessing Officer cannot be accepted that, in order to sell goods worth Rs.3.56 crores the assessee has inflated the purchases by Rs. 3.51 crores. Further, it was found that there was a total of 10 transactions entered by the assessee with regard to the sale and purchase of goods. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

■

Hence, keeping in view the above facts, and the order of the Co- ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of Grishma Hemanshu Mody v. CIT(A) [IT Appeal No. 895 (Mum.) of 2023, dated 25-10-2023], and in the case of ITO v. Siddheshwar Impex (P.) Ltd. [IT Appeal No. 153 (Mum.) of 2024, dated 26-08-2024] wherein the issue of bogus purchases pertaining to M/s. Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. involving Shri Deepak Babel have been adjudicated, the order of the CIT(A) cannot be interfered with. [Para 12]

■

In the result, the appeal of the revenue is dismissed. [Para 13]

applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14] It is an admitted fact that the assessee was having sufficient cash balance as per cash book maintained for the relevant period. In fact, cash in hand as on the date of demonetization i.e. 8-11-2016 was at Rs. 48,84,03,169/- and said cash balance is backed by cash receipts recorded in the books of account before the date of demonetization. Further, cash receipts from various persons have been further substantiated with sales made to them before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed various evidences, including sales bills to support its arguments. The Assessing Officer never disputed sales declared by the assessee nor pointed out any discrepancy in purchase or stock-in-trade held in the business of the assessee before the date of demonetization. In fact, the assessee has filed comparative sales for the month of April, 2016 to November, 2016 and corresponding April-15 to November, 2015 and there is no abnormal deviation found in sales declared for the month of November, 2016 when compared to earlier periods. It is not a case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee has declared sales without purchases. In fact, a sale declared by the assessee is backed by corresponding purchases, and is supported by necessary purchase bills. The Assessing Officer could not point out any discrepancy in stock register maintained by the assessee nor made out a case that the assessee has declared sales without there being any stock in hand. Therefore, in absence of any contrary findings to the effect that the sales declared by the assessee is not backed by any corresponding purchase or supported by stock in hand, it is opined, simply sales cannot be rejected on the ground that sale for the particular month or period is higher when compared to corresponding previous period. There cannot be any reason for uniform sales in all days or month or year. There may be various reasons for increase or decrease in sales which depends upon various factors, including festival sales, clearing sales, year end sales, etc. Therefore, the explanation of the assessee that it has received cash from various customers towards sale of jewellery and subsequently the advances have been converted into sales, appears to be bona fide and reasonable. [Para 15]

Coming back to second observation of the Assessing Officer in rejecting explanation of the assessee with regard to source for cash deposits. Initially, assessee claims that source for cash deposits is out of trade advances received in cash from various persons. However, during the course of assessment proceedings itself, the assessee claimed that it was an error in making a submission that it has received trade advances from various persons before the date of demonetization, but fact remains that authorized representative who appeared and made submissions before the Assessing Officer made an inadvertent error of copying submission made in another group case which is also pending for assessment. Further, immediately after noticing the above inadvertent error, the assessee has submitted details of cash book along with bank statements and explained that it has sufficient cash withdrawal aggregating to Rs. 150 Crores from very same bank account on various dates before the date of demonetization and after utilization of the cash for the purpose, for which, it has been drawn the net withdrawal was at Rs. 136.85 Crores. The assessee was carrying cash balance in books and once demonetization was announced, the available cash balance in Specified Bank Notes, has been deposited into bank account. After perusing relevant cash book and bank statements which are available in paper book and after considering relevant materials, force is found in the arguments of the assessee for simple reason that as per the details furnished by the assessee like bank statements, cash book, it is undoubtedly clear that assessee was having sufficient withdrawals from very same bank accounts before the date of demonetization which was recorded in the books of account of the assessee. Further, the cash balance maintained by the assessee as per books of account as on 8-11-2016 was much higher than the amount of cash deposited to bank account during demonetization period. Therefore, view, when the assessee is able to file necessary evidences to prove that there was sufficient cash withdrawal from very same bank account which is further backed by bank statements, where it has been clearly evident that there are sufficient cash withdrawals, there is no reason for the Assessing Officer to reject explanation of the assessee that cash deposits are out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. [Para 16]

Thus the Assessing Officer has erred in making additions towards cash receipts received for sale of jewellery, which has been subsequently converted into sales, for the impugned assessment year as unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The Commissioner (Appeals) after considering relevant facts has rightly deleted the additions made by the Assessing Officer, and thus, the findings of the Commissioner (Appeals) are to be upheld the appeal filed by the revenue is dismissed. [Para 19]

The sale of shares of KAFL which was dematerialized in Demat account has taken place through recognised stock exchange and assessee received money through banking channel. So, the assessee has explained the nature and source of the money with supporting documents and thus has discharged the onus casted upon him by producing the relevant documents, accordingly, the question of treating the said gain as unexplained cash credit under section 68 cannot arise unless the Assessing Officer is able to find fault/infirmity with the same. The source of the receipt of the amount has been explained and the transaction in respect of which the said amount has been received by assessee has not been cancelled by the stock exchange/SEBI. So, it is difficult to countenance the action of the Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals) in the aforesaid facts and circumstances explained. [Para 13]

Even assuming that the brokers may have done some manipulation then also the assessee cannot be held liable for the illegal action of the brokers when the entire transactions have been carried out through banking channels duly recorded in the Demat accounts with a Government depository and traded on the stock exchange unless specific evidence emerges that the assessee was in hand in gloves with the broker for committing the unscrupulous activity to launder his own money in the guise of LTCG. [Para 14]

There was also nothing on record which could suggest that the assessee gave his own cash and got cheque from the alleged brokers/buyers. The assessment refers also to some third party statement of one SD which was admittedly recorded behind the back of the assessee and the assessee has neither been allowed to cross examine this person by the assessee nor the statement of SD furnished to assessee, so the statements even if adverse against the assessee cannot be relied upon by the Assessing Officer to draw adverse inference against the assessee and in the light of the documents to substantiate the claim of LTCG, which has not been found fault with by the Assessing Officer. For the reasons given in the case the action of the Commissioner (Appeals)/Assessing Officer cannot be accepted, since the scrip of KAFL cannot be held to be bogus; and based on the finding of fact supra which are supported by documents which have not been adversely commented upon by Assessing Officer/Commissioner (Appeals), the appeals of the assessee are inclined to be allowed and the Assessing Officer is directed to allow the claim of LTCG on sale of scrips of KAFL in respect of all the assessees. Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

On revenue's appeal to the High Court: HELD: Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

The assessee had also filed necessary books of account, including cash book, sales register, sale bills, purchase details along with bills and stock details to prove that there is no discrepancy in books of account and also the assessee has reported sales made before the date of demonetization to GST authorities. [Para 12] In light of above factual matrix, if one examines the issue, the Assessing Officer has rejected the contention of the assessee on two grounds. The first and foremost reasons given by the Assessing Officer to reject the explanation of the assessee is that persons from whom assessee claims to have been received advance are not responded to summons issued under section 131(1) and in few cases, they have denied any kind of transactions with the assessee. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee could not discharge its onus cast upon as per the provisions of section 68, in respect of cash receipts, and thus, opined that cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee from various persons is unexplained cash credits taxable under section 68. The second reason given by the Assessing Officer was that there is a contradiction in the claim of the assessee insofar as source for cash deposits are concerned inasmuch as initially, the assessee claims to have explained cash deposits out of cash receipts from various persons towards sale of jewellery and subsequently changed its stand and argued that source for cash deposits is out of cash withdrawals from very same bank account. Insofar as the first and foremost reason given by the Assessing Officer to assess cash receipts under section 68, we find that there is a distinction between cash credits and cash receipts towards sales. If assessee claims certain cash credits in his books of account and not able to explain credits to the satisfaction of the Assessing Officer, then, such cash credits need to be examined in light of provisions of section 68. In case, the assessee claims that it has received trade advances in cash and the same has been subsequently converted into sales by issuing sale bills, then, said trade advance cannot be examined in light of provisions of section 68, because, trade advances have been subsequently converted into sales and sales has been accounted in the books of account of the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has committed a fundamental mistake in examining the cash receipts claimed to have been received by the assessee towards sale of jewellery in light of provisions of section 68. [Para 13]

Be that as it may. The fact remains that, the assessee has furnished name and address of the customers from whom it has received cash for sale of jewellery. The assessee need not obtain confirmation and submit to the Assessing Officer, because, the law does not mandate collecting PAN details of the persons, if sale value of jewellery does not exceed Rs. 2 lakhs as per rule 114B of Income-tax Rules, 1962. In so far as compliance of KYC norms, it is mandatory under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, with effect from 4-5-2023 onwards and not applicable for the impugned assessment year. Therefore, when the assessee has furnished name and address of the persons from whom it has received trade advances for sale of jewellery, the assessee has satisfactorily discharged onus cast upon to furnish name and address of the persons. Therefore, the observation of the Assessing Officer in light of provisions of section 68, that the assessee has not satisfactorily explained cash receipts is unwarranted and devoid of merits. [Para 14]

The certificate issued by the revenue under the VDIS, 1997 to the effect that the assessee had diamond jewellery weighing 65.75 carats continued to be valid and subsisting and no proceedings had been initiated by the revenue till relevant time to cancel the certificate. [Para 12]

When the assessee claimed that the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 had been sold to T for Rs. 10,35,562, the same was accepted in the original assessment. However, in the reassessment order, the claim was disbelieved mainly by relying on the statement of 'T' recorded on 31-3-2000, wherein he had stated that the transactions recorded in his books were hawala transactions. It was further held that the above statement was corroborated by the non-availability of the diamond jewellery allegedly sold by the assessee to T and the bank accounts of T showed that he had received cash before issuing cheques to various parties including the assessee. [Para 13]

T had retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, which was received by the Assessing Officer on 17-4-2000. The retracted confession of T could be relied upon only if there was independent and cogent evidence to corroborate the statement of T made on 4-4-2000. [Para 14]

In the instant case, the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal was that T had not only retracted his statement recorded on 31-3-2000 vide letter dated 4-4-2000, but had also participated in the reassessment proceedings and stated on oath that the purchase of diamond jewellery from the assessee was a genuine transaction. The Tribunal had recorded a finding that the statement of T recorded on 31-3-2000 was a general statement and nowhere in the said statement it was recorded that the transaction with the assessee was not genuine . On evaluation of the evidence on record, the Tribunal had arrived at a finding that the assessee had successfully shown the existence of diamond jewellery prior to the sale, the person to whom it was sold and also the consideration received and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not justified in making the addition. Thus, the decision of the Tribunal was based on appreciation of evidence. [Para 15]

As the VDIS, 1997 certificate issued by the department was valid and subsisting, it was not open to the revenue to contend that there was no jewellery which could be sold by the assessee on 20-1-1999. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee continued to be in possession of the said diamond jewellery even after the alleged sale effected on 20-1-1999 or that the said jewellery had been sold to third parties. In those circumstances, the decision of the Tribunal in accepting the claim of the assessee that the amount of Rs. 10,35,562 represented the sale proceeds of the diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 could not be faulted. [Para 16]

The fact that the diamond jewellery claimed to have been sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser T or his associates could not be held against the assessee, because, admittedly, the said diamond jewellery declared under the VDIS, 1997 was also not found with the assessee after the sale was effected. If existence of the diamond jewellery with the assessee prior to the sale was evidenced by the VDIS, 1997 certificate and on sale of the said jewellery the assessee had received the consideration which was duly accounted for, then the mere fact that the jewellery sold by the assessee was not found with the purchaser could not be a ground to hold that the transaction was bogus and the consideration received by the assessee was the undisclosed income of the assessee. [Para 17]

The assessee was a dealer in HDPE plastic powder. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the entire addition on the ground that the third parties to whom sales were made, were found to have been genuine and if sales were genuine, then purchase must be genuine and transaction could not be said to be havala transaction. INCOME TAX: Where assessee’s long-term capital gains from sale of diamonds were supported by declaration under IDS, 2016 and valid holding period, additions under sections 68 and 69C treating sale proceeds and alleged commission as unexplained were unsustainable and liable to be deleted.

It was seen from records that the Assessing Officer had come to the conclusion that the amount of Rs. 66.90 lakhs found credited in the bank account of the assessee was unexplained credit simply on the ground that the assessee was not able to produce the broker before him for examination and basing on the statement of the assessee recorded under section 131, and the purchase price was paid by the assessee in eight instalments spreading over a period of two months, but the assessee had produced the share certificate issued by 'C' for acquisition of 3,50,000 equity shares. Subsequently, those shares were sold by the assessee for consideration of Rs. 70.40 lakhs through a stock broker 'R' and thereby earned long-term capital gains of Rs. 66.90 lakhs. The 'C' was a public limited company where public were substantially interested. Its shares were listed in the Ahmedabad Stock Exchange. The said company was regularly filing statutory return as required under the Companies Act, 1956. If the Assessing Officer really doubted the genuineness of transaction, he ought to have obtained the list of shareholders coupled with the holding of the said shareholders together with the share certificate numbers and folio numbers of the shares held by each shareholder. This was cogent evidence, which went to the root of the matter to find as to the genuineness of the purchase and sale of shares by the assessee, but this was not done by the Assessing Officer though he had abundant powers under section 131. The Assessing Officer had also not written to the stock exchange of Ahmedabad as to the trading of those shares by the said broker in the stock exchange. In the absence of all these material facts, it could never be said that the transactions of purchase and sale conducted by the assessee through broker were not genuine. Therefore, it was opined that under the facts and circumstances of the case, the Assessing Officer was not able to make out any material except for presumptions and assumptions to come to the conclusion that the purchase and sale of shares claimed by the assessee were not genuine. More so, in the presence of letter communicated by the broker giving the details of shares purchased and sold on behalf of the assessee, mentioning therein the commission charged by him as well as proceeds available with him for purchase of shares as well as realization of sale proceeds and crediting the same to the bank account of the assessee. Hence, the impugned order of the Commissioner (Appeals) deleting the additions made by the Assessing Officer did not require any interference. As a result, appeal filed by the Department was to be dismissed.

Issue relating to bogus purchases

The Commissioner (Appeals) has categorically noted that assessee has submitted the evidences with respect to the Ledger accounts of the transactions with purchase parties, purchase invoices and bank statements of the assessee showing the payment made to the parties. Assessee has also shown the mapping of corresponding purchases and sales. The argument of the department is that one-to-one mapping shown by the assessee is not correct for the reason that in the purchase bills of these parties there is no narration with respect to the quantity i.e. number of diamonds as well as the colour etc. To support the same, the assessee has submitted the other beans of the other parties, which have been accepted by the Assessing Officer as genuine purchases. On perusal of those bills, also there is no mention of number of diamonds as well as the colour of the diamonds. Therefore, it cannot be said that in the purchase bills the assessee should have mentioned this details as that is not the trade practice and that is also not the reason why the Assessing Officer has rejected those purchases. [Para 21]

With respect to one-to-one mapping therefore only criteria is the sale of carats of the diamond. Assessee has shown that number of carats purchased from the three entities is 585.88 carats and the sale of the diamond is also 585.88 carats. The amount of purchases recorded is 6.27 crores whereas the sale of the same diamond is shown at 6.71 crores. facts. Unless there was some evidence in support of the claim that the money reached back to the assessee, it could not be held that the finding arrived at by the revenue authorities was the right one. Suspicion alone, however, strong was not sufficient. It was true that the Assessing Officer clearly established the modus operandi in this line of business. But unless there was some evidence against the assessee, however, weak, the decision had to go in the assessee’s favour. As regard the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that the assessee made purchases to the tune of Rs. 5,30,87,813, there was not an iota of evidence, except the reasoning of the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee made purchases by making cash payments. Not even a single question was put to any of the parties from whom the statements were recorded by the Assessing Officer, as to whether the payment made by the assessee by cheque was withdrawn and paid back to the assessee. In the absence of any other evidence on facts, the reasoning of the Assessing Officer that the assessee made the cash purchases could not be accepted. In view of the above facts, the further addition made to the income of the assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) did not survive. In view of the above, it was also held that there was no material to recompute the profits for the purpose of deduction under section 80HHC.

Since there was no basis for making any addition on account of cash purchases, the excess peak investment worked out by the Commissioner (Appeals) automatically did not survive.

There was no case for the revenue that the assessee was not maintaining books of account. The purchases were recorded in the books of account. Payments were made by cheque to the immediate purchasers. They accepted and confirmed the sale. To hold otherwise, there should be some evidence in the possession of the revenue. Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of evidence and that alone cannot be the criteria for deciding the matter.

Though search was conducted during the period under consideration, yet nothing incriminating was found during the search action. There was no evidence to show that the money had come back to the assessee or claim of the payment was bogus. In such circumstances, for the subsequent period to hold that the entire purchase was bogus was a conclusion that was very difficult to arrive at. Another reasoning of the Assessing Officer to come to the conclusion that the assessee had not actually purchased the diamonds from the immediate suppliers was that their suppliers from Surat had no capacity and even if they had the capacity, there was no evidence that they transported it to Mumbai. According to the Assessing Officer, the diamonds worth crores of Rupees, if they claimed to have transported these diamonds should have been insured and the mode of transportation or at least the details of tickets, etc. of the persons who brought diamonds should have been mentioned. No question had been put to immediate suppliers of the assessee whether they purchased the material from the open market other than the parties who said to have supplied them from Surat. Therefore, the proposition that in the absence of insurance, mode of transportation, etc. the claim that the diamonds came from Surat could not be accepted, was not a sound conclusion arrived at. It was true that the profit shown by the assessee was extremely high. But, then, no similar cases of export had been mentioned anywhere by the Assessing Officer or by the Commissioner (Appeals) to discredit the assessee’s claim of higher profit. Export of the assessee was accepted by the Customs Department, which showed that the export of diamonds could not be doubted.

The results of the inquiry made by the Assessing Officer with the third parties and the reliance placed by the assessee that no opportunity was provided to the assessee, had not much relevance. Summons issued were received by these parties. They confirmed the sales. Payment made by cheque was confirmed. The only reasoning of the Assessing Officer to disallow assessee’s claim was that subsequently these parties withdrew the amount reflected in their accounts by cash and disappeared. But there was no evidence to show that the money had come back to the assessee. Further, the reasoning of the Assessing Officer, as confirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals), was that there was no evidence to show that the material had been transported from Surat to Mumbai. The third parties were not the parties who sold to the assessee directly. Surat parties claimed that they had delivered the goods to the sellers from whom assessee made purchases. Therefore, this point also could not be strictly taken against the assessee.

Hence, the order of the revenue authorities were liable to be set aside as there was no evidence on record to show that the payments made by the assessee had come back to the assessee, except the modus operandi said to be prevalent in this line of business.

Further, there was no evidence to show that the assessee had made purchases on payment of cash, because the payment was made by the assessee by cheques, which was also reflected in the books of account of the purchasers as well as of the assessee.

In the result the appeal was to be allowed.

The assessee, a partnership firm engaged in manufacturing and trading of cut and polished diamonds, filed its return declaring income of about Rs. 4.74 lakhs. The case was reopened under section 148 based on Investigation Wing information following search/survey in the Bhawarlal Jain group, alleging accommodation purchase entries from Mohit Enterprises and Nice Diamonds aggregating to about Rs. 46.46 lakhs.

■

In response, the assessee furnished purchase bills, stock register, sales and purchase registers, bank statements evidencing payments through banking channels, export invoices and shipping bills, and bank realisation advices, and correlated the impugned purchases to export sales to SR Exports (HK) Ltd. and Lotus Gems BVBA with proceeds realised through banking channels.

■

The Assessing Officer, emphasizing the modus operandi of the Bhawarlal Jain syndicate and terming the documentation unilateral, treated the purchases from the two parties as bogus and disallowed 100% of about Rs. 46.46 lakhs, completing the assessment under section 144, without pointing out discrepancies in the evidences filed or disputing the sales.

■

In first appeal, the assessee reiterated that disallowance could not be made merely on third-party statements without corroboration and highlighted that sales were not doubted. The Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the full disallowance.

On appeal to the Tribunal.

■

In the present case, on the basis that the assessee has deposited cash amounting to Rs. 12.25 lakhs, during the demonetization period in his bank account, the Assessing Officer made the addition by treating the same as unexplained money under section 69A. On the other hand, it is the plea of the assessee that the amount deposited in cash in the bank account during the demonetization period was received by him from his customers to whom he had earlier granted loans against the gold ornaments. As per the assessee, against such gold ornaments, he took loans from the Federal Bank and earns interest income from the customers. In order to support the submission that the assessee availed gold loans from Federal Bank, the assessee has placed on record the statement of its bank account maintained with Federal Bank for the period 13-9-2015 to 13-9-2019. From the perusal of the bank statement, it is evident that the same pertains to 'Fast Track Gold Loan/Gold Loan' availed by the assessee from the Federal Bank and the loan disbursements were made to the assessee from time-to-time. As per the assessee, the amount received from the Federal Bank against the gold ornaments was given as a loan by him to his customers against the gold ornaments. The assessee has also placed on record the list of his customers to whom loans were given against the gold ornaments, which were repaid in cash. From the perusal of the list, it is found that apart from providing the name and address of the customers, the assessee has also provided the PAN details of all these 23 customers. From the perusal of these details, it is further found that these loans were given to the customers as early as 4-5-2016 and as late as 8-11-2016. It is further found that, except in two cases where the loan was repaid on 30-8-2016, the rest of the 21 customers repaid the loan during the demonetization period. It is found that though the assessee furnished all these documents before the lower authorities, however, none of these documents were rejected, nor despite the availability of the information regarding the customers, any verification was made by the Assessing Officer from them. [Para 9]

■

Further, as regards the findings of the lower authorities that the assessee was not authorized to accept the repayment made by the customers in cash in Specified Bank Notes after 8-11-2016, it is found that merely for the reason that there is a violation of certain notifications/GO issued by the Government in transacting with Specified Bank Notes, the genuine explanation offered by the assessee towards the source of cash deposit cannot be rejected, unless the Assessing Officer makes out the case that the assessee has deposited unaccounted cash into bank account in Specified Bank Notes. [Para 10]

■

Therefore, having carefully perused the documentary evidence filed by the assessee, it is viewed that the assessee has duly explained the source of cash deposited by him in his bank account during the demonetization period, and same cannot be treated as unexplained money under section 69A. Accordingly, the impugned addition of Rs. 12.25 lakhs made by the Assessing Officer, being the cash deposits in the bank account during the demonetization period under section 69A, is deleted. [Para 11]
