68. Cash Credits

Where any sum is found credited in the books of an assessee maintained for any previous year, and the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source thereof or the explanation offered by him is not, in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, satisfactory, the sum so credited may be charged to income-tax as the income of the assessee of that previous year:"

From the plain reading of the above section 68, it is abundantly clear that the essential and mandatory pre-requisite for making an addition under this section is that the unexplained sum must be found credited in the books of an assessee maintained by him for any previous year. If the assessee is not maintaining any books of accounts, then addition u/s 68 is unsustainable. The existence of books of account is a condition precedent for invoking of the power u/s 68 of the Act.

The reliance in this regard is placed on the following Judicial Pronouncements viz.

(i)

Judgement of Hon'ble Guwahati High Court in the case of Anand ram Raytani v. CIT, [1997] 223 ITR 544;

The relevant extract of the aforesaid judgement (para 8) is reproduced below for Your Honours' ready reference,

"8. ............We have gone through Section 68 of the Act. The Assessing Officer before invoking the power under Section 68 of the Act must be satisfied that there are books of account maintained by the assessee and the cash credit is recorded in the said books of account and if the assessee fails to satisfy the Assessing Officer, the said sum so credited has to be charged to income-tax as the income of the assessee of that previous year. The existence of books of account is a condition precedent for invoking of the power. Discharging of burden is a subsequent condition. If the first point is not fulfilled the question of burden of proof does not arise."

Whether Bank Pass Book can be considered as Books of Accounts u/s 68?

In several judicial pronouncements especially in the case of CIT v. Bhaichand N. Gandhi [1983] 141 ITR 67/11 Taxman 59 (Bom.), it has been held that the bank statement can't be considered as books of accounts, for the purpose of making addition u/s 68 of the Income Tax Act.

Presumptions in inter-connected transactions:

7. There may be several inter-connected transactions in the conversion of tainted money into untainted money. It is possible that during the course of investigation only one transaction is proved to be involved in money laundering process. Therefore, Section 23 of the PMLA provides that, where money laundering process involves two or more interconnected transactions and one or more such inter-connected transactions are proved to be involved in money laundering, then for the purposes of adjudication or confiscation or for the trial of offence of money laundering, it shall, unless otherwise proved to the satisfaction of the adjudicating authority, or the Special Court, be presumed that the remaining transactions form part of such inter-connected transactions.

Burden of proof:

8. Several persons, including professionals, may be involved in processing of the proceeds of crime for converting it into untainted money. The ultimate beneficiary of the proceeds of crime in the untainted form may be made the prime accused and all those persons who had knowledge or who were involved may also be made co-accused. There may be other persons who may be charged for abatement, but that cannot be under PMLA as no such provision exists in this Act. The charge of abatement/conspiracy can be brought under Section 120B of IPC. Therefore, where a person is charged with the offence of money laundering under section 3, then as per Section 24 of the PMLA, the Authority or Court shall, unless the contrary is proved, presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering: and, in the case of any other person (who is not charged u/s 3of PMLA) the Authority or Court may presume that such proceeds of crime are involved in money laundering. The use of the word "may" in this Section provides a discretion to the Court, whether to cast burden on the accused to prove his innocence. Thus, Section 24 casts the burden of proving that alleged proceeds of crime are not involved in money laundering, on the accused charged u/s 3 of PMLA. However, this does not relieve the prosecution of making specific (and not a vague and omnibus) allegation or charge, supported by substantive evidence that money involved in laundering is earned from or through a scheduled offence and, therefore, are proceeds of crime. Once a charge is made, the accused has to establish that investment (assets or properties) alleged to be out of tainted money, are, in fact, acquired legitimately by lawful means. This can be proved on a standard of preponderance of probability.

Cash Transaction

The above mechanism is useful for transactions made through banking channels, but for cash transactions, it is near to impossible to catch them as the cash system works in the same fashion as 'hawala' works. The word 'hawala' is a local version of the English word 'reference'; this system works only on a reference basis. An anonymous person cannot go directly to the 'hawala' dealer for transfer of money between cities or countries. A reference from some known person is required. These dealers are not maintaining any written record; once a transaction is completed, the record is erased. Even if any record is found during the course of the survey or search, nothing can be made out of these jotted entries. Generally, these transactions are very smooth. Trust and risk are primary conditions. So dealing with cash crypto is almost like dealing with 'hawala' transactions. No separate provisions of the law are applicable, and no special expertise is required to crack these transactions. Traditional hawala methods were mainly operating through two methods. Firstly, the quantum of money of the sender and receiver should be the same. The second method is 'under-invoicing or over-invoicing' of import and export bills as required. But transfer through crypto is not based on any such conditions, the money can be sent unilaterally. So the emphasis is required only on those transactions which are done through banking channels.

Major Challenge

The main danger of cryptocurrencies is the convenience of transferring money to offshore places. A person can buy crypto in cash in India and transfer it to some person living abroad. That person would sell it and receive money in the local currency. Same as in the case of international debit or credit cards, where the deposits are made in one country in local currency, but ATM withdrawals can be made in any country. The central banks are honouring the transactions of debit and credit cards, as in the case of crypts also. The central bank has to honour at least in those countries that have given legal status to some cryptocurrencies. So why have some countries, like China, completely banned any transaction in these currencies. Section 194S comes into the picture when the amount is credited to a resident. Hence the money sent outside of the countries is out of the purview of these provisions. The first-time buyers of the crypto are also required to bring under these provisions.

24. Payment of advance salary to defeat purpose of demonetisation won't come under purview of benami transaction

[G. Bahadur v. ACIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 179 (PBPTA - AT)]

The appellant was employed in a College run by a Trust. He received Rs. 50 thousand as advance salary from the said trust. The appellant deposited entire amount in his bank account, which was subsequently withdrawn by him and used for own purposes.

The Initiating Officer (IO) assumed that Chairman of trust had forced employees to distribute, deposit and retain their own money in demonetized currency in guise of loan received, which had to be repaid after some time in new currency. Thus, IO held chairman of college as beneficial owner and appellant as benamidar and passed order provisionally attaching bank account of appellant.

The Appellate Tribunal held in favour of appellant as under:

Every cash transaction couldn't be termed as a 'benami' transaction. As per section 2(9) of Benami Act the following twin conditions are needed to be satisfied to construe any transaction as benami: (1) the property being held by a person who has not provided the consideration, (2) the property is held by that person for the immediate or future benefit, direct or indirect of the person who has provided the said consideration.

The characteristic of a 'benami' transaction is that there must be a mere lending of name without any intention to benefit the person in whose name it is made, i.e., a mere name lender. The mischiefs sought to be punished by the Act are only such transactions which have a name lending element without deriving any benefit therein, i.e., 'benami' transactions.

The transaction where cash was paid to person in lieu of a future promise couldn't be a 'benami' transaction, as there was no lending of name. There could be no 'benami' transaction if the future benefit was due from the person who was also the holder of property.

The impugned order was not sustainable as it intended to punish the appellants for wanting to defeat the purpose of demonetization and was beyond the purview of the Act.

CONCLUDING OBSERVATION AND SUGGESTIONS Based on the above observation, it can be stated that the introduction of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 was a much-needed step for the prosecution of fugitive economic offenders. This Act is a tailor-made specific statute that deals with a typical form of white collar crime which constitutes a huge chunk of economic offences in the country. It can also be stated that there are various unique features in this statute. This brings out various positive points that the legislators have tried to implement through this Act. The Act provides for time-bound prosecution of the offenders of economic crimes. To ensure this, the Act is formulated in such a way that there is no delay in the trial and other judicial proceedings. The distinctive feature of this Act is the attachment and confiscation of different types of properties that are not acquired by legal means. Such attachment and confiscation are based on the United Nations Convention against Corruption. Thus it can be said from the above observation and analysis that this legislation is drafted keeping in mind the speedy trial and recovery of monetary value in question. The above provisions of the Act are closely associated with the nature of offenses that the country has faced in the past few years. Economic offenses of grave nature affect the country's GDP and become a hurdle in the path of progress of the economy. Therefore such accused who are declared as fugitive economic offenders under the Act must be brought to justice so that the sanctity of the rule of law is maintained. This will also ensure the removal of the block in the path of the country's economic progress. This legislation was the need of the time and the Central Government has been successful in bringing out a law that deals with all major aspects of offices whose offenders have turned fugitive and are trying to avoid prosecution. The powers granted to the authority and the designated officers are wider in nature as compared to previous money laundering and economic offenses legislations.

On one hand where the government's move towards tackling such nature of offenses is being appreciated, on the other hand, the implementation of the said Act is also put to question with several lacunas. The lacuna lies in the fact that as per Section 4 of the Act, a person is straightway declared as a fugitive if sufficient evidence is against him. It also observes that imbalanced power is granted to the special court and nodal agency for conducting search and seizure and attaching the property of the accused. The law is subject to proper judicial review from the higher courts to be perfectly implantable since it violates basic human rights and laws of natural justice prima facie on its implementation. The pre-confiscation of the property of the accused before the conviction of the offence violated the basic principle of criminal law which states that every person is to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Thus, it is important to note that this legislation should go under judicial review by the appropriate court. To make the implementation of the law more effective, the Central Government needs to bring amendments as per the rule of law observing the principles of natural justice, the right to free and fair trial, and in consonance with the fundamental rights provisions of the Indian Constitution. The Act is a much-needed step to recover and prevent economic offenses of modern times and will prove a milestone shortly if implemented and executed with due care.

In today's world, financial fraud instances are on the rise, and with advancements in technology, fraudsters are smarter to contrive new ways to carry out their nefarious schemes. Money laundering is one of these crimes that has been exploiting businesses for a long time. Criminals have devised alternate methods for concealing the source of money obtained unlawfully. Money laundering is a significant concern for financial institutions and Fintech firms. Placement, layering, and integration are the three stages of money laundering. The most difficult yet vital of these is placement. Most of the evidence that could aid in tracking the funds is destroyed during this stage. The funds are then layered in the second stage, which means they are given a frame that makes them appear legitimate. The funds are brought back into the legal economy during the last step of integration. Several bank accounts from different jurisdictions are used during the layering stage. Multiple account transfers obstruct tracking and circumvent value constraints. Authorities should be unable to track the origins of incriminated monies during the integration stage.

Given the recent significant surge in money laundering cases, firms anticipate an upsurge in the future as well. Regulatory authorities are functioning to prevent money laundering globally. Every company must follow the Financial Actions Task Force's rules (FATF) recommendations to combat Money Laundering cases that intend to protect enterprises from many sorts of illegal activities, particularly money laundering. Furthermore, the guidelines have highlighted specific actions that can assist businesses in detecting money laundering. FATF recommends these acts as red flags, making money laundering detection simpler.

If resources are valuable, fraudsters will try taking advantage of them. They enjoy precious jewels, stones, gold, diamonds, and other glistening materials as they are easy to conceal and give higher worth. Vulnerabilities can motivate the offenders to perpetrate fraud by dodging taxes, laundering money, or smuggling at virtually every level of the precious metals and stone trades, from extraction to refining to sale or re-sale of finished products. Gold and diamonds perfect for money laundering

Recently there have been several gold-related financial crime cases. According to the United States "Financial Action Task Force," criminals prefer to launder money through global gold and diamond markets because they offer predictable profits, participants deal mostly in cash, tracing transactions is complex, and gold and diamonds are easier to transport.

Many case studies have crammed how drug traffickers accept diamonds or gold as payment for drugs, smugglers convert gold into common unidentifiable objects like belt buckles, corrupt payments, bribes, and illegal gold and diamond mining to fund terrorism avoiding taxes. In most cases, Shell companies are established as a front business for illicit trades. Money laundering and shell companies share an old camaraderie, and in most cases of reported money laundering and smuggling, shell companies have played a significant role. This is prevalent worldwide. Shell companies are the entities that generally have no physical presence otherwise than an address and generate no or little economic value. They can be formed for legitimate purposes, too; yet, they have become a common tool for money laundering due to their ability to hide ownership and mask the financial details.

Money laundering occurs in a variety of ways. For example, someone might form a shell company to trade precious metals and use the shell company's name and bank account to receive the sale proceeds. Apart from this, the schemes involving magnified valuations of precious metals or stones due to a lack of expert valuation knowledge are also widespread. In such cases, the owner of a stone usually hires a third party to help evaluate the stone. The valuer doing the valuation often provides a deceptive report to the seller by claiming the stone to be of low value per carat. The stone's market worth may be high, but due to the seller's lack of knowledge, it will be presented to the seller at a marginally lower price.

Though FATF provides recommendations on Anti-Money Laundering practices, specific regulations to combat money laundering using precious metals and jewels have been provided by the "Kimberley Process," which was formed in 2003 and today has 56 participants from 82 nations. (The EU's 27 member states are counted as single participants.) The certification process oversees the requirements and provisions, such as creating national conflict legislation, commitment to transparency, statistical data exchange, prohibition of diamond trade with non-members, and provision of conflict-free certification for shipments. However, some nations are not Kimberley Process participants, and this is a big issue in the possibility of illicit trade involving stones from those countries.

The RBI has an anti-money laundering cell in operation, to whom banks are expected to report suspicious transactions.

MONEY-LAUNDERING VIS-A-VIS OTHER ACTS 6. Money-laundering in somewhat different way is sought to be tackled through Income-tax Act and Banking cash transaction tax Act, though the scope is not limited to proceeds of crime. A cash credit in the books of account not explained as to its source (section 68), unexplained investment (section 69), unexplained expenditure (section 69C), and possession of undisclosed assets (section 69B) are deemed to be income and subjected to tax. Transfer of immovable property at understated consideration could have been frustrated by the Government acquiring the property on those terms (Chapter XXC). The provision of acquiring the property now stands deleted. Payments exceeding prescribed monetary limits and loans/ advances and repayment thereof (section 269SS and 269T) can be made otherwise than by crossed cheques, only at the risk of consequences by way of disallowances and penalty. Banking cash transactions tax recently introduced subjects to tax, cash withdrawals from bank accounts exceeding the specified limit and requires the banks to submit details of such withdrawals to the authorities. The object of all these provisions is to track the tainted money and provide for consequences of attempt to legitimise such money.

It may not be easy to link the property which is the proceed of crime with the actual commission of offence which is essential for the offence of money laundering.... Provisions need to be made real and effective deterrence should be provided for frivilous and motivated actions on the part of administrators as well as informants.

MULTIPLICITY OF INFORMATION

7. Operation of these provisions, like the provisions of Money Laundering Act, is dependent upon the proper information system. The newly introduced section 285BA in the Act enjoin on the banks, credit card companies, Mutual Funds, a company issuing shares, bonds and debentures, Registrar of properties and the officer of RBI to furnish Annual Information Return (AIR) of transactions above specified limit. Further the TDS provisions require banks to submit details of deposits and interest paid on deposits of whatever nature. The BCTT Act requires banks to submit details of cash withdrawals. The Money Laundering Act requires banks, financial institutions and intermediaries to submit information as specified. Enactments other than Money Laundering Act also seek to deal with introduction of unaccounted funds into the mainstream. Even though the scope of these legislation is not limited to proceeds of crime the information required to be furnished is more or less similar. The requirement of furnishing similar or almost similar information under different statutes for dealing with objects of similar nature places avoidable burden on banks and other agencies. If a co-ordinated view can be taken and the information is designed so as to subserve the purposes of these legislations, the burden of the information providers will be reduced resulting in reduced cost of compliance.

PROBLEMS/ISSUES INVOLVED

8. Even though the objective of the legislation is unquestionably laudable, much will depend on the implementation. It is not uncommon to find that the persons actually committing the crime and those enjoying the proceeds of crime are not the same. Most of the activities of drug trafficking, smuggling, etc., are carried on through carriers and the identity of real culprits remain concealed. It may not be easy to link the property which is the proceed of crime with the actual commission of offence which is essential for the offence of money-laundering. Failure to link the two may frustrate the very objective of the Act. Further there is need of utmost caution to be exercised in execution to ensure that genuine business activities are not subjected to process under the Act. Even though the Legislature has taken care to see that innocent people are not subjected to treatment under the Act by adding the word ‘knowingly’ to the act of assistance or being a party in the definition of money-laundering which will make the fact of ignorance a defence, such safeguards will have no meaning unless the adjudicating authority acts fairly and judiciously. Such words generally, have relevance in appellate proceedings when the damage is already done. The Act also makes a vexatious search without recording reasons, a punishable offence and so is the act of providing wrong information leading to search or arrest action. These provisions need to be made real and effective deterrence should be provided for frivolous and motivated actions on the part of administrators as well as informants.

10. Concluding comments

Much more can be written about the issues likely to emerge consequent to the decision to demonetize the high denomination notes on the basis of present situation. More are likely to surface as the work relating to exchange and conversion proceeds. 10.1 The decisions to demonetize notes of Rs.500/- & Rs.1,000/- is a bold decision of the Govt., though taken in haste and without required preparedness but there may not be dissenters to the decision taken by the Govt. in principle. But, doing so, without proper preparations, cannot be excused. Why should there be restriction of Rs.20,000/- withdrawal a week when one wish to withdraw his disclosed money with the bank. Further, mere issue of Rs.2,000/- notes to start with is of no use unless notes of smaller denominations of Rs.100/- and Rs.50/- are simultaneously issued. Why so far there has been no issue of new notes of Rs.500/- is a mystery. The inconvenience that the common man is suffering because of unpreparedness of the Govt. to meet the resultant problems is un-excusable. Merely saying 'suffer these for better future' can hardly be a consolation.

10.2 Also, demonetization is only one way for tackling black money problem. People do not generate black money to keep it idle in chests at home. They churn it out to add more money by investments in real estate, gold/silver jewellery, precious stones, investments in India and abroad and in many other ways, including its use in political funding. Hence, tackling in parts the problem of black money is likely to be counterproductive. Consolidated effort in this direction is needed. Measures like demonetization inconvenience merely the small traders and common man across the country. Hence, simultaneous efforts are necessary to check investments in aforesaid avenues. Further, measures will have to be thought of to dis-incentivise fresh generation of black money and clean up the political funding and keep check on the finances of political parties. All parties must be, through law, made to mandatorily declare their monthly receipts and expenditure, which must be open to public scrutiny and vetted by the Election Commission. That would be a real step in the direction of checking black money – not measures like demonetization – which tackle the stock – not theflow.

10.3 Terror financing through counterfeit Indian notes and their smuggling may stop for some time, but further action on these lines will stop only when the new notes cannot be duplicated. The claim of the RBI is that these cannot be but time alone would show how far such claim is justified. However, the more important step, to be taken, is checking strongly their infiltration in the country.

10.4 The success of the decision can only be known after the period of conversion allowed is over. If large chunk of 14.95 lakh crore notes come back to the economy, it will indicate that the demonetization has not served its purpose – the evaders have been more smart than the administrative action from the side of the Finance Ministry.

11. Urgent action needed from GOI's side

Considering the confusion created by the unpreparedness of the Govt. and its own estimate that it will take 2-3 weeks more for making the ATMs work and non-availability of new notes in sufficient numbers, the time limit upto 30th December for conversion/deposit in bank accounts needs to be extended upto 31st March, 2017 and thereafter, with the RBI upto 30th June, 2017. This needs to be done immediately to remove the hervousness and hurried approach to banks.

TAXMANN ADVISORY AND RESEARCH TEAM (INCOME TAX)

Introduction

1. Demonetization has encouraged people to shift towards digital mode of payment while making financial transactions. By adopting digital mode of payment, no financial transactions would remain undisclosed and Consequently, an enhanced turnover of business might get reflected in the books of account.

Under the circumstances, an apprehension has been caused that increased turnover in the current year may lead to reopening of earlier years' cases causing undue harassment to taxpayers.

Thus, CBDT and CBEC (vide Circular No. 40/2016 and Circular No. 137/155/2012-Service tax) have advised tax officials not to re-open past assessments in income-tax and indirect tax cases only because increased turnover is reflected in books of account of business on account of increased use of digital means of payment.

2. Points to be considered for interpreting such circulars:

It would be incorrect to construe the above Circulars as giving any amnesty to tax-evaders.

The above circulars do not say that any spurt in turnover reported in books of account of businesses of current financial year (and consequently in their ITRs or indirect tax returns) is not need to be explained.

The Circulars do not give businessmen a license to show their accumulated black money in the form of demonetized notes as current year's turnover and get away scot-free without any interest or penalty and by paying normal tax for current year. If such a license is given by the circulars, the proposed PMGKY Scheme and proposed amendments to section115BBE of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and proposed new section 271AAC of that Act would be redundant.

The two circulars clarify the following points which is mere re-iteration of the existing law:

Suppose any business reported Rs.1cr to Rs.1.5 cr as its turnover in service tax and VAT in last 5 years. If the business reports a turnover of Rs.5 cr in financial year 2016-17, then it is natural for any tax official to suspect that increased turnover;

However, such suspicion alone is not sufficient to entail reopening of past assessments in income-tax and well as service tax/customs;

The Circulars do not take away the powers of tax officials to make inquiries into the sudden spurt in reported turnover;

If the results of enquiries yield information which can form basis of "reason to believe" escapement of turnover/income in the past periods, the assessments can be reopened.

The Circulars are innocuous and merely caution tax officials to adopt systematic approach under the law to enquire into sudden jumps and reopen past assessment only if enquiry throws up reason to believe that past turnovers/incomes escaped assessment. Sudden jump in turnover may give reason to suspect that turnover/income had escaped assessment in past years. But that suspicion should not lead to reopening of past assessments without making necessary inquiries and verification regarding causes of the sudden increase.

Huge increase in reported turnover can be due to genuine reasons as well as due to book-keeping sophistry.

3. Examples of genuine reasons for increased turnover due to increased use of digital means of payments:–

(1)

Credit cards offer EMI terms on purchases made through credit cards. This may have resulted in increase in sales. So, a business which was selling only on cash basis may experience a jump in turnover on account of this reason.

(2)

Impolitic purchases through plastic cards

(3)

Special cash back schemes of mobile wallets/debit cards/credit cards.

(4)

Expansion of facility of service provider/increase in manpower enabling him to service more customers.

4. Comments

Increased turnover reflected in books of accounts may also be due to past unaccounted money now shown in current year's books as current year's turnover and thereafter these notes are banked.

Whatever be the reasons, taxpayers can (and should be) asked to explain the huge increase in current period's turnover. If they are able to explain the same by valid reasons and also show corresponding increase in stocks and purchases (or expansion in size of facilities/manpower), then their explanation will be believed and past assessments will not be reopened. If they cannot explain the sudden increase in reported turnover, they can always declare their huge unexplained cash/bank deposits in proposed PMGKY Scheme and pay 49.9% tax and deposit 25% in PMGKY deposit (no interest; 4 years lock-in). If they declare their unaccounted cash/bank deposits in PMGKY, then obviously, there would be no question of reopening their past assessments of income-tax or indirect taxes. If they do not declare in PMGKY and opt to show it as current year's turnover, then they should be able to justify it.

Abstract

Gold has regained prominence as a universal store of value amid rising geopolitical uncertainty, inflation, and distrust in fiat currencies. Its surge to record highs in 2025 reflects both legitimate economic behaviour and increasing compliance challenges. This article analyses how global gold dynamics intersect with taxation, money-laundering laws, and white-collar crime, particularly within India's regulatory ecosystem. It also examines cross-border trade complexities, enforcement coordination, and the evolving standards of global financial governance. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for policymakers and corporate stakeholders to balance economic opportunity with legal responsibility.

Keywords: Gold, Taxation, Compliance, PMLA, FATF, GAAR, Cross-Border Trade, Corporate Governance, White-Collar Crime

I. Research Objective and Context

Gold remains more than a commodity. It is an emotion, a financial anchor, and a barometer of public confidence. In 2025, its value has soared not only because of market mechanics but also due to geopolitical tension and financial distrust. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the legal, tax, and compliance implications of gold's renewed prominence in the global economy.

The research aims to:

1.

Examine the global and Indian gold market trends shaping 2025.

2.

Analyse the legal and regulatory architecture governing taxation, anti-money-laundering, and cross-border transactions.

3.

Identify vulnerabilities that enable gold to be used for white-collar crime.

4.

Recommend policy and governance strategies that uphold transparency and accountability without impeding legitimate trade.

Gold's unique attributes such as liquidity, anonymity, and universal acceptance make it both an asset of stability and a tool of concealment. Understanding this duality is essential for designing laws that protect integrity while enabling commerce.

II. The Global Gold Surge: Economics, Emotion and Law

A. Price Trends and Market Forces

According to Reuters and the World Gold Council, gold prices in 2025 have risen nearly 50 percent year-on-year, reaching around US $3,950 per ounce internationally and crossing Rs. 1,25,000 per 10 grams in India. This dramatic rise stems from persistent inflation, high global debt, and growing investor preference for tangible assets.

Central banks across Asia and the Middle East have purchased record quantities of gold to diversify reserves. Goldman Sachs has forecast prices could approach US $4,900 per ounce by 2026 if inflation remains elevated and interest rates stabilise.

This global pattern underscores gold's transformation from a passive store of value into a geopolitical hedge. It reflects both market sentiment and institutional strategy.

B. India's Domestic Context

India's relationship with gold is historical and deeply cultural. Demand peaks during festivals and marriage seasons, creating a recurring impact on trade balances. India imports nearly all its gold, which has implications for the current account deficit and currency stability.

High import duties and fluctuating exchange rates have incentivised smuggling and under-invoicing. In March 2025, the government discontinued parts of the Gold Monetisation Scheme to limit fiscal exposure. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has since reported a notable increase in illegal inflows through land and maritime borders.

C. Geopolitical Context

Gold's rally cannot be separated from the global political landscape. The continuing Russia–Ukraine conflict, instability in the Middle East, and trade tensions between the United States and China have disrupted global supply chains. Sanctions against Russian bullion refineries have redirected trade to Asian hubs such as Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

As trade flows realign, enforcement agencies must address differing compliance standards among jurisdictions. Some free-trade zones have become conduits for gold trading with limited regulatory oversight, increasing risks of mis-invoicing and money laundering.

III. Legal Framework Governing Gold and Financial Compliance

A. Income-Tax and Disclosure Laws

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, unexplained gold holdings can be taxed as income under Sections 69 and 69B. High-net-worth individuals and corporations are required to declare gold holdings accurately to avoid reassessment and penalty.

Cross-border transactions in gold attract transfer-pricing scrutiny under Section 92F. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued guidelines requiring documentation that justifies arm's-length pricing.

Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor.

Judicial Review of Demonetization in 2016

On January 2, 2023, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India [2023] 146 taxmann.com 36 upheld the Central Government's decision to demonetise currency notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1,000 denominations. The Constitution Bench, led by Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, inter-alia, held that demonetization was proportionate to the Union's stated objectives and was implemented reasonably.

The Petitioners before the Apex Court had contended that demonetization could only be initiated on the RBI's Central Board recommendation, highlighting a lack of evidence of deliberation and consultation between the Union and the RBI. They further argued that, under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act 1934, which allows the Central Government to declare that "any series of bank notes of any denomination shall cease to be legal tender" after a recommendation from the Central Board of RBI, the Union could only announce demonetization for a specific series, not all notes. This, they claimed, significantly impacted the economy, as 86% of circulating currency was in demonetized notes.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court deemed it an Executive's economic policy, immune to reversal as judicial review did not apply to economic policy decisions. The Hon'ble Bench accepted the Government's claim of consultation with the RBI prior to demonetization, asserting a reasonable connection between the Government and the RBI in implementing the measure.

Consequently, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that demonetization did not violate the "Doctrine of Proportionality" asserting that the demonetization process involved deliberation, and application of mind, and lacked procedural flaws.

In hindsight, when the Hon'ble Apex Court rendered its verdict, the question of the Constitutionality of demonetization seemed moot. The deed was done, and the repercussions were evident. With over 99% of the currency returned within the stipulated deadline, the dust had settled and possibly little was left to reverse or rectify.

Methods include:

• over-invoicing,

• under-invoicing,

• phantom shipments,

• duplicate invoicing,

• false declarations.

India presently lacks sophisticated, integrated trade data analytics capable of real-time anomaly detection. (Trade Intelligence & Analytics (TIA) Portal - A New Integrated Platform for India’s Trade Insights, 2025)

This trend of bringing in amendments in the legislature, and that too with retrospective effect, to overcome decisions favourable to the tax payer rendered by various courts will surely keep the tax payers on their toes even after succeeding in appeals at various levels of the judiciary and would thereby create uncertainty to the complete system of taxation in India.

banks. Countries with less stringent banking laws become tax-haven for the criminals, who by striking an understanding with the bank officials, deposit the crime proceeds in bank accounts and discreetly purchase some property with that money.

Electronic transfer has further facilitated criminal organizations in swift and almost risk-free transfer of funds between countries. With increased automation in banking and financial systems, there is lesser face-to-face contact between the customers and the bank officials. As a result, the chances of smelling a suspicious transaction turn remote. The actual modus operandi of money-laundering activity can be divided into 3 stages, viz., introduction, conversion and merger. The three stages are described as follows :

Initially the launderer introduces the criminal proceeds into the banking system. This can be done in more than one way; the most common being by disintegrating the proceeds into smaller sums which bear lesser chances of arousing suspicion. Alternatively, the launderer may transfer funds in various accounts in different locations through a number of financial instruments of smaller denomination.

The next stage is of conversion, which is achieved by making a series transactions, with a view to distance the final application of proceeds from their original source. The basic objective is to camouflage the source by multiplicity of transactions so that it becomes more difficult to find trail of the criminal source. This is done simply by serial transfer of funds from one account to another, either physically or electronically. The objective is better served, if the various accounts are spread over different countries. At times, the transfer of funds may be disguised as payment for goods or services.

The last stage is merger of proceeds into the mainstream economy under disguise of a legitimate transaction such as investment in immovable property, or in establishment of a business, or in buying expensive items or luxuries.

Banks, thus, become an integral part of transactions of money-laundering, intentionally or more often unintentionally. The law on prevention of money-laundering has, therefore, assigned a major role for banks in fulfilling the international endeavour.

Assessing Authorities' Stand in OCM/Demonetisation Assessment Cases concerning Assesses' Claims of Cash deposits being made out of Cash Sales in Business

5. In the cases of persons engaged in business and maintaining books of accounts, the most common and natural explanation and justification for the cash deposits being made by them in the post demonetisation period has been cash sales being made by them in their businesses.

The assessing authorities, in majority of the OCM assessment cases, have declined to accept the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made out of cash sales of business in post demonetisation period and have made huge income-tax demands under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in the regular assessment orders in such OCM/demonetisation cases. The most common arguments and contentions being made by the assessing authorities in rejecting the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made by the assessees out of their cash sales in business post demonetisation period are discussed as under:

i.

Since w.e.f. 8.11.2016 midnight, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes (SBNs) were declared invalid and were not to be considered as legal tender, therefore, for the assesses carrying on business, booking of cash sales and accepting such SBNs for transacting business transactions, during post demonetisation period, was prohibited.

ii.

The money measurement concept of accounting underlines the fact that in accounting and economics generally, every recorded event or transaction is measured in terms of money, i.e., the local currency monetary unit of measure. Since the SBNs were just a piece of papers and they bear no value on 9th November 2016 or after, as Central Government, the guarantor, had withdrawn its guarantee and hence, the receipt of these SBNs can't be journalized in books of account. Therefore, the transactions made in SBNs on or after 9th November 2016 cannot be entered into cash books.

iii.

Therefore, if the assessee has received any SBN notes after 09.11.2016 on account of any monetary transactions and utilizes the same for making cash deposits into the bank account, then the credit of the same into the books of accounts is not to be considered as valid and has to be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act and brought to tax.

In some other cases, where the cash deposits have been explained by the assessees as pertaining to cash sales being made by them prior to the demonetisation period, the assessing authorities have again rejected the genuineness and authenticity of such claims believing that the assessees might have backdated the cash sales just before the demonetisation period so as to reflect cash in hand as on 8.11.2016 consisting of banned notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000, which they have deposited in their bank accounts post demonetisation.

Swiss Legal Position: Reliance on Stolen Information

Till 2019, a total of 628 cases of HSBC Bank, Geneva, were reported accounting for undisclosed income of INR 8,465 crores were brought to tax. Out of these, over 208 cases were found to be "non-actionable because of no balances in account's information, non-residents, not traceable, an amount taxable in some other hand."

On administrative assistance relating to tax matters, on July 17, 2018 [decision no. 2C_648/2017], Swiss Supreme Court ('SSC') rendered a decision concerning stolen data. The court categorically distinguished its decision from an earlier decision dated March 17, 2017 on the same subject matter.

The decision rendered by the SSC on March 17, 2017 was based on the 'principle of good faith' as envisaged under the Swiss Criminal law, violation of which is a criminal offence. The court applied the principle and concluded that Swiss Federal Tax Administration ('FTA') cannot provide administrative assistance for any request made by foreign tax authorities based on the theft of data.

The subsequent decision of the SSC dated July 17, 2018, ruled that exchange of information based on stolen information will not per se be in violation of the 'principle of good faith' as contemplated under Article 7 of the Swiss Tax Administrative Assistance Act ('STAA'). The principle may defer basis the facts and circumstances of each case.

The exchange of stolen information would constitute violation if there were an explicit arrangement between India and Switzerland to not use the stolen data. As per SSC, there was no explicit declaration or assurance given by the Indian Tax Authorities to not use the stolen data and therefore, Indian Tax Authorities could use the said information.

The theory on administrative tax assistance was also considered in yet another decision of Swiss Supreme Court rendered on July 26, 2019, which makes it easier for foreign tax authorities to submit a general request for obtaining information without having to demonstrate concrete indication of alleged tax transgressions by account holders at Swiss banks.

For administrative tax assistance, the most crucial requirement is to depict that the request made by the tax authorities is for 'foreseeable relevance' and not for 'speculative requests' which are prohibited. With this premise, the tax authorities will be able to put in broad requests without having to showcase alleged tax transgressions.

Impact Analysis

Another aspect which is significant relates to the Fundamental Principle under Laws of Evidence i.e., the concept of 'beyond reasonable doubt.' Given the recent Pandora leaks, tracing the ultimate beneficiary, and establishing live link with the illicit money being stacked outside India would require arduous efforts. Even if the efforts get the ball rolling, Revenue would be required to prove their case 'beyond reasonable doubt.'

Further, the settled principle of a mere possibility of 'maybe guilty' cannot result in conviction, further would act as a hindrance for Revenue to trace and prove ultimate beneficiary.

It is generally accepted principle under the Evidence Laws is that when a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it.

17. Reopening of cases of Rahul Gandhi and Sonia Gandhi is valid as they failed to disclose shares allotted in excess of FMV: HC

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

Smaller businesses might be involved in the supply chain, and they may fall below the GST registration threshold, contributing to the presence of non-registered entities in the expenses. By examining these factors and obtaining a clear understanding of the nature of the expenses and the entities involved, the auditor can make a more informed assessment and mitigate the risk of misinterpretation or misreporting.

As a corollary, when the figures reported in the mentioned column are substantial, and the following instances are present, the auditor should exercise heightened vigilance to ensure the authenticity of the transactions:

(a)

Taxable Products: If the products purchased are taxable under GST, it raises the significance of these transactions and warrants closer scrutiny.

(b)

Cash Payments: Payments made in cash can increase the risk of irregularities or inaccuracies in reporting, and therefore, require careful examination.

(c)

Absence of TDS: Transactions not subjected to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) can potentially indicate a need for closer inspection, as TDS is a common regulatory requirement for certain types of payments.

(d)

Internal Documentation: Transactions primarily supported by internal vouchers, bills, or purchase notes, as opposed to external invoices or receipts, may necessitate a more thorough examination to verify their legitimacy.

If the auditor encounters difficulties in forming a conclusive opinion based on the data provided by the assessee, it is essential to include appropriate comments in the main report. These comments should clearly convey an concerns or uncertainties regarding the reported transactions, ensuring transparency and clarity in the audit process.

Expenses covered under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM):

In case of expenditures that were subjected to tax on reverse charge basis, we may encounter with two issues-

(a)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by a person registered under GST but issuing RCM invoices;

(b)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by an unregistered person where the assessee pays tax under RCM on voluntary basis.

In the first scenario, the expenditure under the said category ought to be reported under column 5 of clause 44 i.e., "Relating to other registered entities".

In the second scenario, the expenditure under the said category should be reported under column 7 i.e., Expenditure relating to entities not registered under GST".

Judicial update

Recently, Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in Rajmandir Estates (P.) Ltd. v. Pr. CIT [2016] 386 ITR 162/240 Taxman 306/70 taxmann.com 124, had an occasion to deal with the issue of validity of reopening of assessment by CIT u/s. 263, in the backdrop of possible money-laundering.

The CIT in his order dated 22.03.13 passed under Section 263 opined that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went undetected due to lack of requisite enquiry and non-application of mind. He entertained the belief "that unaccounted money is laundered as clean share capital by creating a façade of paper work, routing the money through several bank accounts and getting it the seal of statutory approval by getting the case reopened u/s.147 suo motu. Accordingly he concluded that assessment order passed u/s. 143(3)/147 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. He, therefore, set aside the same and issued directions for a thorough enquiry.

Hon'ble High Court in its elaborate order after referring to the PMLA and observing various facets and evidences of possible money laundering under the peculiar facts of the case upheld the order of CIT u/s. 263 in following words:

"We have indicated above the pieces of evidence which go to show that the Commissioner had reasons to entertain the belief that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went unnoticed because the assessing officer did not hold requisite investigation except for calling for the records. ……. The fact that the assessing officer did not apply his mind to those pieces of evidence would be evident from the assessment order itself.

The question for consideration is whether in the presence of materials discussed above the Commissioner was justified in treating the assessment order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. That question in the facts and circumstances has to be answered in the affirmative."

It is important to note that, Hon'ble High Court distinguished some of the Supreme Court precedents cited by the appellant to support his case inter alia on the ground that The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 was not there on the statute at that point of time. Therefore, though offences under the Income Tax act, 1961 per se are not scheduled offences for the purpose of PMLA, nevertheless assessing officer can proceed in assessment or CIT can direct further investigation in order to verify possibility of income/assets added or declared u/s. 68, 69, 69A etc. of the IT act being sourced out of proceeds of crime as defined u/s. 2(u) of the PMLA, so that further action under PMLA, if necessary, can be taken.

Conclusion

It has to be kept in view that India has a problem of black economy, which is unacounted and many a time the holders of black money also launder the black money in order to acquire legitimate assets. Legal or illegal income which evades tax and illegal income that comes within the exempted taxation slab constitute the unreported Gross Domestic Product or black economy. Laundering the black money and laundering proceeds of crime are two different issues, although there is frequent overlap between the two. While laundering black money is to be handled through taxation laws or similar laws, the laundering of proceeds of crime is to be handled through special anti-money-laundering laws. [Dr. M. C. 13. Review and Contemporary Analysis

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act has become one of the most important economic laws in India’s regulatory system. Over the years, it has strengthened the government’s ability to trace illegal money, investigate financial frauds, recover public assets, and tackle organized economic offences. Enforcement actions against banking scams, shell companies, Ponzi schemes, cyber frauds, and cross-border laundering networks have played a major role in protecting investors, financial institutions, and the broader economy.

Recent data released by the Enforcement Directorate shows the increasing scale of enforcement under the PMLA. As of March 2026, the ED had registered more than 8,800 ECIRs, issued over 3,500 provisional attachment orders, and attached assets worth nearly ₹2.36 lakh crore. During the financial year 2025–26 alone, attachments reportedly crossed ₹81,000 crore, marking a sharp rise compared to previous years.

These enforcement measures have also produced significant economic benefits. Official figures indicate that assets worth more than ₹63,000 crore have either been returned or steps have been taken to return them to banks, investors, financial institutions, and homebuyers affected by large-scale frauds. In several real-estate and infrastructure cases, attached properties were used to safeguard the interests of thousands of affected investors and purchasers.

The scale of recent investigations further highlights the expanding role of the ED in financial regulation. In the TDI Infrastructure case, properties worth around ₹349 crore were attached in matters relating to the alleged diversion of homebuyers’ funds affecting over 14,000 investors. Likewise, in proceedings involving Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Ltd., assets exceeding ₹313 crore were attached to protect the interests of affected homebuyers.

India has also strengthened international cooperation in tracing illegal financial flows and fugitive offenders. Through Mutual Legal Assistance Requests and Letters Rogatory issued to countries such as the United Kingdom, Singapore, Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, investigative agencies have expanded their efforts in evidence collection, extradition, and asset tracing.

At the prosecution stage, nearly 2,400 complaints have been filed before Special Courts under the PMLA. Parliamentary disclosures further indicate that courts have delivered judgments in a number of concluded cases, with convictions secured in a large majority of them. These figures are often cited to demonstrate the strengthening of India’s anti-money laundering framework and its growing institutional capacity.

The impact of these actions extends beyond prosecution alone. Recovery and attachment of illegally acquired assets have helped improve banking recovery mechanisms, discourage circulation of unaccounted money, strengthen financial discipline, and improve India’s standing within the global anti-money laundering framework developed by the Financial Action Task Force.

46. (1) The procedure for export from Special Economic Zone through seaports or airports or Inland Container Depot or Container Freight Station or Land Customs Station or by Post or by Courier or by Personal Carriage, as the case may be, shall be as under:—

(a)

the Unit shall file Shipping Bill, in quadruplicate, with the Authorized Officer of Customs in the Special Economic Zone together with relevant documents, namely, invoice, packing list and Currency Declaration Form (GR) (in duplicate):

Provided that there shall be exemption from declaration in the forms, GR or SDF or PP or SOFTEX as referred in the Foreign Exchange Management (Export of Goods and Services) Regulations, 2000 notified vide Reserve Bank of India Notification No. FEMA 23/2000-RB dated 3rd May, 2000 as amended from time to time 1[for export value as may be notified by the Reserve Bank of India, from time to time];

(b)

the Shipping Bill shall be registered, assigned a running serial number and assessed by the Authorized Officer in the manner and procedure as is followed in case of exports under free shipping bill without any requirement of the counter signature;

(c)

the goods shall not be subjected to routine examination and 'Let Export Order' shall be given on the basis of self certification by the Unit 2[, however, in case Merchandise Exports from India Scheme benefit is claimed then examination of export cargo shall be done as per examination norms set by Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs 2a[for the scheme]] :

Provided that goods may be sealed after examination, as per the norms prescribed for free shipping bills, at the option of the Unit, by the Authorized Officer Provided further that if services are exported in non-physical form, the export value is to be furnished by the Unit on self certification basis as per the instructions of the Reserve Bank of India.

Explanation.—"Self-certification" means the certification regarding sealing of container or package of goods under export given by the Unit and includes the certificate regarding contents and sealing of the container or package given by the owner or the working partner or the Managing Director or the Company Secretary of the said Unit or any person authorized in this behalf by the owner or company or working partner, as the case may be, on the copies of Shipping Bill stating that the package or container in respect of goods under export have been sealed in his presence;

(d)

the goods may be examined at the port, airport Inland Container Depot or Container Freight Station or Land Customs Station only in case of specific intelligence or information after obtaining the written permission of Deputy or Assistant Commissioner of Customs having jurisdiction over the said port, airport, Inland Container Depot or Container Freight Station or Land Customs Station, as the case may be, in writing;

(e)

the Unit may export through Inland Container Depot located in the Special Economic Zone, or through any port or airport or Inland Container Depot:

Provided that in case of export of large quantities of cargo where it may not be possible to ship the cargo from the Special Economic Zone in one consignment, the Specified Officer may allow the export of such cargo on execution of a Bond for the duty involved subject to the condition that the Unit shall submit the proof of export within ninety days of removal of such cargo under Bond, failing which applicable duty on the goods not exported shall be payable in terms of the Bond;

the shipping bill and the invoice alongwith packing list presented to the authorized officer shall contain the following:

description of the items;

weight and purity of gold or silver or platinum and the type of gems stone, such as, diamond, ruby, sapphire, cubic zircon and the like which has been used for studding and its weight in carats; and

free on board price rate of the jewellery item and quantity in pieces and the total value;

the Unit may export jewellery on the basis of a notional rate certificate issued by the Nominated Agency and this rate will be based on the prevailing Gold or US Dollar rate and the US Dollar or Indian Rupees rate given in the notional rate certificate:

the Unit obtaining gold or silver or platinum from the Nominated Agency on loan basis shall export gold or silver or platinum jewellery within the period prescribed for the same under the Foreign Trade Policy:

Stock of slow moving jewellery ("dead stock")

.

13. (1) An assessee maintaining separate stocks of manufactured and traded articles and showing the value of such manufactured and traded articles separately in his first sale invoice shall treat his dead stock as that of manufactured articles or traded articles depending upon whether such dead stock is part of his stock of manufactured articles or traded articles, as the case may be.

(2) For an assessee, who opts to pay the excise duty as per the optional scheme under rule (12), if at the end of a particular return cycle, the cumulative sales for three types of articles, namely 'silver studded articles; 'gold or platinum articles studded with diamonds' or 'other gold or platinum articles', as the case may be, on which duty has been paid or which have been exported till the end of that return cycle are more than or equal to the cumulative receipts of manufactured stock of such articles till the end of the return cycle, then the whole of the dead stock of such articles would be deemed to be that of traded articles, and new articles made out of such dead stock on its receipt back by the manufacturer or principal manufacturer, as the case may be, would form part of his traded stock of such articles.

(3) For an assessee who opts to pay the excise duty as per the optional scheme under rule (12), the cumulative sales of a particular type of articles on which duty has been paid or which have been exported till the end of a particular return cycle are less than the cumulative receipts till the end of that return cycle of such manufactured articles, then the dead stock of such articles at the end of such return cycle, equal to the difference between the cumulative receipts of manufactured stock and the cumulative sales till the end of such return cycle shall be deemed to be that of manufactured articles, and balance, if any, shall be considered as that of traded articles.

(3) Illustration. - Thus, two alternative situations can be considered in treatment of the dead stock at the end of the quarter:

Situation 1 - Cumulative sales at the end of return cycle are more than the cumulative receipts of manufactured articles:

i.

Cumulative receipts of manufactured silver studded articles till the end of a quarter are 100 kg.

ii.

Cumulative sales of manufactured silver studded articles till the end of the quarter are 110 kg (out of which on 100 kg the manufacturer or principal manufacturer, as the case may be, has paid excise duty or which have been exported).

iii.

Then, whole of the dead stock silver studded articles at the end of such quarter shall be treated as that of traded stock and new articles made out of such dead stock on its receipt back would form part of traded stock.

Situation 2 - Cumulative sales at the end of return cycle are less than the cumulative receipts of manufactured articles:

i.

Cumulative receipts of manufactured silver studded articles till the end of a quarter are 100 kg.

ii.

Cumulative sales of manufactured silver studded articles till the end of the quarter are 90 kg (out of which on 90 kg the manufacturer or principal manufacturer, as the case may be, has paid excise duty or which have been exported).

iii.

Then, 10 kg [100 kg - 90 kg] of dead stock of silver studded articles at the end of such quarter shall be treated as that of manufactured stock and new articles made out of such dead stock on its receipt back would form part of manufactured stock. Any dead stock of silver studded articles at the end of such quarter in excess of 10 kg shall be deemed to be that of traded stock.

Illustration

A house property (H1) located outside India was bought in 1997 for twenty lakh rupees. It was sold in 2001 for twenty five lakh rupees which were deposited in a foreign bank account (BA). In 2002 another house property (H2) was bought for thirty lakh rupees. The investment in H2 was made through withdrawal from BA. 1. All these appeals involve common facts and propose identical questions of law, for which we are deciding them by a common order. For the purpose of clarity and convenience, facts of ITA No. 675/2025 are however, being taken into consideration.

2. The respondent/assessee deals in diamonds, which he imports from various countries in accordance with the provision of Customs Act, 1962 and other relevant law. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer (AO) found that the assessee had issued 6,358 bills of cash sales (each being less than Rs.2 lacs in value), amounting to total of Rs. 97,12,70,670/-. This being the position, the AO was of the view that since the source of purchase was the cash received from these sales, the purchases amounting to Rs.97,13,70,670/-, (being the amount of cash sales) was not properly explained and made addition under Section 69C of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as 'the Act of 1961').

3. While passing the assessment order the AO clearly stated that he has no doubt so far as the genuineness of purchase is concerned and accepted the factum of purchase as such, but has taken recourse to Section 69 C of the Act of 1961 to disallow the expenses relating to such purchase, as according to him, the source of expenditure (being cash) not duly explained.

4. Against the assessment order so passed by the AO on 19.12.2016, the assessee preferred an appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) (hereinafter referred to as 'CIT(A)'), which was allowed by the Appellate Authority vide its order dated 10.01.2017.

5. Against the order of the Appellant Authority, the Income Tax Department preferred an appeal before the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (hereinafter referred to as 'Tribunal'), which was rejected by the Tribunal by its impugned order dated 18.12.2024.

6. While rejecting the appeal, the Tribunal has observed that all the purchases made by the assessee were made through proper banking channels and after paying applicable duties in accordance with provision of The Customs Act 1962 and other applicable rules. The Tribunal has also recorded that all the purchases were duly supported by bills/vouchers, import bills, bills of entry, airlines bills and custom documents etc. and such purchase cannot be disallowed. The Tribunal held that the AO has proceeded on mere assumption and conjuncture.

7. Having observed so, the Tribunal has also expressed its concern that when the AO had found the purchases to be genuine, how could he take the sale to be bogus without rejecting the books of account.

8. Mr. Guarav Gupta, learned Senior Standing Counsel for the appellants submitted that the Tribunal and the CIT(A) have erred in deleting the addition made by the AO, simply because the purchases were found to be through proper banking channels and supported by documents. He argued that it is an admitted case of the AO that purchases were genuine but what he had disallowed is the expenditure of the purchase itself, because source of purchase was unexplained. Explaining the arguments, Mr. Gaurav Gupta submitted that the amount in the bank account had come from the cash sales out of the transactions (6358) which were cash bills for less than Rs.2 lacs each. He read the order of the AO and showed that all the transactions have been made only in the span of 44 days with only 8 to 10 employees were engaged, which raises a doubt about the sales affected by petitioner.

9. Learned counsel for respondent/assessee, on the other hand, submitted that the assessee had an opening stock of Rs.114.62 crores to begin with and such stock has not been disputed by AO. He further submitted that all the purchases were from abroad and all the documents, bills, payment slips, bill of entry, courier receipts etc. have been produced and as a matter of fact, the purchases have been found to be genuine by the AO. He submitted that simply because the invoices were issued to the retailers and the sales were made in cash, which cash from time to time was deposited in the bank, it does not mean that the deposits were unexplained and hence, the source of purchase was not properly explained.

10. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

11. Both the Appellant Authorities namely the CIT(A) and Tribunal have concurrently held that the AO has erred in disallowing the purchases and making addition under Section 69C of the Act of 1961. Not only the Appellate Authority even the AO himself had accepted the fact that the purchases are genuine.

Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

14. The conclusion of the Assessing Officer, briefly, is as under :

Assessing Officer held, the statement of the assessee is that it is not the duty of the assessee to verify from where the purchase party procures goods and a mere failure of a sub-creditor cannot in the absence of clinching evidence be treated as income of the assessee derived from undisclosed sources. Assessing Officer held, in this case the sub-creditors were not found. All their accounts show cash withdrawals every day with a minimum balance and this is not a mere co-incidence. The supplier to the assessee-firm earns a profit of less than Rs. 10 lakhs on a total turnover of Rs. 500 crores, whereas the assessee earns income of about Rs. 1.6 crores by mere 11 transactions. The fact that finance incharge even after date of search on 11th October, 2000 confirmed that this was a money laundering activity itself is a proof that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business. Hence he rejected assessee’s contentions. He worked out the peak credit on account of purchases of Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment.

15. Assessee shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent during the year under consideration. Assessing Officer held, it was not realistic profit. The profit could be somewhere 5 to 6 per cent. He held, in view of this it can be presumed that the assessee has invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. In view of the above, he computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as unexplained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204 (the same being 82 per cent of market price), which covers the actual cost of diamonds at the prevailing market rate, taking into account the fair market profit of around 6 per cent.
