The assessee, engaged in the business of trading in diamonds, filed its return of income for A.Y. 2019-20 declaring about Rs. 1.32 crores. Reassessment was initiated under section 148. A search was conducted at the premises of M/s. Ratnakala Exports Pvt. Ltd. (REPL) where software allegedly recording unaccounted sales and purchases was found; based on this, it was alleged that the assessee made unaccounted cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs from REPL.

■

During reassessment proceedings, the assessee submitted that it had purchased cut and polished diamonds from REPL of about Rs. 3.66 lakhs, furnishing purchase bills, its ledger of REPL, confirmation from REPL, and details of payments through banking channels. It stated that the goods were exported and the income therefrom was offered to tax, supported by sales invoices and stock records. The AO, relying only on the third-party software found at REPL, treated cash purchases of about Rs. 6.65 lakhs as unexplained expenditure under section 69C and assessed income at about Rs. 1.39 crores. The assessee had sought copies of the corroborative material and the statement of the authorized person of REPL, and requested cross-examination, which were not provided.

■

In appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the assessee's contentions, observing that the assessee failed to offer comments on the material recovered during the search of REPL showing unaccounted purchases as per ledgers extracted from the software, had not produced matching entries in books, bank records and purchase invoices regarding the alleged cash purchases, and had not provided proof of having requested cross-examination.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal.

HELD: ■

Insofar as the merits of the impugned addition are concerned, the addition rests solely on the alleged recovery of a software during the search action on M/s. REPL, which according to the AO indicated that separate accounts were maintained by M/s. REPL in respect of unaccounted purchases and sales. The said material was not supplied to the appellant and no opportunity of cross-examination was granted. The observation by the CIT(A) that no opportunity of cross-examination was claimed is factually incorrect. The reply dated 05.04.2023 filed by the appellant before the AO shows that the appellant sought a copy of the statement of the authorized person of M/s. REPL and the corroborative material to support the allegation of cash paid by the appellant to M/s. REPL against purchase of diamonds, as well as the opportunity to cross-examine. [Para 13]

■

It is settled that if the AO proposes to rely on any material for making the impugned addition, the same must be supplied to the assessee and an opportunity of cross-examination must be granted wherever claimed. Failure in this regard is a breach of the principles of natural justice. The appellant cannot be expected to establish a negative. The onus to disprove arises only when material is brought on record and appropriate opportunity is granted to the assessee to challenge it. The matter would depend upon facts and circumstances of each case. In the present case there was failure on the part of the AO to supply the corroborative material and to grant opportunity of hearing and, therefore, the impugned addition cannot be sustained. [Para 14]

■

As the ground raised on merits is accepted, it is not necessary to deal with the additional ground raised. [Para 15]

The whole controversy can also be seen from the another angle, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases to the tune of Rs. 48.78 crores during the subject assessment year as the payments for these purchases were stated to be made out of cash deposited in bank accounts out of so-called cash sales of gold made by the assessee of which identity of the buyers was not revealed by the assessee. The assessee in the instant case could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit of huge magnitude of more than Rs. 49 crores in his bank account which he claimed to be from cash sales from gold bars to the persons wherein the identity of the buyers are not revealed by the assessee. Thus, the assessee could not satisfactorily explain the sources of cash deposit in the bank account and consequently sources of incurring expenditure by way of purchases claimed by the assessee in its profit and loss account of Rs. 48.78 crores could not be satisfactorily explained by the assessee and onus cast under section 69C was not satisfied which would make amount covered by such expenditure represented by purchases of gold bars to be deemed income of the assessee under the deeming fiction of section 69C. The said section 69C is further controlled by proviso which has an overriding effect and provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of the 1961 Act, such unexplained expenditure which is deemed to be the income of the assessee shall not be allowed as a deduction under any head of income. Thus, section 69C read with proviso makes it abundantly clear that the amount represented by expenditure incurred by the assessee towards purchases of gold bars constitute income within deeming fiction of section 69C. Thus, the order of Commissioner (Appeals) and confirm the addition to the tune of Rs 49.17 crores for detailed reasons as cited above. Thus, revenue succeeds on this ground while the assessee fails on this issue in their respective appeals. [Para 10]

FACT: ■

The assessee was engaged in the business of trading of gold & diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. It had filed its return of income which was processed under section 143(1).

■

The Assessing Officer thereafter issued a notice under section 148 on the basis of the information received from Investigation Wing that diamonds shown by the assessee as purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14 were bogus. Accordingly, he made an addition in the hands of the assessee.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) had upheld the addition made by the Assessing Officer.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The assessee was engaged in the trading of diamonds.

In relation to the assessment year 2017-18, the Assessing Officer selected the case of the assessee for scrutiny and having found that during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016, the assessee made a cash deposit in various bank accounts issued a show cause notice to the assessee narrating the various bank accounts, names of bank and amount deposited therein and asked the assessee to furnish the details of cash deposits and source thereof and if the cash was received on sales provide details of purchases of items and sold in cash including quality, quantity, GIA/IGI certificate to substantiate the cash deposits.

The assessee filed a detailed reply and submitted that out of total sales of Rs. 9.54 crores, the cash deposit in the banks was only Rs. 33 lakhs.

The Assessing Officer did not accept the reply of the assessee and by taking view that the assessee had not provided the details of purchases and the names of the parties and had also not produced the persons to whom sales made with documents showing the colour and size of diamonds made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to the income of the assessee on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68 and brought the same for taxation at the rate of 60 per cent under section 115BBE.

The Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the addition made by the Assessing Officer by holding that the assessee had to prove the nature and source of deposit with three conditions as per provisions of section 68 and the assessee could not explain the nature and source of aforesaid amount of Rs. 29.66 lakhs.

Pawaskar was contradictory and hence he held "it is not worthy of credence". Assessee submitted, while framing the block assessment, the revenue has given a clean chit but for part of the assessment year taken steps just contrary to the one taken in the block period. Hence, assessee requested, the enhancement proceedings are to be dropped.

28. However, the learned first appellate authority rejected the claim. He held that Assessing Officer had fixed the opportunity of cross-examination on 19th and 20th January, 2005 not with an intention. The marriage was to take place on 21st January, 2005. But this claim is not supported by any evidence; whereas the fact remains that the assessee failed to avail the opportunity. Hence he rejected the assessee’s claim of violation of principles of natural justice. He further held, Assessing Officer has not brought any fresh evidence during the remand proceedings; but merely examined the parties and reiterated the conclusions drawn by him during assessment proceedings. There is nothing objectionable. CIT(A) held, it is true, all the parties confirmed the sales and receipts by cheque, which were duly deposited in their regular bank accounts. However, the assessee is not having any other evidence except this to prove the genuineness of purchases from these seller parties. On the other hand, he held, Assessing Officer conducted extensive investigation to prove that these seller parties did not have any capacity actually to sell the impugned diamonds to the assessee, as their own suppliers were not traceable at the given address. He further held, examination by the Assessing Officer of the bank accounts of the seller parties and their supplier parties convince that the purchase consideration paid by the assessee through cheques has been finally withdrawn in cash after its movement through various bank accounts, which leads to a reasonable suspicion that the amount has been received back by the assessee in cash. Hence he agreed with the Assessing Officer. He held, mere production of sale bills and payments through cheques is not conclusive proof that the assessee in fact purchased the impugned goods from the same parties if the subsequent investigation indicates that all this was stage managed.

29. CIT(A) held that the addition can be made on the basis of preponderance of probability and it is not necessary to prove the facts leading to such an addition, beyond any reasonable doubt. In the case of the assessee, he held, the facts clearly indicate that the assessee has not purchased the diamonds from its disclosed seller parties against cheque payments and the only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn is that same were actually purchased against cash consideration in open unorganized market. Hence he held, provision of sections 69B and 69C is applicable in the instant case of the assessee. He held, assessee has understated the value of purchases and has not disclosed correct identity of the seller parties. He held, assessee has invested more money in effecting the purchases of diamonds than what is disclosed in the regular books of account. He held, assessee recorded only 82 per cent of the actual expenditure on effective purchases of diamonds. In other words, the balance 18 per cent of the expenditure was unexplained. Hence he held, the provision of sections 69B and 69C are clearly applicable in the instant case of the assessee.

During the assessment proceedings the Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that assessee had indulged in bogus purchases and disallowed the entire purchases worth Rs. 1.35 crores holding it to be unexplained expenditure under section 69C.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) concluded that since the Assessing Officer did not doubt the genuineness of payments made through banking channels and accepted the total sales, the entire purchases couldn't be disallowed. Instead, only the profit element was considered, restricting unexplained expenditure to 8 per cent of total purchases.

INCOME TAX : Where assessee, engaged in trading of diamonds, deposited Rs. 33 lakhs in cash in bank account during demonetization period of 9-11-2016 to 30-12-2016 and Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 29.66 lakhs to assessee's income on account of unexplained/unaccounted income under section 68, since purchases of assessee were not doubted and account books were not rejected,

one - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, reasoning of Assessing Officer that assessee made cash purchases could not be accepted and as such addition made to income of assessee on account of cash purchases was not justified - Held, yes - Whether in view of above, addition made to income of assessee by resorting to section 40A(3) was also not justified and also there was no material to recompute profits for purposes of deduction under section 80HHC - Held, yes FACT: For the relevant assessment year, the assessee, a trader in diamonds and VCD rights claimed deduction under sections 80HHC and 80HHF. The assessee had declared that during the previous year it had purchased diamonds from eleven parties for Rs. 5,30,87,813 and had sold the same for Rs. 6,90,23,486 and thus earned net profit of 23.4 per cent on sales. The net profit on the sales in the earlier year was 28.11 per cent. The Assessing Officer noted that the profit earned by the assessee on account of sale of diamonds was much higher than the profit earned by the parties from whom the assessee had made purchases as profit earned in assessee’s line of business normally was 6 per cent; thus, he examined all the parties except two which did not appear before the Assessing Officer and noticed that though all of such parties confirmed the transactions, yet none could reply satisfactorily the amount of credit given, i.e., number of days and their profit margin; that all the supplier parties were from Surat, whereas the purchase parties were from Mumbai; but none of these supplier parties were traceable; that cheque books signed by the operating parties at the account opening stage itself were in possession of the bill providers, who encashed self cheques by depositing them in these accounts and the money was returned to the exporter; that there were other parties who were heavy weight bill providers, who did the same in the second or third layer by introducing three or four purchase parties and then the cash was withdrawn and the one who imported had added benefits, as at most of the time these bill providers in part transfered the amount received on accommodation bill to import payments and; that seller parties withdrew their money, which was received by cheque and ultimately it reached back to the assessee. Therefore, the Assessing Officer concluded that the assessee made purchases of diamonds from the open market in cash and in turn had taken accommodation bills from these parties to arrive at higher deduction of income under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer further held that the assessee was not conducting a bona fide business and accordingly worked out the peak credit on account of purchases at Rs. 2,83,17,204 and treated the same as assessee’s unexplained investment. The Assessing Officer also held that the assessee had shown a net profit of 23.4 per cent, which was not realistic profit; that the profit could be somewhere between 5 to 6 per cent; that therefore, the assessee had invested around 18 per cent in unaccounted cash to inflate its net profit to avail the deduction under section 80HHC. The Assessing Officer, therefore, computed Rs. 3,45,33,175 as un-explained investment in the business of the assessee, being the cost of diamonds, which were exported at market value, being 1/0.82 times of the peak credit of Rs. 2,83,17,204. The Assessing Officer, therefore, made an addition of Rs. 3,45,33,175 to the income of assessee as unexplained investments. The Assessing Officer further while computing the deduction under section 80HHC rejected the purchases declared by the assessee. He held that the sales during the year (excluding exchange fluctuation which was allowed as it being beyond the control of the assessee) was at Rs. 6,90,23,486 and the total trading and establishment expenses were at Rs. 2,93,120, and that the actual cost of purchase and expenses treated at 94 per cent of the sales came to Rs. 6,48,82,076. He further allowed indirect expenses to the tune of Rs. 2,93,120 and thus treated the actual purchase at Rs. 6,45,88,956. The Assessing Officer also made an addition of Rs. 1,29,77,912 to the income of the assessee under section 40A(3) being 20 per cent of the cash purchases of Rs. 6,45,88,956. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the contentions raised by the assessee and increased the assessee’s unaccounted peak investment in effecting purchase of diamonds from Rs. 3,45,33,175 to Rs. 4,67,01,433. On second appeal : HELD: In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

On second appeal :

HELD: As regards the sale of diamonds to ‘S’, at Surat it was found that the identity of the party had been established, the transaction was genuine and the creditworthiness of jeweller had been proved beyond doubt by the assessee. The bank accounts of ‘S’ which were collected by the Assessing Officer showed that the amounts were received by account-payee DDs from Mumbai. The DDs were taken by ‘S’ and sent to the assessee which were credited in his bank account and used for business purposes of his business entities. It was not the duty of the assessee to prove the sources of the credits in the bank account of ‘S’. The assessee could not establish the source of the source. The decision of the Madras High Court in S. Hastimal v. CIT [1963] 49 ITR 273, also supported this view of the assessee. [Para 30]

As regards the assessee’s presence at Surat on the dates of sale of jewellery on 22-2-1998, 15-3-1998 and 25-3-1998, credit card statements and bank account entries on 25-3-1998 could not be relied upon as these were collected behind the back of the assessee and were never put to the assessee for rebuttal, as held by the Supreme Court in Kishinchand Chellaram v. CIT [1980] 125 ITR 713/4 Taxman 29 at 720. [Para 31]

Notwithstanding the above, although the revenue claimed that the assessee was in restaurant, Hyderabad, on 22-2-1998, when the first sale of diamonds took place, no evidence had been brought on record to show that he was present during the day time on 22-2-1998. It was also found as a matter of fact that the sale of diamonds of other members in the family were on 3-12-1997, 8-12-1997, 16-12-1997 and 12-1-1998. The travel time from Mumbai to Hyderabad was an hour as noted by the Assessing Officer at page 24 of his order and the travel time from Mumbai to Surat was 3 to 4 hours and, therefore, the presumption of the Assessing Officer that the assessee was at Hyderabad during the day when the business was transacted was not supported by any documentary evidence. The submission of the authorised representative of the assessee that he was at Surat/Mumbai on 21-2-1998 and 22-2-1998 had also equal force to support that he was in Hyderabad on 22-2-1998 only in the late hours of the night. [Para 32]

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ A perusal of the record would suggest that the assessee is engaged in the business of trading of gold and diamond jewellery, platinum jewellery/silver ornaments/articles and bullion etc. It has been maintaining its proper books of account. The accounts were duly audited. The assessee has filed its return of income on the strength of those accounts. When the Assessing Officer has confronted the assessee for explaining its position with regard to certain purchases made from Daksh Diamonds and Jewel Diamonds in assessment year 2007-08 and Nazar Impex (P) Ltd. in assessment year 2013-14. The assessee has submitted copy of the audited balance-sheet, Profit & Loss account along with auditor’s report, the complete stock tally of the ornaments. It has also filed copy of the stock register exhibiting opening stock, purchase, sales and closing stock. The assessee thereafter filed purchase bills issued by Daksh Diamonds, Jewel Diamonds and Nazar Impex in the respective years. The assessee has made the payments to its suppliers through banking channel. The seller of the diamonds was having PAN, VAT, TIN and CST no. Those details were submitted by the assessee to the Assessing Officer during the course of assessment proceedings. The assessee had made request that the person, who has disclosed from its back that he was engaged in providing bogus entries, then, such a person be subject to cross examination. The Assessing Officer had issued summons under section 131 to Bhanwar Lal Jain for appearance, he never appeared. The assessee thereafter brought it to the notice of the Assessing Officer that a perusal of the statement given by Bhanwar Lal Jain would suggest that he has not specifically taken the name of assessee disclosing therein that the assessee has availed accommodation entries. The information disclosed by him is a general nature whereby he disclosed that he controls 68 firms mentioned therein and such firms were engaged in providing accommodation entry. It is not specific whether such firm has specifically provided accommodation entry to the assessee or not. The assessee further produced details of the sales made by it. [Para 19]

■

It is also pertinent to note that in assessment year 2013-14, the assessee has requested that Sanjay Chaudhary managing the affairs of Nazar Impex be produced for cross examination. The Assessing Officer has issued the summons for the appearance of Sanjay Chaudhary before the Assessing Officer. However, he has expressed his inability to appear before him at Jalandhar. Ultimately the Assessing Officer could not ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination by the assessee. The Assessing Officer has expressed her inability to produce the witness at Jalandhar. The assessee again requested the Assessing Officer to produce the witness for cross examination, but no such steps were taken by the Assessing Officer to ascertain the presence of Sanjay Chaudhary for cross examination. [Para 20]

■

A perusal of the record would suggest that there are two sets of evidence available with the Assessing Officer. On the one hand, he has an information transmitted by the Investigation Wing exhibiting the fact that certain concerns of Bhanwar (Mumbai) and Rajendra were engaged in providing accommodation entries to various beneficiaries. The list of all those companies/firms are mentioned in that report. According to the Assessing Officer, the assessee has made purchases from three concerns. In the second set of evidence is the material submitted by the assessee before the Assessing Officer. This set contains audited accounts of the assessee, stock register, purchase register, details of payments of purchases through banking channel, details of suppliers/sellers, namely PAN, VAT, TIN, CST numbers. [Para 21]

■

The assessee has produced quantitative details, which were verifiable and also tallied. For example, if 100 kgs. of raw material is being purchased, then sales also represent those 100 kgs. or unsold items are reflected in the closing stock. [Para 22]

■

The short question is, whether on the basis of the information collected from the back of the assessee from a third party, its purchases could be doubted and disallowance of expenditure is to be made. [Para 23]

■

The Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Odeon Builders (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 64/266 Taxman 461/418 ITR 315, had held that disallowance based on third party information gathered by the Investigation wing of the Department without independent verification of the Assessing Officer cannot be made. In other words, the information transmitted by the DIT (Investigation) was a material to ignite assessment machinery in motion but it cannot be treated as gospel truth for disallowing the claim of the assessee without independent cross verification of those information by the Assessing Officer. [Para 24]

The Assessing Officer having found that during the search proceedings in the case of a party it was gathered that the said party was engaged in the business of issuing non-genuine purchase bills, unsecured loans and accommodation entries to various parties made disallowance at the rate of 100 per cent of purchases made by the assessee on account of unexplained purchases being accommodation entries and added the entire quantum of purchases to the assessee's income.

On appeal to the Tribunal, the main grievance of the revenue was that since all the purchases were bogus and in the nature of accommodation entry, the addition made by the Assessing Officer should be sustained, whereas the grievance of the assessee was that it had submitted bills and vouchers, stock registers and the transactions were though banking channels and, therefore, addition at the rate of 5 per cent sustained by the Commissioner (Appeals) should be deleted.

The Tribunal having noted that the issue under consideration was squarely covered by the judgment of the co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in the case of ITO v. On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: There is no dispute about the business of assessee in dealing and trading of diamonds. Further there is no dispute about the total sale of assessee which is 9.54 crores. During the assessment, the assessee furnished various details of purchases and sales including accounts confirmation. The dispute is only with regard to addition made by Assessing Officer about the cash deposited by assessee in a high denomination bank notes. The books result of assessee was not disputed and was not rejected by Assessing Officer. Further the sales of assessee is also not in dispute. When the nature and activities of assessee were not in dispute nor against the explanation and the evidences furnished by assessee, the Assessing Officer has to bring any adverse material to justify his action in treating the entire cash deposit as unaccounted income. There is merit in the submission of the assessee that business and state of accounts and its dealing are justified, reasonable inference that for smooth and convenience, it could keep the part of sale proceed in a high denomination notes.

By furnishing all the details, the assessee has prima facie discharged its initial burden. The Assessing Officer while making addition made a general observation that required details were not furnished. Once the assessee has discharged its initial burden, the onus shifts on the Assessing Officer to prove it otherwise. [Para 10]

The Assessing Officer has not investigated the facts and only doubted the cash deposited. When the purchases of assessee were not doubted and books were not rejected, the component of sales in cash cannot be rejected. However, in order to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage, a reasonable disallowance out of total cash deposits would meet the ends of justice. Therefore, taking a consistent view as has been taken in other cases, disallowance of 10 per cent of alleged cash deposit would be reasonable to avoid the possibility of revenue leakage. [Para 11]

Since substantial part of addition was deleted, the addition sustained would not be liable to tax at the enhanced rate under section 115BBE. The Assessing Officer is directed to tax the same at normal rate of tax applicable on assessee. [Para 12]

Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Cash credits (Purchase) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery - Pursuant to a search conducted at premises of assessee Assessing Officer found that assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N' and accordingly, made addition - Assessee contended that allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law as Assessing Officer had ignored overwhelming factual evidences - Confirmations of both parties were placed on record and purchases made from these parties had entered in stock register and corresponding sales had not been disputed by revenue authorities - Further, payments for such purchases had been carried out through banking channel - He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances - Whether in light of factual context and balance of probabilities, issue would be adjudicated in favour of assessee, and disallowances made on this count were to be cancelled - Held, yes [Para 9.1.2] [In favour of assessee]  II. Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Unexplained moneys (Cash) - Assessment year 2015-16 - Pursuant to a search conducted at branch office of business premises of assessee-firm, unaccounted cash amounting to Rs. 3 crore were found and seized - On being inquired about source of cash found in course of search, assessee pointed out that aforesaid cash of Rs. 3 crore was accumulated out of cash sales affected during immediately preceeding period between 5-9-2014 to 21-9-2014 prior to search - Assessing Officer on basis of statement of partners of firm who stated that firm did not maintain books of account invoked provisions of section 69A read with section 115BBE to tax cash as unexplained - It was noted that branch office was searched, not main establishment, and partner statements were extracted under questionable circumstances, and subsequently retracted - Whether where stock so purchased and corresponding sales were duly recorded in stock book and stock stand tallied without any perceptible discrepancy in stock qua cash sales made, source of cash found was to be regarded as sufficiently explained and hence could not be treated as unexplained money under section 69A - Held, yes - Whether further, assessee could not be blamed for towering failure of search team to keep main office out of purview of search action and it was rather inexplicable that only a branch office was covered under search and a statement of partner was regarded as gospel truth despite visible lack of business activities, attendant work force, books, records etc. - Held, yes -Whether benefit of doubt, in peculiar circumstances, thus need to go in favour of assessee and therefore, action of revenue authorities to make additions towards unexplained cash sales under section 69A being without any sound basis deserved to be set aside - Held, yes [Paras 9.2.3, 9.2.6 and 9.2.7] [In favour of assessee]  III. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted addition holding that when turnover disclosed by the assessee in audited books of account were found to be in order, cash realised on account of sales of stock could not be held to be unexplained deposits.

On revenue's appeal : HELD: The only reason given by the Assessing Officer for treating the entire cash deposited in the bank account is that there was abnormal growth on the cash sales in the month of November 2016 and corresponding cash deposits from the month of November to December, which alone cannot be the ground when deposits are directly linked with sales duly disclosed in the books. Another point raised by him was that, some of the cash sales made to different parties cannot be identified and the parties who responded were unable to explain the source of their funds. From the perusal of the material placed on record and also the explanation given by the assessee before the Assessing Officer, it is seen that assessee has maintained regular books of account which was subject to audit and has produced the entire sale bills, stock register and purchases and also quantitative tally of sales and corresponding stock. The assessee has also demonstrated that there was a direct correlation of cash outflow from the books of account with cash deposit in the bank accounts and also produced day wise stock report, wherein the outflow of stock against sales has been clearly reflected. Apart from that, sales declared under the Maharashtra VAT Act and the VAT return completely tallied with the sales of the assessee shown in the books of account. Even the Assessing Officer before whom all these documents were furnished has not pointed out any discrepancy in the sales bills, sales register, purchases and stock. Neither he has admitted the quantity of purchases at the stock with assessee and the corresponding quantity of sales made by the assessee during the year. [Para 12]

Another important fact is that assessee has duly filed cash compliance report with respect to cash sales in Form 61A giving all the details with respect to cash sales. Nowhere, the Assessing Officer has pointed out that assessee did not have sufficient stocks in its possession or otherwise found any defect in the stock register. If that finding has not been given and no discrepancy has been pointed out, then how the corresponding sales of same stock and quantity can be treated as 'undisclosed income' of the assessee. Once, the Assessing Officer has accepted the sales and there is direct nexus with the closing stock and the sales along with movement of stock linked to purchases then such credit on account of sales cannot be added under section 68. If the cash sales have been accepted, then deposit of the same cash in the bank account which is tallying with the entries in regular cash book, cannot be treated as deposits made out of any undisclosed income. [Para 13]

Addition under section 68 on account of cash deposits could not be made simply on the reason that during the demonetization period, cash deposits vis-a-vis cash sales ratio was higher. If the parties during the period of demonetization has purchased huge quantity of jewellery on cash which has been duly recorded in the books of account of the assessee and also tallying with the quantity of stock, then simply because there was a huge cash sales in that particular month cannot be the reason for treating it as undisclosed income from undisclosed sources. In this case the parties to whom notices under section 133(6) were issued have confirmed the purchases but also filed the purchase bills. The Assessing Officer cannot disbelieve the purchases made from the assessee simply on the ground that those parties could not submit the source of their funds which is not the requirement of the assessee to prove specifically when assessee is a retail seller of jewellery and even law does not prohibit any cash sales or there is any requirement to seek any further detail. For this compliance assessee has also filed Form 61A before the Assessing Officer. Once, it has been established that sales representing outflow of stocks was duly accounted in the books of account and there are no abnormal profits during the year, then there is no justification why Assessing Officer treat the deposits made in the bank account out of cash sales to be income from undisclosed sources. Thus, since aforesaid finding recorded by the Commissioner (Appeals) is based on correct appreciation of facts on record and there is no adverse finding by the Assessing Officer with regard to the availability of stock and quantity of items shown in the stock register and the corresponding sales, no addition can be made. Accordingly, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is confirmed. [Para 14]

On revenue's appeal to the High Court: HELD: Section 69C provides that where in any financial year the assessee has incurred any expenditure and offers no explanation about the source of such expenditure or part thereof or the explanation, if any, offered by him is not in the opinion of the Assessing Officer satisfactory, the amount of such expenditure is deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year. [Para 21]

In nuce, the section covers a situation where no explanation has been offered about the source of the expenditure or the explanation offered is not found to be satisfactory by the Assessing Officer. In such a case, the unexplained expenditure would be deemed to be the income of the assessee. [Para 22]

The entire bedrock of the Assessing Officer's case appears to be that the assessee has not produced the parties from whom the assessee had made the subject purchases although admittedly parties' ledger accounts, bank statements were produced before him and even though there were sales against purchases and payments were made by account payee cheques through banking channels. The Commissioner (Appeals) also records that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him and the Assessing Officer. [Para 23]

The Assessing Officer came to a conclusion that though the goods were certainly purchased by assessee but not from persons, who had supplied the bills. Statedly relying upon the purported affidavits filed before the Sales Tax Authorities, the Assessing Officer was of the view that the goods were purchased in cash from the market and sale bills were obtained from hawala dealers for that purpose. No material has been brought on record by the Assessing Officer to show that the assessee purchased material from the market or from unexplained cash. In the alternate, he presumed that the sales were affected from unaccounted stock and held the said amounts as unexplained investment under section 69. No evidence or material appears to have been brought on record or finding given by the authorities to arrive at this presumption. [Para 24]

On the basis of the above, the Assessing Officer propounds a hypothesis that the money which was given by cheques to such persons has come back to the assessee in the form of cash. The Commissioner (Appeals) has found that neither the Assessing Officer has made available any documents nor is there any evidence to demonstrate the same. [Para 25]

There is no dispute that the subject purchases were in fact made, that the assessee has made payments by account payee cheques which have been cleared through the normal banking channels, the assessee had furnished the bills, delivery challans relating to the said purchases, the transactions appear to have been duly accounted for in the books of assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has observed that all the purchases were reflected in the stock reconciliation furnished before him in respect of the subject purchases made by the assessee. There is no evidence or material brought on record by the Assessing Officer that the purchases made were for cash or that the purchasers had returned the cash corresponding to the cheque payments received from the assessee. The Commissioner (Appeals) has recorded that there is no evidence of money flowing back to the assessee and that the Assessing Officer had made the addition merely on the basis of presumption. The Assessing Officer had not made available copies of the documents relied upon by him for the purpose of making the addition. These are all findings of fact for which the Tribunal is the last fact-finding authority. [Para 26]

It is observed that the assessee has discharged his onus in respect of the subject purchases. The Assessing Officer has also not doubted the sales arising out of the said export activity and its GPR. This is not a case which falls within the ambit of section 69C as held by the Assessing Officer. [Para 27]

The assessee’s family members had disclosed jewellery and diamond under VDIS, 1997. The loose diamonds were sold by these family members for Rs. 86,46,406. The Assessing Officer held the voluntary disclosure by these family members bogus and treated the sale proceeds as undisclosed income of the assessee for the block period by observing that in the VDIS, these family members had disclosed holding of unexplained loose diamonds which were subsequently sold but the assessee and his family members never had any loose diamonds. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition.

On revenue’s appeal :

It was obvious that the assessee made purchases from J.R. New Delhi, on 5-1-1990 to the tune of 1970 quintals and the sales in cash of the same were made on 8-1-1990 and thereafter. As the purchase as well as sales were duly recorded in the books of account and the assessee had shown the profits on these sales made in the return of income, one failed to understand as to how the figure of total cash sales amounting to Rs. 35,48,005 could be treated as unexplained cash credit under section 68. The assessee made available to the Assessing Officer all the necessary particulars of the party from whom the assessee purchased the goods which were sold in cash and became the subject-matter of controversy at hand. The Assessing Officer in his wisdom thought it fit not to examine the supplier. It indicated that he was satisfied with the genuineness of the purchase aspect of the transaction. It was not the case of the revenue that the assessee had not shown any purchase in its books of account against which the sales had been recorded. The case law cited by the revenue as to the burden of proof on the assessee was not applicable to the facts of the present case, because the factum of purchase and sale of the goods in the assessee’s books of account stood established beyond a shadow of doubt. Under these circumstances, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld.

FACT: The assessee was a partnership-firm engaged in trading bullion and jewellery. Pursuant to a search conducted at the premises of the assessee the Assessing Officer found that the assessee had made bogus purchase from two parties namely 'A' and 'N'.

The assessee contended that the allegation towards bogus purchases was wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contended that the Assessing Officer had ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties were placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. Further, the payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. He submitted that purchases could not be disbelieved in such circumstances.

The Assessing Officer was however, dissatisfied with the documentary evidences filed to support the purchases made from these two parties, and treated same as bogus and made addition.

On second appeal:

HELD: As noted above, the assessee contends that the allegation towards bogus purchases is wholly misconceived in law. To prop up its case, the assessee contends that the Assessing Officer has ignored the overwhelming factual evidences. The confirmations of both the parties are placed on record. The purchases made from these parties have entered in the stock register and the corresponding sales have not been disputed by the revenue authorities. The payments for such purchases have been carried out through banking channel. It is also the contention of the assessee that both the parties from whom the assessee has made purchases are existing parties and such parties have independently filed their confirmation with regard to the supplies made by such parties to the assessee and mere non-attendance per se after a lapse of time could not be viewed adversely.[Para 9.1]

Having regard to the nature of business, i.e. trade in bullion, where stocks are identifiable and the price is also governed by market forces with little scope for manipulations; the purchases duly accounted for; the transaction of only 2 parties doubted despite extensive enquiry on 122 parties etc. there was potency in the plea of bonafides. There can be variety of reasons for non-attendence by unrelated third parties and it is not always within the domain of assessee to enforce attendance of third parties. Nothing adverse need to be imputed in such circumstances, more so, where the payments have been made through banking channel. [Para 9.1.1]

The assessee-HUF filed its return of income for the assessment year 1998-99 and declared certain sum as long-term capital gains arising on sale of diamonds. To verify the genuineness of the said sale of diamonds, extensive investigations were carried out by the Assessing Officer. The assessee submitted that the said diamonds had been declared under the voluntary disclosure of income scheme (VDIS) and produced the VDIS certificate issued by the Commissioner. The assessee further explained that the sale was effected in five lots to four different parties at Surat, and that the total sale consideration of diamonds was received by way of demand drafts (DDs) and was deposited in the savings bank account of the assessee-HUF. The assessee also placed before the Assessing Officer the confirmation letters from the buyers of the diamonds; sale invoices containing the description of goods; weight in carats; rate per carat; copy of the extract of the bank account and valuation report of diamonds. The Assessing Officer issued letters to all the parties calling for confirmation and further details about the sale of diamonds. Since no confirmations were forthcoming, he made enquiries through the departmental officials posted at Surat and they reported to the Assessing Officer that the main activity of the aforesaid purchasing parties was of providing accommodation entries. The Assessing Officer also called for reports from the Mumbai branches of the banks from where the DDs were purchased, specifically calling for information regarding the names of the persons who had applied for the DDs and if they were purchased by cheques, then to indicate from whose accounts the cheques were issued. On the basis of the report received from the banks he concluded that the DDs were purchased by depositing equivalent amount of cash in the bank account. The Assessing Officer then scrutinised the details of the travel undertaken by the assessee to Surat purportedly to sell the diamonds and noted that the assessee had travelled alone while carrying the diamonds and that five such visits were made by him; that the assessee had travelled by unreserved compartment in the train without any insurance for the diamonds, and had stayed in a dharmashala under a fictitious name, and had not properly explained as to how he selected the parties to whom the diamonds were sold. The Assessing Officer also took note of the statement of one 'G' who was connected with the purchasing parties, who in his statement had stated that he was doing only billing work without actually delivering or taking delivery of goods and earning commission in between. The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Assessing Officer, therefore, treated the transactions of sale of diamonds as non-genuine and unexplained and further, rejecting the claim of capital gains of the assessee made addition to his total income under section 68. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the action of the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal :

HELD: The assessees had jewellery in respect of which the certificate had been issued under the VDIS, 1997 and on sale of the said jewellery the assessees had established the person to whom it was sold, and had accounted for the sale proceeds received from him. Once the identity of the purchasers was established and the amounts received from the said purchasers were accounted for in the absence of any material to the contrary it was difficult to hold that the transactions were not genuine. Even if the assessees had paid commission to the middleman for effecting the sale without examining the middleman and without adducing any evidence to the contrary it could not be said that the transactions were not genuine. Moreover, the genuineness of the sales in the hands of the purchaser had not been doubted by the revenue. [Para 6]

It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32] The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. Under the provisions of section 68, if the explanation with regard to nature and source of deposit is found unsatisfactory, only then, the amount so credited may be added as income. In the instant case, there was no evidence of any ‘hawala’ transaction. [Para 37]

The fact that ‘V’ admitted that his son was the proprietor of ‘R’ and that he had no experience of the diamonds trade and the business was handled by him and his son was nowhere connected with ‘R’ personally, was not a determinative factor of the issue that the transaction by the assessee with ‘V’ or ‘D’ was not genuine. In the instant case, the diamonds were declared in the VDIS, in support of which the certificate issued by the Commissioner was placed on record. Therefore, the presumption was that the diamonds were in the possession of the assessee unless contrary was proved by the Assessing Officer. This had not been done by the Assessing Officer. Further, sale invoices giving full description and details had been placed on record. The Assessing Officer had not been able to find any fault with these invoices. It was also not his case that the description in the invoices did not tally with any other corroborating material on record. The confirmation letters were on record with which also no fault had been found by the Assessing Officer. It was also confirmed by the departmental officials themselves that they were the existing assessees on the records of the department and, hence, there was no gainsaying that the buyers were fictitious persons. The Assessing Officer had also called for certain details from the banks from where the DDs were purchased. Amongst the details called for, the most important was ascertaining the names of the persons applying for the DDs or if they were purchased by cheques, then the names of the account holders who issued the cheques. It was mentioned by the Assessing Officer that the reports of the banks were received and were placed on record. However, the Assessing Officer had not revealed the contents of the reports in his order except mentioning that the day the DD was purchased, equivalent cash was deposited in the account. The information called for by the Assessing Officer was really pertinent. If the identity of the applicant of the DD had been revealed, or if the account on which the cheque was drawn had been revealed, the source of the money deposited in the account could have been traced back. But the Assessing Officer failed utterly in doing so. Therefore, there was a strong presumption in favour of the assessee that there was nothing adverse in the bank's report. Because the Assessing Officer had failed to nail the assessee, he diverted his attention and energies to the purported trips of the assessee to Surat. Assuming that the assessee had travelled in an unreserved compartment carrying the diamonds uninsured, yet these facts would not affect the transactions which were otherwise well documented and supported by evidence. Even going by the theory of human probabilities, it was just possible that the assessee might have wanted to pose as an ordinary person so that no one might have doubted that he was carrying valuables with him. This might have been a good security measure according to the assessee's own perception and which perception could not be regarded as obsurd. It was true that 'G' had deposed that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries, but his statement could not be taken as a gospel truth for three reasons: firstly, the assessee had not been provided the opportunity to cross-examine him; secondly, there was neither any direct nor indirect evidence to show that the assessee was accommodated by him in any manner; thirdly, though the statement was that he indulged only in providing accommodation entries yet, this statement had to be understood in the sense that by and large he indulged in providing entries only. Existence of exceptions to a person's normal and avowed activity is a natural phenomenon and in the case of 'G' also, the same had to be presumed. Therefore, the transactions of sale of diamonds by the assessee had to be considered to be genuine. Therefore, the impugned addition made to the income of the assessee was liable to be deleted and the Assessing Officer was to be directed to accept the capital gains computed by the assessee. [Para 7]

The income based on the books of account of ‘V’ was accepted in his case under the Act which included the said transaction. [Para 25]

Similarly, ‘V’ being the registered dealer under the BST and CST Act had filed the returns under those Acts, duly disclosing the said transaction with the assessee much before the date of survey. [Para 26] The observation of the Commissioner (Appeals) that since ‘V’ was denying the explanation given at the time of survey, it was upon him to explain the cash deposits in his bank accounts and the lack of closing stock was not convincing. The assessee had received the payment by account payee cheque from ‘V’ and it was department’s case that the cash might have been given by the assessee and deposited in the bank account of ‘R’/’D’ ,which was the ultimate source of the payment of cheque. The Commissioner (Appeals), therefore, could not be said to be right in concluding that the statement given at the time of survey ‘remained’. The two statements were conflicting and as to for which statement he said ‘remained’, was not known. It would be more logical, if it was so for the first statement given on 30-3-2000, which was confirmed by him vide letter dated 4-4-2000 and his affidavit thereafter and also on oath when he appeared before the Assessing Officer under section 131 on 25-10-2002. [Para 27]

The fact that the letter dated 4-4-2000, retracting from his statement, was not given on oath, was of no consequence as it was supporting the earlier statements dated 30-3-2000 and as affirmed in the statement recorded under section 131 subsequently on 25-10-2002, though it should be accepted that between those contradictory statements, those made under oath would have greater value. It was a fact that ‘V’ had retracted from his statement given on 31-3-2000. The fact that it was without offering any explanation as to the large cash deposits and the absence of stock, had nothing to do with that, because it was the department who claimed that the money had been given by the assessee. [Para 28]

The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath, recorded by the Assessing Officer, ‘V’ claiming that while he knew ‘S’, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, could not raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs.10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as ‘hawala’ transaction in the statement given to the department. The acknowledgement of ‘S’ as a business associate and then to delink the transaction in question from those transactions did not show any contradiction in the statement, later being supplementary one. [Para 29]

The claim of the assessee that ‘V’ was, in fact, the witness of the department could not be accepted as it was the department who was relying upon his statement to allege that what was apparent was not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remained with the department and did not shift to the assessee. [Para 30]

It was true that at the time of survey, it was not the case of ‘V’ that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants, but the fact remained that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee was concerned throughout. [Para 31]

Large amounts of cash were deposited in various bank accounts of ‘D’ on various dates by ‘R’, but there was no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there was no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It might be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another, the payment to the assessee had been made but how the assessee was responsible for that. Nothing was on record that said money was given by the assessee. [Para 32]

The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS; they were sold to ‘D’; payment was received by account payee cheques. In those circumstances, it could not be a cash credit, the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person,who paid it, was identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment was the bank account of the payer, it was stated to be in consideration for sale of diamond, there was no material on record that source of that money was the assessee or it was given for any services rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. In those circumstance, it could not be said to be the income of the assessee, in any circumstance, much less under the deeming provisions of section 68 as applied by the revenue authorities since the source was satisfactorily explained by the assessee. [Para 33]

The Assessing Officer, thus, concluded that the assessee had not travelled to Surat and that it was merely a cooked up story of having sold the diamonds to the Surat based parties. The Supreme Court in CIT v. Noorjahan (P.K.) (Smt.) [1999] 237 ITR 570/ 103 Taxman 382 , held that the discretion postulated in section 69 before making the addition has to be judiciously exercised. In the instant case, in spite of the facts pointing in the direction of genuineness and identity of ‘S’ and their creditworthiness not being in doubt, the addition had been made on presumptions, surmises and suspicions and, therefore, the judgment of the Supreme Court (supra ) applied to the facts of the instant case. The entire case of the revenue is built upon the basis of suspicion regarding the sales booked by the assessee prior to the start of demonetization period. The Assessing Officer has rejected the books of account merely because there was a spike in cash advances on three dates. However, the comparative data furnished by the assessee clearly dispels this suspicion. A perusal of the chart reveals that the cash sales in the year under consideration were in fact significantly lower than the preceding year. When the assessee has demonstrated that in the previous year, during the corresponding period, the cash sales were much higher, the allegation of ‘abnormal’ sales during the demonetization period falls flat. The data furnished by the assessee shows that the assessee’s total sales as well as cash sales during the year under consideration including the relevant demonetization period were comparatively very less than the preceding financial year. This data shows that the assessee’s cash sales were not abnormal during the relevant period and Assessing Officer’s suspicion of cash sales is not based on any reliable material. [Para 11]

■

Further, the Assessing Officer has not pointed out any discrepancy in the stock register, and the assessee was evidently possessed of the requisite stock to effect the impugned sales. It is a matter of record that the purchases have been made through banking channels out of duly accounted for receipts/income. The notices issued under section 133(6) were largely complied with, and the mere fact that one party went into bankruptcy does not make the entire purchases bogus. Though the Assessing Officer has doubted the purchases, it is not the case of the Assessing Officer that the assessee had not debited the amount of purchases from its books or that the assessee had made purchases out of its unexplained income. Once the purchases are accepted and the stock is not disputed, the sales flowing out of such stock cannot be treated as non-genuine. The sales have been recorded in the books of account and the profit arising therefrom has been offered to tax. Therefore, the entire receipts from the corresponding sales cannot be treated as unaccounted income of the assessee; only the profit element embedded in such sales can be taxed, which the assessee has duly offered for taxation. Taxing the gross receipts again under section 68 would amount to double taxation of the same amount. [Para 12]

■

Even, at the most, it can be alleged, though not proved, by the Assessing Officer that the assessee had made certain sales and accepted SBN/demonetized currency during the relevant period. Even assuming so, the assessee may have breached or violated the relevant circular/notification of the RBI/Demonetization Scheme, however, even then it cannot be held a case of income from unexplained sources. [Para 14]

■

In view of the above discussion, it is held that the addition made by the Assessing Officer is not sustainable. The assessee has successfully explained the source of cash deposits as sales/advances which are duly recorded in the books of account. The suspicion of the Assessing Officer regarding the genuineness of sales is not supported by any concrete evidence and is contradicted by the comparative sales data. The Assessing Officer had wrongly rejected the books of accounts of the assessee merely on suspicion of advance received on sales, without any justification. Even the violation of RBI notification, if any, does not attract the provisions of section 68. Accordingly, the impugned addition is ordered to be deleted. [Para 16]

Overview of section 69C

Any type of expenditure (be it capital or revenue or personal) is incurred by the assessee in any financial year [Para 17.2];

Source from which expenditure is incurred is not explained or not satisfactorily explained by assessee [Para 17.3];

If source of expenditure is not explained or is not satisfactorily explained, the expenditure may be deemed to income of the financial year;

To invoke section 69C, AO has to establish existence or under-statement of expenditure incurred by the assessee [Para 17.4];

100% addition u/s 69C not to be made for grey market purchases where sales figures are not doubted [Para 17.5]

100% addition not justified for bogus purchases which were just accommodation entries [Para 17.6]

No additions u/s 69C for purchases paid through banking channels and evidenced by delivery challans, purchase bills etc. [Para 17.7]

Where assessee did not furnish any evidence to rebut bogus purchase allegation but stated that 2% of these may be added, 100% addition was justified, [Para 17.8]

Addition u/s 69C not justified for mere 11 lakhs of credit card payments by cash in case of HNI assessee who had filed ITR for crores every year [Para 17.9]

No addition u/s 69C towards site expenses where assessee had filed vouchers, detailed sample appointment letters, cheques etc. [Para 17.10]

Power of AO to refer matter of valuation of assets to Valuation Officer [Section 142A] [Para 17.11]

Additions cannot be made solely on the basis of statements made by the assessee during survey proceedings [Para 17.12].

No deduction of expenditure or set-off of loss while computing income under section 69C [See Para 17.13]

In that also under the Voluntary Disclosure Scheme, 1997, the assessee made disclosure of undisclosed income which was represented by diamonds, silver utensils, gold bars, etc. The said voluntary disclosure was duly accepted and a certificate relating to the same was issued. The assets declared under VDIS, 1997 had been sold in relevant assessment year and such sale proceeds had been credited in the books. As regards the sale of silver utensils, the Assessing Officer made enquiries with the valuer, who issued valuation report for the said utensils; the transporters, who issued consignment notes for transportation of the same from Calcutta to Delhi; the jewellers of Delhi who purchased the said goods. On the basis of the said enquiries, the Assessing Officer came to the conclusion that the alleged sale proceeds of silver utensils was nothing but unexplained cash credit in the assessee’s hands and added the said amount in his hands income from other sources. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the impugned addition and, thus, allowed the assessee’s appeal. On revenue’s appeal, the Special Bench held :

"There was no dispute that the assessee had made a disclosure under the VDIS, 1997, which was accepted by the Commis-sioner vide certificate issued under section 68(2) of the VDIS, 1997. Vide circular No. 754, dated 10-6-1997 [(1997) 226 ITR 8 (St)] it was clarified by the CBDT that in respect of jewellery if it was acquired prior to 1-4-1987, the value would be trim as on 1-4-1987, as certified by valuer. Accordingly, the assessee got till valuation of jewellery from the registered valuer and filed the valuation report along with the VDIS declaration. The Commissioner after verifying the same had issued the certificate under section 68(2) of the VDIS, 1997. Despite the fact that the Commissioner had issued certificate under section 68(2) of the VDIS, 1997 on the basis of the disclosure made by the assessee supported by valuers certificate, the Assessing Officer had made enquiry from the registered valuer about the valuation done by him and observed that the conduct of the valuer showed that he had given bogus valuation report in respect of silver utensils without actually examining said silver articles. Under the VDIS, it had been provided that such disclosure, when accepted, would offer complete immunity to be declare in respect of the income so disclosed. In the absence of any material task that such certificate had been cancelled or withdrawn or amended by the CIT under the VDIS, 1997, the Assessing Officer had grossly erred in holding that such silver utensils allegedly sold never existed. Such train of the Assessing Officer was beyond his jurisdiction and against the scheme of the VDIS, 1997. Even otherwise the finding of the Assessing Officer that valuer did not issue valuation report after physically seeing the entire silver utensils, was not sustainable in view of the remand report of the Assessing Officer."

He records briefly : parties open a bank account in their name and also simultaneous bank accounts in the name of their relatives and employees. These accounts are opened for a short period, less than a year. Bills are provided when approached from a party, who needs accommodation bill, as is the case of most of the exporters. They arise an invoice on the party, like assessee and charge commission of 1 to 3 per cent depending on their standing in the market. The exporter who takes the bill normally does not pay immediately. The payments are made only on export realisation. If the payments are received in the next financial year, it goes to a different entity of the bill provider group as most of these parties operate for only one financial year or perhaps even less. He further records, the parties with dummy accounts have accounts in the same branch of the bill providers and these dummy account parties have a very nominal amount in a year. The fact that in the subsequent statement on oath recorded by the Assessing Officer, VDT claiming that while he knew Saxena, the transactions entered into by him with the assessee were not through him but through family friends whose names he did not remember, cannot raise doubt as to the genuineness of the transaction with the assessee of purchase of diamonds worth Rs. 10,35,562 or that it was covered by the transaction to which reference was made as hawala transaction in the statement given to the Income-tax Department. The claim of the assessee that VDT was in fact the witness of the department cannot be accepted as it is the department who is relying upon his statement to allege that what is apparent is not real and, therefore, the onus of proof remains with the department and does not shift to the assessee.

It is true that at the time of survey it was not the case of VDT that he was doing some part of his business as genuine and only some part of the business was on paper for facilitating the VDIS declarants but the fact remains that he affirmed the transaction as genuine insofar as the assessee is concerned throughout.

Large amounts of cash deposited in various bank accounts of Dhananjay Diamonds on various dates by Ratnakar, but there is no evidence on record to establish that those were deposited by or from the money received from the assessee to whom subsequently cheques were issued. Looking to the totality of the circumstances, there is no nexus between the cash deposited and the cheque drawn. It may be true that the facts remained uncontroverted that out of the funds so transferred from one bank account to another the payment to the assessee has been made but how the assessee is responsible for that. Nothing is on record that money was given by the assessee.

33. The diamonds were declared by the assessee under VDIS, they were sold to Dhananjay, payment was received by account payee cheques. In these circumstances how it can be a cash credit the source of which could be said to be unexplained. The person who paid it is identified, he confirmed it, the source of payment is the bank account of the payer, it is stated to be consideration for sale of diamond, there is no material on record that source of that money is the assessee or it was given for any services have been rendered by him, or the source of income thereof was that of the assessee. ■ The Tribunal duly considered the facts and circumstances of the case. The Tribunal noticed from the assessment order that the AO has proceeded to hold the sales of the assessee to be bogus, primarily on account of the fact that the figures of purchases and sales in the period immediately prior to demonetization were at wide variance with the figures of purchases and sales in the corresponding period of the previous year and also at variance with the figures of the previous months in the present financial year. The AO also noted that the purchases on the basis of which the sales were made were effected from certain sister concerns and that too, only upto the period of demonetization. He could not find any nexus between the purchase and the payment made to the persons from whom the purchase had been made and from the same he came to the conclusion that a channel of purchase and sale was created just to give colour to unexplained cash deposit under the garb of sale and for this the VAT return had been utilized as a tool. In consideration of these findings, the Tribunal observes that a departure in trading patterns cannot in itself be a ground to make an addition by holding such departure to be bogus. It can at best be a ground for further investigation to determine the reason for such departure and if the assessee is unable to prove that the enhanced figures were genuine, then only could the credits purported to be made on account of such sales be brought to tax under the provisions of section 68. However, before section 68 could be invoked, the AO was obliged to demonstrate with evidence as to why the explanation furnished by the assessee for cash sales in that particular period were not acceptable. Such evidence could be the fact that the assessee did not have the inventory to make the sale that it claimed, or that the assessee had not made corresponding purchases which stood subsequently effected by way of sales. Unless the AO could find sufficient material to disturb the trading results declared by the assessee in the audited accounts, he would not be at liberty to regard the explanation offered by the assessee for the said cash deposits as unexplained. The Tribunal noticed that in the instant case, the AO had voiced suspicion that the purchases had been shown to have been made from sisterconcerns only so as to create a channel of purchase and sales to explain the deposit of money. He comes to this conclusion on account of the fact that he was unable to relate payment for such purchases to the actual purchases made. The Tribunal again notes that the suspicion could only be a starting point for further investigation and the purchase of goods on credit cannot in itself be a ground to reject the genuineness of the purchase. The Tribunal further notes from the assessee's submission that the AO had issued notices under section 133(6), but could not find anything adverse in this regard. On the contrary, the Tribunal notes from the paper book filed by the assessee that the assessee had inventories amounting to Rs. 4.61 crores as on the first day of the accounting year and that the assessee is able to explain an opening stock of worth Rs.4.41 crores as on 1-10-2016 as per the perpetual inventory method, prepared on the basis of its VAT returns filed upto September, 2016, which the Tribunal notes had been filed on 20-10-2016 i.e. before the date of demonetization. In the circumstances, there do not appear to be any reasons to question the sales made by the assessee in the month of October, 2016 were not due till later, out of those stocks or even in November, 2016 out of the residual stocks that remained on 31-10-2016 and purchases made during the period. The AO has pointed out that there was possibility for manipulation in sales on account of the fact that the VAT returns for the month of October, 2016 but the Tribunal notes that even if that were so, it would not change the nature of the receipt from being realization of sales of stocks that was available unless it could be demonstrated that such sales were not made or that the stock to make such sales was not available. No credence can be given to the AO's views that such sales were shown only with a view to deposit cash during demonetization and the stocks were later on actually sold outside the books of accounts as no such evidence has been brought on record by the AO to back up this suspicion. The Tribunal is therefore in agreement with the decision of the ITAT Chennai Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. Viswa and Devji Diamonds (P.) Ltd. [2025] 171 taxmann.com 474 (Chennai - Trib.) wherein the ITAT Chennai Bench has held that if no defect could be pointed out in the books of accounts and the cash deposited had been stated to be made out of sales, since the assessee had discharged the burden of proving the source of cash deposited in the bank, the impugned addition was fit to be deleted
