The authorities below were justified in holding that the assessee had failed to discharge the burden cast upon it to establish that the seized diamonds did not belong to the assessee and, consequently, the addition of the value of the seized diamonds as unexplained income of the assessee under section 69A was justified. Assessment order showed that after seizure of the diamonds from the office of the assessee on 3-4-1996, the FERA authorities had recorded the statement of the partner of the assessee on 4-4-1996. It was true that in the said statement, it was stated that the seized diamonds in boxes DD, EE, FF and GG belonged to the brokers, and on proper verification, the diamonds seized by the FERA authorities contained in boxes DD, EE, FF and part of GG were released by the income-tax authorities and only part of GG were seized. [Para 6]

The authorities below had noted that although the partner of the assessee had claimed that diamonds seized on 4-4-1996, and kept in said boxes, belonged to the brokers in question, yet the assessee produced ‘jangads’ (letters/bills issued by diamond owners to whom diamonds were given prior to sale/export, etc.) only on 18-4-1996. Although it was claimed by the assessee that the diamonds in question were seized from the brokers who were present in the office of the assessee on 3-4-1996, yet the panchanama recorded by the FERA authorities on 3-4-1996, did not mention about the presence of the brokers or that the diamonds were seized from the brokers. In any event, the fact remained that ‘jangads’ were submitted almost after 15 days from the date of the seizure. Thereafter, the letters of the ten parties claiming ownership of the seized diamonds were received. The income-tax authorities, with a view to verify the genuineness of the ‘jangads’, conducted a survey under section 133A and it was found that out of the ten parties who were claiming to be the owners of the seized diamonds, as per ‘jangads’, some of them were not available at the given addresses and some were found to be not living at those addresses at all. When confronted with these findings, the assessee sought to file the affidavit of the broker, VP, and also affidavit of the said ten parties and requested that the statement of the ten persons to whom the said diamonds belonged be recorded. After analysing the statements of those ten persons, the authorities had come to the conclusion that the assessee had engineered the evidence in the form of such claims including that of broker VP. It was held that most of the parties, who claimed ownership of the diamonds, were either men of no means or negligible means. It was found that most of them had not even maintained books of account or had maintained them at the instance of the said broker; that the affidavits of the ten parties were stereotyped and were verbatim the same; that some of the parties confessed the involvement of the said broker, in preparation of the papers at Bombay which were sent to the party at Bhavnagar and that one of the parties had admitted that he had not purchased any diamonds from any person as entered in the books. Thus, the authorities below had concluded that the assessee had engineered the evidence and since the assessee failed to prove the identity of some and the creditworthiness and genuineness of the remaining claimants, it was held that the ‘source’ or ‘origin’ itself was not proved and, therefore, the assessee being found in possession of the seized diamonds should be deemed to be the owner thereof. No infirmity was found in the order passed by the authorities below. The panchanama recorded on 3-4-1996, neither showed the presence of any broker in the office of the assessee nor indicated that the diamonds were seized from the brokers. There was no answer as to why the said brokers, if present at the time of search, did not protest or object to their diamonds lying on the table top being seized by the FERA authorities. The broker VP in his affidavit dated 3-7-1997, categorically admitted that the seized diamonds did not belong to him. It was the assessee who, in a bid to establish the source, insisted on recording the evidence of the ten parties who claimed to be the owners of the seized diamonds. Since the conduct as well as evidence of the parties failed to prove the genuineness of the source and the confession thereof failed to inspire confidence in the authorities below, it was rightly held that the seized diamonds represented the unaccounted income of the assessee and the additions made were in accordance with law. 6. Understanding and Interpretation of Law concerning additions being made u/s 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in OCM/Demonetisation cases.

(i) Cash deposits made out of cash sales recorded in post demonetisation period treated as unexplained deposits u/s 69A of the Income Tax Act, on considering the Specified Banned Notes (SBNs) of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 as not a Legal Tender.

The text of section 69A of the Income Tax Act is being reproduced as under:

"Unexplained money, etc.

69A. Where in any financial year the assessee is found to be the owner of any money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article and such money, bullion, jewellery or valuable article is not recorded in the books of account, if any, maintained by him for any source of income, and the assessee offers no explanation about the nature and source of acquisition of the money, bullion, jewellery or other valuable article, or the explanation offered by him is not, in the opinion of the Assessing Officer, satisfactory, the money and the value of the bullion, jewellery or other valuable article may be deemed to be the income of the assessee for such financial year."

The assessing authorities' contentions concerning the rejection of the claims of cash deposits being made out of cash sales being recorded in the books of accounts in the post demonetisation period, on account of their presumption of prohibition on booking of cash sales in SBNs in the books of accounts during the post demonetisation period, and treating the same as unexplained cash deposits u/s 69A of the Income Tax Act, may not hold sustainable legal ground before the higher appellate authorities on account of the express legislative provisions as contained in "the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017" , implemented pursuant to the Demonetisation exercise. These legislative provisions are discussed as under:

a.

Section 5 of the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 provides that "On and from the appointed day, no person shall, knowingly or voluntarily, hold, transfer or receive any specified bank note."

b.

Section 2(1)(a) in Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 provides that "appointed day" means the 31st day of December, 2016.

c.

Further Section 3 of Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 states that "On and from the appointed day, notwithstanding anything contained in the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 or any other law for the time being in force, the specified bank notes which have ceased to be legal tender, in view of the notification of the Government of India in the Ministry of Finance, number S.O. 3407(E), dated the 8th November, 2016, issued under sub-section (2) of section 26 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, shall cease to be liabilities of the Reserve Bank under section 34 and shall cease to have the guarantee of the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 26 of the said Act."

From the above, it is clear that use of Specified Bank Notes (SBN) pursuant to 8th November, 2016 upto 31st December, 2016 was always allowed. It was never the intention of the Legislature to prohibit their use for transactions uptill 31st December, 2016.

Also, the Specified Bank Notes (Cessation of Liabilities) Act, 2017 clearly provides that the specified bank notes shall cease to be liabilities of the Reserve Bank under section 34 and shall cease to have the guarantee of the Central Government under sub-section (1) of section 26 of the said Act from the appointed date, i.e. 31st December, 2016.

The SBNs of 500- and 1000-rupee denominations can be measured in monetary terms since the guarantee of Central Government and liability of Reserve Bank of India does not cease to exist until 31st December 2016 in lieu of the 500 and 1000-rupee SBNs. Since the RBI is obligated to exchange the SBNs of 500 and 1000 and the liability can be measured with certainty amounting to the values imprinted on these bank notes, these bank notes do possess value and were very much amenable to be recorded in the books of accounts. Hence the contention that it cannot be journalized in the books of accounts based on the SBNs having no monetary value is not valid. Therefore, the same cannot be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A and brought to tax, provided that corresponding supporting documents and records are being furnished by the assessees.

Gold has always been associated the symbols of wealth, purity and prosperity in all cultures and India is no exception . The ancient Indian scriptures, give numerous references to gold. Rigveda, mentions gold as 'hiranya', a precious metal of immense value. Mahabharata gives the anecdote of the Rajasuya where items of gold were used for performing the yajna. Ramayana mentions about the golden city of Lanka and the golden deer maricha.

Taking a cue from the examples, is it not interesting that, as per the Prevention of Money Laundering Act of 2002, dealers who deal in gold and precious metals are considered reporting entities?

Applicability of Reporting Requirements.

The government of any country is required to monitor all points of entry, or legal or white channels of transaction, via which black money might be transformed into white money. Jewellery shops are the most common access points for laundering money due to its ease of accessibility and lesser compliance frameworks. To curb these risk factors and to check mate the flow of black money, necessary steps were taken by the government to include the dealers in precious metals to the ambit of the reporting entity.

Background

Notification no G.S.R 799(E) [F NO P-12011/14/2020-ES CELL DOR ] DATED 28.12.2020 says that 2020 In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-clause (iv) of clause (sa) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 (15 of 2003), the Central Government hereby notifies the dealers in precious metals, precious stones as persons carrying on designated businesses or professions - if they engage in any cash transactions with a customer equal to or above Rupees ten lakhs, carried out in a single operation or in several operations that appear to be linked.

Relevance

This means that where a dealer engages in any cash transaction with a customer equal to or above rupees ten lakhs, carried out in a single operation or in several operations that appear to be linked, then the dealer comes under the purview of reporting entity under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act ,2002.

Definitions

Reporting Entity

As per Sec 2 (1) (wa) of Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002 "reporting entity" means a banking company, financial institution, intermediary or a person carrying on a designated business or profession;

Designated Business or Profession is defined under Sec 2 (1)(sa) of Prevention of Money Laundering Act of 2002 which says that

"person carrying on designated business or profession" means,—

i.

a person carrying on activities for playing games of chance for cash or kind, and includes such activities associated with casino;

Inspector-General of Registration appointed under section 3 of the Registration Act, 1908 (16 of 1908) as may be notified by the Central Government;]

real estate agent, as may be notified by the Central Government;

dealer in precious metals, precious stones and other high value goods, as may be notified by the Central Government;

v.

person engaged in safekeeping and administration of cash and liquid securities on behalf of other persons, as may be notified by the Central Government; or

vi.

person carrying on such other activities as the Central Government may, by notification, so designate, from time to time;

The meaning of dealer can be understood as per the definition under Sec 2(1)(ib) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act 2002, "dealer" has the same meaning as assigned to it in clause (b) of section 2 of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956 (74 of 1956);]

Delight Diam Pvt. Ltd. or any other parties. If there were no purchases, then there would be no corresponding sales; then the income of the assessee will be reduced as there is some margin towards the sales and purchase difference and the same has to be taken as profit. In the instant case, the issue of cross-examination does not arise as the assessee has also not attended the office of the Revenue Authorities, though Shri Deepak Babel has also not attended on the said date. All the 10 transactions involved selling of goods/diamonds which has been purchased. [Para 11]

Where credits representing sales proceeds of shares held to be bogus

In the following cases, credits for sale of shares were held to be bogus and additions u/s 68 upheld:

Assessee claimed exemption under section 54F against capital gain arising from transaction of sale of shares. After initial assessment, information was received that transaction of sale of shares by assessee was sham and accommodation entries were given to him by broker after taking cash equal to value of profit; that entries in share register of company whose shares were allegedly purchased and sold revealed that no transaction of shares was entered in said register; and that broker was not member of any stock exchange. Assessing Officer, therefore, reopened assessment and holding said transaction as sham, added amount of sale consideration to income of assessee applying test of human probabilities. As burden of proving genuineness of transaction was on assessee which he failed to discharge and, therefore, test of human probabilities could be relied upon to reject claim of assessee that income was generated from source of sale of shares which was exempted from tax under section 54F. Therefore, amount claimed to be exempted was to be added to income of assessee as income from undisclosed source.

IDENTITY OF THE PERSON PAN card - The word 'identity' meant the condition or fact of a person or thing being that specified unique person or thing. Mere production of Permanent Account Number (PAN) or assessment particulars does not establish the identity of a person. The identification of a person includes the place of work, the staff and the fact that it was actually carrying on business and further recognition of the said company/individual in the eyes of public. PAN cannot be blindly and without consideration of surrounding circumstances treated as sufficiently disclosing the identity of the individual [CIT v. N. R. Portfolio (P.) Ltd. [2014] 42 taxmann.com 339/222 Taxman 157 (Mag.) (Delhi)].

Banking transaction - The very fact that all the transactions were entered into between the parties through account-payee cheques makes the question of identity of creditors fall into oblivion and it becomes absolutely irrelevant [Addl. CIT v. Bahri Bros. (P.) Ltd. [1985] 22 Taxman 3 (Pat.)].

In case of shareholders - If the shareholders exist then, possibly, no further enquiry need be made. But if the AO finds that the alleged shareholders do not exist then, in effect, it would mean that there is no valid issuance of share capital. Shares cannot be issued in the name of non-existing persons. If the shareholders are identified and it is established that they have invested money in the purchase of shares, then the amount received by the company would be regarded as a capital receipt but if the assessee offers no explanation at all or the explanation offered is not satisfactory, then the provisions of section 68 may be invoked [CIT v. Sophia Finance Ltd. [1993] 70 Taxman 69 (Delhi - FB)].

CREDITWORTHINESS OF THE PERSON

Earning capacity - Creditworthiness of the donor would depend upon the income and earning of the donor and whether and did he have necessary funds. Rarely one finds a poor man giving gifts to a rich and powerful, out of natural love and affection [Pawan Kumar Aggarwal v. ITO [2015] 60 taxmann.com 133 = [2015] 234 Taxman 144 (Delhi)].

Payment by cheque, etc. - Creditworthiness is not proved by showing issue and receipt of a cheque or by furnishing a copy of statement of bank account, when circumstances requires that there should be some more evidence of positive nature to show that the subscribers had made genuine investment or had acted as angel investors after due diligence or for personal reasons. There should be some positive evidence to show the nature and resources of the share subscribers [CIT v. Nipun Builders & Developers [2013] 30 taxmann.com 292/214 Taxman 429 (Delhi)].

When payment by cheque did not establish the creditworthiness of the lender, mere examination of the pass book or the bank statement or the letter of confirmation or the balance sheet of the lender was not enough [CIT v. Maithan International [2015] 56 taxmann.com 283/231 Taxman 381 (Cal.)].

Income-tax assessee - When the cash creditor is an income-tax assessee, it cannot be said that he is not a man of means [Kamal Motors v. CIT [2003] 131 Taxman 155 (Raj.)].

Deposits from tenants - In regard to deposit from tenants, it is sufficient if the assessee proves the identity of the tenant and the genuineness of the transaction under which the deposit is made. It will not be necessary for the assessee to prove the capacity of the tenant to make the deposit/advance [CIT v. Nevendram Ahuja [2007] 290 ITR 453 (MP)].

GENUINENESS OF THE TRANSACTION

Burden of proof - The burden of proving genuineness of a transaction of receipt of income by him from a claimed source, particularly income on the basis of which exemption of tax is claimed, is on the assessee. The said burden can be discharged by him either by leading evidence or from the circumstances on record. In absence of positive evidence of the assessee, the AO, by applying test of human probabilities can draw an inference of money being undisclosed income of the assessee [CIT v. Durga Prasad More [1969] 72 ITR 807 (SC); CIT v. Daulat Ram Rawatmull [1973] 87 ITR 349 (SC)].

In today's world, financial fraud instances are on the rise, and with advancements in technology, fraudsters are smarter to contrive new ways to carry out their nefarious schemes. Money laundering is one of these crimes that has been exploiting businesses for a long time. Criminals have devised alternate methods for concealing the source of money obtained unlawfully. Money laundering is a significant concern for financial institutions and Fintech firms. Placement, layering, and integration are the three stages of money laundering. The most difficult yet vital of these is placement. Most of the evidence that could aid in tracking the funds is destroyed during this stage. The funds are then layered in the second stage, which means they are given a frame that makes them appear legitimate. The funds are brought back into the legal economy during the last step of integration. Several bank accounts from different jurisdictions are used during the layering stage. Multiple account transfers obstruct tracking and circumvent value constraints. Authorities should be unable to track the origins of incriminated monies during the integration stage.

Given the recent significant surge in money laundering cases, firms anticipate an upsurge in the future as well. Regulatory authorities are functioning to prevent money laundering globally. Every company must follow the Financial Actions Task Force's rules (FATF) recommendations to combat Money Laundering cases that intend to protect enterprises from many sorts of illegal activities, particularly money laundering. Furthermore, the guidelines have highlighted specific actions that can assist businesses in detecting money laundering. FATF recommends these acts as red flags, making money laundering detection simpler.

If resources are valuable, fraudsters will try taking advantage of them. They enjoy precious jewels, stones, gold, diamonds, and other glistening materials as they are easy to conceal and give higher worth. Here's how countries are combating the smuggling and money-laundering schemes and what it means for fraud investigators.

Vulnerabilities can motivate the offenders to perpetrate fraud by dodging taxes, laundering money, or smuggling at virtually every level of the precious metals and stone trades, from extraction to refining to sale or re-sale of finished products. However, regulations and industry standards are in place to help avoid the violations linked with precious metals and gemstone extraction.

Gold and diamonds perfect for money laundering

Recently there have been several gold-related financial crime cases. According to the United States "Financial Action Task Force," criminals prefer to launder money through global gold and diamond markets because they offer predictable profits, participants deal mostly in cash, tracing transactions is complex, and gold and diamonds are easier to transport.

Many case studies have crammed how drug traffickers accept diamonds or gold as payment for drugs, smugglers convert gold into common unidentifiable objects like belt buckles, corrupt payments, bribes, and illegal gold and diamond mining to fund terrorism avoiding taxes. In most cases, Shell companies are established as a front business for illicit trades. Money laundering and shell companies share an old camaraderie, and in most cases of reported money laundering and smuggling, shell companies have played a significant role. This is prevalent worldwide. Shell companies are the entities that generally have no physical presence otherwise than an address and generate no or little economic value. They can be formed for legitimate purposes, too; yet, they have become a common tool for money laundering due to their ability to hide ownership and mask the financial details.

Money laundering occurs in a variety of ways. For example, someone might form a shell company to trade precious metals and use the shell company's name and bank account to receive the sale proceeds. Apart from this, the schemes involving magnified valuations of precious metals or stones due to a lack of expert valuation knowledge are also widespread. In such cases, the owner of a stone usually hires a third party to help evaluate the stone. The valuer doing the valuation often provides a deceptive report to the seller by claiming the stone to be of low value per carat. The stone's market worth may be high, but due to the seller's lack of knowledge, it will be presented to the seller at a marginally lower price.

Though FATF provides recommendations on Anti-Money Laundering practices, specific regulations to combat money laundering using precious metals and jewels have been provided by the "Kimberley Process," which was formed in 2003 and today has 56 participants from 82 nations. (The EU's 27 member states are counted as single participants.) The certification process oversees the requirements and provisions, such as creating national conflict legislation, commitment to transparency, statistical data exchange, prohibition of diamond trade with non-members, and provision of conflict-free certification for shipments. However, some nations are not Kimberley Process participants, and this is a big issue in the possibility of illicit trade involving stones from those countries.

To the extent the spurt in turnover is due to increase in digital sales, there is nothing to worry

There is nothing to fear if a spurt in cash sales is explainable by adequate purchases/stock/adequate expansion of facilities /increase in manpower

In both the above cases, show turnover in books and returns and pay normal taxes as usual and relax.

If unaccounted money available in the form of cash or deposits in bank accounts, better not to show it as current year's cash sales if one cannot satisfactorily explain as above the resulting increase in turnover. 23. Sum received by Sushmita Sen as compensation for being sexually harassed not taxable

[Sushmita Sen v. ACIT [2018] 99 taxmann.com 252 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The assessee, Sushmita Sen, received a sum of Rs. 145 lakhs from Coca Cola India Limited. Out of total sum, she offered to pay tax only on Rs. 50 Lakhs and claimed that balance Rs. 95 lakhs was capital receipt. She claimed that Rs. 95 lakhs represented the compensation received towards damages caused to her reputation.

The Mumbai ITAT held that compensation received by the assessee was not income liable to tax. Though she had received total amount of Rs. 145 lakhs in lieu of settlement for breach of terms of celebrity engagement contract, yet only an amount of Rs. 50 lakhs was due to assessee under the contractual terms, and additional amount of Rs. 95 lakhs did not arise out of exercise of profession. Rs. 95 lacs was received towards damages arising out of her being sexually harassed by CCIL employee, disparaging her professional reputation by false allegations and for the repudiatory breach of contract by CCIL. Such compensation could not be termed as any benefit, perquisite arising to assessee out of exercise of profession, hence, it couldn't be construed to be assessee's income either under section 2(24) or under section 28.

24. Payment of advance salary to defeat purpose of demonetisation won't come under purview of benami transaction

[G. Bahadur v. ACIT [2018] 100 taxmann.com 179 (PBPTA - AT)]

The appellant was employed in a College run by a Trust. He received Rs. 50 thousand as advance salary from the said trust. The appellant deposited entire amount in his bank account, which was subsequently withdrawn by him and used for own purposes.

The Initiating Officer (IO) assumed that Chairman of trust had forced employees to distribute, deposit and retain their own money in demonetized currency in guise of loan received, which had to be repaid after some time in new currency. Thus, IO held chairman of college as beneficial owner and appellant as benamidar and passed order provisionally attaching bank account of appellant.

The Appellate Tribunal held in favour of appellant as under:

Every cash transaction couldn't be termed as a 'benami' transaction. As per section 2(9) of Benami Act the following twin conditions are needed to be satisfied to construe any transaction as benami: (1) the property being held by a person who has not provided the consideration, (2) the property is held by that person for the immediate or future benefit, direct or indirect of the person who has provided the said consideration.

The characteristic of a 'benami' transaction is that there must be a mere lending of name without any intention to benefit the person in whose name it is made, i.e., a mere name lender. The mischiefs sought to be punished by the Act are only such transactions which have a name lending element without deriving any benefit therein, i.e., 'benami' transactions.

The transaction where cash was paid to person in lieu of a future promise couldn't be a 'benami' transaction, as there was no lending of name. There could be no 'benami' transaction if the future benefit was due from the person who was also the holder of property.

The impugned order was not sustainable as it intended to punish the appellants for wanting to defeat the purpose of demonetization and was beyond the purview of the Act.

Assessments in OCM/ Demonetisation Cases

4. The demonetisation period i.e. period from 9.11.2016 till 30.12.2016, fell in the FY 2016-17 corresponding to the AY 2017-18. So, in the regular assessments for the AY 2017-18, a large number of scrutiny cases were pertaining to the issue of huge and abnormal cash deposits during the demonetisation period.

The earlier deadline for completing regular assessments for OCM/demonetisation cases was 30.9.2019. However, due to the paucity of time, the CBDT has extended the deadline for assessing officers to complete and conclude the assessments of such OCM/demonetisation cases by December 31, 2019, which in any case was the time barring deadline for completion of regular assessment cases for the AY 2017-18, other than transfer pricing cases.

The assessing authorities have segregated such OCM cases separately for business cases and non-business cases and have analysed these in terms of various criterion.

Further, cash deposits made in a financial year have been segmented into three parts, i.e. pre demonetisation period (1.04.2016 till 8.11.2016), post demonetisation period (9.11.2016 till 31.12.2016) and total in the financial year 016-17 and corresponding period in FY 2015-16. The assessing authorities have subjected these data to analytics and have worked out the percentage increase in cash deposits against all the three combinations to derive the meaningful inferences. The analysis of month wise cash sales and deposits for demonetisation period and also the corresponding period in the FY 2015-16 have also been undertaken.

But this cannot be a sole criteria for reaching to the conclusion that the bogus long-term capital gain was generated which is exempted under section 10(38) of the Act. Such observation during the assessment proceedings provides reasons to investigate the matter in detail and the same cannot take the place of the evidence. But in the case on hand, there was no finding that the enquiry conducted either by the SEBI or the stock exchange with respect to rigging up of share price of M/s Shree Nath Commercial & Finance Ltd. Similarly, there was no finding with subsequent market price of the impugned scrip.

The income generated by the assessee cannot be held bogus only on the basis of the modus operandi, generalisation, and assumptions of certain facts. In order to hold income earned by the assessee as bogus, specific evidence has to be brought on record by the Revenue to prove that the assessee was involved in the collusion with the entry operator/stock brokers for such an arrangements. In the absence of such finding, no adverse inference can be drawn against the assessee.

Now the controversy also arises whether a person who genuinely purchases the shares at a low price and sold at high price, therefore, he enjoyed the windfall from such scripts, can he be disallowed the benefit of tax exemption provided under section 10(38) of the Act in a situation where it is established that the share price of the company was rigged up to extend the benefit to certain parties. Justice cannot be delivered in a mechanical manner. In other words, what we see on the records available before us, sometime we have to travel beyond it after ignoring the same. Furthermore, while delivering the justice, we have to ensure in this process that culprits should only be punished and no innocent should be castigated. An innocent person should not suffer for the wrongdoings of the other parties. In the case on hand, admittedly there was no evidence available on record suggesting that the assessee or his broker was involved in the rigging up of the price of the script of M/s Shree Nath Commercial & Finance Ltd. Thus, it appears that the assessee acted in the given facts and circumstances in good-faith.

The above provisions of TDS have taken care of the profit at the time of consideration paid to the resident either in cash/cheque or even crypto. It means when a person shifts from one crypto to another, the provisions are applicable, but this transaction cannot be mapped as the amount is not credited to the bank account.

Strengthening the Provisions One more method can be used to bring these exchanges in the ambit of regulation i.e. by bringing these exchanges under section 285BA and treating them as reportable entities (REs). By this, the obligation of disclosing the transaction lies with the exchange. For the time being, in the absence of the change in section 285BA, a special pilot project by Intelligence and Criminal Investigation (I&CI) can be launched to gather the information for such Specified Financial Transactions (SFT). There is no information available in the organized form that how many exchanges are dealing with crypto currencies. Similarly, only the exchanges located in a country can be brought to the scheme. The exchanges located outside are not obliged to comply either with the provisions of the Act or with any notices issued under Section 133(6) of the Act. At first, for the domestic exchanges, a master list is required to be prepared by collecting information from Google etc.Then these REs may be asked to furnish the SFT, which should contain data of all persons who have made these transactions. The entries during the gain period should be specifically checked. The collected information can be disseminated to the Assessing Officers for further verification or scrutiny. Similarly, Section 194S provides for a deduction of tax, even if the VDA is sold for another VDA. In case the sale is made in any recognised currency, the sale value is determined as per the realised value, but in case, the sale is made in another VDA, the issue of the valuation may arise. The fair market value has not been defined, which is another challenge.

Cash Transaction

The above mechanism is useful for transactions made through banking channels, but for cash transactions, it is near to impossible to catch them as the cash system works in the same fashion as 'hawala' works. The word 'hawala' is a local version of the English word 'reference'; this system works only on a reference basis. An anonymous person cannot go directly to the 'hawala' dealer for transfer of money between cities or countries. A reference from some known person is required. These dealers are not maintaining any written record; once a transaction is completed, the record is erased. Even if any record is found during the course of the survey or search, nothing can be made out of these jotted entries. Generally, these transactions are very smooth. Trust and risk are primary conditions. So dealing with cash crypto is almost like dealing with 'hawala' transactions. No separate provisions of the law are applicable, and no special expertise is required to crack these transactions. Traditional hawala methods were mainly operating through two methods. Firstly, the quantum of money of the sender and receiver should be the same. The second method is 'under-invoicing or over-invoicing' of import and export bills as required. But transfer through crypto is not based on any such conditions, the money can be sent unilaterally. So the emphasis is required only on those transactions which are done through banking channels.

Major Challenge

The main danger of cryptocurrencies is the convenience of transferring money to offshore places. A person can buy crypto in cash in India and transfer it to some person living abroad. That person would sell it and receive money in the local currency. Same as in the case of international debit or credit cards, where the deposits are made in one country in local currency, but ATM withdrawals can be made in any country. But these transactions contain heavy transaction fees, which is not there in the case of crypto. The central banks are honouring the transactions of debit and credit cards, as in the case of crypts also. The central bank has to honour at least in those countries that have given legal status to some cryptocurrencies. So why have some countries, like China, completely banned any transaction in these currencies. Section 194S comes into the picture when the amount is credited to a resident. Hence the money sent outside of the countries is out of the purview of these provisions. The first-time buyers of the crypto are also required to bring under these provisions.

CONCLUDING OBSERVATION AND SUGGESTIONS Based on the above observation, it can be stated that the introduction of the Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 was a much-needed step for the prosecution of fugitive economic offenders. This Act is a tailor-made specific statute that deals with a typical form of white collar crime which constitutes a huge chunk of economic offences in the country. It can also be stated that there are various unique features in this statute. This brings out various positive points that the legislators have tried to implement through this Act. The Act provides for time-bound prosecution of the offenders of economic crimes. To ensure this, the Act is formulated in such a way that there is no delay in the trial and other judicial proceedings. The distinctive feature of this Act is the attachment and confiscation of different types of properties that are not acquired by legal means. Such attachment and confiscation are based on the United Nations Convention against Corruption. Thus it can be said from the above observation and analysis that this legislation is drafted keeping in mind the speedy trial and recovery of monetary value in question. The above provisions of the Act are closely associated with the nature of offenses that the country has faced in the past few years. Economic offenses of grave nature affect the country's GDP and become a hurdle in the path of progress of the economy. Therefore such accused who are declared as fugitive economic offenders under the Act must be brought to justice so that the sanctity of the rule of law is maintained. This will also ensure the removal of the block in the path of the country's economic progress. This legislation was the need of the time and the Central Government has been successful in bringing out a law that deals with all major aspects of offices whose offenders have turned fugitive and are trying to avoid prosecution. The powers granted to the authority and the designated officers are wider in nature as compared to previous money laundering and economic offenses legislations.

On one hand where the government's move towards tackling such nature of offenses is being appreciated, on the other hand, the implementation of the said Act is also put to question with several lacunas. The lacuna lies in the fact that as per Section 4 of the Act, a person is straightway declared as a fugitive if sufficient evidence is against him. It also observes that imbalanced power is granted to the special court and nodal agency for conducting search and seizure and attaching the property of the accused. The law is subject to proper judicial review from the higher courts to be perfectly implantable since it violates basic human rights and laws of natural justice prima facie on its implementation. The pre-confiscation of the property of the accused before the conviction of the offence violated the basic principle of criminal law which states that every person is to be presumed innocent until proven guilty.

Thus, it is important to note that this legislation should go under judicial review by the appropriate court. To make the implementation of the law more effective, the Central Government needs to bring amendments as per the rule of law observing the principles of natural justice, the right to free and fair trial, and in consonance with the fundamental rights provisions of the Indian Constitution. The Act is a much-needed step to recover and prevent economic offenses of modern times and will prove a milestone shortly if implemented and executed with due care.

Assuming that the assessee is a regular investor as was submitted to us by the learned advocates for the assessees that in any manner cannot improve the situation as the claim for LTCG has been only restricted to the shares which were purchased and sold by the assessees in penny stocks companies. Therefore merely because the assessee had invested in other blue chip companies had earned profit or incurred loss cannot validate the tainted transactions.

It has been established by the department that the rise of the prices of the shares was artificially done by the adopting manipulative practices. Consequently whatever resultant benefits which accrue from out of such manipulative practices are also to be treated as tainted. However, the assessee had opportunity to prove that there was no manipulation at the other end and whatever gains the assessee has reaped was not tainted. This has not been proved or established by any of the assessee before us. Therefore, the Assessing Officers were well justified in coming to a conclusion that the so called explanation offered by the assessee was not to their satisfaction. Thus, the assessee having not proved the genuineness of the claim, the creditworthiness of the companies in which they had invested and the identity of the persons to whom the transactions were done, have to necessarily fail.

In such factual scenario, the Assessing Officers as well as the CIT(A) have adopted an inferential process which is a process which would be followed by a reasonable and prudent person. The Assessing Officers and the CIT(A) have culled out proximate facts in each of the cases, took into consideration the surrounding circumstances which came to light after the investigation, assessed the conduct of the assessee, took note of the proximity of the time between the buy and sale operations and also the sudden and steep rise of the price of the shares of the companies when the general market trend was admittedly recessive and thereafter arrived at a conclusion which in our opinion is a proper conclusion and in the absence of any satisfactory explanation by the assessee, the Assessing Officers were bound to make addition under Section 68 of the Act.

Abstract

Gold has regained prominence as a universal store of value amid rising geopolitical uncertainty, inflation, and distrust in fiat currencies. Its surge to record highs in 2025 reflects both legitimate economic behaviour and increasing compliance challenges. This article analyses how global gold dynamics intersect with taxation, money-laundering laws, and white-collar crime, particularly within India's regulatory ecosystem. It also examines cross-border trade complexities, enforcement coordination, and the evolving standards of global financial governance. The paper concludes with strategic recommendations for policymakers and corporate stakeholders to balance economic opportunity with legal responsibility.

Keywords: Gold, Taxation, Compliance, PMLA, FATF, GAAR, Cross-Border Trade, Corporate Governance, White-Collar Crime

I. Research Objective and Context

Gold remains more than a commodity. It is an emotion, a financial anchor, and a barometer of public confidence. In 2025, its value has soared not only because of market mechanics but also due to geopolitical tension and financial distrust. The objective of this paper is to evaluate the legal, tax, and compliance implications of gold's renewed prominence in the global economy.

The research aims to:

1.

Examine the global and Indian gold market trends shaping 2025.

2.

Analyse the legal and regulatory architecture governing taxation, anti-money-laundering, and cross-border transactions.

3.

Identify vulnerabilities that enable gold to be used for white-collar crime.

4.

Recommend policy and governance strategies that uphold transparency and accountability without impeding legitimate trade.

Gold's unique attributes such as liquidity, anonymity, and universal acceptance make it both an asset of stability and a tool of concealment. Understanding this duality is essential for designing laws that protect integrity while enabling commerce.

II. The Global Gold Surge: Economics, Emotion and Law

A. Price Trends and Market Forces

According to Reuters and the World Gold Council, gold prices in 2025 have risen nearly 50 percent year-on-year, reaching around US $3,950 per ounce internationally and crossing Rs. 1,25,000 per 10 grams in India. This dramatic rise stems from persistent inflation, high global debt, and growing investor preference for tangible assets.

Central banks across Asia and the Middle East have purchased record quantities of gold to diversify reserves. Goldman Sachs has forecast prices could approach US $4,900 per ounce by 2026 if inflation remains elevated and interest rates stabilise.

This global pattern underscores gold's transformation from a passive store of value into a geopolitical hedge. It reflects both market sentiment and institutional strategy.

B. India's Domestic Context

India's relationship with gold is historical and deeply cultural. Demand peaks during festivals and marriage seasons, creating a recurring impact on trade balances. India imports nearly all its gold, which has implications for the current account deficit and currency stability.

High import duties and fluctuating exchange rates have incentivised smuggling and under-invoicing. In March 2025, the government discontinued parts of the Gold Monetisation Scheme to limit fiscal exposure. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence has since reported a notable increase in illegal inflows through land and maritime borders.

C. Geopolitical Context

Gold's rally cannot be separated from the global political landscape. The continuing Russia–Ukraine conflict, instability in the Middle East, and trade tensions between the United States and China have disrupted global supply chains. Sanctions against Russian bullion refineries have redirected trade to Asian hubs such as Dubai, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

As trade flows realign, enforcement agencies must address differing compliance standards among jurisdictions. Some free-trade zones have become conduits for gold trading with limited regulatory oversight, increasing risks of mis-invoicing and money laundering.

III. Legal Framework Governing Gold and Financial Compliance

A. Income-Tax and Disclosure Laws

Under the Income-tax Act, 1961, unexplained gold holdings can be taxed as income under Sections 69 and 69B. High-net-worth individuals and corporations are required to declare gold holdings accurately to avoid reassessment and penalty.

Cross-border transactions in gold attract transfer-pricing scrutiny under Section 92F. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued guidelines requiring documentation that justifies arm's-length pricing.

Inadequate valuation or inter-company transfers through low-tax jurisdictions often attract investigation under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule (GAAR).

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor.

Assessing Authorities' Stand in OCM/Demonetisation Assessment Cases concerning Assesses' Claims of Cash deposits being made out of Cash Sales in Business

5. In the cases of persons engaged in business and maintaining books of accounts, the most common and natural explanation and justification for the cash deposits being made by them in the post demonetisation period has been cash sales being made by them in their businesses.

The assessing authorities, in majority of the OCM assessment cases, have declined to accept the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made out of cash sales of business in post demonetisation period and have made huge income-tax demands under sections 68, 69, 69A, 69B, 69C read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act, in the regular assessment orders in such OCM/demonetisation cases. The most common arguments and contentions being made by the assessing authorities in rejecting the genuineness and authenticity of the cash deposits being made by the assessees out of their cash sales in business post demonetisation period are discussed as under:

i.

Since w.e.f. 8.11.2016 midnight, Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000 notes (SBNs) were declared invalid and were not to be considered as legal tender, therefore, for the assesses carrying on business, booking of cash sales and accepting such SBNs for transacting business transactions, during post demonetisation period, was prohibited.

ii.

The money measurement concept of accounting underlines the fact that in accounting and economics generally, every recorded event or transaction is measured in terms of money, i.e., the local currency monetary unit of measure. Since the SBNs were just a piece of papers and they bear no value on 9th November 2016 or after, as Central Government, the guarantor, had withdrawn its guarantee and hence, the receipt of these SBNs can't be journalized in books of account. Therefore, the transactions made in SBNs on or after 9th November 2016 cannot be entered into cash books.

iii.

Therefore, if the assessee has received any SBN notes after 09.11.2016 on account of any monetary transactions and utilizes the same for making cash deposits into the bank account, then the credit of the same into the books of accounts is not to be considered as valid and has to be treated as unexplained money u/s 69A read with section 115BBE of the Income Tax Act and brought to tax.

In some other cases, where the cash deposits have been explained by the assessees as pertaining to cash sales being made by them prior to the demonetisation period, the assessing authorities have again rejected the genuineness and authenticity of such claims believing that the assessees might have backdated the cash sales just before the demonetisation period so as to reflect cash in hand as on 8.11.2016 consisting of banned notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1000, which they have deposited in their bank accounts post demonetisation.

10. Concluding comments

Much more can be written about the issues likely to emerge consequent to the decision to demonetize the high denomination notes on the basis of present situation. More are likely to surface as the work relating to exchange and conversion proceeds. 10.1 The decisions to demonetize notes of Rs.500/- & Rs.1,000/- is a bold decision of the Govt., though taken in haste and without required preparedness but there may not be dissenters to the decision taken by the Govt. in principle. But, doing so, without proper preparations, cannot be excused. Why should there be restriction of Rs.20,000/- withdrawal a week when one wish to withdraw his disclosed money with the bank. Further, mere issue of Rs.2,000/- notes to start with is of no use unless notes of smaller denominations of Rs.100/- and Rs.50/- are simultaneously issued. Why so far there has been no issue of new notes of Rs.500/- is a mystery. The inconvenience that the common man is suffering because of unpreparedness of the Govt. to meet the resultant problems is un-excusable. Merely saying 'suffer these for better future' can hardly be a consolation.

10.2 Also, demonetization is only one way for tackling black money problem. People do not generate black money to keep it idle in chests at home. They churn it out to add more money by investments in real estate, gold/silver jewellery, precious stones, investments in India and abroad and in many other ways, including its use in political funding. Hence, tackling in parts the problem of black money is likely to be counterproductive. Consolidated effort in this direction is needed. Measures like demonetization inconvenience merely the small traders and common man across the country. Hence, simultaneous efforts are necessary to check investments in aforesaid avenues. Further, measures will have to be thought of to dis-incentivise fresh generation of black money and clean up the political funding and keep check on the finances of political parties. All parties must be, through law, made to mandatorily declare their monthly receipts and expenditure, which must be open to public scrutiny and vetted by the Election Commission. That would be a real step in the direction of checking black money – not measures like demonetization – which tackle the stock – not theflow.

10.3 Terror financing through counterfeit Indian notes and their smuggling may stop for some time, but further action on these lines will stop only when the new notes cannot be duplicated. The claim of the RBI is that these cannot be but time alone would show how far such claim is justified. However, the more important step, to be taken, is checking strongly their infiltration in the country.

10.4 The success of the decision can only be known after the period of conversion allowed is over. If large chunk of 14.95 lakh crore notes come back to the economy, it will indicate that the demonetization has not served its purpose – the evaders have been more smart than the administrative action from the side of the Finance Ministry.

11. Urgent action needed from GOI's side

Considering the confusion created by the unpreparedness of the Govt. and its own estimate that it will take 2-3 weeks more for making the ATMs work and non-availability of new notes in sufficient numbers, the time limit upto 30th December for conversion/deposit in bank accounts needs to be extended upto 31st March, 2017 and thereafter, with the RBI upto 30th June, 2017. This needs to be done immediately to remove the hervousness and hurried approach to banks.

Judicial update

Recently, Hon'ble Calcutta High Court in Rajmandir Estates (P.) Ltd. v. Pr. CIT [2016] 386 ITR 162/240 Taxman 306/70 taxmann.com 124, had an occasion to deal with the issue of validity of reopening of assessment by CIT u/s. 263, in the backdrop of possible money-laundering.

The CIT in his order dated 22.03.13 passed under Section 263 opined that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went undetected due to lack of requisite enquiry and non-application of mind. He entertained the belief "that unaccounted money is laundered as clean share capital by creating a façade of paper work, routing the money through several bank accounts and getting it the seal of statutory approval by getting the case reopened u/s.147 suo motu. Accordingly he concluded that assessment order passed u/s. 143(3)/147 was erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. He, therefore, set aside the same and issued directions for a thorough enquiry.

Hon'ble High Court in its elaborate order after referring to the PMLA and observing various facets and evidences of possible money laundering under the peculiar facts of the case upheld the order of CIT u/s. 263 in following words:

"We have indicated above the pieces of evidence which go to show that the Commissioner had reasons to entertain the belief that this was or could be a case of money laundering which went unnoticed because the assessing officer did not hold requisite investigation except for calling for the records. ……. The fact that the assessing officer did not apply his mind to those pieces of evidence would be evident from the assessment order itself.

The question for consideration is whether in the presence of materials discussed above the Commissioner was justified in treating the assessment order erroneous and prejudicial to the interest of the revenue. That question in the facts and circumstances has to be answered in the affirmative."

It is important to note that, Hon'ble High Court distinguished some of the Supreme Court precedents cited by the appellant to support his case inter alia on the ground that The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 was not there on the statute at that point of time. Therefore, though offences under the Income Tax act, 1961 per se are not scheduled offences for the purpose of PMLA, nevertheless assessing officer can proceed in assessment or CIT can direct further investigation in order to verify possibility of income/assets added or declared u/s. 68, 69, 69A etc. of the IT act being sourced out of proceeds of crime as defined u/s. 2(u) of the PMLA, so that further action under PMLA, if necessary, can be taken.

Conclusion

It has to be kept in view that India has a problem of black economy, which is unacounted and many a time the holders of black money also launder the black money in order to acquire legitimate assets. Legal or illegal income which evades tax and illegal income that comes within the exempted taxation slab constitute the unreported Gross Domestic Product or black economy. Laundering the black money and laundering proceeds of crime are two different issues, although there is frequent overlap between the two. While laundering black money is to be handled through taxation laws or similar laws, the laundering of proceeds of crime is to be handled through special anti-money-laundering laws. [Dr. M. C. Mehanathan in his commentary on the Law of Prevention of Money Laundering in India published by Lexis Nexis (2014 edition)]

TAXMANN ADVISORY AND RESEARCH TEAM (INCOME TAX)

Introduction

1. Demonetization has encouraged people to shift towards digital mode of payment while making financial transactions. By adopting digital mode of payment, no financial transactions would remain undisclosed and Consequently, an enhanced turnover of business might get reflected in the books of account.

Under the circumstances, an apprehension has been caused that increased turnover in the current year may lead to reopening of earlier years' cases causing undue harassment to taxpayers.

Thus, CBDT and CBEC (vide Circular No. 40/2016 and Circular No. 137/155/2012-Service tax) have advised tax officials not to re-open past assessments in income-tax and indirect tax cases only because increased turnover is reflected in books of account of business on account of increased use of digital means of payment.

2. Points to be considered for interpreting such circulars:

It would be incorrect to construe the above Circulars as giving any amnesty to tax-evaders.

The above circulars do not say that any spurt in turnover reported in books of account of businesses of current financial year (and consequently in their ITRs or indirect tax returns) is not need to be explained.

The Circulars do not give businessmen a license to show their accumulated black money in the form of demonetized notes as current year's turnover and get away scot-free without any interest or penalty and by paying normal tax for current year. If such a license is given by the circulars, the proposed PMGKY Scheme and proposed amendments to section115BBE of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and proposed new section 271AAC of that Act would be redundant.

The two circulars clarify the following points which is mere re-iteration of the existing law:

Suppose any business reported Rs.1cr to Rs.1.5 cr as its turnover in service tax and VAT in last 5 years. If the business reports a turnover of Rs.5 cr in financial year 2016-17, then it is natural for any tax official to suspect that increased turnover;

However, such suspicion alone is not sufficient to entail reopening of past assessments in income-tax and well as service tax/customs;

The Circulars do not take away the powers of tax officials to make inquiries into the sudden spurt in reported turnover;

If the results of enquiries yield information which can form basis of "reason to believe" escapement of turnover/income in the past periods, the assessments can be reopened.

The Circulars are innocuous and merely caution tax officials to adopt systematic approach under the law to enquire into sudden jumps and reopen past assessment only if enquiry throws up reason to believe that past turnovers/incomes escaped assessment. Sudden jump in turnover may give reason to suspect that turnover/income had escaped assessment in past years. But that suspicion should not lead to reopening of past assessments without making necessary inquiries and verification regarding causes of the sudden increase.

Huge increase in reported turnover can be due to genuine reasons as well as due to book-keeping sophistry.

3. Examples of genuine reasons for increased turnover due to increased use of digital means of payments:–

(1)

Credit cards offer EMI terms on purchases made through credit cards. This may have resulted in increase in sales. So, a business which was selling only on cash basis may experience a jump in turnover on account of this reason.

(2)

Impolitic purchases through plastic cards

(3)

Special cash back schemes of mobile wallets/debit cards/credit cards.

(4)

Expansion of facility of service provider/increase in manpower enabling him to service more customers.

4. Comments

Increased turnover reflected in books of accounts may also be due to past unaccounted money now shown in current year's books as current year's turnover and thereafter these notes are banked.

Whatever be the reasons, taxpayers can (and should be) asked to explain the huge increase in current period's turnover. If they are able to explain the same by valid reasons and also show corresponding increase in stocks and purchases (or expansion in size of facilities/manpower), then their explanation will be believed and past assessments will not be reopened. If they cannot explain the sudden increase in reported turnover, they can always declare their huge unexplained cash/bank deposits in proposed PMGKY Scheme and pay 49.9% tax and deposit 25% in PMGKY deposit (no interest; 4 years lock-in). If they declare their unaccounted cash/bank deposits in PMGKY, then obviously, there would be no question of reopening their past assessments of income-tax or indirect taxes. If they do not declare in PMGKY and opt to show it as current year's turnover, then they should be able to justify it.

Smaller businesses might be involved in the supply chain, and they may fall below the GST registration threshold, contributing to the presence of non-registered entities in the expenses. By examining these factors and obtaining a clear understanding of the nature of the expenses and the entities involved, the auditor can make a more informed assessment and mitigate the risk of misinterpretation or misreporting.

As a corollary, when the figures reported in the mentioned column are substantial, and the following instances are present, the auditor should exercise heightened vigilance to ensure the authenticity of the transactions:

(a)

Taxable Products: If the products purchased are taxable under GST, it raises the significance of these transactions and warrants closer scrutiny.

(b)

Cash Payments: Payments made in cash can increase the risk of irregularities or inaccuracies in reporting, and therefore, require careful examination.

(c)

Absence of TDS: Transactions not subjected to Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) can potentially indicate a need for closer inspection, as TDS is a common regulatory requirement for certain types of payments.

(d)

Internal Documentation: Transactions primarily supported by internal vouchers, bills, or purchase notes, as opposed to external invoices or receipts, may necessitate a more thorough examination to verify their legitimacy.

If the auditor encounters difficulties in forming a conclusive opinion based on the data provided by the assessee, it is essential to include appropriate comments in the main report. These comments should clearly convey an concerns or uncertainties regarding the reported transactions, ensuring transparency and clarity in the audit process.

Expenses covered under Reverse Charge Mechanism (RCM):

In case of expenditures that were subjected to tax on reverse charge basis, we may encounter with two issues-

(a)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by a person registered under GST but issuing RCM invoices;

(b)

Expenses incurred in respect of supplies made by an unregistered person where the assessee pays tax under RCM on voluntary basis.

In the first scenario, the expenditure under the said category ought to be reported under column 5 of clause 44 i.e., "Relating to other registered entities".

In the second scenario, the expenditure under the said category should be reported under column 7 i.e., Expenditure relating to entities not registered under GST".

13. Review and Contemporary Analysis

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act has become one of the most important economic laws in India’s regulatory system. Over the years, it has strengthened the government’s ability to trace illegal money, investigate financial frauds, recover public assets, and tackle organized economic offences. Enforcement actions against banking scams, shell companies, Ponzi schemes, cyber frauds, and cross-border laundering networks have played a major role in protecting investors, financial institutions, and the broader economy.

Recent data released by the Enforcement Directorate shows the increasing scale of enforcement under the PMLA. As of March 2026, the ED had registered more than 8,800 ECIRs, issued over 3,500 provisional attachment orders, and attached assets worth nearly ₹2.36 lakh crore. During the financial year 2025–26 alone, attachments reportedly crossed ₹81,000 crore, marking a sharp rise compared to previous years.

These enforcement measures have also produced significant economic benefits. Official figures indicate that assets worth more than ₹63,000 crore have either been returned or steps have been taken to return them to banks, investors, financial institutions, and homebuyers affected by large-scale frauds. In several real-estate and infrastructure cases, attached properties were used to safeguard the interests of thousands of affected investors and purchasers.

The scale of recent investigations further highlights the expanding role of the ED in financial regulation. In the TDI Infrastructure case, properties worth around ₹349 crore were attached in matters relating to the alleged diversion of homebuyers’ funds affecting over 14,000 investors. Likewise, in proceedings involving Ansal Properties and Infrastructure Ltd., assets exceeding ₹313 crore were attached to protect the interests of affected homebuyers.

India has also strengthened international cooperation in tracing illegal financial flows and fugitive offenders. Through Mutual Legal Assistance Requests and Letters Rogatory issued to countries such as the United Kingdom, Singapore, Switzerland, the United Arab Emirates, and the United States, investigative agencies have expanded their efforts in evidence collection, extradition, and asset tracing.

At the prosecution stage, nearly 2,400 complaints have been filed before Special Courts under the PMLA. Parliamentary disclosures further indicate that courts have delivered judgments in a number of concluded cases, with convictions secured in a large majority of them. These figures are often cited to demonstrate the strengthening of India’s anti-money laundering framework and its growing institutional capacity.

The impact of these actions extends beyond prosecution alone. Recovery and attachment of illegally acquired assets have helped improve banking recovery mechanisms, discourage circulation of unaccounted money, strengthen financial discipline, and improve India’s standing within the global anti-money laundering framework developed by the Financial Action Task Force.

B. Anti-Avoidance and GAAR Principles

GAAR empowers authorities to disregard transactions structured primarily to avoid tax. The Supreme Court's decision in Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India [2012] 19 taxmann.com 217 reaffirmed that genuine commercial purpose is the defining factor. Gold trading entities often use complex cross-border arrangements for warehousing and invoicing. Such structures, if devoid of economic substance, can be recharacterised by tax authorities. The growing collaboration between Indian regulators and international counterparts has made tax arbitrage more difficult to conceal.

C. Money Laundering and the PMLA Framework

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) forms the backbone of India's anti-money-laundering regime. Jewellers, refiners, and bullion dealers are designated as reporting entities. They must verify customer identity, maintain records, and report suspicious transactions exceeding Rs. 10 lakh to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU-IND).

The Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India [2022] 140 taxmann.com 610 (SC) upheld the constitutional validity of the PMLA, emphasising its deterrent role. Non-compliance now attracts criminal prosecution, with attachment and confiscation of assets linked to proceeds of crime.

Gold, due to its liquidity and global mobility, remains a preferred medium for layering and integration in money-laundering chains. Enforcement agencies have therefore prioritised the bullion trade in their investigative strategies.

D. Benami and Black-Money Legislation

The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988, as amended in 2016, prohibits holding gold or other assets in another person's name. The Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ganpati Dealcom Pvt Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 389/289 Taxman 177/447 ITR 108 clarified that the 2016 amendments are prospective, giving enforcement agencies clear timelines for action.

The Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) Act, 2015 criminalises undisclosed offshore holdings, including gold kept in foreign vaults or nominee accounts. Residents must report such assets in Schedule FA of their tax returns or face penalties and imprisonment.

E. Customs and FEMA Compliance

Gold imports and exports are regulated under the Customs Act, 1962 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA). Importers must obtain authorisation from the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT) and route payments through authorised banking channels.

Under-invoicing and over-invoicing are treated as contraventions under both Customs and FEMA. Such activities may trigger proceedings under Section 111 of the Customs Act and attract compounding penalties under FEMA.

IV. Cross-Border Trade and International Coordination

A. The FATF and Global Standards

The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) has repeatedly identified the gold trade as a high-risk sector for money laundering and terror financing. Its 2024 evaluation called upon member countries to expand reporting obligations and enhance beneficial ownership transparency. India, through the Asia-Pacific Group on Money Laundering, is implementing these standards across its financial institutions and bullion exchanges.

B. OECD and Transfer-Pricing Guidelines

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) mandates country-by-country reporting for multinational enterprises engaged in commodities trading. Gold refiners and trading houses must justify pricing models and inter-company margins. The Central Board of Direct Taxes has aligned domestic rules with OECD recommendations to ensure consistency in valuation.

C. Information Sharing and Treaties

India's participation in the Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and multiple Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) enables exchange of financial information with more than 100 countries. This allows regulators to trace offshore holdings and identify beneficial owners of foreign gold accounts.

Under the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) framework, Indian institutions also report US-linked gold-backed assets, ensuring reciprocity in disclosure.

D. Digital Gold and New-Age Risks

Digital gold platforms have transformed retail investment. While convenient, they raise jurisdictional and compliance questions because the underlying bullion is often stored overseas. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)and Reserve Bank of India (RBI) are now evaluating mechanisms to regulate digital gold and tokenised bullion under a unified compliance regime.

Proper regulation is critical to prevent misuse of digital assets for cross-border transfer or concealment.

V. Corporate Governance and Enforcement Trends

Corporate scandals involving misreporting of gold inventories and false collateral declarations have drawn scrutiny under the Companies Act, 2013. Section 447 defines such manipulation as fraud, punishable by imprisonment and fines.

Investigations today employ digital forensics, audit analytics, and blockchain tracing to verify authenticity of gold-backed financial products. Collaboration among the Enforcement Directorate, Income Tax Department, Customs, and FIUhas improved substantially.

India's cooperation with foreign regulators, especially in the UAE and Singapore, facilitates tracing of assets and repatriation of proceeds of crime. The country's growing adherence to FATF and OECD frameworks enhances its credibility in global financial governance.

5. We are engaged in manufacture of Synthetic (Industrial) Diamond (Heading 7102 29 90 of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985) through the Microwave Plasma Chemical Vapour Deposition Process, which results into Rough Diamonds. The said Rough Diamonds are subjected to Bruiting, Cutting and Polishing on job-work basis and become saleable Items, viz., Final Product (classifiable under Heading 7102 31 00). Discuss liability, if any, under Central Excise and/or Service tax.

Your query has been replied in following parts —

(A)

Manufacture - As already stated by you that the process amounts to 'manufacture', the rate of duty for goods falling under Heading 7102 is 'NIL'. Hence, there is manufacture of goods, but not liable to any duty.

(B)

Manufacture not liable to service tax -A process amounting to manufacture under section 2(f) of the Central Excise Act, 1944 falls within the negative list entry under section 66D(f), read with section 65B(40), of the Finance Act, 1994 [Negative list of Services - Process amounting to Manufacture or Production of Goods] and not liable to service tax.

(C)

Job work - The job-work carried out as an intermediate production process on independent basis and not amounting to manufacture under section 2(f), is exempt from service tax if it is in relation to 'cut and polished diamonds and gemstones or plain and studded jewellery of gold and other precious metals, falling under Chapter 71 of the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985 (5 of 1986)' as per Entry 30(b) of Notification No. 25/2012-ST, dated 20-6-2012. Accordingly, Bruiting, Cutting and Polishing on job-work basis would be exempt.

(D)

Conclusion - There will not be any liability of central excise duty or service tax on the entire transaction.

9. Technological Challenges in Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement

9.1 Crypto currency and Decentralized Finance

Modern laundering systems increasingly rely upon:

• decentralized exchanges,

• privacy coins,

• peer-to-peer transfers,

• offshore wallets,

• mixers and tumblers,

• cross-chain bridges.

Traditional banking-based AML systems are often ineffective against decentralized financial ecosystems.

9.2 Trade-Based Money Laundering

Trade-Based Money Laundering (TBML) remains one of the least detected forms of financial crime. (Hanson, 2025)

Methods include:

• over-invoicing,

• under-invoicing,

• phantom shipments,

• duplicate invoicing,

• false declarations.

India presently lacks sophisticated, integrated trade data analytics capable of real-time anomaly detection. (Trade Intelligence & Analytics (TIA) Portal - A New Integrated Platform for India’s Trade Insights, 2025)

9.3 Shell Companies and Beneficial Ownership Concealment

Complex ownership structures spread across tax havens continue to conceal beneficial ownership through:

• nominee directors,

• layered subsidiaries,

• offshore trusts,

• shell corporations.

The absence of centralized beneficial ownership intelligence weakens financial investigations. (Beneficial Ownership Transparency: The Missing Link in AML Investigations, 2024)

10. Major Enforcement Actions Resulting in Economic Recovery

10.1 PACL Ponzi Scheme

Despite constitutional concerns, anti-money laundering enforcement has generated substantial economic benefits for the economy, the banking sector, and investors. Even with ongoing constitutional concerns, anti-money laundering enforcement has brought major economic benefits to the economy, banks, investors, and the government’s largest Ponzi-style investment scams are affecting millions of investors.

The proceedings:

• preserved assets,

The investigation strengthened:

• international cooperation,

• trade-finance monitoring,

10.3 Vijay Mallya–Kingfisher Case

Recovery and attachment proceedings significantly benefited public sector banks and reduced pressure arising from non-performing assets.

8. Weak spots, which could lead to laundering of black money white without any consequences

The Govt. has announced that no enquiry will be made in regard to deposits upto Rs.2.5 lac in Jandhan A/cs or new accounts opened for depositing old notes. Report in this regard have started surfacing in print media showing misuse of such declaration. According to a report in TOI of Nov. 13, there is sudden influx of deposits in almost dead Jandhan a/cs. The report shows that in one city – Agra – alone, around 170 crores have been deposited in the past 3 days in such a/cs. Similar could be the situation in other parts of the country. While the Govt may not question deposits made upto Rs.2.5 lac, how such deposits are used later needs to be watched to trace back their return journey to the actual owner. This could be a stupendous task considering the fact that there are crores of such a/cs and chasing outflow from these a/cs to reach the ultimate owners of money would require large manpower. This, apart, how a person can be questioned legally in respect of dispersal of his disclosed income under the I.T. law would also need consideration. Sustained interrogation can only bring out the nexus between black money-holders and depositors of such money. The I.T.Dept. does not have such manpower and thus, more than 5 lac crore could be rendered white through such processes.

9. Has demonetization made the IDS declarants loosers?

In the just concluded IDS on 30th Sept., 2016, undisclosed income of nearly Rs.66,500 crore has been declared, netting a tax of Rs,30,000 crore (inclusive of penalty and cess) @45%..After declaration of demonetization, the undisclosed income in the form of Rs.500/- and Rs.1,000 crore can be shown as current year's income and subjected to payment of advance tax in coming two quarters. Thus, the evaders can escape by paying 30% tax and surcharge [wherever applicable] with some interest for delay in payment of advance tax in the first 2 quarters as against 45% paid by the IDS declarants. Already, the assessees for payment of excise duty andVAT have started doing so by showing such income as sales and paying applicable taxes on the same.
