It is generally accepted principle under the Evidence Laws is that when a person is bound to prove the existence of any fact, it is said that the burden of proof lies on that person. The burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it. In ITO v. Pradip Burman [CC No. 525792/16] & ITO v. Ashok Jaipuria [CC No. 527354/2016], Hon'ble Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate ('ACMM') Court had given ample opportunity to the prosecution/complainant i.e., Income-tax Department, to lead material evidence as to prove the factum of bank account viz who had opened the bank account at a particular branch or carried out any transaction with the foreign bank during relevant year or had availed the services of bank for any purpose, received benefit therefrom or had live link with the entries as stated in foreign bank account details.

Having given sufficient opportunities, prosecution miserably failed to substantiate the question raised by the opposition with cogent material/facts which culminated into quashing of conviction. The Hon'ble Prosecution Court having perused the entire evidence and taking into consideration the scheme of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (specifically, onus of proving) has held that complainant department has not proved their case beyond 'reasonable doubt.'

Therefore,it all boils down to the million-dollar question- whether the Tax department. or Enforcement Directorate ('ED') would go after everyone named in Pandora Papers. The Government vide Press Release dated October 04, 2021 had emphasized that investigations in Pandora Paper leaks will be monitored through multi-agency groups and appropriate actions would be taken in such cases as per law.

Source: Economic Times dated October 22, 2021, New Delhi

The media reports suggests that the Tax Department has also been asked to send an update on actions taken every month to SIT. Subsequently summons would be issued seeking explanations about the money trail and financial structures. If the explanations provided are not found satisfactory, action will be initiated under the black money act.

The very recent data emanating from National Crime Records Bureau ('NCRB') highlights that only around 33.6% of economic offences end up in convictions. A total of 56.5% of completed trials ended in acquittals and the remaining 9.9% of trials ended with discharge.

The Tax department may approach the other countries/sovereigns to verify the Pandora Papers, however, the fate of each case would be decided upon judicial scrutiny. The outcome of Pandora Papers is likely to result being charged with Economic Offences and one may face trial, but the statistics suggest that only a fraction of them i.e., one-third actually would end up in conviction.

It is noteworthy that in 2016, the Income Declaration Scheme ('IDS') was announced (in the backdrop of the advent of Black Money Act) and a four-month window was provided which ended in September 2016. As on September 2016, the declarations made under IDS was approx. 64,275 declarations disclosing a meagre amount of INR 65,250 crores.

In the end, it is imperative that the Government which has the prerogative of making legislative reforms must strive for finding a sustainable solution to overcome the menace of black money, in particular the money stashed abroad!!

Swiss Legal Position: Reliance on Stolen Information

Till 2019, a total of 628 cases of HSBC Bank, Geneva, were reported accounting for undisclosed income of INR 8,465 crores were brought to tax. Out of these, over 208 cases were found to be "non-actionable because of no balances in account's information, non-residents, not traceable, an amount taxable in some other hand."

On administrative assistance relating to tax matters, on July 17, 2018 [decision no. 2C_648/2017], Swiss Supreme Court ('SSC') rendered a decision concerning stolen data. The court categorically distinguished its decision from an earlier decision dated March 17, 2017 on the same subject matter.

The decision rendered by the SSC on March 17, 2017 was based on the 'principle of good faith' as envisaged under the Swiss Criminal law, violation of which is a criminal offence. The court applied the principle and concluded that Swiss Federal Tax Administration ('FTA') cannot provide administrative assistance for any request made by foreign tax authorities based on the theft of data.

The subsequent decision of the SSC dated July 17, 2018, ruled that exchange of information based on stolen information will not per se be in violation of the 'principle of good faith' as contemplated under Article 7 of the Swiss Tax Administrative Assistance Act ('STAA'). The principle may defer basis the facts and circumstances of each case.

The exchange of stolen information would constitute violation if there were an explicit arrangement between India and Switzerland to not use the stolen data. As per SSC, there was no explicit declaration or assurance given by the Indian Tax Authorities to not use the stolen data and therefore, Indian Tax Authorities could use the said information.

The theory on administrative tax assistance was also considered in yet another decision of Swiss Supreme Court rendered on July 26, 2019, which makes it easier for foreign tax authorities to submit a general request for obtaining information without having to demonstrate concrete indication of alleged tax transgressions by account holders at Swiss banks.

For administrative tax assistance, the most crucial requirement is to depict that the request made by the tax authorities is for 'foreseeable relevance' and not for 'speculative requests' which are prohibited. With this premise, the tax authorities will be able to put in broad requests without having to showcase alleged tax transgressions.

The certification process oversees the requirements and provisions, such as creating national conflict legislation, commitment to transparency, statistical data exchange, prohibition of diamond trade with non-members, and provision of conflict-free certification for shipments. However, some nations are not Kimberley Process participants, and this is a big issue in the possibility of illicit trade involving stones from those countries. The "Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development" (OECD) provides due diligence standards for metal and mineral supply-chain management in high-risk countries. The rules include advice and models to follow but lack the punishment provisions for those who break them.

The London Bullion Market Association also provides standards and guidance on the over-the-counter wholesale bullion market. This global precious metals market trades bilaterally with standardized contract sizes, delivery dates, and settlement locations. These standards and guidelines certify compliant entities as "Good Delivery" entities and help the responsible trade of precious metals. Many countries have regulations on the trade of precious metals and stones, but their enforcement may not be strict enough to prevent the use of gold or diamonds in fraudulent schemes. The challenges associated with precious metals are frequently related to legislation and its enforcement, particularly in the case of illegal mining. Also, the laws in some countries, particularly those that are not Kimberley Process participants, are lax and easy to manipulate.

Managing the risk

Many jurisdictions have enacted legislation to combat the fraud risks associated with precious metals and stones. International organizations also provide helpful advice, suggestions, and red flags. However, anti-fraud specialists and organizations, such as financial institutions that deal in gold or diamonds, must take steps to detect and manage those risks.

For example, the identification of precious metals and stones in an individual or corporation's asset portfolios or commercial activities could result in a high-risk categorization. In such cases, banks might beef up their due diligence by engaging the help of precious metals and gemstone experts. They can give information on transactions and companies that would otherwise be unavailable to the general public.

As a result, gold, diamonds, and precious stones remain the highly sought-after commodity with a wide range of both legitimate and criminal applications. It is a bearer instrument that is easily exchanged and often has a stable price, making it appealing to both criminals and investors.

The professionals, i.e., Auditors, fraud experts, banks, etc., must enhance know-your-customer (KYC) standards and assign high risks to manage the fraud risks successfully. Though there has been global awareness in the detection of such malpractices, still, gold-related money laundering remains a grey area to solve. Even after many regulations have been formed, when one looks at the gold money laundering schemes, it is apparent that not much has changed. In practice, anti-financial crime experts can do more to mitigate risks. While typical enhanced due diligence (EDD) approaches may work for smaller gold accounts, larger amounts require extra care. There is no substitute for enhanced due diligence for larger accounts in the precious metals market, as external due diligence reports can give information not commonly available in the public domain.

Gold has intrinsic value, is easily transported, and maybe secretly sold anywhere. Reports, investigations, and first-hand accounts all confirm that the risks in this industry are not new and that they will continue to exist for the foreseeable future. When there is a link to the gold sector, anti-financial crime specialists and financial institutions should evaluate the following factors:

Gold-related transactions necessitate a high-risk rating.

Clients must pay attention to how they get their gold, their customer base, and EDD methods for managing industry risks.

External EDD is used for larger/higher-risk clientele.

Human rights abuse hazards are considered part of the gold mining, processing, and transportation operations.

Conclusion

Gold is a potentially attractive money laundering vehicle because it is easily transportable. The governments have promoted the worldwide gold trade as a frequent means of laundering illegally mined gold, narcotics, and other criminal proceeds. Unlawful gold is usually traded through the illegal shell or front businesses that use forged or incomplete documentation. The gold is frequently smuggled through third-party countries before being sold in base countries.

Despite substantial international efforts to combat money laundering, authorities have yet to succeed in eliminating the problem. While money laundering can be costly at times, it is frequently lucrative in the end. Because most anti-money laundering efforts are concentrated in the banking sector, most compliance experts believe that money launderers are moving to less regulated industries, e.g., retail, real estate, and consulting services, which are not subject to anti-money laundering legislation.

Regulators seem to be particularly concerned in industries where cash transfers are widespread. Antiquities, jewelry, gold, and raw diamonds are examples of cash-intensive companies.

VI. The Human Dimension of Compliance Beyond statutes and audits lies the behavioural aspect of compliance. Gold's emotional significance in India often translates into informal holdings within families. Many citizens view gold as a private inheritance rather than a financial instrument. This cultural mindset complicates formal disclosure.

Legal practitioners and policymakers must recognise this human element. Compliance should be accompanied by public education, awareness campaigns, and accessible disclosure mechanisms. Incentivising legitimate investment through Sovereign Gold Bonds, Exchange-Traded Funds, and regulated exchanges can help channel informal wealth into transparent avenues.

[Sonia Gandhi v. ACIT [2018] 97 taxmann.com 150 (Delhi)]

The assessees, Mr. Rahul Gandhi and Mrs. Sonia Gandhi, extended a loan to the National Herald to write off the accumulated debts and recommence the newspaper publication. The said loan was assigned by the assessee to a newly incorporated non-profit company 'Young India' (YI) and in lieu of that they were allotted shares of YI. However, in Income-tax returns, they failed to pay tax on the shares allotted by Young India. The assessees argued that the allotment of shares did not trigger any taxing event. It was also argued that since they were shareholders of a non-profit and charitable company, they were under no obligation to disclose the value of shares.

The High Court held in favour of revenue that sub-clause (ii) of clause (c) of Section 56(2) provides that if certain shares or property are acquired at a price which is less than its aggregate fair market value by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, the fair market value as reduced by the considered paid shall be charged to tax. In the instant case, the assessee bought the shares at Rs. 100 per share which could not be deemed as its fair market value. The assesse had nowhere disclosed the fair market value of such shares and had not recorded the facts relating to above taxing event. Further, it couldn't be held that the individual was exempted altogether from disclosing her or his interest in the acquisition of shares merely because shares were of not-for-profit Company. Therefore, the AO was justified in reopening the cases.

Judicial Review of Demonetization in 2016

On January 2, 2023, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Vivek Narayan Sharma v. Union of India [2023] 146 taxmann.com 36 upheld the Central Government's decision to demonetise currency notes of Rs. 500 and Rs. 1,000 denominations. The Constitution Bench, led by Justice S. Abdul Nazeer, inter-alia, held that demonetization was proportionate to the Union's stated objectives and was implemented reasonably.

The Petitioners before the Apex Court had contended that demonetization could only be initiated on the RBI's Central Board recommendation, highlighting a lack of evidence of deliberation and consultation between the Union and the RBI. They further argued that, under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act 1934, which allows the Central Government to declare that "any series of bank notes of any denomination shall cease to be legal tender" after a recommendation from the Central Board of RBI, the Union could only announce demonetization for a specific series, not all notes. This, they claimed, significantly impacted the economy, as 86% of circulating currency was in demonetized notes.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court deemed it an Executive's economic policy, immune to reversal as judicial review did not apply to economic policy decisions. The Hon'ble Bench accepted the Government's claim of consultation with the RBI prior to demonetization, asserting a reasonable connection between the Government and the RBI in implementing the measure.

Consequently, the Hon'ble Apex Court held that demonetization did not violate the "Doctrine of Proportionality" asserting that the demonetization process involved deliberation, and application of mind, and lacked procedural flaws.

In hindsight, when the Hon'ble Apex Court rendered its verdict, the question of the Constitutionality of demonetization seemed moot. The deed was done, and the repercussions were evident.
